The post Top 10 Best Enterprise DRM & Information Rights Management Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Perimeters don’t follow files. The deal model emailed to a counterparty, the design doc shared with a contractor, the board pack synced to a trustee’s tablet enterprise DRM (information rights management) keeps policy attached to the document itself: who can open, edit, print, screenshot, and until when, revocable after the file is long gone.

We scored ten options on protection depth, cross-platform friction, and the adoption killer nobody demos external-recipient experience. Microsoft Purview takes 1; Seclore and Fortra’s Vera complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Microsoft Purview Information Protection rights management where the documents already live.

• Podium: Purview (ecosystem gravity), Seclore (deepest independent IRM), Vera under Fortra (persistent-control pioneer lineage).

• The adoption killer: recipient friction if a counterparty can’t open the file in two clicks, users stop protecting files.

• 2026 driver: AI-leak anxiety rights that survive upload into tools you don’t control.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: persistence and revocation depth, usage-control granularity (view/edit/print/copy/expiry/watermark), external-recipient friction, format and platform breadth, classification integration, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: recipient experience 25%, control granularity 25%, persistence/revocation 20%, format breadth 15%, pricing clarity 15%.

The 2026 Enterprise DRM/IRM Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Microsoft Purview — Best Ecosystem-Native IRM

Snapshot: E5/add-on licensing | Sensitivity labels + rights enforcement | Office-native

Why it earns 1: Rights management wins or dies on friction, and Purview enforces inside the apps where documents are born label a file in Word and encryption, usage rights, and revocation travel with it through Outlook, Teams, and SharePoint with zero recipient plugins inside the Microsoft world.

For the majority of enterprises already on M365, it’s the shortest path to protection users won’t route around.

Pros: Native authoring-app enforcement; classification-to-rights pipeline; bundle economics.

Cons: Friction rises outside Microsoft formats and tenants; cross-org scenarios need care.

Bottom line: The default where the documents already live.

2. Seclore — Best Independent IRM Depth

Snapshot: Quote | Platform-agnostic rights | Strong external-collaboration focus

Why it earns 2: Seclore built its platform for the hard case files crossing company boundaries into estates you don’t control with granular usage policies, browser-based access for recipients, and automation hooks that attach rights as files leave DLP, ECM, or ERP systems. It’s the deepest answer unbound to any one ecosystem.

Pros: Ecosystem-neutral; strong recipient experience for external parties; automation integrations.

Cons: Separate platform to own alongside suite-native options.

Bottom line: Independent rights management built for cross-company reality.

3. Fortra (Vera) — Best Persistent-Control Lineage

Snapshot: Quote | Vera’s follow-the-file encryption | Now in Fortra’s data-security portfolio

Why it earns 3: Vera pioneered the follow-the-file model encryption, dynamic policy, and kill-switch revocation wherever the file travels and under Fortra it sits beside Titus/BoldonJames classification for a label-to-rights chain.

Buyers should confirm current packaging within Fortra’s consolidated portfolio.

Pros: Mature persistent control; revocation after delivery; classification synergy in-portfolio.

Cons: Portfolio-era packaging clarity.

Bottom line: The pioneer’s capability, consolidated under Fortra.

4. Fasoo — Best Enterprise-Wide Deployment Pedigree

Snapshot: Quote | Document-centric security platform | Large-scale deployments, strong APAC base

Why it earns 4: Fasoo has run enterprise-wide DRM at organizations protecting millions of documents for two decades automatic protection at creation, centralized policy, derivative-document control, and screen-capture defense pedigree that shows in deployments where DRM is the default state of every file, not an exception workflow.

Pros: Protect-at-creation automation; derivative and screen controls; proven mega-scale.

Cons: Western brand visibility trails capability.

Bottom line: DRM as the organization’s default, proven at scale.

5. Virtru — Best Email-First Encryption & Control

Snapshot: Published tiers | Gmail/Outlook-native | TDF open-standard foundation

Why it earns 5: Virtru attacks the most common leak path email and attachments with sender-side controls (expiry, disable-forward, revoke, watermark) that recipients open without accounts or plugins. Built on the open Trusted Data Format it’s the lowest-friction entry into rights-managed sharing for M365 and Workspace shops alike.

Pros: Minimal recipient friction; fast deployment; open-standard foundation.

Cons: Document-lifecycle depth narrower than full IRM platforms.

Bottom line: Rights-managed sharing where leaks actually start the inbox.

6. Kiteworks — Best Governed-Exchange DRM

Snapshot: Quote | Private content network | DRM within governed file exchange

Why it earns 6: Kiteworks wraps rights controls inside a governed exchange network email, MFT, file sharing, and web forms through one policy and audit plane so DRM arrives as part of provable third-party communication governance rather than a standalone tool.

Pros: One governed channel for external content; unified audit for compliance.

Cons: Platform purchase, not a point DRM tool.

Bottom line: Rights management inside a compliance-grade exchange lane.

7. NextLabs — Best Policy-Driven (ABAC) Rights

Snapshot: Quote | Attribute-based policy engine | Strong in engineering/ERP estates (SAP, PLM)

Why it earns 7: NextLabs enforces rights from centralized attribute-based policy user, project, nationality, contract which is exactly how export-control and joint-venture rules are actually written.

Its depth in SAP and engineering/PLM environments serves the manufacturers this problem bites hardest.

Pros: ABAC policy sophistication; export-control alignment; ERP/PLM integrations.

Cons: Policy-engineering investment required.

Bottom line: Rights decided by policy, not by folder.

8. Vitrium Security — Best Secure PDF & Document DRM

Snapshot: Commercial | Secure web viewer + protected PDF | Persistent document controls

Why it earns 8: Vitrium protects PDFs and other sensitive documents with persistent DRM controls, secure browser access, protected downloads, expiry, watermarking, and user-level permissions even after files leave the organization.

Pros: Strong document controls; browser-based access; flexible DRM policies.

Cons: More document-distribution focused than broad enterprise IRM suites.

Bottom line: Persistent protection for PDFs and sensitive documents beyond the perimeter.

9. Digify — Best Deal-Room Simplicity

Snapshot: Published tiers | Virtual data rooms + file rights | Watermark, expiry, revoke, tracking

Why it earns 9: Digify packages rights controls into deal-shaped workflows virtual data rooms, send-and-track links, dynamic watermarks, remote shredding at published prices a corp-dev or fundraising team can expense today, no IRM program required.

Pros: Minutes-to-value; transparent pricing; recipient-friendly viewer.

Cons: Enterprise policy/automation depth limited.

Bottom line: Deal-grade document control without a deployment.

10. Locklizard — Best Zero-Password PDF Lockdown

Snapshot: Published licenses | Secure PDF viewer model | No passwords, no plugins for Adobe stack

Why it earns 10: Locklizard takes the hard-shell approach: PDFs locked to licensed devices through its secure viewer no passwords to share, printing/expiry/watermark enforced client-side a focused answer for publishers and training providers whose product is the document itself.

Pros: Strong copy-control for sold/licensed content; no password leakage vector.

Cons: Proprietary viewer is the trade-off; collaboration workflows aren’t the aim.

Bottom line: When the document is the product, lock the product.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Test the Counterparty, Not the Console

IRM programs die at the recipient, so run the real test: send a protected file to an outside counterparty on a different ecosystem and time their path to reading it every extra step is future shadow-sharing.

Scope by leak path: email-dominant risk points to Virtru-class controls; deal documents to Digify-class rooms; firm-wide default protection to Purview (Microsoft estates) or Seclore/Fasoo (mixed estates); export-controlled engineering data to NextLabs-grade ABAC.

Wire classification to rights so labels, not users, decide protection; insist on revocation and audit you can demonstrate to a regulator; and for 2026, ask every vendor the AI question directly what happens when a protected file is fed to an external AI tool, and what evidence do you get?

FAQs

What is the best enterprise DRM solution in 2026? Microsoft Purview ranks 1 for ecosystem-native rights in M365 estates, Seclore for the deepest independent cross-company IRM, and Fortra’s Vera for persistent-control lineage with Virtru leading email-first control and Digify the deal-room lane.

What’s the difference between DRM, IRM, and DLP? DLP decides whether data may leave; IRM/enterprise-DRM controls what happens after it leaves usage rights that persist and can be revoked. Mature programs chain them: DLP triggers, IRM protects.

Does rights protection survive forwarding? With file-attached models (Seclore, Vera, Fasoo-class), yes the policy travels with the file and the viewer checks entitlement at open, wherever the copy sits.

Can recipients without the software open protected files? Increasingly yes browser-based and no-plugin paths (Seclore, Virtru, Digify, Purview in-ecosystem) are now the adoption differentiator. Viewer-locked models trade that convenience for stronger copy control.

Can DRM stop screenshots and photos of screens? Software screen-capture blocking exists (Fasoo is notably strong); a phone photographing a screen cannot be technically prevented watermarking with user identity is the honest deterrent.

Verdict

Purview protects by default where documents are born, Seclore and Vera keep control after files cross company lines, Fasoo makes protection the organization’s default state, and Virtru fixes the inbox first pick by leak path, let labels drive rights, and judge every finalist by the counterparty’s first two clicks.

articles.title: Fortinet Urges Customers to Patch Critical Flaws Affecting FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer
articles.description:
Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-assisted security testing. The company said customers should address internet-facing devices first. In an October 21 announcement, Fortinet Chief Information Security Officer Carl Windsor warned […]

The post Fortinet Urges Customers to Patch Critical Flaws Affecting FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-assisted security testing. The company said customers should address internet-facing devices first.

In an October 21 announcement, Fortinet Chief Information Security Officer Carl Windsor warned customers against treating these fixes as routine maintenance. The update follows security releases for FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, extending the patching effort across several key products.

Fortinet said its testing program uses advanced AI models to examine code paths, protocol handling, and configuration logic. The company thanked Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceX for their work with its security teams.

The concern extends beyond finding new bugs. Fortinet warned that attackers can use AI to compare patched and older software, identify changed code, and build exploits within hours or days. This process, known as patch diffing, can expose weaknesses before customers finish upgrading.

AI may also help attackers combine lower-severity flaws into a more serious attack chain. However, the announcement does not provide individual CVE identifiers, CVSS scores, or detailed attack conditions for this release. It also does not report active exploitation of these newly addressed flaws.

Its earlier testing report also stressed human review. Security analysts validate AI findings and test whether they are exploitable, helping separate real vulnerabilities from false alarms and recommend product security improvements.

Affected Versions and Required Updates

FortiOS customers should move to version 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13, or 7.2.14, depending on their current branch. Affected releases span 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.12, and 7.2.0–7.2.13.

FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer share the same minimum fixed releases: 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12, and 7.2.13. Their affected versions cover 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.11, and 7.2.0–7.2.12. Fortinet lists October 22 availability for all these updates.

For FortiMail, the fixed versions are 8.0.2, 7.6.7, and 7.4.9. Customers running affected FortiMail 7.2 releases must move to the 7.4 branch or later. FortiAuthenticator users should install 8.0.4 or 6.6.11, depending on their branch.

Fortinet plans to publish public advisories on its PSIRT page on November 10. Its notice says FortiSASE will receive automatic updates before the coordinated release. FortiManager Cloud updates may require manual action, while public cloud updates follow the relevant cloud provider’s release process.

The gap between firmware availability and full public disclosure gives customers time to upgrade before detailed advisories appear. It does not mean exposed devices can safely wait until November. Fortinet explicitly asks customers to act when the updates become available, rather than delay for technical details.

PHP and Node.js Add Patching Pressure

The warning comes alongside separate PHP and Node.js security releases. These are distinct issues, not confirmed components of the Fortinet vulnerabilities.

PHP released emergency patches on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, known as PHP2Shell. Both can allow remote code execution without authentication. One involves memory exhaustion leaving incomplete request data, while the other involves stale request state surviving after memory is freed.

Cybersecurity News’s PHP2Shell coverage explains the risks across different server setups. Fixed PHP releases are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The PHP Foundation also described how AI-assisted research contributed to investigating these weaknesses.

Separately, the Node.js security update addresses ten vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. CVE-2026-111497 affects Brotli decompression and can allow code execution through an out-of-bounds memory write. Other high-severity fixes address TLS hostname verification bypasses and DNS name truncation. The affected supported branches are 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

Fortinet recommends identifying exposed systems, backing up configurations, and scheduling urgent maintenance windows for October 22–23. Teams should review logs for unusual administrator access and unauthorized configuration changes before and after patching.

Where upgrades cannot happen immediately, administrators should restrict HTTPS and SSH management to trusted addresses, remove FortiManager administration from the public internet, and enforce multifactor authentication with unique passwords. These controls reduce exposure but do not replace installing the security updates.

articles.title: Samsung and Vizio Smart TVs Still Send Tracking-Like Traffic After Users Turn It Off
articles.description:
Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings. The findings raise questions about whether smart TV privacy controls stop viewing-related data flows, while also clarifying an important limit. Encrypted traffic prevented researchers from confirming exactly what these devices […]

The post Samsung and Vizio Smart TVs Still Send Tracking-Like Traffic After Users Turn It Off appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings.

The findings raise questions about whether smart TV privacy controls stop viewing-related data flows, while also clarifying an important limit. Encrypted traffic prevented researchers from confirming exactly what these devices transmitted.

The Watching the Watchers study examined 12 commercial televisions from ten manufacturers across eight operating systems representing roughly 95% of the U.S. smart TV market.

Researchers ran 5,943 automated experiments, comparing network activity with automatic content recognition enabled and disabled.

Samsung TV Tracking After Users Turn It Off

ACR identifies screen content using short audio or video samples, or digital fingerprints derived from them. Providers compare these signals against known content to identify programs. Viewing records can support audience measurement, targeted advertising, and data sharing.

Samsung, Vizio TVs Continue Tracking After Opt-Out

The feature can monitor content beyond streaming apps, including antenna broadcasts and HDMI devices. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of smart TV tracking described how ACR can operate even when a television serves mainly as an external display.

For the new analysis, researchers captured network packets. At the same time, televisions played controlled content through antenna inputs, HDMI connections, streaming services, and screen mirroring. Each viewing scenario was repeated with ACR enabled and after opting out.

Samsung’s Tizen television showed ACR-consistent traffic in all 30 opted-out tests involving its built-in streaming service. Similar traffic appeared in 41 of 60 antenna tests, 18 of 30 HDMI tests, and six of 30 Tubi tests.

Vizio’s SmartCast television continued contacting its identified Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint in every opted-out run for the affected scenarios. Researchers observed no decrease when the feature was disabled.

These findings do not prove that Samsung or Vizio continued recording viewing histories. Most ACR traffic was encrypted, so researchers relied on destinations, timing, volume, and other network patterns. They could not determine what information reached company servers or whether companies stored it.

Opt-outs worked in the tested LG webOS, Sony Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and VIDAA systems. Roku’s setting did not cover its own streaming service, a restriction disclosed on the tested TCL television but not the Roku-branded model.

The research paper also describes risks beyond uncertain encrypted traffic. VIDAA transmitted ACR messages over MQTT without encryption, exposing device identifiers, app names, input sources, and audio fingerprints.

An unauthenticated server exposed more than 57 million detection results linked to over one million televisions. VIDAA subsequently added login requirements, according to the researchers, but transmissions remained unencrypted.

Separately, Vizio’s WatchFree+ service placed readable program or channel information in network names visible through DNS requests and TLS server-name information. This could reveal viewing choices to network observers even with ACR disabled.

Researchers recommend disconnecting the television from the internet or blocking identified ACR endpoints. Their published blocklist did not disrupt viewing in tested scenarios, but it does not stop the WatchFree+ title leak.

Smart TV risks also extend beyond ACR. Separate research into proxy-enabled television apps highlights why app permissions and bundled services deserve scrutiny. These findings apply to the tested devices and firmware, not every television from these brands.

articles.description:
Hackers are exploiting a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center to run malware through a trusted, signed application. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936, the weakness affects versions before 4.0.9.8. Siemens has confirmed active exploitation and released a fix, and existing installations will receive the update the next time the application starts. Siemens published security advisory SSA-580366 […]

The post Hackers Actively Exploiting Siemens Software Center Flaw in ClickFix Malware Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are exploiting a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center to run malware through a trusted, signed application. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936, the weakness affects versions before 4.0.9.8.

Siemens has confirmed active exploitation and released a fix, and existing installations will receive the update the next time the application starts.

Siemens published security advisory SSA-580366 on October 15 and added a reference to active exploitation on October 19. According to the company’s campaign details, attackers distributed a genuine Siemens executable alongside malicious files outside official channels.

Siemens said it was unaware of any breach involving its systems, products, or update channel. The attackers used Siemens Software Center version 3.5.8.7 to deliver their malware.

The executable retained its valid digital signature and was not modified. Instead, attackers placed malicious DLL files beside it, exploiting how the vulnerable application searched for supporting libraries.

Siemens Software Center Flaw Exploited

According to Siemens, DLL side-loading occurs when an application loads an untrusted library from its folder without proper validation, allowing malicious code to execute with the application’s privileges due to an uncontrolled search path.

This makes the executable’s location and behavior important. A valid signature on SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe does not establish that neighboring DLLs are safe. Defenders who check only the genuine executable’s fingerprint could miss the files responsible for the infection.

The activity is linked to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign. ClickFix tricks users into running commands through fake verification or repair prompts.

Previous reporting on the ROMULUS ClickFix platform described hidden PowerShell scripts, modified installers, and malicious libraries loaded through legitimate software.

Cyber Security News has also covered ClickFix attacks using Python tunnels, where trusted executables, nearby malicious DLLs, and scheduled tasks formed part of the infection chain. These cases show why signed software still requires behavioral checks.

Siemens identified 96.62.218[.]59 and wizardexpensive[.]com as payload-hosting and command-and-control infrastructure. Both were active when its campaign notice was published.

Another address, 2.27.248[.]127, previously distributed the malicious AllMyBasic.msi bundle but was no longer serving files. Earlier downloads still require investigation.

Warning signs include Siemens Software Center appearing in startup apps or Task Scheduler on computers where users never installed it.

Indicators of Compromise

Investigators should check for a folder named SM Software Provisioning Service under AppData\Local\Programs and unexpected execution of SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe from that location, particularly when launched by msiexec.

Other reported traces include activate.bak or statinfosta.DB beside the executable and an FTSuite folder containing ftc. uml under AppData\Local. Connections to the reported infrastructure should trigger further investigation rather than being treated as harmless software-update traffic.

Users should install Siemens Software Center 4.0.9.8 or later. Starting an existing installation triggers its automatic update. Downloads should come from the official Siemens Software Center page, not third-party bundles.

Defenders should block the listed infrastructure, review historical logs, and isolate compromised systems. Stop the malicious process, remove startup entries and scheduled tasks, then reset affected passwords through the incident response process.

Users should never paste commands from webpages into Run or PowerShell. A genuine “I am not a robot” check does not require running a command on the computer.

articles.title: Critical Signal Vulnerability Could Keep Your Mic and Camera Live Even After Hang Up
articles.description:
A critical vulnerability in Signal’s calling library could allow a malicious call participant to keep hearing audio after another user tries to hang up. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-113380, affects RingRTC versions before 2.72.0 and carries a CVSS severity score of 9.3. Video could also remain active, although the published description does not confirm that […]

The post Critical Signal Vulnerability Could Keep Your Mic and Camera Live Even After Hang Up appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical vulnerability in Signal’s calling library could allow a malicious call participant to keep hearing audio after another user tries to hang up.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-113380, affects RingRTC versions before 2.72.0 and carries a CVSS severity score of 9.3. Video could also remain active, although the published description does not confirm that behavior.

RingRTC powers Signal’s voice and video calling features across its mobile and desktop apps. The issue affects how calls shut down, not how Signal encrypts conversations. A secure connection can still carry private audio if the software fails to close it when the user presses the end-call button.

The problem involves an internal event queue used by RingRTC’s finite-state machine, or FSM. This component tracks a call’s state and handles instructions that control its operation. A malicious participant can overwhelm the queue and interfere with the steps needed to end the call.

Signal Vulnerability

According to Imahian’s GitHub vulnerability description, a remote peer can saturate the event queue and prevent a local hang-up from fully ending the call, potentially leaving audio accessible to the other participant after the user believes the conversation has ended.

The attack requires a malicious participant in a call. It is not described as a way for an unrelated outsider to switch on any Signal user’s microphone.

Available reporting also leaves important details unresolved, including what affected users would see onscreen and how long unwanted transmission might continue.

The Python demonstration simulates how queued events can block hang-up handling but runs offline and does not attack Signal or prove real-world exploitation.

The fix makes call termination less dependent on the overloaded event queue. RingRTC 2.72.0 introduces a separate termination flag that call and connection state machines can check independently. It also adds five-second limits to shutdown waits, allowing cleanup to continue when individual steps fail.

The patch analysis describes tests covering full queues and failed application notifications. They check that hang-up closes the simulated connection, turns off outgoing audio, and clears the component handling outgoing media packets. The change strengthens shutdown behavior rather than replacing Signal’s encryption.

Signal users should install available updates on every phone and computer they use. Developers building applications with RingRTC should use version 2.72.0 or later.

However, the reviewed reports do not establish the first fixed Signal app version for every platform, so the library version should not be presented as an app version.

This flaw differs from previously reported Signal linked-device attacks, which targeted account access, and Signal support impersonation campaigns, which tricked users into sharing registration details. Those incidents used different attack methods, not this call-shutdown failure.

The reviewed coverage reported no known exploitation. Even so, the potential exposure matters for sensitive calls. Updating addresses the underlying software risk, while checking that call and microphone indicators have stopped provides an additional practical precaution before discussing private information nearby.

articles.title: Hackers Are Using Real Dell and Staples Emails to Make Their Scams Look Legitimate
articles.description:
Hackers are abusing genuine Dell and Staples order emails to make fake purchase alerts look credible. Instead of sending a forged message, they place scam instructions inside order details that trusted retail systems deliver, pushing recipients toward phone numbers controlled by the attackers. The emails describe expensive purchases that recipients may not recognize. Their aim […]

The post Hackers Are Using Real Dell and Staples Emails to Make Their Scams Look Legitimate appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are abusing genuine Dell and Staples order emails to make fake purchase alerts look credible. Instead of sending a forged message, they place scam instructions inside order details that trusted retail systems deliver, pushing recipients toward phone numbers controlled by the attackers.

The emails describe expensive purchases that recipients may not recognize. Their aim is to make someone call a supposed support line to cancel the order.

The sender and email design can look genuine because the message travels through the retailer’s notification system, even though parts of its content serve the scam.

Cisco Talos researchers identified two campaigns involving roughly 1,400 messages, according to an October 21 report by Diana Brown.

The findings describe phishing and phone-based fraud, not a confirmed malware infection. Talos also observed abuse of more than 25 legitimate platforms during the past year across several service categories.

Hackers Are Using Real Dell and Staples Emails

The Staples sample presented an Apple iPad purchase with an order number, delivery details, pricing, billing information, and the retailer’s standard footer.

The suspicious instructions appeared inside fields normally used for shipping or billing data. Similar Microsoft Teams notification scams have used trusted messages to direct recipients toward fraudulent support calls, showing how familiar branding can hide dangerous instructions.

The Dell example followed the same pattern. It described a Microsoft Project Standard 2024 purchase costing $736.09.

Its shipping and billing sections contained order confirmation wording and a supposed helpline, making the phone number appear connected to an established sales process rather than an outside scammer.

Neither example depended on persuading the recipient to open an obvious phishing link. The intended next step was a phone call.

Once contact moved away from email, attackers could attempt payment fraud, password theft, or remote assistance scams. Talos did not establish which follow-on actions occurred in these two campaigns.

The Staples message showed aligned DKIM authentication and passed DMARC checks. Dell-related infrastructure also passed DKIM, while its order domain passed DMARC.

These results supported the messages’ apparent origin, but they did not prove that the purchase details or embedded support instructions were genuine.

This reflects the same weakness seen in GitHub and Jira notifications, where attackers place harmful content inside fields that legitimate services later include in automated emails.

Why Email Authentication Did Not Prove Safety

Talos calls this platform-as-a-proxy abuse: the attacker supplies the misleading content while a trusted service handles delivery. The distinction matters for email security. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help establish whether sending infrastructure is expected.

They do not decide whether a shipping field should contain cancellation instructions, whether a purchase makes sense, or whether a listed phone number belongs to the retailer.

Talos also described registration abuse, where attackers enter scam text into name, company, or project fields. Automated welcome messages then repeat that text to recipients.

In some cases, list bombing becomes more than inbox disruption: legitimate registration emails themselves become carriers for attacker-controlled messages.

Related email bombing support scams show how inbox confusion can support social engineering, although that separate activity should not be treated as evidence of the same operators.

Talos additionally found a WeTransfer-themed lure inside a delivery failure notification, extending the problem to returned email content.

Talos recommends checking user-controlled fields before storing them and again before generating emails. Unexpected phone numbers, links, urgent language, and support instructions should trigger review when they appear in address or name fields.

Security gateways should inspect complete messages, including content nested inside delivery reports, rather than trusting the outer sender alone.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cybercrime group used artificial intelligence (AI) agents to coordinate attacks against more than 400 banks, payment providers and other financial organizations across Latin America, according to a report by cybersecurity company Straiker.

The group, known as CyberCartel, reportedly used AI models from Anthropic, xAI and Moonshot AI to help plan and carry out parts of its operations. The reported targets span several countries, but Straiker did not name the institutions.

Researchers said the system, called CARLIY0S, was built to help a small team handle more targets and reduce the time spent on manual tasks.

It connected AI models with software and shared data, allowing different agents to review target information, suggest actions and help coordinate activity.

The report describes an investigation of the group’s own systems, rather than a claim that every one of the more than 400 targets was successfully breached.

Straiker researchers identified CARLIY0S and linked it to operators working as the Tr4nsHack Team under the name Hexagon Security Labs Mexico.

It is best described as an AI-driven attack framework, not a single malware file. The report says the system relied on PentAGI, an automated security-testing framework, alongside scripts, AI model settings and other tools.

Security News readers can learn more about PentAGI’s automated testing framework, which can be used for authorized security work but may be misused.

Hackers Used Claude and Grok

The report describes a system in which Claude models were assigned separate roles. Some analyzed target information and proposed ways forward; another reviewed suggestions and returned a final decision.

The framework also used Grok models, which Straiker says helped collect secrets into a database called FinancialSoft. Moonshot AI’s Kimi models were also part of the setup, including as a fallback when other systems refused requests.

This arrangement matters because the models were part of a larger workflow, not simply used as chatbots to answer occasional questions.

The system linked model output to tools that could inspect web traffic, manage data and support automated tasks. Straiker says the operators framed requests as authorized testing or academic work, a tactic intended to make harmful requests appear legitimate to AI systems.

The case adds to wider reporting on Claude agents used in cyberattacks, though the activity and evidence in that reporting are separate.

Straiker’s report says CARLIY0S used automated browser software and residential proxy services as part of its operations. It also describes attempts to exploit financial organizations’ web systems and search for credentials and sensitive information after gaining access.

These details come from the company’s review of the group’s files and systems; the report does not publicly identify the affected organizations. Straiker says it removed or altered sensitive data in the published material.

The group’s collected information reportedly included email addresses, account numbers, passwords, API keys and other access details. Straiker counted 4,493 records in the FinancialSoft database snapshot it reviewed.

The report also describes credentials linked to payment services and infrastructure, including Mexico’s SPEI interbank payment system. The presence of such records raises the risk of fraud or further access, but does not by itself confirm that every credential was used successfully.

Why the finding matters

The case shows how AI can help criminals scale familiar activities, such as researching targets, working with stolen credentials and coordinating technical tasks.

It does not mean AI independently selected every target or carried out every step without people. Straiker’s findings point to a system where human operators, scripts, infrastructure and commercial AI models worked together.

That distinction is important: the risk comes from how these parts are connected and what access they are allowed to use. The report also notes that the operators had fallback methods when an AI model rejected a request, including local code that did not depend on a model.

That means a provider blocking one account may disrupt access to a service, but may not stop the wider operation if the group can switch tools or use existing scripts.

Straiker says Anthropic revoked a credential linked to the activity, while xAI was notified and was investigating the reported use of Grok.

For defenders, the practical response is to protect identity and payment systems, limit the access granted to automated tools, and watch for unusual account or API activity.

Financial firms should review connected services as well as core banking systems, since support portals and payment interfaces may also hold sensitive data.

Security teams can also study related reporting on AI agents and attack automation and AI-assisted attack frameworks, while treating each investigation’s evidence and scope separately. The investigation is a warning about the speed and reach that automation can add to cybercrime.

It is not proof that AI has replaced human attackers; rather, AI appears to have helped CyberCartel organize work across a broad set of targets. For banks and payment firms, strong access controls, careful monitoring and rapid credential revocation remain central defenses.

articles.title: October 21 Cybersecurity Nightmare: PHP and Node.js Flaws, LiteLLM Backdoor, and Active Attacks
articles.description:
October 21, 2026 brought a demanding mix of emergency security updates, poisoned software releases, and warnings about attacks already underway. PHP servers needed urgent patches. An AI software package was stealing credentials. Other investigations exposed weaknesses in certificate trust, remote management, and VPN access. Several incidents began before October 21, but their recovery work collided […]

The post October 21 Cybersecurity Nightmare: PHP and Node.js Flaws, LiteLLM Backdoor, and Active Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
October 21, 2026 brought a demanding mix of emergency security updates, poisoned software releases, and warnings about attacks already underway. PHP servers needed urgent patches.

An AI software package was stealing credentials. Other investigations exposed weaknesses in certificate trust, remote management, and VPN access.

Several incidents began before October 21, but their recovery work collided with fresh disclosures that day. For teams running production systems, the immediate task was to identify affected services, patch exposed software, and investigate whether attackers had already gained access. Installing an update could close a vulnerability while leaving stolen credentials or backdoors active.

Emergency Patches Across Web Platforms

The PHP emergency release addressed CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws known as PHP2Shell. Both received CVSS scores of 9.2 and could allow unauthenticated remote code execution under affected configurations. One corrupts memory when an operation runs out of memory. The other lets later requests reach invalid data left behind by earlier requests.

Researchers demonstrated code execution against Apache mod_php before application code even ran. Cloudflare reported early attack attempts without confirming successful compromises. Administrators should deploy PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, then restart affected services and confirm that web workers actually use the patched build.

The Node.js security updates fixed ten vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. CVE-2026-111497 affects Brotli decompression and can allow code execution through a memory write outside its intended area. Other flaws weaken TLS hostname checks or mishandle DNS names. Patched releases are 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4. These updates also refresh certificate trust following the eMudhra incident. Rebuild container images so deployments include the updated runtime.

That workload followed two critical Next.js RCE fixes released on October 14. They covered specific React Server Components caching behavior and SVG image processing on Linux systems using glibc. Teams should move affected Next.js deployments to 16.4.1 or 15.5.28, as appropriate. Updating Node.js alone does not update these application dependencies.

Apache Tomcat’s eight security fixes added another priority. CVE-2026-101296 allows authentication without the correct password when JNDIRealm uses non-GSSAPI SASL mechanisms. Other issues can mix responses between users or leak data through AJP processing. The HTTP/2 flaw involves errors during asynchronous processing that leave internal objects available for reuse. Apache disclosed the flaws on October 20. Fixed releases are 11.0.27, 10.1.61, and 9.0.123, with exposure depending on configuration.

Supply Chain Attack

The LiteLLM supply chain compromise directly threatened cloud and AI environments. Version 1.107.0 reached PyPI and container registries carrying a credential stealer and remote code loader. All seven Python wheels were affected, along with container tags including latest and main-stable. The vendor said stolen GitHub credentials let attackers redirect a release workflow to a lookalike repository.

Malicious Python startup hooks could run when an unrelated Python command started, without the application importing LiteLLM. Targets included cloud credentials, SSH keys, and AI service secrets. Wiz observed stolen AWS credentials being used about four and a half hours after data theft. The vendor advised pinning to 1.106.2. Affected teams also need clean rebuilds and credential rotation. Running pip inside a contaminated environment can trigger the hooks again, making a simple downgrade an unsafe first response.

The WordPress backup developer breach showed how stolen management keys can defeat normal trust checks. Attackers accessed TeamUpdraft’s website during October 17–18 and used UpdraftCentral connection keys to install malicious plugins on connected sites. The UpdraftPlus download packages themselves were unchanged. Administrators should verify installation of 1.26.13 Free or 2.26.13 Premium, remove exposed connection keys, and inspect sites for backdoors and unexpected administrators. Updating cannot remove malware already installed.

Attackers also hijacked OVHcloud CLI releases after compromising a developer account. They replaced binaries for versions 0.11.0 through 0.15.0 during a 94-minute window on October 19. Earlier clean downloads were unaffected. OVHcloud released version 0.16.0 and urged exposed users to replace secrets stored on affected machines. The incident showed why a familiar download location cannot guarantee that a release file is safe.

Certificate Authority Compromise

The eMudhra certificate authority incident reached deeper into internet trust. Eight intermediate signing keys were compromised. The updated disclosure says incorrect key generation made them recoverable from public certificates, creating a risk of forged certificates. Mozilla found that all eight affected P-384 private keys were integers below 256, allowing almost instant recovery.

Browser vendors issued blocks, but applications that use separate certificate bundles or skip revocation checks may remain exposed. Organizations must update browsers, operating systems, runtimes, and trust stores. Public evidence has not established attacks against users through these keys.

Meanwhile, Palo Alto GlobalProtect exploitation showed how a VPN weakness can lead to wider network access. CVE-2026-0257 lets attackers bypass authentication, including MFA, in affected configurations. Exploitation requires authentication override cookies and a vulnerable certificate setup.

Unit 42 described attackers reaching VMware vCenter, weakening ESXi controls, and extracting credentials directly from a domain controller’s virtual disk. Reading the disk outside the guest operating system avoided its endpoint monitoring. Defenders should patch affected gateways and investigate suspicious successful VPN sessions.

Plex servers were also under active attack. The Plex2Shell chain combines four flaws to run code without authentication. It abuses internal requests, exposes an owner token, writes a file, and loads a malicious codec. Attackers deployed cryptocurrency miners and proxy software on exposed servers. Plex says version 1.43.3.10861 and later contain the fixes.

Administrators should check NAS installations and containers, examine unexpected processes, and rebuild systems where compromise is found or cannot be ruled out.

The State Bank of India data disclosure added a separate concern. SBI identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information within roughly 375,000 reviewed dark-web records.

That larger figure should not be treated as a confirmed count of affected customers. Reported fields included names, mobile numbers, addresses, and loan-related details. The bank said services remained operational while investigators examined the data’s authenticity and source. The disclosure did not establish a breach of core banking systems or theft of customer funds.

Start with exposed systems facing active attacks, then address vulnerable runtimes and affected dependencies. After restarts, check running versions, rebuild compromised environments, and revoke secrets from clean systems.

Review cloud activity, VPN sessions, and administrator changes for evidence of misuse. October 21’s lasting lesson is that recovery must cover every route an attacker gained, including access that survives a successful patch.

articles.title: Hackers Are Breaking Into FortiGate, FortiWeb and Palo Alto GlobalProtect Systems to Steal Passwords
articles.description:
Internet-facing firewalls and VPN systems are under attack in a campaign that aims to steal credentials and gain lasting access to corporate networks. The activity targets FortiGate and FortiWeb devices from Fortinet, as well as Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect portals. Once inside, operators can collect passwords stored in device configurations and use them to move […]

The post Hackers Are Breaking Into FortiGate, FortiWeb and Palo Alto GlobalProtect Systems to Steal Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Internet-facing firewalls and VPN systems are under attack in a campaign that aims to steal credentials and gain lasting access to corporate networks.

The activity targets FortiGate and FortiWeb devices from Fortinet, as well as Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect portals. Once inside, operators can collect passwords stored in device configurations and use them to move deeper into a victim’s network.

The campaign is linked to an operator known as k0t. Group-IB and NyxLab say the activity affected organizations across different industries and regions.

Their investigation identified more than 70,000 exposed credentials and related data, including network-device credentials and LDAP records. The researchers warn that this total does not confirm that every listed credential led to a successful compromise.

Analysts from Group-IB, working with NyxLab, identified the campaign and described its methods in a report published on October 21, 2026.

They said operators search for exposed network equipment in bulk, then try to break in by exploiting software flaws or guessing weak passwords. Their findings include stolen credentials, signs of persistent remote access and cases of data theft.

Hackers Are Breaking Into FortiGate, FortiWeb and Palo Alto GlobalProtect Systems

The operators use public search services to find internet-facing VPN portals and firewalls. They then check discovered systems for weaknesses and attempt to gain access.

Group-IB says the activity is broad rather than focused on a single industry. The number of devices exposed online and their settings may help explain which organizations appear in the collected data.

FortiWeb devices were targeted with CVE-2025-64446, a path traversal flaw that can let an unauthenticated attacker run administrative commands through crafted web requests.

Group-IB observed a custom tool attempting to use the flaw to create a new administrator account. FortiGate devices are not vulnerable to this FortiWeb flaw; instead, operators tried common username and password combinations against exposed FortiGate systems.

Fortinet describes CVE-2025-64446 as an improper access control issue affecting FortiWeb. The FortiGate activity can have effects beyond the firewall itself. After gaining access, operators may download a device configuration file and recover credentials stored in it, including administrator and LDAP or Active Directory account details.

Group-IB says the attackers used a known default encryption key to decrypt some stored secrets. Organizations should therefore treat a potentially exposed configuration as a possible password disclosure, not just as a device-management issue.

The campaign also targets Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect systems. Group-IB observed attempts to exploit CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass flaw in GlobalProtect portals and gateways under specific PAN-OS settings.

The flaw can allow an unauthorized VPN connection. Palo Alto Networks’ advisory describes the same risk and advises administrators to follow its remediation guidance.

Cybersecurity News has previously covered FortiWeb flaw exploitation and a FortiWeb exploit tool release. These reports provide background on the FortiWeb weakness; the current investigation adds evidence of operators using it as part of a wider campaign against network-edge devices.

What happens after access

After entering a network, operators may use legitimate administration and security tools to discover systems, seek additional credentials and expand access.

Group-IB observed tools including NetExec, Impacket and Mimikatz, alongside remote-management software such as MeshCentral and Atera. Their use can be hard to spot when defenders review only one event at a time, since legitimate tools may also appear in normal IT work.

Researchers found 28 active device groups with 84 compromised devices linked to a MeshCentral server during their review. They also saw signs of other remote-access tools and a command-and-control framework.

In some cases, data was copied to cloud storage using Rclone. Group-IB said some victims later appeared on ransomware leak sites, but it has not confirmed that k0t is directly affiliated with the ransomware groups involved.

Organizations can read more about FortiGate configuration theft and GlobalProtect authentication bypass activity in earlier Cybersecurity News coverage.

These related reports describe risks that matter after an edge device is compromised: stolen credentials may enable further access, even if the initial entry point is later patched.

Security teams should check whether FortiGate, FortiWeb and GlobalProtect systems are exposed to the internet, confirm that they run fixed software, and restrict administrative access to trusted networks where possible.

They should review logs for unexpected administrator accounts, configuration exports, unusual VPN sessions, repeated login failures and management access from unfamiliar locations.

Palo Alto Networks’ advisory provides remediation instructions for CVE-2026-0257; Fortinet’s advisory covers CVE-2025-64446.

If a device may have been accessed, teams should investigate connected accounts and systems, rotate credentials stored in or linked to the appliance, and review VPN and identity logs for suspicious follow-on activity.

FortiGate administrators should also check whether private-data encryption is enabled with an organization-controlled key. A lack of matching indicators does not prove that a device or network is safe; defenders should correlate appliance, VPN, identity and endpoint records.

The post China-Linked Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Target 2,250 Microsoft 365 Tenants After ConnectWise Breach appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
China-state-aligned hackers used ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework, to attempt access to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants following the ConnectWise Cloud Backup breach.

Microsoft attributed the attack to Storm-0940 and reported 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute, leaving security teams little time to investigate and block access.

The attackers abused stolen application credentials and permissions already approved by customers, rather than requiring users to enter passwords.

Earlier reporting on compromised ConnectWise backup credentials documented unauthorized sign-ins across 173 tenants.

That confirmed-access figure differs from Microsoft’s broader targeting count: not every attempted sign-in succeeded, and successful authentication alone does not prove data theft.

Researchers from Zscaler and Microsoft teams separately documented ARTEX abuse in reports published October 21. ARTEX is a security-testing framework, not a newly discovered malware family.

Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise attack to Storm-0940, while Zscaler examined a Chinese-speaking operator’s broader workflow without establishing that both investigations covered the same actor.

China-Linked Hackers Use ARTEX AI

According to Microsoft’s technical investigation report, Storm-0940 used ARTEX for scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse.

Between October 10 and 14, its infrastructure targeted 327 accounts across eight organizations, generating more than 151,000 failed logons. Microsoft observed no successful authentication during that password-spray activity.

The group previously used stolen accounts for network access, as coverage of Storm-0940 password spray attacks explains. In the ConnectWise incident, however, stolen application credentials provided another route.

The attackers authenticated as trusted applications, using permissions already granted inside customer tenants without an interactive user sign-in.

After gaining control of multiple ConnectWise application identities, the attackers used Microsoft Graph to inspect environments and change application credentials.

Some activity involved identities, groups, and privileged roles. These changes could preserve access through other applications even after the original ConnectWise connection was disabled. Microsoft said several ARTEX-driven attacks reached privileged cloud access in under three hours.

Zscaler’s investigation showed how an operator combined ARTEX with Claude Code, Codex, and other AI workspaces. The framework divided goals into tasks, ran security tools, and retained findings.

Custom additions included nmap, sqlmap, nuclei, and Android analysis tools, extending its reach across websites, networks, and mobile applications.

The findings expand on earlier South Korean financial breaches involving ARTEX, with Zscaler finding targets across many countries and sectors.

Saved prompts requested personal records, phone numbers, payment credentials, and transaction data. Questions about selling stolen records suggested financial motives, but did not establish that any sale occurred.

Shared notes and synchronization scripts let separate AI sessions resume unfinished work. Prompts assigned DeepSeek initial research and GLM review duties, while other sessions used Grok configurations.

Zscaler cautioned that configured model names did not prove which underlying models answered requests. The operator also instructed agents to assume targets were authorized and reduced approval requirements.

What Defenders Should Check

Microsoft recommends keeping affected ConnectWise connections disabled until formal restoration guidance arrives.

Teams should preserve evidence before deleting applications and examine service-principal sign-ins, application credential additions, consent grants, and role changes.

Investigations should include previously authorized integrations, because removing the original connection may leave attacker-added credentials elsewhere.

Review should extend beyond published IP addresses to unusual Microsoft Graph activity, mailbox access, file downloads, forwarding rules, and unexpected owners. Microsoft said the activity did not stem from a vulnerability or compromise in its own systems, products, or services.

articles.description:

The cloud platform warned that the affected data could contain API keys, database passwords, and private registry credentials, and urged all customers to replace stored secrets. The company published its security disclosure on […]

The post Railway Security Incident: Hackers May Have Accessed Customer Environment Variables appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Railway has disclosed a security incident in which an unauthorized third party may have accessed customer environment variables, including some decrypted values. The cloud platform warned that the affected data could contain API keys, database passwords, and private registry credentials, and urged all customers to replace stored secrets.

The company published its security disclosure on October 21, 2026, after detecting unusual activity in systems that store these variables. Its initial findings suggest that only some users may be affected. However, Railway has not released an affected account count, identified the attacker, or explained how access was gained.

Railway Security Incident

Environment variables hold settings that applications need during builds and normal operation. Railway’s documentation explains that these values can include configuration details and secrets supplied to services. This makes the storage system a sensitive target because stolen credentials could give attackers access to connected services beyond Railway itself.

The key distinction is that Railway reported possible access to encrypted variables and, for some, decrypted contents. This does not establish that attackers broke the encryption. The notice does not explain how readable values may have been obtained, leaving that part of the investigation unresolved.

Railway believes the incident forms part of a recent series of attacks against platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers. These providers run AI models in response to user requests. Railway said it notified upstream providers and asked them to revoke keys proactively, but did not identify those providers.

The suspected focus on AI access reflects a wider credential theft risk. Cybersecurity News previously covered an LLMjacking attack involving a leaked AWS key, where stolen access was used to run paid AI models at the victim’s expense. Railway has not confirmed that similar misuse occurred in this incident.

Related reporting on AI agents exposing API keys and cloud secrets also shows why secret handling matters across modern development tools. That report describes exposure through configuration files, command output, and model context. It is background on credential risk, not evidence of how attackers entered Railway’s systems in this case.

Deployments Paused as Credential Resets Continue

Railway paused deployments during its investigation, preventing customers from releasing new application versions. Its incident status page confirmed that builds remained unavailable at 02:19 UTC on October 22. The restriction also affects recovery because some credential changes require services to be redeployed before applications can use the replacement values.

The company also began rotating all Railway storage bucket credentials as a precaution. Replacement credentials will appear automatically in customer dashboards. However, Railway said applications cannot be redeployed to pick up those credentials until builds return, creating an additional recovery hurdle for customers with services that depend on storage buckets.

Railway recommends immediately rotating all secrets stored as environment variables, including API keys and private registry credentials, and checking connected service logs for unusual activity. Customers should not wait for confirmation that their account was affected. The company has published guides covering database passwords, AI provider usage, cloud access, and GitHub activity.

Railway said it will email customers directly as affected accounts are confirmed. The investigation remains ongoing, with the full scope still unclear.

The post 12-Year-Old GitLab Vulnerability Allows Remote Code Execution on Self-Managed Server appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
GitLab has released urgent security updates for a critical vulnerability that could let attackers run code on self-managed servers without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw carries the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and affects both GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. The company published the fixes on October 21, 2026.

The affected code reaches back to GitLab 7.0, released in 2014, giving the vulnerability a roughly 12-year history. That does not mean attackers have been using it for 12 years. GitLab’s advisory describes the risk but does not report confirmed attacks or provide a public exploit.

GitLab Remote Code Execution Flaw

According to GitLab’s official security advisory, the vulnerability involves an integer overflow when the server compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Regular expressions are patterns used to match text. Under certain conditions, processing an attacker-controlled pattern could allow arbitrary code to run on the server.

GitLab’s CVSS assessment describes a network-based attack with low complexity, no account privileges, and no required user interaction. It rates the possible impact on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability as high. However, the company has not disclosed the full conditions needed to reach the vulnerable code.

GitLab credited security researcher joaxcar with reporting the issue through its HackerOne bug bounty program. Its release notes also list Ruby regular-expression patches, providing further context about the affected software layer without revealing a complete attack path. Administrators should not assume the flaw requires access to a particular project or feature unless GitLab confirms that restriction.

Affected Versions and Available Fixes

The vulnerability affects GitLab CE and EE versions starting with 7.0. GitLab has fixed it in versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3, and 19.5.1. Earlier releases within those branches remain affected. The company extended the fix to four older branches beyond its standard patch releases.

Self-managed customers should upgrade immediately. GitLab.com already runs patched software. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0, or later already include the fixes and require no action, according to the notice. GitLab also says that when an advisory does not name a specific deployment type, all deployment types are affected.

This issue should not be confused with the earlier GitLab code execution vulnerability patched on October 12. That separate flaw, CVE-2026-97229, also involved regular-expression handling but affected a different version range. Installing that earlier update does not address this newly disclosed vulnerability.

GitLab has published two detection guides for self-managed environments, named “Onigmo native worker crash” and “Org mode render error burst.” These resources are intended to help security teams identify possible exploitation attempts. Their publication is not evidence that attacks have occurred, and the release notice does not establish either signal as proof of a successful compromise.

The patch release addresses 12 vulnerabilities overall. Another serious issue, CVE-2026-15723, carries a CVSS score of 8.2. When OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking are both enabled, an authenticated attacker could take over an existing LDAP-backed account without the victim’s involvement. CVE-2026-112212, rated 7.5, concerns poisoned OAuth and OpenID Connect discovery responses that could redirect certain flows to an attacker-controlled server.

These fixes follow other recent GitLab security updates, including a separate AI Gateway remote command execution vulnerability. Those reports concern different components and attack requirements, making accurate version checks more useful than assuming one GitLab update covers every related product.

Administrators should review GitLab’s upgrade instructions before deployment. The notice warns that database migrations can affect the process, with downtime for single-node installations and zero-downtime procedures available for suitable multi-node setups.

Versions 19.3.6 and 19.4.3 include regular migrations. GitLab normally makes detailed security issues public 90 days after patching, so teams should not delay updates while waiting for full technical details.

The GitLab fixes arrive alongside security updates for Node.js and PHP, adding to the patching workload for teams running web applications and development services.

Cyber Security News reports that Node.js released security updates addressing ten vulnerabilities across its 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches, with patched versions listed as 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4.

Meanwhile, PHP issued emergency patches for PHP2Shell, a pair of critical memory-handling flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The post GoDaddy Revoking 404,607 TLS Certificates Following Compliance Failures appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
GoDaddy launched a mass revocation of 404,607 SSL/TLS certificates after finding that issued certificates did not match its published certificate policies. The company missed its required revocation deadline, creating a second compliance issue. An updated customer notice says the incorrectly issued certificates were revoked on October 21, 2026.

The incident affects certificates issued under GoDaddy and Starfield certificate chains. Customers still using an affected certificate may face browser security warnings or website access problems until they install a replacement, according to GoDaddy’s customer guidance. Receiving a replacement alone does not confirm that the website is using it.

GoDaddy Revoking 404,607 TLS Certificates

According to the original incident report, a third party flagged differences between issued certificates and the profiles described in Starfield’s Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement, known as CP/CPS. These documents set out the rules the certificate authority follows when issuing certificates.

The differences involved certificate policy information, including policy object identifiers, or OIDs, and CPS URI policy qualifiers. These fields identify certificate policies and reference the authority’s published practices. The issued certificates did not match the documented profiles. The reports describe a compliance failure, not a confirmed theft of private keys.

GoDaddy stopped certificate issuance after confirming the report. Its investigation uncovered additional differences across affected profiles. The company corrected and published its documentation before resuming issuance. Further checks found similar problems in the older Starfield G2 chain, which was no longer actively issuing certificates.

Domain validated certificates made up most of the affected population. Starfield R1 DV accounted for 208,896 certificates, while Starfield G2 DV accounted for 187,159. Smaller numbers of organization validated and extended validation certificates were also affected across the GoDaddy and Starfield chains.

GoDaddy Missed the Revocation Deadline

The delayed revocation report cites Section 4.9.1.1 of the TLS Baseline Requirements. For the stated policy violation, affected certificates should be revoked within 24 hours and must be revoked within five days, except for short-lived subscriber certificates. The specified revocation reason is “superseded.”

GoDaddy began contacting subscribers on October 14. Its outreach included customers holding large certificate inventories and organizations providing government, financial, and health services. However, only 170,566 certificates had been revoked when the October 18 deadline passed at 23:45 UTC.

By 05:29 UTC on October 19, the revoked total had reached 227,422. GoDaddy said dedicated teams were handling customer contact, replacement, revocation, and progress tracking through email, SMS, and phone calls. Its later customer notice states that the incorrectly issued certificates were revoked on October 21.

Affected administrators should review the SSL certificate section of their GoDaddy account and follow any replacement notice. GoDaddy warns that an updated certificate can exist in the account while the domain continues serving the old certificate. Customers receiving an installation alert should download and install the replacement immediately.

The case echoes earlier DigiCert certificate revocations following a DNS validation error, although the underlying failures differ. It also highlights the operational concerns covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on certificate mismanagement.

The post Arrakis Security Report Finds 76% of AI Agents Are Dormant but Keep Their Credentials and Connections appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York, NY, USA, October 21st, 2026, CyberNewswire

According to the 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report, published by Arrakis Security, 76% of active agents have not run in 60 days, but their credentials still work and their triggers still fire. 44% have not run in 180 days.

24% of dormant agents can be started by an unsigned webhook from outside the organization.

The report is based on anonymized, unidentifiable production telemetry from thousands of AI agents in Arrakis customers’ environments, collected over a 12-week period.

“There’s a lot of discussion about AI agent risk, and very little data”, said Tal Baron, CEO and co-founder of Arrakis Security. “When an employee leaves, their access is removed the same day.

When an agent stops being used, nobody removes anything, because in most companies nobody owns it”.

﻿Other findings:

  • 22% of agents can send content to a model run by a third party and act on the answer.
  • 20% of agents can pass a task to another agent with different permissions, and get back results they aren’t allowed to produce themselves.
  • 70% of agents can reach sensitive systems, such as cloud storage, AI services, and marketing platforms, and almost none of those connections have verified data loss prevention (DLP).
  • 82% of agents carry at least one exposure, and 46% of those carry more than one.

The full report is available at https://arrakis.security/2026-threat-report.

About Arrakis Security

Arrakis secures autonomous agents through behavioral intelligence across three layers: what an agent is, what it does, and why.

AI-SPM scans each agent’s structure, permissions, tools, and metadata hourly, including agents that never run, surfacing shadow agents, exposed keys, and misconfigurations.

AI-TDR monitors actions in real time for deviations from defined rules and policies. The behavioral intelligence engine models each agent from its own history, posture, runtime, and context: how it got there and what it could do next.

For each action, it decides whether to continue, escalate, or intervene.
