articles.title: The AI Adoption Blind Spot: How Fake AI Tools Put Enterprises at Risk
articles.description:
AI adoption is accelerating across enterprises, with employees increasingly relying on platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, and Microsoft Copilot for everyday work. Cybercriminals are exploiting this growing trust, distributing malicious applications disguised as legitimate AI tools to steal credentials, deliver malware, and gain access to corporate environments.  Recent research by ANY.RUN reveals how attackers are impersonating […]

The post The AI Adoption Blind Spot: How Fake AI Tools Put Enterprises at Risk  appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
AI adoption is accelerating across enterprises, with employees increasingly relying on platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, and Microsoft Copilot for everyday work.

Cybercriminals are exploiting this growing trust, distributing malicious applications disguised as legitimate AI tools to steal credentials, deliver malware, and gain access to corporate environments. 

Recent research by ANY.RUN reveals how attackers are impersonating popular AI brands to target corporate users, including developers and marketing teams.

The findings highlight a growing challenge for security leaders: identifying threats hidden behind familiar applications before they lead to credential theft, compromised accounts, or wider business disruption. 

Who Is Most Exposed to Fake AI Attacks? 

Between April 15 and October 5, 2026, ANY.RUN researchers identified 1,258 public sandbox analyses linked to fake AI campaigns.

The United States accounted for 16% of submissions with country information, ranking second after India (20%). US submissions also led in two major campaign groups involving fake Claude downloads and ChatGPT-themed attacks. 

The activity spans multiple industries. Technology appeared across all seven campaign queries examined by researchers, followed by telecommunications (six), education and consulting (five each), and manufacturing, healthcare, government, and finance (four each).

Among US submissions, telecommunications and manufacturing appeared most frequently across the campaign queries. 

Attackers also tailor their methods to specific employee roles: 

  • Developers: Fake AI coding assistants and installation instructions can put source code, cloud credentials, and API keys at risk. In one sandbox session, researchers observed a counterfeit GitHub Copilot CLI page delivering malicious installation instructions. 
  • Marketing teams: Counterfeit AI advertising programs target employees with access to advertising budgets, billing systems, and business accounts. A fake Claude Ads campaign used a fraudulent Google sign-in window to capture credentials. 
  • Other corporate users: Fake desktop applications can expose employees to malware and browser-session theft. One trojanized Claude installer launched the legitimate application while secretly collecting browser data in the background. 

For business leaders, these findings show that fake AI threats are not limited to technology companies or IT departments.

Exposure can arise wherever employees install AI applications or connect business accounts without adequate security oversight. 

Reduce the Impact of Fake AI Attacks.
Detect malicious behavior earlier and contain threats faster. Strengthen Threat Response 

How Fake AI Attacks Unfold: From Trusted Brand to Corporate Compromise 

ANY.RUN’s research highlights how attackers move from AI-branded lures to malicious execution and potential corporate compromise: 

  1. Initial lure: Attackers impersonate ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini through counterfeit websites, advertisements, and shared AI conversations. 
  2. Malicious delivery: Fake installers and setup instructions trick users into downloading malware or executing malicious commands disguised as legitimate installation steps. 
  3. Payload execution: Once launched, malicious code can deploy information stealers or other malware on the employee’s device. 
  4. Credential theft: Attackers attempt to collect passwords, session cookies, authentication tokens, and other sensitive data. 
  5. Business impact: Stolen credentials and compromised sessions can enable unauthorized access to corporate systems, potentially leading to data exposure or further intrusion. 

Fake AI Threats Extend Beyond Windows 

Windows remains a major target for malware campaigns, but macOS devices are not immune.

Fake AI installation pages can trick Mac users into copying malicious commands into Terminal, presenting dangerous actions as routine software setup instructions. 

For enterprises with mixed operating systems, this creates an additional investigation challenge. Limited visibility into macOS activity can leave security teams without the evidence needed to assess an incident, potentially delaying containment and leaving affected accounts or devices unidentified. 

Cross-platform behavioral analysis helps address this gap. For example, ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox supports Windows, Linux, Android, and macOS, allowing analysts to investigate suspicious files and URLs in isolated environments.

Teams can observe malicious behavior, examine network connections, extract indicators of compromise (IOCs), and trace attack chains to determine what happened and what requires further investigation. 

With consistent investigation capabilities across operating systems, SOC teams can reduce blind spots, avoid fragmented investigations, and make more informed response decisions without relying on separate analysis workflows for every platform. 

Closing the AI Security Visibility Gap 

As AI adoption grows, enterprises need to ensure their security teams can investigate threats disguised as legitimate applications.

This means looking beyond suspicious downloads to understand what executes on employee devices, which credentials may be exposed, and whether an attack has progressed further into the corporate environment. 

More than 16,000 organizations worldwide use ANY.RUN to investigate cyber threats and strengthen SOC operations.

Teams using the solution report up to 36% higher detection rates, 21 minutes less MTTR per incident, and 30% fewer Tier 1-to-Tier 2 escalations.

For enterprises, these improvements mean faster investigations, fewer unnecessary escalations, and more time for analysts to focus on critical threats. 

As attackers continue to exploit trusted AI brands, the priority for security leaders is clear: give SOC teams the cross-platform visibility and behavioral evidence they need to identify malicious activity early and contain threats before they cause wider business disruption. 

Help Your SOC Stop More Threats with the Same Team.
Cut investigation time and reduce escalations. Scale SOC Performance

articles.title: Node.js Releases Security Updates to Fix High-Severity TLS, DNS, and Brotli Vulnerabilities
articles.description:
Node.js has released security updates for its 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches to address ten vulnerabilities, including four high-severity flaws affecting DNS lookups, TLS certificate checks, and Brotli decompression. The supplied release details identify 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4 as the patched versions. The most serious potential outcome is remote code execution through the Brotli decoder. […]

The post Node.js Releases Security Updates to Fix High-Severity TLS, DNS, and Brotli Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Node.js has released security updates for its 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches to address ten vulnerabilities, including four high-severity flaws affecting DNS lookups, TLS certificate checks, and Brotli decompression.

The supplied release details identify 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4 as the patched versions. The most serious potential outcome is remote code execution through the Brotli decoder.

The October security update also covers HTTP connection handling, repeated random values, ZIP processing, and filesystem permission checks. Node.js scheduled the releases for October 21, 2026, and listed high severity as the highest risk across all three supported branches.

CVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder in all three release lines. The supplied advisory describes an out-of-bounds write that permits remote code execution.

This means the decoder can write outside its intended memory area. Applications that process untrusted Brotli-compressed content should receive particular attention during patch planning. However, the supplied notice does not explain the exact conditions needed for exploitation.

Two high-severity vulnerabilities involve TLS certificate hostname checks. CVE-2026-105483 allows a hostname verification bypass when an IP address uses full-width digits, affecting Node.js 26.x and 24.x.

Node.js Releases Security Updates

CVE-2026-106069 involves hostnames that loosely resolve to an IP address and affects all three branches. Both concern whether a certificate correctly matches the intended destination.

The fourth high-severity issue, CVE-2026-105482, causes dns.resolve to truncate names containing a NUL character. It affects all three release lines. The flaw raises concerns for applications that depend on consistent name handling before performing DNS lookups.

These fixes follow earlier Node.js TLS authentication bypass patches, which also addressed differences in hostname handling and certificate verification.

Three medium-severity issues broaden the update’s scope. CVE-2026-105481 allows a keep-alive socket to process a response written before its request was sent.

CVE-2026-106072 concerns improper certificate validation for nonstandard IPv4 hostnames, allowing DNS certificate names to authenticate IP endpoints.

CVE-2026-106074 affects cached random data stored in startup snapshots and single executable applications. Processes created from these artifacts can repeat values returned by crypto.randomUUID() and crypto.randomInt(). All three medium-severity flaws affect the 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches.

The remaining issues carry low ratings. CVE-2026-106070 concerns attacker-controlled bytes returned after failed ZIP header checks. CVE-2026-106071 can grant excessive filesystem access through wildcard matching. Both affect 26.x.

CVE-2026-106073 bypasses Permission Model checks through fs.realpathSync across all three branches. Previous Node.js Permission Model vulnerabilities also exposed gaps in filesystem restrictions.

The release details also list updates to c-ares, CA certificates, Undici, OpenSSL, and SQLite, with branch coverage varying by component.

Administrators should deploy the matching patched release, rebuild application images where needed, and restart affected services. Testing should cover outbound HTTPS connections, DNS handling, compressed content, and permission-restricted workloads.

Teams should consult the official Node.js security announcement and avoid unsupported versions. The project warns that end-of-life branches remain affected even after security releases, so migrating to a supported branch is an important part of remediation.

Editorial verification note: The live announcement retrieved during research still displayed the advance release notice, without the detailed CVEs or patched downloads. Those details above come from the release text you supplied and should be checked against the updated announcement before publication.

articles.title: Hackers Use AI-Powered Browsers to Hide Thousands of Fake Accounts and Bypass Security Detection
articles.description:
Cybercriminals are using AI-enabled “antidetect” browsers to manage large networks of fake online accounts while making each profile appear to come from a different person, device, or location. Check Point Research reported that these tools can help a single operator or small group run thousands of accounts across social media and other platforms, making it […]

The post Hackers Use AI-Powered Browsers to Hide Thousands of Fake Accounts and Bypass Security Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cybercriminals are using AI-enabled “antidetect” browsers to manage large networks of fake online accounts while making each profile appear to come from a different person, device, or location.

Check Point Research reported that these tools can help a single operator or small group run thousands of accounts across social media and other platforms, making it harder for services to spot linked activity.

The browsers have legitimate uses, but researchers documented their presence in criminal forums and marketplaces and described their use in fraud and account-takeover operations.

Analysts at Check Point Research identified Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin as three tools with features that can support this activity.

Their October 20, 2026 report says the platforms combine profile isolation and identity masking with automation, and in some cases AI integrations.

The report does not claim that the browsers themselves are malware; it warns that criminals can misuse commercially available software to conceal coordinated operations.

Hackers Use AI-Powered Browsers

A website can collect details about a browser and device, including screen size, time zone, language, user agent, and graphics settings.

Together, these details can help create a browser fingerprint. Platforms may compare fingerprints and activity patterns to identify accounts that appear to share a device or operator.

Check Point says antidetect browsers can change or assign different values to profiles, making that comparison more difficult.

The tools may also keep each profile’s cookies, local storage, and session information separate. Some can work with proxy services, which may make profiles appear to connect from different network locations.

That can complicate checks based only on an account’s IP address or location. Cybersecurity News has also described how residential proxies can hide malicious traffic, although proxy use alone does not prove that activity is criminal.

A more serious risk arises when criminals use stolen session cookies. A cookie can keep a user signed in after authentication; if it is stolen and reused, an attacker may access an active account without repeating the usual login process.

Check Point says criminals can place stolen session data into a browser profile, potentially making the session appear familiar to a service.

This is related to the risks in session-cookie theft and account takeover, where access to a logged-in session can undermine protections that focus on the initial sign-in.

AI and automation increase the scale

The report says AI features and automation can reduce the manual work needed to run many accounts. AdsPower, for example, advertises a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for connecting large language model workflows to browser profiles.

The researchers describe a possible pipeline in which AI-generated text is paired with automated account activity and distribution. That does not mean every user of these products is conducting a campaign, but it can make coordinated misuse easier to scale.

Some platforms also offer templates for repetitive actions and tools to build activity histories over time. This “warming” can make a new profile look less like a newly created account.

Check Point warns that accounts may build credible histories or pass identity checks, which can delay detection until fraudulent activity begins.

Potential misuse includes account takeover, payment fraud, fake loan applications, advertising fraud, phishing, malware distribution, and coordinated efforts to influence online discussion.

The same concern applies to organizations whose staff accounts or customer accounts are targeted. A stolen session may be used to reach email, financial services, or other connected systems.

The Cybersecurity News report on Microsoft 365 session theft after MFA offers a related example of why security teams need to monitor active sessions, not just passwords and login challenges.

Check Point recommends looking beyond account behavior, because antidetect tools are designed to make individual profiles appear unrelated.

Security teams should review network and infrastructure signals, including large-scale residential proxy activity, unusual browser fingerprint changes, and suspicious session-cookie patterns. Organizations should also check whether their session monitoring can identify unusual access to an already authenticated account.

For platforms, account-level signals may still matter, but the report argues they should be combined with infrastructure analysis and investigation of suspicious patterns across profiles.

For companies, security reviews should include scenarios in which a valid session is used from an unexpected device or network, even when no new password prompt appears.

As with other session-hijacking methods, invalidating active sessions may be necessary when an account is confirmed compromised. The key point is that antidetect browsers are not a single malware family with one fixed signature.

They are tools that can mask identity signals, while automation and AI can help criminals operate at greater scale. Defenders therefore need to link signals across accounts, devices, networks, and sessions instead of relying on one indicator alone.

articles.title: Hackers Use Gentlemen Ransomware to Disable Windows Defender and Destroy Backups
articles.description:
A ransomware operation known as The Gentlemen is using a mix of security tampering, service disruption and file encryption to make recovery harder for affected organizations. Its Windows malware can turn off Microsoft Defender’s real-time protection, add broad exclusions that reduce scanning, stop backup-related services and delete Volume Shadow Copies. These steps weaken defenses and […]

The post Hackers Use Gentlemen Ransomware to Disable Windows Defender and Destroy Backups appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A ransomware operation known as The Gentlemen is using a mix of security tampering, service disruption and file encryption to make recovery harder for affected organizations.

Its Windows malware can turn off Microsoft Defender’s real-time protection, add broad exclusions that reduce scanning, stop backup-related services and delete Volume Shadow Copies. These steps weaken defenses and remove common ways to restore files after encryption.

The malware also targets more than files. It can clear event logs and other system records that investigators may need to understand what happened.

The group uses a double-extortion model: attackers can steal data as well as encrypt it, raising the risk of public exposure even when a victim has backups. The sequence is a reminder that a successful ransomware response depends on protecting both systems and recovery data.

Analysts from Acronis’ Threat Research Unit identified these behaviors in its technical analysis of The Gentlemen ransomware and associated tools. The report describes a Go-based ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in 2025 and targets Windows, Linux, network-attached storage and BSD systems.

Acronis says the group has claimed more than 800 victims, though that figure reflects the group’s claims rather than independently confirmed infections.

On Windows, the ransomware attempts to disable Defender’s real-time monitoring and add its process and the C: drive to the exclusion list.

That may allow the malware to run with less interference while it prepares to encrypt files. It also stops selected processes and services linked to security tools, databases, virtual machines, email and backup products.

Cyber Security News has previously covered how Gentlemen operators disable defenses and backup services during intrusions.

The impact is not limited to security software. Stopping database or virtualization services can free files for encryption, while disrupting backup software may prevent routine recovery jobs from running.

Hackers Use Gentlemen Ransomware

Before encryption, the malware also attempts to remove available Volume Shadow Copies, which Windows can use to restore earlier versions of files.

It can clear selected Windows logs, prefetch data and PowerShell command history, reducing the local evidence available to responders.

Acronis found that the ransomware can establish persistence through scheduled tasks and Windows startup registry entries. It can also search for connected drives and, when the relevant option is used, network shares.

With its spreading feature enabled, it can identify a domain and use PsExec to copy and run the ransomware on other workstations.

This behavior connects one compromised machine to broader network risk, a pattern also detailed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Gentlemen ransomware spreading across networks.

The encryption process is designed to move quickly. The report says files under 1 MB are encrypted in full, while larger files may be encrypted in sections.

The malware uses ChaCha20 for file encryption and elliptic-curve cryptography to protect the file keys. Encrypted files receive an extension that can vary between builds, and the malware leaves a ransom note in affected folders.

Acronis also identified a separate tool used to terminate security processes. It drops vulnerable drivers, installs them as services and uses them to stop selected processes at the kernel level.

One driver is linked to Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver, associated in the report with CVE-2025-70795; the other is Lenovo’s BootRepair.sys.

The technique is known as “bring your own vulnerable driver”: attackers abuse a driver with a weakness to gain actions that ordinary user-level tools may not permit. For more context, see Cyber Security News’ report on vulnerable drivers used against EDR.

For defenders, the warning signs include unexpected Defender setting changes, security or backup services stopping, unfamiliar driver installations, log clearing and rapid file changes across multiple systems.

Organizations should investigate

Organizations should investigate these events together rather than as isolated alerts. Acronis recommends keeping endpoint detection tools active, patching systems and drivers, limiting administrative access, monitoring PowerShell and remote administration tools, and segmenting networks to restrict spread.

Backups should be regularly tested and protected with access controls that prevent ordinary compromised systems from deleting or changing them.

Keeping critical copies offline or isolated from production can preserve a recovery path if attackers reach administrator accounts. Microsoft likewise advises restoring from verified offline or immutable backups after ransomware incidents.

These measures cannot prevent every intrusion, but they can reduce the chance that one compromised device turns into a prolonged outage.

articles.title: Google Upgrades Chrome With Gemini AI to Detect Fake Antivirus and Browser Update Scams
articles.description:
Google has upgraded Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode with a more powerful Gemini AI model to detect fake antivirus alerts, browser update scams, and other deceptive websites. Announced on October 20, 2026, the changes also introduce suspicious site warnings and protection against ClickFix attacks that trick users into running malicious commands. The update expands Google’s earlier […]

The post Google Upgrades Chrome With Gemini AI to Detect Fake Antivirus and Browser Update Scams appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google has upgraded Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode with a more powerful Gemini AI model to detect fake antivirus alerts, browser update scams, and other deceptive websites.

Announced on October 20, 2026, the changes also introduce suspicious site warnings and protection against ClickFix attacks that trick users into running malicious commands.

The update expands Google’s earlier work on AI scam detection. Chrome previously used an on-device Gemini model on supported devices to identify tech support scams.

Google has now moved this analysis to a server-side model, extending the feature to all users who enable Enhanced Protection rather than limiting it to compatible hardware.

Chrome Gemini AI Detects Fake Scams

According to Google’s announcement, Gemini examines page content for signs of fraud. It identifies the brand a website claims to represent, assesses the page’s purpose, and produces a score showing how likely it is to be a scam.

Safe Browsing combines these findings with domain reputation and other security signals before reaching a final verdict. This means Gemini does not decide whether to block a website by itself.

Its analysis provides another layer of evidence, helping Chrome assess pages that use convincing security messages or browser branding to pressure visitors into taking unsafe actions.

Google says Chrome sends page text for analysis only when a website shows strong scam indicators. The company says it processes this content temporarily and never logs, retains, or uses it to train its models. These safeguards apply to page content sent for this detection process.

Chrome is also introducing two levels of site warnings for Enhanced Protection users. Suspicious site warnings flag deceptive patterns when Google has lower confidence about the threat. These warnings differ in appearance, wording, colors, and icons from warnings for confirmed dangerous websites.

Known malicious sites will continue to trigger Chrome’s familiar full-page red warning. This approach lets Google warn about more potentially harmful pages while keeping possible risks separate from high-confidence threats.

The update also addresses ClickFix, a technique that asks visitors to copy and run commands to repair a fake problem. Cybersecurity News has previously covered fake Chrome error pages that guide users into executing hidden PowerShell scripts.

These attacks move malware downloads into tools such as PowerShell or cmd.exe, outside Chrome’s normal download checks. Related reporting on DriveSurge’s fake browser updates shows how attackers combine familiar update prompts with command-based infection methods.

Chrome now detects suspicious commands copied during potential ClickFix attempts. It removes personally identifiable information from the copied content before sending it to Safe Browsing. A dangerous verdict triggers a warning, with checks designed to limit disruption to legitimate developer work.

Users must enable Enhanced Protection to receive these features. Google provides instructions in its Chrome Safe Browsing guide. Google also stresses that Chrome will never ask users to repair the browser by copying and running commands from a webpage.

articles.title: LiteLLM Compromised – Hackers Injected an Infostealer and RAT in the Latest 1.107.0 PyPI Release
articles.description:
LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was compromised on PyPI on October 21, 2026, spreading a credential stealer and a remote access trojan through all seven distributed wheel files. The malicious release also reached Docker images, putting developer systems, build runners, and AI services at risk. Aikido warned that anyone who installed the affected release should assume credentials […]

The post LiteLLM Compromised – Hackers Injected an Infostealer and RAT in the Latest 1.107.0 PyPI Release appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was compromised on PyPI on October 21, 2026, spreading a credential stealer and a remote access trojan through all seven distributed wheel files. The malicious release also reached Docker images, putting developer systems, build runners, and AI services at risk.

Aikido warned that anyone who installed the affected release should assume credentials were exposed. PyPI removed version 1.107.0, but taking down the package does not remove malware already installed or invalidate secrets attackers may have stolen.

Socket’s investigation said its scanner flagged all seven wheels seven minutes after publication. Detection speed matters because automated dependency updates can pull a poisoned release into multiple environments before a human reviews the package change.

How the LiteLLM Malware Runs

The attack uses Python startup hooks rather than relying on an application to import LiteLLM. According to Wiz’s technical analysis, installation places three files, cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py, directly inside Python’s site-packages directory.

When Python starts, cook.pth imports cook.py, which decodes its hidden code and starts the credential theft routine. This means an unrelated Python command can trigger the payload after installation, even when the user never opens LiteLLM directly.

The stealer searches for system information, browser data, developer secrets, cloud credentials, and authentication files used by AI tools. Reported targets include SSH private keys, AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials, browser passwords, and tokens for tools such as Claude and GitHub Copilot.

Collected information is encrypted and sent through an HTTP POST request to www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck. Wiz identifies the destination as attacker controlled and designed to resemble LiteLLM infrastructure. The stealer also writes a marker at /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb, although that path can fail on Windows.

A separate startup file, sitecustomize.py, provides the remote code loading path on Linux and macOS. It tries to retrieve domain.txt from the GitHub repository letters9813/pythonclient-test, then uses the returned address to download and execute another Python script from a /codepy endpoint.

This gives attackers a route to run additional code when affected Python environments start again. However, capability should not be confused with confirmed activity. Wiz reported that domain.txt had not been populated during its analysis and that the repository was subsequently taken down.

Container users also need to investigate. Wiz identified affected LiteLLM images on GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub, including v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable. A familiar image tag therefore does not establish that a deployment is clean.

The public incident discussion also points to build records naming Berri-AI/litellm, a lookalike repository that differs from the legitimate BerriAI/litellm project by one hyphen. That finding raises questions about release source validation, but does not establish the full intrusion path or attacker identity.

Teams that installed LiteLLM 1.107.0 should isolate affected hosts and runners, preserve relevant logs, and treat accessible secrets as potentially stolen. Investigations should cover package installation records, container deployments, Python startup files, and outbound connections to the reported collection endpoint.

Rotate and revoke exposed cloud keys, SSH keys, browser sessions, repository tokens, and AI service credentials from a clean system. Replacing only the LiteLLM package is not enough when stolen credentials can still provide access elsewhere.

Wiz identified 1.106.2 as the most recent safe version in its report. Rebuild affected environments from trusted sources and pin container deployments to verified image digests rather than relying on moving tags. Review cloud and source control logs for unexpected access after installation.

This is LiteLLM’s second reported supply chain compromise this year. Cyber Security News previously covered the LiteLLM supply chain attack involving versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 and the later investigation into exposed cloud keys and CI/CD secrets.

Those earlier findings do not prove the same attackers caused this incident. They show why brief package exposure can create a much longer security problem. Removing a malicious release limits new downloads, while recovery still depends on finding affected systems, removing startup backdoors, and cutting off stolen access.

articles.title: China-Linked Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Applications Into Backdoors to Steal Credentials
articles.description:
China-linked hackers are using trusted Windows applications to load hidden backdoors, collect system details, and steal Active Directory credential data. The group, tracked as BRONZE SANDCASTLE, places malicious files beside legitimate software, allowing familiar programs to run attacker-controlled code without changing the original application. cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
China-linked hackers are using trusted Windows applications to load hidden backdoors, collect system details, and steal Active Directory credential data.

The group, tracked as BRONZE SANDCASTLE, places malicious files beside legitimate software, allowing familiar programs to run attacker-controlled code without changing the original application.

The campaign shows how genuine software can become part of an attack chain. Similar China-linked DLL sideloading attacks have abused trusted applications to hide malicious activity, although shared techniques alone do not establish a connection between threat groups.

Researchers from Sophos’ Counter Threat Unit and SophosLabs identified the malware while investigating incidents across Asia and Africa.

Their technical report on the campaign, published October 20, describes attacks observed between August 2025 and August 2026 involving victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea.

China-Linked Hackers Turn Trusted Windows Applications

Sandboxie DLL sideloading is the group’s clearest technical marker. Attackers placed legitimate Sandboxie programs beside a malicious supporting library.

When launched, the trusted application loaded that library and handed execution to the attackers. The report also documents abused components from Java, Krita, NVDA, LINE, and Microsoft Sysinternals.

The malicious libraries typically read an encrypted payload from a local configuration file, decode it, and execute code in memory.

This separates the visible application from the hidden backdoor and lets operators change payload behavior without replacing the loading library. Renamed executables further help the files blend into compromised systems.

Other ShadowPad DLL sideloading campaigns have used a comparable three-part structure: a legitimate program, a malicious library, and an encrypted payload.

That similarity provides useful context, but Sophos tracks BRONZE SANDCASTLE separately because its observed activity could not be reliably linked to BRONZE PRESIDENT or BRONZE ATLAS.

Modified Meterpreter Payload Steals System Data

The decoded backdoor uses a reflective loader, which places an embedded Windows program into memory. Although its structure resembles Metasploit shellcode, Sophos found custom function-resolution routines and a larger, more complex codebase than standard examples. Elements of COFFLoader also suggest custom features for use after a system is compromised.

Researchers identified payload versions 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. The backdoor sends its control server a structured JSON message containing computer and user names, domain details, operating system version, internal and public IP addresses, process information, working directory, processor type, and startup time.

Version 1.1.5 contacted dedicated control domains, while version 1.1.7 downloaded encrypted configuration files through GitHub.

Connections to legitimate file-sharing and messaging services may also have supported operator instructions, although Sophos did not confirm that purpose.

After gaining access, the operators used Windows network commands to inspect accounts and local networks. They also created Volume Shadow Copies before copying the Active Directory database.

This activity connects the backdoor’s remote access with attempts to obtain sensitive domain credential data. Previous Windows shadow copy abuse shows why this sequence matters: snapshots can expose protected database contents.

Sophos recommends detecting libraries that read local files and immediately execute code in memory, alongside unusual executable headers and reflective loading. Behavior and memory monitoring are important because encrypted payloads can weaken static file detection.

articles.description:
PHP has released emergency security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that could let unauthenticated attackers run code on vulnerable web servers. The PHP project rates both vulnerabilities 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. Administrators should […]

The post PHP Releases Emergency Patches for PHP2Shell Flaws Threatening Millions of Web Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
PHP has released emergency security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that could let unauthenticated attackers run code on vulnerable web servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and collectively called PHP2Shell, the flaws affect PHP’s handling of memory during web requests. The PHP project rates both vulnerabilities 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. Administrators should update PHP as soon as possible.

The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The vulnerabilities affect earlier versions in those branches. PHP 8.1 and older are no longer supported by the project, though some Linux distributions and long-term support providers may offer backported fixes. Administrators using older releases should check with their vendor or plan a move to a supported version.

PHP2Shell Flaws

According to the PHP2Shell research website, researchers from Wiz Research, OpenAI Codex Security, and Calif uncovered two critical vulnerability classes in PHP’s core engine.

CVE-2026-109618 stems from how PHP responds to an out-of-memory condition. PHP previously used a mechanism called longjmp() to exit the current operation when memory ran out. In some situations, that sudden exit could leave request data partly initialized. PHP’s later shutdown process could then read or act on the invalid data, opening a path to remote code execution.

The PHP advisory explains that multipart form data can help trigger the memory problem. For example, a request may contain many headers within a part, or many empty file fields that still make PHP create metadata.

Nested field names can add to the memory needed to process the request. The advisory also describes a case where a multipart request without a usable content length can pass an early size check while PHP continues parsing data. These conditions can exhaust memory even when a request appears to stay within some configured limits.

The impact is especially clear for Apache’s mod_php. The PHP security advisory says researchers validated unauthenticated code execution over HTTP against this setup, using default PHP input and memory limits. The request can reach the vulnerable state before the application’s own code starts. The risk differs across server setups. For PHP-FPM, the advisory says source analysis indicates susceptibility, but the same complete exploit was not demonstrated for that server setup.

CVE-2026-109619 involves stale global state in long-running PHP workers. A worker may retain a reference to memory from a request after PHP has freed that memory. If an error or other event interrupts cleanup, and a later request reaches that leftover state before PHP resets it, the worker may use invalid memory.

The advisory describes confirmed paths involving fatal errors, error-reporting data, and session upload-progress handling. Whether a specific server is exposed depends on its PHP setup, configuration, application, and extensions.

The second flaw matters because web workers handle requests one after another. A state left behind by one request can affect a later request handled by the same worker. The PHP advisory’s confirmed cases include a mod_php scenario. It also describes a PHP-FPM path that depends on an application operation and a later request reaching the same worker. These details make the setup important, but they do not reduce the urgency of patching.

The fix for CVE-2026-109618 changes PHP’s handling of out-of-memory errors. Instead of abruptly leaving an operation in a way that can expose incomplete request state, PHP delays a graceful memory error until a safe point.

A separate hard limit handles more severe memory pressure. The related fix for CVE-2026-109619 resets a wider range of request-related global state so that a worker is less likely to carry invalid references between requests.

Researchers identified flaws that impact PHP web deployments across various server configurations, including Apache with mod_php and PHP-FPM. Estimates of exposure highlight the seriousness of the issue: BleepingComputer reported that VirusTotal estimated there are over 5.1 million PHP hosts visible online. This figure represents an estimate of potentially exposed hosts, rather than a count of confirmed vulnerable or compromised servers.

PHP Team Recommends Updating

The PHP project says updating to a release with the fixes is the complete mitigation. After upgrading, administrators should restart PHP workers and check that all web-facing pools and services are using the patched version. Updating the command-line PHP package alone may not update a separate PHP-FPM service or an Apache module.

If an update cannot happen immediately, temporary measures can reduce some risk but do not replace patching. For CVE-2026-109618, the advisory names an administrative memory_limit=-1 setting as a primary configuration step, while warning that it is not complete protection. It also recommends limiting request sizes and multipart inputs at the frontend. Administrators should avoid RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA, which can cause allocation failures on the vulnerable path.

For the stale-state flaw, the advisory says there is no complete general configuration workaround. On PHP 8.5, disabling fatal_error_backtraces can remove the producer used in one confirmed case. Disabling session upload progress can reduce exposure to a demonstrated session-related path.

Neither setting addresses every possible producer and consumer of stale state, so organizations should treat them only as temporary risk-reduction steps.

Cybersecurity News has also reported on a public PHP2Shell testing tool and early exploitation attempts. These reports are a reason to prioritize upgrades, not a substitute for checking a system’s actual version and vendor guidance. The primary references are the PHP advisory for CVE-2026-109618 and the related advisory for CVE-2026-109619.

If organizations can’t patch immediately, reduce public exposure where possible, review PHP and web-server logs, and confirm which worker processes handle live traffic. Log checks can help identify errors, but clean logs don’t prove a system is safe. The strongest defense is to move every web-facing PHP installation to a fixed release and verify that the updated workers have restarted.

articles.title: APT28 Hackers Open Secret SSH Tunnel Into NATO Country’s Naval Shipbuilder Network
articles.description:
Russian cyberespionage group APT28 used the Hookedge backdoor to reach a naval shipbuilder’s network in a NATO member state, steal login material and set up a hidden SSH tunnel. The intrusion lasted at least two months, according to a report by Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team. The report does not name the shipbuilder or the country. […]

The post APT28 Hackers Open Secret SSH Tunnel Into NATO Country’s Naval Shipbuilder Network appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Russian cyberespionage group APT28 used the Hookedge backdoor to reach a naval shipbuilder’s network in a NATO member state, steal login material and set up a hidden SSH tunnel.

The intrusion lasted at least two months, according to a report by Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team. The report does not name the shipbuilder or the country.

It also describes activity against organizations in a second NATO member state, including a law enforcement agency and a maker of military aircraft engines.

APT28, also known as Fancy Bear and Forest Blizzard, is referred to as Swallowtail in Symantec’s report. Researchers from Symantec identified Hookedge activity at the three organizations.

Their findings add detail to earlier public reporting on the malware, including this report on Hookedge targeting, which described the backdoor’s use of Word documents and web services.

APT28 Hackers

At the shipbuilder, the activity began on July 24, 2026, when a malicious Word document was opened from the Outlook attachment cache. Its hidden macro wrote several files to the user’s profile and started the infection chain.

One of those files launched Hookedge, a backdoor that can fetch instructions, run commands and send back their output. The malware used a hidden Microsoft Edge window to contact webhook.site, a public web service.

The use of a familiar browser and a legitimate service could make the traffic harder to spot among normal web activity. An earlier Hookedge campaign analysis also describes how the backdoor used Edge and webhook services to receive instructions and return results.

The first commands gathered basic details about the infected computer and checked whether it could reach common online services.

After a gap of about three days, the operators returned with a more active stage that used a dedicated server at 185.82.218[.]119 for tasking and data transfer.

Symantec observed a burst of seven commands in about 30 seconds, suggesting an operator was working directly on the compromised system.

Stolen key enabled a route back in

The operators placed an SSH private key on the host and used it to open a connection to their server. The tunnel gave them a route from their own infrastructure back into the shipbuilder’s internal network.

Unlike a short remote session, a tunnel can provide a continuing path through a compromised machine. Soon after it was opened, the operators checked internal hostnames, indicating that they were mapping the network.

The SSH tunnel was one of two ways the attackers sought to obtain or use account credentials. They also ran a PowerShell script that caused the computer to send an NTLM authentication response to a local listener. NTLM is a Windows method for proving a user’s identity.

Captured responses can create further risk if attackers can crack them or use them to try to access other systems.

The operators checked account and group details, looked up more internal systems, and gathered information about running processes and installed updates.

They stopped the SSH process the following day, but Hookedge continued to contact the operators’ server in later bursts. The report does not confirm why the tunnel was closed or what data, if any, was taken.

This use of tunnels fits a wider pattern in which APT28 has relied on less obvious routes and services to support its operations.

Cyber Security News has also reported on APT28 abuse of cloud services, a separate campaign that highlights why defenders should check how programs behave, not just whether a website is known or trusted.

On July 31, the operators ran a program named ld.exe with an encrypted file called Events.dat. The loader decrypted its input in memory and called a function named ExecuteLoader.

Symantec found that the file supplied to the loader was not recovered, so the final payload and its purpose remain unknown. The loader was still present on the host weeks later, and the Hookedge launcher was seen again on September 24.

The report places the shipbuilder incident within a wider campaign against defense and government-related targets in two NATO countries.

The combination of a backdoor, credential theft, internal network checks and a tunnel suggests a sustained effort to gain access and collect intelligence.

The available evidence does not show whether the attackers reached other systems or obtained sensitive shipbuilding information.

Organizations should investigate suspicious Word attachments, unexpected scripts in user folders, hidden Edge activity and unapproved SSH connections.

They should review endpoint, email, DNS and proxy logs for the indicators below, check for signs of NTLM credential exposure, and rotate affected credentials if compromise is suspected.

The report advises treating Hookedge activity as a possible ongoing intrusion rather than assuming that removing one file ends the threat.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack 333 Tor Exit Nodes to Intercept SSH Logins and Steal Credentials
articles.description:
Hackers compromised 333 Tor exit nodes and redirected SSH connections to password-stealing servers, according to a researcher’s account published October 20, 2026. The campaign began October 2 and targeted unencrypted email traffic alongside remote server logins. The affected nodes represented roughly one in ten of the approximately 3,000 Tor exit relays cited in the report. […]

The post Hackers Hijack 333 Tor Exit Nodes to Intercept SSH Logins and Steal Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers compromised 333 Tor exit nodes and redirected SSH connections to password-stealing servers, according to a researcher’s account published October 20, 2026. The campaign began October 2 and targeted unencrypted email traffic alongside remote server logins.

The affected nodes represented roughly one in ten of the approximately 3,000 Tor exit relays cited in the report. Attackers reportedly gained access to the underlying Linux servers in August and installed Ebury 1.8.3, an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer.

Exit relays carry traffic from the Tor network to its destination. In this campaign, compromised relays forwarded encrypted web traffic normally but redirected SSH connections on port 22 to one of 12 interception servers.

The researcher discovered the activity after an SSH connection produced a “REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED” warning. That message meant the presented server key did not match the previously trusted key.

Hackers Hijack 333 Tor Exit Nodes

According to the account, users who ignored the warning and continued with password authentication exposed their credentials. Attackers could then connect to the intended server, watch commands entered during the session, and open another connection to try to install Ebury.

The attack therefore depended on defeating verification, rather than simply breaking SSH encryption. A changed host key was the visible warning that the connection might no longer reach the expected server.

The report also described changes to allowed ports that steered affected exits toward unencrypted mail traffic, giving attackers another source of readable data.

To identify compromised exits, the researcher built a test around exitmap, a tool for checking Tor exit behavior. Each test selected an exit relay and opened an SSH connection between two controlled servers.

One server checked the SSH fingerprint. The other checked whether the incoming connection originated from the selected exit or an interception server. About a dozen exits returned false fingerprints, while more than 300 routed connections through the same interception infrastructure.

A separate honeypot test using sshesame reportedly revealed Paramiko, a Python SSH library, on the attacker’s side. Captured commands checked user privileges and sudo access before attempting to run a Base64-encoded Perl installer.

Ebury’s role fits its established history. Cyber Security News previously covered Ebury infections affecting over 400,000 Linux servers, including credential theft and SSH traffic interception inside hosting environments.

Researcher kaba reported the findings to Tor’s network health team on October 2, and operators alerted affected relays with the BadExit flag on October 4.

Tor’s bad-relay guidance confirms that BadExit prevents a relay from serving as an exit. The project also accepts reports containing relay identifiers and evidence of suspicious behavior.

Attackers reportedly restarted several relays on October 5, but the flags prevented them from serving as exits. The account says all identified infected servers were shut down that day.

The initial access method remains unknown. A hosting-provider breach is one theory, not a confirmed finding. Attribution also remains unresolved.

The case reinforces why relay monitoring matters, a subject covered in Cyber Security News’ report on Tor’s network safety measures. For SSH users, the researcher’s central lesson is to investigate host-key warnings rather than bypass them and replace password logins with SSH keys.

articles.description:

Google says the release will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The patched versions are 156.0.8078.47 for Linux and 156.0.8078.47/.48 for Windows and Mac, according […]

The post Google Releases Massive Chrome Security Update Fixing 353 Flaws, Including 6 Critical Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google released Chrome 156 for Windows, macOS, and Linux on October 20, 2026, fixing 353 security flaws, including six critical bugs across graphics, accessibility, rendering, and communication features.

Google says the release will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The patched versions are 156.0.8078.47 for Linux and 156.0.8078.47/.48 for Windows and Mac, according to the supplied release notice. Users should check their installed version and restart the browser after updating to ensure the fixes take effect.

According to Google’s security advisory, five critical vulnerabilities involve memory corruption. They are CVE-2026-113341 in Skia, CVE-2026-113279 in Accessibility, CVE-2026-113072 in CSS, CVE-2026-113280 in Paint, and CVE-2026-113303 in WebRTC. The sixth, CVE-2026-113271, is a use-after-free flaw in Accessibility.

Use-after-free bugs occur when software accesses released memory, creating security risks. However, the public notice does not detail how each critical flaw can be exploited or confirm a complete attack chain, so severity ratings alone do not prove full device compromise.

Chrome Security Update Fixing 353 Flaws

Google reported the Skia issue internally. Researcher Xinyang Ge reported memory corruption flaws in Accessibility, CSS, and Paint. The advisory credits Ge of Anthropic, assisted by Claude, for the Accessibility use-after-free finding. OpenAI Codex Security, identified as kylebot, reported the critical WebRTC vulnerability on October 15.

The credits show AI tools appearing alongside researchers in browser security work. However, the advisory doesn’t explain the extent of AI involvement in each finding, and the listed credits shouldn’t be read as evidence that every discovery was fully automated.

Beyond the critical issues, Chrome 156 fixes high-severity weaknesses in SiteIsolation, FileSystem, ANGLE, V8, GPU, Network, and other components.

The reported bug types include memory corruption, use-after-free, improper input validation, and out-of-bounds reads. Google awarded $10,000 for CVE-2026-113101, a SiteIsolation use-after-free flaw reported by Quyen Son at VinFast.

This release follows earlier October patch rounds covered by Cybersecuritynews.com, including a Chrome update that fixed 247 vulnerabilities and another that addressed 37 Chrome vulnerabilities. Those releases also included critical memory-safety bugs, making the latest update part of a busy month for browser patching.

Google’s announcement does not state that these six critical vulnerabilities are being exploited in active attacks. It also says access to bug details may remain restricted until most users receive fixes, or until affected third-party projects address shared issues. The available information therefore leaves important exploitation details undisclosed.

Users can follow Google’s update instructions by opening the browser menu, selecting Help, and choosing About Google Chrome. Chrome checks for available updates on that page. Select Relaunch when prompted.

Downloading a patch alone doesn’t complete the installation because Chrome applies the update when it restarts. For managed devices, administrators can use Chrome Enterprise policies to prompt or require browser restarts after pending updates.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Orlando, Florida, United States, October 20th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Industrial Defender Unifies Endpoint Intelligence and Network Monitoring for CIP-015, Adds Risk Signal to Turn Findings into Prioritized Patch Plans

New internal network security monitoring correlates every anomaly with deep asset intelligence; Risk Signal converts findings into verified remediation

Industrial Defender, an OT cybersecurity leader serving the global critical infrastructure industry, today released its latest version, adding internal network security monitoring (INSM) and Risk Signal.

The release builds on Industrial Defender’s decades of leadership serving NERC-CIP regulated utilities, pairing its deep endpoint visibility with network traffic monitoring, providing OT/ICS operators a single path from detection to prioritized remediation.

“Network monitoring tells you something changed. Our customers need to know what that change means and what to do next,” said George Kalavantis, Chief Executive Officer, Industrial Defender.

The FERC-approved NERC CIP-015-1 standard requires entities with high and medium impact BES Cyber Systems to monitor internal network traffic, detect and evaluate anomalies, and retain and protect the resulting data.

Built into the existing platform, the INSM solution learns each device’s baseline communications and flags deviations such as new connections, unexpected protocols, anomalous traffic volume and unknown devices communicating.

“Our platform now associates network traffic with deep endpoint intelligence to provide a more comprehensive cybersecurity,” Kalavantis said.

Each anomaly is correlated with the asset data Industrial Defender maintains, including configuration changes, vulnerabilities and risk score, so operators understand immediately what a network change means to operations.

Every review decision is captured with reviewer, timestamp and rationale, creating audit-ready evidence mapped to CIP-015 requirements.

Beyond CIP-015, INSM serves industrial control system environments across sectors like oil & gas, petrochemical processing and manufacturing, connecting rich asset data with network visibility to strengthen cybersecurity posture.

Risk Signal: Patch what matters first

Detection and visibility are only half the job. Risk Signal closes the loop by turning asset, vulnerability and network findings into action.

Building on each customer’s existing risk model, it identifies the patches and upgrades that deliver the greatest risk reduction for the least operational effort, then packages them into prioritized playbooks that publish directly into existing work-management systems.

After remediation, Risk Signal verifies each patch was applied and updates the asset’s risk score.

“The latest version of our trusted platform connects network activity with the asset intelligence we’ve engineered for two decades, and Risk Signal turns that insight into a defensible plan. It’s the shortest path from visibility to reduced risk for critical infrastructure” Kalavantis said.

Industrial Defender will demonstrate these capabilities at GridSecCon 2026 in Orlando.

About Industrial Defender

Industrial Defender provides OT and ICS cybersecurity and compliance solutions for critical infrastructure operators, including electric utilities, oil & gas, chemical, water, and manufacturing organizations.

The platform delivers continuous OT asset visibility, vulnerability management, and audit-ready compliance reporting across frameworks including NERC CIP, NIS2, IEC 62443, and NIST CSF.

articles.title: Scattered Spider Hackers Exploit Help Desk Calls to Bypass MFA and Breach Corporate Networks
articles.description:
A convincing phone call can be enough to open a path into a company network. Scattered Spider has repeatedly used social engineering to persuade help desk workers to reset passwords or move multi-factor authentication (MFA) to a device controlled by an attacker. Instead of breaking the security technology directly, the caller exploits the support process […]

The post Scattered Spider Hackers Exploit Help Desk Calls to Bypass MFA and Breach Corporate Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A convincing phone call can be enough to open a path into a company network. Scattered Spider has repeatedly used social engineering to persuade help desk workers to reset passwords or move multi-factor authentication (MFA) to a device controlled by an attacker.

Instead of breaking the security technology directly, the caller exploits the support process designed to help employees regain access.

The approach turns routine account recovery into a serious security risk. An attacker may pose as a worker who has lost a phone, changed numbers or been locked out before an important meeting.

Personal details gathered from public sources and stolen data can make the story sound genuine. If a support agent accepts those details as proof of identity, the attacker may gain access to the employee’s account and, from there, other company services.

Researchers at Flare, including cybersecurity researcher Jon DiMaggio, describe Scattered Spider as an intrusion cluster that uses social engineering to target help desks, identity systems and account-recovery processes.

Their analysis also warns that a help desk call alone does not prove that Scattered Spider carried out an incident; attribution needs more supporting evidence.

The group is also known by names including UNC3944 and Octo Tempest, while security agencies track related activity under different labels.

Scattered Spider Hackers Exploit Help Desk Calls

MFA asks users to prove their identity in more than one way, such as with a password and a phone prompt. But if an attacker persuades a help desk to reset the account or register a new authentication device, the attacker may be able to pass the next login check as if they were the real employee.

The weak point is not always the MFA product; it can be the process for changing the methods tied to an account. Scattered Spider operators may first collect information about a target from professional profiles, company websites, breached data or other public sources.

They can then call support and claim they cannot use their usual device. A successful reset can give them access to email, single sign-on (SSO) portals, virtual private networks and cloud services.

Flare describes this as a people-centred route into enterprise identity systems, rather than a campaign that depends on a new software flaw.

The method has appeared alongside other ways to pressure or trick users. In MFA fatigue, an attacker sends repeated login prompts in the hope that a tired or distracted employee will approve one.

In a SIM-swap attack, the attacker tries to take control of a phone number used to receive verification codes. CISA and its partners have documented these techniques, along with calls that persuade help desk staff to reset passwords or MFA tokens.

Cyber Security News has previously reported on help desk MFA bypass tactics, including how impersonation can lead to account access.

Other coverage has examined phishing frameworks used by Scattered Spider and the wider risks described in the joint Scattered Spider advisory.

These reports illustrate why companies should treat identity recovery as part of their security boundary, not as a routine service task.

What attackers may do after access

A successful account takeover can provide a foothold for further activity. Attackers may access company services, seek higher privileges, create ways to retain access or use legitimate remote-management tools.

That can make activity harder to distinguish from normal IT work. In some cases, access is followed by data theft and extortion or ransomware deployment.

The impact can extend beyond the first compromised account. If that account has broad access through SSO or administrative tools, an attacker may be able to reach multiple systems without separately breaking into each one.

The scale of any breach depends on the victim’s permissions, security controls and response speed; a help desk reset does not automatically mean the entire network is compromised.

Flare’s report also makes an important distinction about attribution. Help desk vishing is now used by actors across a wider cybercrime ecosystem, so it should not, by itself, be treated as proof of Scattered Spider involvement.

Investigators need to assess the full picture, including technical evidence, infrastructure and other behavior. That caution matters for companies reporting incidents and for readers assessing claims made by threat actors.

CISA recommends phishing-resistant MFA, including FIDO/WebAuthn or public-key-based methods, because these are designed to resist phishing and are not vulnerable to push bombing or SIM-swap attacks in the same way as some other methods.

Organizations should also strengthen how help desks verify identity before changing a password, phone number or MFA method. A safer reset process should use a trusted second channel or a verified contact method already on file, rather than details supplied during the call.

High-risk changes can require approval from a manager or security team, and staff should be trained to pause when a caller creates urgency or asks to bypass normal checks. Companies should also alert on unusual MFA registrations, repeated prompts and account recovery followed by unfamiliar logins.

The main lesson is straightforward: MFA remains valuable, but it cannot compensate for a weak recovery process. Security teams need to protect the people and procedures that control account access, as well as the devices and applications that enforce it.

Scattered Spider’s playbook shows how a familiar voice and a plausible story can turn a customer-support interaction into a path toward corporate systems.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Rust 1.100 will introduce optional security cooldowns in Cargo, giving developers a way to delay newly published dependencies before they enter projects.

Scheduled for November 12, 2026, the release aims to give security teams and package maintainers time to spot malicious updates before automated builds pull them in.

The feature is available in beta but has not reached stable Rust. Its default waiting period remains zero, so upgrading alone will not enable protection. Teams must set a minimum package age to reduce exposure during the risky hours after a release appears.

Researchers from Socket.dev documented the malicious proc-macro1 crate behind an August compromise involving arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec.

Its build script downloaded a payload, showing how a trusted dependency can bring malware into developer systems without obvious changes to application code.

Rust 1.100 Introduces Cargo Security Cooldowns

The three compromised releases remained on crates.io for 86, 90, and 107 minutes, respectively, before removal, according to Rust security responders cited by Socket.

All disappeared within two hours, but automated updates could still reach developer machines and continuous integration systems before defenders finished checking them.

During the incident, attackers added a harmful dependency to trusted packages. Reporting on compromised Rust package releases explains how Cargo ran the malicious build script during compilation, allowing code execution before developers used the affected library.

That makes dependency selection a security decision, not simply routine maintenance. Work on the cooldown began before that attack. The tracking issue opened on May 18, and nightly Cargo gained support on June 21.

The stabilization change merged on August 28, with the feature listed for Rust 1.100 in draft release notes.

How the Waiting Period Works

Developers can enable a seven-day cooldown in .cargo/config.toml by setting global-min-publish-age = "7 days" under [registry].

Cargo accepts periods expressed in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, or months. Its incompatible-publish-age rule defaults to "deny", so teams normally need no separate resolver setting.

When Cargo selects dependencies, it excludes releases younger than the chosen limit. It can select an older version that meets the project’s requirements. If none qualifies, dependency resolution fails rather than accepting a fresh release simply to complete the build.

This strict behavior addresses a specific risk: attackers could publish malware and withdraw safe versions, pushing a weaker policy toward the malicious update.

Attackers withdrew legitimate arrayref versions during the August incident. Cargo also reports skipped releases and their ages, helping developers understand blocked updates.

The approach shares a goal with GitHub’s Dependabot cooldown protection, which delays routine version updates. Cargo places the age check within dependency selection itself, rather than relying only on an update bot to hold back new releases.

Cargo preserves versions already recorded in Cargo.lock, even when they fall below the age threshold. Enabling cooldowns therefore will not remove a malicious release already locked into a project. The feature also excludes cargo install, Git dependencies, local paths, and registries without publication timestamps.

For urgent fixes, developers can run CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update -p some-crate --precise 1.2.3, replacing the example package and version.

This bypass applies to that command, including indirect dependencies it resolves. Once recorded in the lockfile, those versions remain usable under normal settings.

A cooldown buys time; it does not scan code or prove safety. Earlier malicious Rust logging crates stole wallet keys while keeping normal logging functions, showing why familiar behavior cannot establish trust. Malware that escapes detection can simply outlast the waiting period.

Socket also noted a September warning about attackers targeting Rust project members and crate owners through fake job and project offers. Attackers arranged video calls, then tried to persuade targets to install software or run commands.

That campaign highlights the account security problem behind poisoned releases: delaying updates does not stop criminals from stealing the access used to publish malicious code.

Cloudflare says the rules are available to all customers, including those on free plans, […]

The post Cloudflare Detects Early Exploitation Attempts Targeting Two Leaked PHP Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cloudflare says it is seeing early attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities whose details surfaced before the PHP security team’s planned release. The company has deployed an initial set of Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules to block known exploit patterns. Cloudflare says the rules are available to all customers, including those on free plans, and that it is updating them as new patterns appear.

The warning raises the urgency for teams running PHP websites, but the firewall rules are only a temporary layer of protection. Cloudflare’s chief technology officer, Dane Knecht, said customers should patch as soon as PHP publishes its security update. At the time of writing, the release is scheduled for 14:00 UTC on October 21, or 19:30 IST.

Public reports track the flaws as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The PHP security team has rated both critical, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Researchers and security reports describe them as remote code execution vulnerabilities, a type of flaw that could let an attacker run code on a vulnerable server. However, PHP has not yet published full technical details, including the affected components, precise attack paths, or confirmed vulnerable versions.

The information became public before the planned disclosure and security update. The PHP team announced an earlier release date after the leak, and said it could move the release forward again if technical details became public or it found evidence of active exploitation. Cloudflare’s warning now indicates attempts are emerging, although the company has not shared evidence or details that would allow readers to assess their scale or success.

A WAF checks web requests and can block traffic that matches known harmful patterns. These rules can reduce exposure while administrators prepare updates, but they cannot replace fixes to the underlying PHP code.

New PHP2Shell exploit patterns may also evade rules written for known requests. Cloudflare says it is adjusting its protections as new vectors appear, but it has described the rules as a stopgap.

Organizations should identify every internet-facing system that runs PHP, including sites built with content-management systems and software that bundles its own PHP runtime. Administrators should monitor PHP’s official security notices and their operating-system or hosting provider’s update channels.

Once fixed releases are available, they should verify the affected versions and apply the right update promptly. Teams should also check that their WAF is enabled and that relevant rules are set to block, not merely log, suspicious requests, as Cloudflare has advised paying customers.

After patching, defenders should review web-server and PHP logs for unusual requests and check whether PHP worker processes launched unexpected programs. Security teams should investigate suspicious activity rather than assuming that a WAF block means a system was never reached. If a server shows signs of compromise, preserve logs and follow the organization’s incident-response process.

The incident also shows how a vulnerability disclosure leak can compress defenders’ preparation time. PHP’s broad use across websites and hosting services means administrators may need to locate runtimes outside their main application inventory.

Reports say the flaws may affect older PHP versions, but the official affected-version list is still pending, so organizations should avoid relying on preliminary claims.

For continuing coverage, see Cyber Security News’ report on PHP’s planned emergency security update and its coverage of other recent PHP vulnerabilities.
