articles.description:
Ransomware operators used commercial AI tools to help plan intrusions, manage victim information and prepare extortion, according to a new investigation. But the systems they relied on also kept detailed records of their work. A publicly accessible server exposed AI chat sessions, stolen credentials, campaign notes and source code, giving researchers a view into the […]

The post Hackers Use Claude AI to Plan Ransomware Attacks, Then Accidentally Expose Their Secrets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ransomware operators used commercial AI tools to help plan intrusions, manage victim information and prepare extortion, according to a new investigation.

But the systems they relied on also kept detailed records of their work. A publicly accessible server exposed AI chat sessions, stolen credentials, campaign notes and source code, giving researchers a view into the operators’ workflow.

The exposed files linked the activity to affiliates operating with INC Ransomware and The Gentlemen Ransomware. They included 46 INC encryptor builds prepared for six victims and evidence that an encryptor had run on a victim’s computer.

The researchers cautioned that the records showed organizations at different stages: some were only listed for reconnaissance, while others had deeper access or had reached extortion. SOCRadar’s technical report describes the findings in detail.

Analysts from the SOCRadar Threat Research Unit (STRU) identified the exposed infrastructure in late September 2026. The team found one open server containing AI session data, a shared knowledge base and code for a framework called Phantom.

Logs, configuration files and credentials on that server led researchers to six more exposed servers. Together, the systems held records of victim activity, tools, malware and extortion plans.

Hackers Use Claude AI to Plan Ransomware Attacks

The operators used OpenCode as an interface to models hosted through OpenRouter. STRU reviewed 8,257 messages across 133 sessions and found that the AI helped plan reconnaissance, select techniques, generate commands, troubleshoot tools, review stolen data and draft extortion material.

Claude Opus 4.6 and Kimi K3 were among the commercial models named in the report; the findings describe an AI-supported operation, not proof that Claude alone carried out every task.

Human operators remained involved. The AI was told to coordinate actions and wait for approval, making the setup closer to a human-directed assistant than an independent system.

When a model refused a request, an operator sometimes rewrote it as an authorized red-team assessment. The operators also used a “WormGPT” persona prompt, but STRU says this was a prompt label, not evidence that they were using a separate uncensored model.

The system’s memory became a major weakness. Its knowledge base tracked victims, credentials and campaign progress, while the chat logs showed how operators planned and adjusted their work.

Recorded AI spending exceeded $23,920, according to SOCRadar’s account records. The exposure turned those private work notes into evidence that investigators could examine.

Edge systems were a key way in

Operator records describe attempts to gain access through internet-facing management and remote-access products. They report exploitation of FortiClient EMS flaw CVE-2026-35616, SimpleHelp flaw CVE-2024-57727 and cPanel/WHM flaw CVE-2026-41940.

These figures come from the operators’ own records and were not independently verified by STRU. For SimpleHelp, the records claim 242 affected IP addresses; the earlier SimpleHelp vulnerability report explains why flaws in remote support tools can put connected customer networks at risk.

CISA has separately warned that ransomware actors have exploited CVE-2024-57727 in unpatched SimpleHelp systems. The agency urged organizations to update vulnerable instances and check for signs of compromise, including where a service provider’s system connects to customer environments.

Attackers in the SOCRadar investigation also reportedly used stolen or reused credentials to move between systems. In one case, a reused password opened access to multiple services, including remote access, servers and backup tools.

After getting inside, the operators searched networks, gathered credentials and focused on finance, human resources, legal and executive files. The exposed toolkit included Phantom, Ghost command-and-control software and RevSocks, which can tunnel traffic.

Researchers also found a tool designed to interfere with some security products. The report says the operators prepared INC encryptors for Windows and Linux, but the planned October 1, 2026 deployment against those targets was not confirmed. A September 30 screenshot did show an encryptor running in a victim environment.

The records suggest that stealing data and threatening to publish it could matter as much as encrypting files. Operators used victim financial and customer information to shape demands and plan pressure, including scripted calls.

This broader shift toward data theft and threats is also seen in other cases; Cybersecurity News has reported on ransomware extortion without encryption.

SOCRadar linked the exposed systems to activity involving both INC and The Gentlemen, but did not conclude that the two groups had a formal alliance.

The researchers considered a shared operational environment or service provider supporting different ransomware partners a more likely explanation.

Their records named 62 organizations, but only four were publicly listed for extortion; others were at earlier stages, including reconnaissance or initial access.

For defenders, the case highlights the need to patch exposed edge and remote-access systems, restrict management interfaces, use multifactor authentication for remote administration and review accounts and VPN settings for unexpected changes.

Organizations should also protect backups from direct access by compromised accounts and monitor remote-management tools and large outbound transfers.

The incident’s central lesson is straightforward: AI can help criminals coordinate complex work, but poorly secured infrastructure and retained logs can expose the operation behind it.

The update includes a maximum-severity Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that allows attackers without login credentials to take over an affected Workflow component through network access. The headline figure reflects security patches rather than […]

The post Massive Oracle Security Update – 1295 Flaws Patched, Including Critical E-Business Suite Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Oracle has released its October 2026 Critical Patch Update, delivering 1,295 new security patches across its software portfolio. Published on October 20.

The update includes a maximum-severity Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that allows attackers without login credentials to take over an affected Workflow component through network access.

The headline figure reflects security patches rather than 1,295 separate flaws. Oracle notes that the same vulnerability can affect several products and appear in multiple risk matrices.

Tenable’s analysis counts 1,209 unique CVEs across 33 Oracle product families, highlighting the scale of this release. The most urgent E-Business Suite issue is CVE-2026-101809, which affects the Workflow Notification Mailer component in versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15.

It carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 10.0, the highest possible rating. An attacker can exploit the weakness over HTTP without authentication, and Oracle describes it as easy to exploit.

A successful attack can lead to takeover of Workflow, putting its data and operation at risk. Oracle also warns that the impact could extend to other products.

The flaw therefore deserves attention beyond the affected mailer component, particularly where connected business systems depend on the same application environment.

Oracle Security Update

Another serious issue, CVE-2026-101767, affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library. Rated 9.8, it allows remote exploitation over HTTP without credentials or user interaction.

Supported versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15 are affected, with high potential impact on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability.

The Oracle October 2026 advisory also lists CVE-2026-75803 in the Database Server’s OpenSSL component. This 9.8-rated vulnerability can allow an unauthenticated attacker using TLS network access to take over the affected component. Database versions 19.3 through 19.32 and 23.4.0 through 23.26.3 are affected.

Oracle APEX receives a critical fix for CVE-2026-101521, another 9.8-rated issue. It allows takeover through HTTPS without authentication and affects versions 24.1.0–24.1.21, 24.2.0–24.2.20, and 26.1.0–26.1.4. Oracle provides further impact details in its technical risk descriptions.

Earlier incidents highlight the risks of delaying Oracle patches. Cybersecurity News previously reported active exploitation of CVE-2026-4681, affecting Oracle Payments.

A separate mass exploitation campaign targeting E-Business Suite was linked to CVE-2025-61882. Neither incident confirms exploitation of the newly disclosed Workflow flaw.

Oracle says it continues to receive reports of successful attacks against customers who have not installed available patches. The company urges organizations to remain on supported versions and apply security updates without delay.

Administrators should check installed versions against Oracle’s affected-product tables and follow the patch availability documents for installation instructions.

E-Business Suite customers must also review the underlying Database and Fusion Middleware components, whose fixes are listed separately.

emporary network restrictions may reduce exposure, but Oracle warns that they can disrupt applications and do not fix the underlying flaws. Test these changes before production use, and treat them only as short-term protection until patches are deployed.

articles.description:

The flaw affects FortiSIEM 7.5.0. Fortinet released a fix in version 7.5.1, while version 7.6 is not affected, according to published reporting on the advisory. Fortinet […]

The post Fortinet FortiSIEM RCE Vulnerability Gets Public Exploit That Requires No Login appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public proof-of-concept exploit has been released for CVE-2026-106173, a critical vulnerability in Fortinet FortiSIEM that can let a remote attacker write files and run code without logging in.

The flaw affects FortiSIEM 7.5.0. Fortinet released a fix in version 7.5.1, while version 7.6 is not affected, according to published reporting on the advisory.

Fortinet disclosed the vulnerability on October 13, 2026, in its FortiGuard security advisory. Horizon3.ai later published technical research and a proof-of-concept on GitHub.

The research shows how an unauthenticated client can reach a gRPC service on TCP port 27918 and abuse its SendQueryResult method to write attacker-controlled data to the FortiSIEM appliance.

The gRPC service accepts query-result data and builds a file path using values supplied by the client. Horizon3.ai found that the service does not properly check the query ID before adding it to the path. By using directory-traversal sequences, an attacker can direct the file write outside the expected query-results folder.

The service also adds its own text to the end of the filename. But Horizon3.ai found that a null byte in a crafted field can cause the operating system to treat the path as ending early.

Fortinet FortiSIEM RCE Vulnerability

This can let an attacker target an exact existing filename instead of being limited to the service’s generated filename. The research says sending the specially formed request requires manually building the gRPC message because common tools and libraries restrict null bytes in headers.

The file-write flaw can become remote code execution if an attacker overwrites a script that the appliance runs automatically. Horizon3.ai identified /opt/charting/redishb.sh, a script it says is run by a scheduled job, as a file of interest.

The researchers also named /opt/phoenix/bin/phLicenseTool as a file administrators should inspect. The published proof-of-concept demonstrates the risk, but its release alone does not show that a particular FortiSIEM system has been compromised.

Administrators should check whether their FortiSIEM appliances run version 7.5.0 and upgrade to 7.5.1 or later. FortiSIEM 7.6 is reported as not affected. If an immediate upgrade is not possible, restrict access to TCP port 27918 to trusted systems and keep it unreachable from the public internet.

Horizon3.ai says it did not find application logs that clearly identify exploitation of this flaw. Teams investigating possible compromise should review file modification times and inspect the named scripts for unexpected changes. A mismatch with nearby system-file timestamps may warrant closer investigation. However, it is not proof of exploitation on its own.

The issue adds to a history of FortiSIEM vulnerabilities reported by Horizon3.ai, including CVE-2024-23108 and CVE-2025-64155. Earlier flaws involved the phMonitor service, while CVE-2026-106173 involves a separate gRPC service. That difference matters for defenders because reviewing protections around one FortiSIEM service does not automatically secure another.

articles.description:
A public proof-of-concept repository shares verification tools and a lab setup to test two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as php2shell. The flaws, tracked by researchers as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are reported to affect PHP’s session.upload_progress feature and could lead to remote code execution under certain conditions. The release adds technical detail to a fast-moving security […]

The post PHP2Shell Vulnerability Gets a Public PoC Exploit for Security Testing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public proof-of-concept repository shares verification tools and a lab setup to test two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as php2shell. The flaws, tracked by researchers as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are reported to affect PHP’s session.upload_progress feature and could lead to remote code execution under certain conditions.

The release adds technical detail to a fast-moving security issue. PHP’s security team announced that an emergency release would address two critical vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and urged users to prepare to upgrade.

Its notice scheduled the release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. At the time of writing, that release time has not yet passed, so PHP’s official notice has not confirmed the technical details, affected versions or fixed builds described in the research repository.

The repository says the vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. It lists PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 as planned fixed versions, but administrators should verify these against the PHP team’s release advisory before updating. The PHP project’s advance notice confirms the severity and planned release, but not those version details.

These are the branches eligible for official security updates. PHP 8.1 and older—including PHP 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x—are end-of-life and will not receive official PHP project fixes.

PHP2Shell Vulnerability PoC Exploit

The researcher’s write-up describes several paths to code execution, rather than one universal exploit that works against every PHP website. One chain combines session-file injection with a local file inclusion flaw in an application.

According to the repository, this path depends on upload progress being enabled and an application flaw that allows a local file to be included. A local file inclusion bug occurs when an application can be made to load a file from its server in an unintended way.

The repository says PHP’s upload-progress handler stores a supplied filename in session data without validating it. It also reports that a session identifier sent in a POST body can bypass the session.use_only_cookies setting, which is meant to restrict how session IDs are accepted.

These claims describe how a weakness in PHP’s session handling could combine with a separate application bug. They should not be taken to mean that every PHP site is immediately exploitable through this route.

A second reported issue involves a use-after-free, a memory error that can occur when software continues to use data after it has been released. The researcher says that re-entry into a var_destroy destructor can trigger this condition and reports confirming it with AddressSanitizer, a tool used to find memory errors.

The repository also describes a PHP-FPM serializer state that may persist across requests, and a handler mismatch that may cause a destructor to run after deserialization fails. The researchers say some of these paths need additional conditions, such as an application gadget or access to a local file.

These technical claims remain those of the independent research project until they can be compared with PHP’s full advisory and patches. Security teams should avoid treating every listed path as independently confirmed for all versions or configurations. The project’s verification repository provides the research overview and lab files. Its stated purpose is controlled testing, not use against systems without permission.

PHP runs a wide range of websites and applications, so a flaw in its core session handling could affect many types of deployments. The risk can be greater when an application already has a file inclusion weakness or unsafe deserialization behavior.

Mallory report highlights the scale of outdated PHP deployments as administrators prepare for the php2shell security updates. Using Shodan data collected on October 20, the company identified 883,717 internet-facing hosts running PHP 8.1 or earlier.

These represent about 59% of the roughly 1.5 million hosts that disclosed a PHP version. Those branches no longer receive official PHP project security fixes, making migration to a supported release a key concern.

As previous PHP security coverage has shown, memory errors in PHP components can have a serious impact, though the technical causes differ. This report also covers another example of application-level risk on ScriptCase vulnerabilities.

The reported score of 9.2 signals a critical issue, but it does not tell administrators whether a particular server is exposed. That depends on the PHP version, configuration, application behavior, and whether the necessary conditions for a specific chain exist. The public repository includes a PHP-FPM and Nginx lab for testing. Organizations should use such environments only for authorized validation and should not run proof-of-concept code against production systems.

Administrators should inventory PHP installations across web servers, containers and managed hosting environments, then check the official PHP security release for confirmed affected and fixed versions. Once a suitable update is available, apply it promptly and restart PHP-FPM or the relevant web service so the new binaries take effect.

Systems running end-of-life PHP branches require special attention because they may not receive official fixes. The repository identifies PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0 and 8.1 as unsupported, but teams should confirm support status with the PHP project.

The researcher lists disabling session.upload_progress and setting session.use_only_cookies to On as temporary safeguards. These settings may reduce exposure to some reported paths, but the repository warns that they do not address every attack chain.

They are not a substitute for a security update. Review applications for local file inclusion and unsafe deserialization issues, and check server logs for unusual requests involving PHP session handling while the official advisory is being reviewed.

For now, the public proof-of-concept is best treated as a signal to prepare and validate safely. The key next step is to compare the research claims with PHP’s official release details, then patch affected systems as soon as the project publishes confirmed fixed versions.

The post Microsoft Offers $40,000 for Complete Azure Vulnerability Reports, Just $4,000 for Incomplete Ones appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has introduced a new report-assessment system across its bug bounty programs, making the evidence security researchers submit a key factor in their rewards.

Under the Azure bounty program, eligible critical remote code execution and privilege escalation reports can earn $40,000 when assessed as Complete, compared with $4,000 when marked Not Complete.

The change applies to reports submitted from October 20, 2026, at 8 AM Pacific Time. Earlier submissions remain subject to the previous report quality requirements.

Microsoft says the update aims to reduce requests for missing details and help its security teams reproduce and assess vulnerabilities faster.

The $40,000 figure is not a standard payment for every Azure vulnerability. Microsoft’s Azure Bounty Program ties awards to security impact, severity, and report completeness.

Microsoft Offers $40,000 for Complete Azure Vulnerability Reports

Critical information disclosure reports carry general awards of $12,000 when complete and $1,200 when incomplete. Critical spoofing and tampering reports qualify for $8,000 or $800, respectively.

Important remote code execution reports can receive $30,000 when complete, against $3,000 when incomplete. Azure’s published award range remains $400 to $60,000, with additional rewards possible at Microsoft’s discretion. Certain high-impact scenarios also carry percentage increases.

A complete report does not automatically qualify for payment or make a vulnerability critical. Microsoft assesses severity and security impact separately. Azure submissions must also meet program rules, including demonstrating an eligible issue on the latest, fully patched service or product.

Microsoft expects clear reproduction steps, a reliable proof of concept, the vulnerability type, and accurate technical analysis. Researchers must identify the affected environment, relevant versions, attack requirements, and what an attacker could achieve. They should explain the root cause where possible.

The key test is whether an engineer unfamiliar with the finding can reproduce and assess it using the initial submission. Missing a required detail or supporting file can result in a Not Complete assessment, even if Microsoft later requests more information.

Evidence requirements depend on the vulnerability. Memory corruption reports may need crash data, call stacks, and proof-of-concept source code.

File redirection findings may require Process Monitor logs, while NTLM coercion or relay reports may need packet captures. Web application findings can require videos and scripts.

Researchers must enter reproduction steps and technical details directly into the MSRC Researcher Portal fields. An attached document does not replace those entries. Microsoft’s report completeness guidance explains the required evidence.

Microsoft says AI-assisted research makes it easier to submit potential findings at scale. It welcomes AI use, but reports must still contain accurate analysis and evidence that demonstrates the issue.

Previous reporting on Azure application spoofing flaws shows why the exact bypass matters. Researchers demonstrated how invisible Unicode characters could defeat restrictions on reserved application names.

Coverage of a Microsoft authentication flaw also illustrates the link between research, disclosure, and remediation. After receiving the report, Microsoft restricted the affected endpoint and awarded the researcher $5,000.

For researchers, the practical change is that documentation now carries a clear financial consequence. A valid finding needs a reproducible demonstration, supported technical claims, and the required files from the start. Testing must still stay within Microsoft’s rules rather than exceed permitted access simply to prove greater impact.

articles.description:
Microsoft has introduced a new command-line tool that gives IT admins a faster way to check and manage OneDrive sync across company devices. Microsoft introduced the OneDrive Sync Client Command Line Interface (CLI) at the OneDrive + Copilot event held today. It is aimed at teams that look after large Microsoft 365 setups. The tool […]

The post Microsoft Unveils New OneDrive Command-Line Tool to Manage Sync Deployments appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has introduced a new command-line tool that gives IT admins a faster way to check and manage OneDrive sync across company devices. Microsoft introduced the OneDrive Sync Client Command Line Interface (CLI) at the OneDrive + Copilot event held today. It is aimed at teams that look after large Microsoft 365 setups.

The tool runs with a simple command called odsync and can be used from PowerShell. In the live demo, Microsoft’s Andrey Esipov showed how admins can pull detailed device health information without clicking through settings screens or digging through log files.

According to the demo, the CLI lists every OneDrive account set up on a device, including machines with more than one account, and it can narrow the results down to a single account. It also shows the version of both the sync client and the CLI, whether OneDrive is running, and how it was installed on the system.

Admins can also see Folder Backup settings, including which folders are being backed up to the cloud. One of the most useful features for security teams is the ability to view the Group Policy settings applied to the sync client. This helps confirm that a device actually follows company rules.

The tool also reports overall status at the client, account, and Folder Backup level. When something goes wrong, admins can switch on verbose output for deeper troubleshooting.

Built for Scripts, Automation and AI Agents

A key detail is that the CLI can return results in JSON format. This makes it easy to plug the output into scripts, Microsoft Intune remediation jobs, or reporting tools. Microsoft says the tool works in both interactive and non-interactive modes. It is designed for admins, developers, scripts, and AI agents such as GitHub Copilot CLI.

For example, an admin could run a script across many devices to spot machines where Folder Backup is turned off or where OneDrive is not running at all. Until now, this kind of check often needed custom scripts, registry checks, or third-party utilities.

OneDrive sync is a common blind spot in many companies. Settings that drift away from policy can leave sensitive files outside approved storage or sync them to places they should never reach.

Cyber Security News has earlier reported how OneDrive auto-sync exposed enterprise secrets in SharePoint Online, showing how small sync mistakes can grow into real data leaks. Threat actors have also abused the sync client itself, as seen when hackers exploited OneDrive.exe through DLL sideloading to run malicious code.

A tool that quickly shows the sync client’s real state on each device gives defenders better visibility. It also helps them catch weak setups before they turn into security incidents.

The OneDrive Sync CLI is not yet generally available. Microsoft says it is coming soon to private preview. The company has not shared a public release date, the supported platforms, or a full list of commands. Based on what has been shown so far, the tool focuses on reading and reporting device state rather than changing settings.

Admins who want to get ready can review Microsoft’s guidance on planning file sync for SharePoint and OneDrive and watch the official OneDrive sync release notes for updates.

articles.title: Apache Tomcat Fixes 8 Security Flaws That Could Let Hackers Bypass Authentication
articles.description:
Apache Tomcat has fixed eight security flaws that could let attackers bypass password checks, expose data between users, and disrupt connections under specific conditions. Apache disclosed the vulnerabilities on October 20, 2026, after releasing fixes in Tomcat 11.0.27, 10.1.61, and 9.0.123. The eight issues span different release branches, so not every flaw affects every version. […]

The post Apache Tomcat Fixes 8 Security Flaws That Could Let Hackers Bypass Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apache Tomcat has fixed eight security flaws that could let attackers bypass password checks, expose data between users, and disrupt connections under specific conditions.

Apache disclosed the vulnerabilities on October 20, 2026, after releasing fixes in Tomcat 11.0.27, 10.1.61, and 9.0.123. The eight issues span different release branches, so not every flaw affects every version.

Apache rates three flaws as Important and five as Low. The most serious problems involve authentication, HTTP/2 request handling, and AJP response processing. Their impact depends on the Tomcat version and the features enabled, making configuration checks an important part of assessing exposure.

CVE-2026-101296 affects JNDIRealm when configured with a non-GSSAPI SASL authentication mechanism. A missing validation step lets attackers authenticate without supplying the correct password.

The flaw affects Tomcat 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.26, 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.60, and 9.0.0.M1 through 9.0.122. It is not a universal login bypass across all Tomcat installations.

Apache Tomcat Fixes 8 Security Flaws

The issue differs from the earlier GSSAPI-related JNDIRealm bypass covered in Cyber Security News’ report on Apache Tomcat authentication vulnerabilities.

The latest advisory concerns other SASL mechanisms, so administrators should check the actual authentication settings rather than rely on the component name alone.

CVE-2026-101356 involves incorrect recycling and reuse of internal objects during HTTP/2 processing of asynchronous servlets. Following a processing error, requests or responses can become mixed between users.

Affected releases include 11.0.22 through 11.0.26, 10.1.55 through 10.1.60, and 9.0.118 through 9.0.122. This creates a risk that information crosses user boundaries.

CVE-2026-103119 affects AJP response handling in Tomcat 11.0.0-M25 through 11.0.26. A buffer under-read during a large non-blocking write can split a response body between the current request and the next request on the same connection.

Apache says the likely result is failure of the second request, with possible leakage from the first response. CVE-2026-88041 allows HTTP/2 trailer information from an earlier request to leak into a later request because cleanup is incomplete.

Another cleanup flaw, CVE-2026-93446, can cause intermittent TLS 1.3 connection failures. Apache rates both issues Low, separating them from the more serious cross-user request and response mix-up.

CVE-2026-74049 affects Jasper’s JSTL <c: redirect> plug-in. Processing does not stop immediately after a redirect, allowing the remaining page code to run.

CVE-2026-74048 affects OpenSSL-FFM configurations using FIPS mode. If FIPS activation fails, Tomcat logs an error but continues with JSSE in non-FIPS mode instead of stopping startup.

The eighth flaw, CVE-2026-80353, concerns Tomcat 9’s APR connector. A race condition when creating a Unix Domain Socket can give an unauthorized local user access. Apache says the earlier fix for CVE-2026-65183 did not cover this connector. Versions 9.0.47 through 9.0.122 are affected.

Administrators should upgrade affected deployments to the fixed release for their branch. Apache’s Tomcat 11 security advisory and Tomcat 9 advisory provide affected ranges and patch details.

Earlier Tomcat access-control flaws offer useful background, but their older patched versions do not resolve this new batch. Apache’s notices do not report active exploitation. However, the password bypass and cross-user data risks warrant prompt patching wherever the affected features are in use.

articles.description:
Every breach eventually touches a file a dropped binary, an edited config, a replaced DLL and file integrity monitoring is the control that notices. The 2026 challenge isn’t detection, it’s signal: PCI DSS 4.x demands FIM, but a tool that pages on every patch Tuesday trains the SOC to ignore the one change that matters. […]

The post Top 10 Best File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every breach eventually touches a file a dropped binary, an edited config, a replaced DLL and file integrity monitoring is the control that notices.

The 2026 challenge isn’t detection, it’s signal: PCI DSS 4.x demands FIM, but a tool that pages on every patch Tuesday trains the SOC to ignore the one change that matters.

We scored ten options on noise discipline as much as detection depth. Fortra’s Tripwire takes 1; Qualys and Netwrix complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Fortra (Tripwire) the category’s reference implementation, with change-reconciliation depth nobody matches.

• Podium: Tripwire (reconciliation), Qualys (cloud-agent scale), Netwrix (change context across the estate).

• Free lane is real: Wazuh delivers audit-grade FIM at open-source cost with engineering sweat as the price.

• The differentiator: reconciling changes against authorized tickets/patches raw change feeds are noise generators.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: detection depth (hashes, attributes, registry, real-time vs scan), change reconciliation against authorized activity, compliance reporting (PCI DSS 4.x, NIST, CIS), scale and agent footprint, SIEM integration, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: noise discipline/reconciliation 30%, detection depth 25%, compliance reporting 20%, scale/integration 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 FIM Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Fortra (Tripwire) — Best Change Reconciliation

Snapshot: Quote | Tripwire Enterprise | The FIM reference since the category existed

Why it earns 1: Tripwire defined FIM and still does the hard part best: reconciling detected changes against authorized change tickets, patch manifests, and known-good baselines, so what reaches a human is the unauthorized residue, not the change firehose.

Deep platform coverage (servers, network devices, databases) and audit-ready PCI/NIST reporting round out the Tripwire Enterprise reference implementation, now under Fortra’s roof.

Pros: Reconciliation depth unmatched; compliance-report pedigree; broad platform reach.

Cons: Enterprise weight and quote pricing.

Bottom line: The FIM auditors already believe.

2. Qualys FIM — Best Cloud-Agent Scale

Snapshot: Per-asset subscription | Rides the Qualys Cloud Agent | Real-time kernel-level capture

Why it earns 2: If Qualys agents already blanket your estate, FIM becomes a toggle, not a deployment: real-time change capture streamed to the cloud platform, correlated with the vulnerability and inventory context the agent already owns.

Scale economics and single-agent consolidation make it the pragmatic enterprise pick.

Pros: Zero new agents for Qualys shops; real-time capture; platform correlation.

Cons: Best value only inside the Qualys ecosystem.

Bottom line: FIM as a feature of the agent you already run.

3. Netwrix — Best Change Context

Snapshot: Licensed/quote | Change Tracker + auditing suite | Who/what/when across AD, files, configs

Why it earns 3: Netwrix answers the question FIM alerts beg: who made the change and what else did they touch? Pairing integrity monitoring with its auditing estate Active Directory, file shares, configurations turns a hash mismatch into a narrated incident, which is what responders actually need.

Pros: Change attribution and context; CIS-benchmarked baselines; approachable operations.

Cons: Deepest value when adopting the wider Netwrix suite.

Bottom line: Not just changed changed by whom, with what else.

4. Cimcor (CimTrak) — Best Real-Time + Remediation

Snapshot: Licensed | Real-time detection with rollback | Trusted-file-registry integration

Why it earns 4: CimTrak detects in real time and can act: unauthorized changes rolled back to baseline automatically, with a trusted-file registry suppressing known-good noise.

For teams who want FIM to be a control rather than a camera, remediation is the feature that separates it.

Pros: Automatic rollback; real-time capture; strong noise suppression.

Cons: Smaller vendor ecosystem than the anchors.

Bottom line: FIM that undoes the change, not just reports it.

5. Wazuh — Best Open-Source FIM

Snapshot: Free/open source | Syscheck engine | Real-time + scheduled, SIEM built in

Why it earns 5: Wazuh ships serious FIM real-time monitoring, hash/attribute/registry tracking, who-data via auditd inside a free open-source SIEM platform.

The capability is audit-defensible; the cost is engineering ownership: tuning, scaling, and rule curation are yours.

Pros: $0 license; genuinely deep FIM; integrated detection platform.

Cons: You are the vendor tuning and scale engineering required.

Bottom line: The budget-honest answer for teams with engineers.

6. Rapid7 — Best SIEM-Converged FIM

Snapshot: Subscription | InsightIDR-integrated FIM | Change events in the detection timeline

Why it earns 6: Rapid7 puts file-change telemetry where investigations happen the InsightIDR timeline so a modified binary lands next to the authentication anomaly that preceded it. For Insight-platform shops, that correlation beats a standalone FIM console.

Pros: Detection-timeline integration; platform consolidation.

Cons: FIM depth lighter than specialists; platform-scoped value.

Bottom line: File changes as first-class detection evidence.

7. Trend Micro — Best Workload-Security FIM

Snapshot: Per-workload | FIM inside Cloud One/Deep Security lineage | Server & container focus

Why it earns 7: Trend delivers FIM as one module of its workload-protection stack alongside anti-malware, IPS, and application control on the same agent within its Cloud One/Deep Security lineage, offering a sensible consolidation for hybrid server fleets already standardized on its platform.

Pros: Single-agent workload consolidation; hybrid/cloud server focus.

Cons: FIM is a module, not the product’s center of gravity.

Bottom line: Integrity monitoring bundled where the agent already lives.

8. ManageEngine — Best Value IT-Suite FIM

Snapshot: Published tiers | FIM across ADAudit Plus/EventLog Analyzer/Log360

Why it earns 8: ManageEngine spreads FIM capability across its affordable IT-management suite, including ADAudit Plus/EventLog Analyzer/Log360, giving mid-market teams change monitoring with who-data and compliance reports at published prices pragmatic coverage without enterprise procurement.

Pros: Published pricing; suite synergy; mid-market fit.

Cons: Capability split across products; depth below specialists.

Bottom line: Mid-market FIM without the enterprise invoice.

9. SolarWinds — Best Observability-Adjacent FIM

Snapshot: Licensed | FIM within Security Event Manager | Ops-team ergonomics

Why it earns 9: SolarWinds offers FIM through Security Event Manager with the operational ergonomics its ops-tooling base expects a reasonable fit where the same team runs monitoring and security and wants one vendor relationship.

Pros: Ops-friendly; consolidated tooling.

Cons: Security-depth perception post-2020 still a diligence topic for some buyers; specialist depth below anchors.

Bottom line: The ops-team’s convenient FIM.

10. Trellix — Heritage Endpoint FIM (Status Check)

Snapshot: Quote | McAfee-lineage integrity monitoring/application control

Why it earns 10: Trellix’s McAfee-lineage integrity and application-control lines still serve installed bases; buyers should verify current product status, roadmap, and support commitments before renewal rather than assuming continuity.

Pros: Installed-base continuity; endpoint-suite ties.

Cons: Roadmap diligence required.

Bottom line: A renewal conversation with questions attached.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Baseline Small, Reconcile Everything

Scope beats sprawl: start FIM on the files that decide incidents system binaries, web roots, critical configs, boot paths, payment flows for PCI to maintain cloud and server baseline integrity, not “all servers, all paths,” which guarantees alert bankruptcy by week two.

Make reconciliation the purchase criterion: can the tool suppress changes that match an approved ticket or patch manifest automatically? Run a patch Tuesday through the proof of concept and count the alerts a human must touch; that number is your real operating cost.

Wire survivors into the SIEM with who-data attached, and for PCI DSS 4.x, map each requirement to a named report before signing auditors accept evidence, not features.

FAQs

What is the best file integrity monitoring tool in 2026? Fortra’s Tripwire ranks 1 for change-reconciliation depth, Qualys for scale on its existing cloud agent, and Netwrix for who-did-what context with CimTrak leading rollback and Wazuh the open-source lane.

Is FIM required for PCI DSS? Yes PCI DSS requires change-detection on critical files with weekly comparisons at minimum, and 4.x expectations push toward timely detection and response. Map requirements to specific reports during evaluation.

Why do FIM deployments drown in alerts? Over-broad scope plus no reconciliation. Patching legitimately changes thousands of files; without suppression of authorized change, FIM becomes a log of IT doing its job.

Is open-source FIM audit-defensible? Wazuh’s FIM capability is technically strong and widely accepted when properly configured and evidenced the audit risk is operational discipline, not the license.

FIM vs EDR do I need both? Yes, they answer different questions: EDR watches behavior in flight; FIM proves integrity state and catches quiet persistence (configs, scheduled tasks, web shells) that behavioral engines deprioritize.

Verdict

Tripwire still owns the hard part knowing which changes were supposed to happen while Qualys makes FIM a toggle at scale, CimTrak undoes what shouldn’t have changed, and Wazuh prices the control at engineering effort. Buy for reconciliation, scope ruthlessly, and adopt Zero Trust baseline verification to let patch Tuesday grade every demo.

articles.title: Top 10 Best Data Masking Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
The fastest way to leak production data is to copy it somewhere less defended and most organizations do exactly that every sprint, cloning customer records into test, analytics, and now AI-training environments with a fraction of production’s controls. Data masking closes that gap by making the copies worthless to steal while keeping them useful to […]

The post Top 10 Best Data Masking Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The fastest way to leak production data is to copy it somewhere less defended and most organizations do exactly that every sprint, cloning customer records into test, analytics, and now AI-training environments with a fraction of production’s controls.

Data masking closes that gap by making the copies worthless to steal while keeping them useful to developers.

We scored ten options across masking fidelity, referential integrity, delivery speed, and estate reach.

Delphix (Perforce) takes 1; Informatica and K2view complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Delphix, now under Perforce masking fused with data virtualization, so masked copies arrive in minutes.

• Podium: Delphix (speed + integrity), Informatica (enterprise breadth), K2view (entity-based consistency).

• New 2026 driver: AI training sets masked data is becoming the default feedstock for internal model work.

• Referential integrity is the real test: masks that break cross-table joins get bypassed by developers within a month.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: masking technique depth (static, dynamic, deterministic), referential integrity across heterogeneous sources, delivery speed to downstream environments, format preservation, database/warehouse coverage, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: integrity & fidelity 30%, delivery speed 20%, estate coverage 20%, technique breadth 20%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Data Masking Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Delphix (Perforce) — Best Masking + Delivery

Snapshot: Quote | Masking fused with data virtualization | Now part of Perforce

Why it earns 1: Delphix solved the problem that kills most masking programs delivery. Masked data that takes three weeks to provision gets bypassed; Delphix virtualizes databases so masked, referentially intact copies spin up in minutes, which is why its masking actually gets used.

The Perforce acquisition folds it into a DevOps portfolio; buyers should confirm packaging and roadmap under the new owner.

Pros: Masked-copy delivery speed no rival matches; strong deterministic masking; CI/CD-friendly.

Cons: Perforce-era packaging and pricing need confirmation.

Bottom line: Masking developers don’t route around.

2. Informatica — Best Enterprise Breadth

Snapshot: Quote | Persistent + dynamic masking | Rides the CLAIRE data-management stack

Why it earns 2: Informatica masks wherever its integration fabric already reaches hundreds of sources, static and dynamic techniques, discovery-driven policies making it the natural pick for enterprises standardized on its data-management stack.

Pros: Source coverage breadth; discovery-to-policy integration; enterprise governance ties.

Cons: Heavyweight for masking-only buyers.

Bottom line: The platform estate’s masking arm.

3. K2view — Best Entity-Based Consistency

Snapshot: Quote/tiered | Entity (business-object) architecture | Consistent masks across systems

Why it earns 3: K2view organizes data by business entity one customer, every system so the same person masks identically across CRM, billing, and warehouse copies.

That cross-system determinism is the hardest masking property to achieve and the one test-data teams feel daily.

Pros: Cross-system consistency by design; strong test-data-management lane.

Cons: Entity modeling is an upfront investment.

Bottom line: One person, one mask, every system.

4. IBM (Optim) — Best Legacy-Estate Pedigree

Snapshot: Quote | Decades of TDM heritage | Mainframe-to-distributed reach

Why it earns 4: Optim still masks the estates others can’t reach DB2, IMS, mainframe flat files alongside distributed targets, with archiving and subsetting depth earned over decades.

Where legacy platforms hold the crown jewels, Optim remains the realistic answer.

Pros: Mainframe/legacy coverage; subsetting + archiving in one lineage.

Cons: Modernization pace; interface age.

Bottom line: The legacy estate’s masking workhorse.

5. Immuta — Best Policy-Based Dynamic Masking

Snapshot: Quote/tiered | Attribute-based policies | Warehouse-native enforcement

Why it earns 5: Immuta masks at query time on Snowflake/Databricks-class platforms: policies written once in plain language enforce k-anonymization, hashing, and nulling per user attribute no copies, no pipeline rework.

It’s dynamic masking built for the warehouse era rather than retrofitted onto it.

Pros: Policy-as-code clarity; native warehouse pushdown; no data movement.

Cons: Analytics-platform scoped; not a test-data tool.

Bottom line: Dynamic masking the lakehouse actually enforces.

6. Oracle (Data Masking & Subsetting) — Best Oracle-Native

Snapshot: Licensed pack | Enterprise Manager-integrated | Format-preserving library

Why it earns 6: On Oracle estates the first-party pack masks and subsets with native awareness of Oracle datatypes and relationships the lowest-friction answer where the database vendor is already the platform.

Pros: Native integration; proven format library.

Cons: Oracle-scoped; pack licensing.

Bottom line: Oracle data, Oracle-masked.

7. Microsoft — Best Bundled Dynamic Floor

Snapshot: Bundled | Dynamic Data Masking in SQL/Azure SQL + Purview ties

Why it earns 7: SQL Server and Azure SQL ship dynamic masking as a platform feature presentation-layer protection you can enable this afternoon.

It’s a floor, not a program: DDM doesn’t protect copies or privileged users, so treat it as the start, not the strategy.

Pros: Zero-additional-cost entry; instant enablement.

Cons: Presentation-layer only; copies remain unmasked.

Bottom line: The floor every Microsoft estate should enable.

8. Mentis (Mage) — Best Discovery-to-Mask Specialist

Snapshot: Quote | Discovery, masking, monitoring suite | Operates as Mage Data

Why it earns 8: The Mentis lineage now marketed as Mage Data pairs sensitive-data discovery with static and dynamic masking in one focused suite, a specialist alternative when the anchors feel oversized. Confirm current branding and packaging.

Pros: Discovery-driven masking focus; right-sized suite.

Cons: Smaller ecosystem; brand-transition diligence.

Bottom line: The focused specialist lane.

9. Broadcom (CA Test Data Manager) — Renewal-Lane Veteran

Snapshot: Quote | CA-heritage TDM with masking + synthetic generation

Why it earns 9: CA TDM’s masking and synthetic-data depth still serves large installed bases, but under Broadcom’s portfolio economics we frame it as a renewal-evaluation conversation rather than a new-logo default: existing customers should weigh roadmap commitments against migration cost at renewal.

Pros: Mature TDM + synthetic generation; installed-base continuity.

Cons: New-buyer momentum; Broadcom-era packaging.

Bottom line: Evaluate at renewal; rarely a fresh shortlist pick.

10. DataVeil — Best Free/Low-Cost Entry

Snapshot: Free tier + licenses | Desktop static masking | SQL database targets

Why it earns 10: DataVeil (with its FileMasker sibling) masks SQL databases and files at a price point including free use on smaller databases that lets small teams start masking this week instead of budgeting next year.

Pros: Genuinely accessible entry; straightforward static masking.

Cons: No enterprise orchestration; limited source breadth.

Bottom line: The honest starting point for small estates.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Test the Joins, Then Time the Delivery

Two failure modes kill masking programs, so test for both before buying. First, referential integrity: mask a customer whose ID appears in six tables across two databases and verify every join still works a mask that breaks application behavior gets disabled by the first blocked sprint.

Second, delivery time: measure hours-to-masked-copy in the proof of concept, because a three-week provisioning cycle guarantees developers quietly revert to production clones.

Static masking (Delphix, K2view, Optim-class) protects non-production copies; dynamic masking (Immuta, DDM-class) protects live query paths most regulated estates need both, and they are different purchases.

Enable bundled floors (SQL DDM, Oracle packs) immediately regardless, and if AI training is on the 2026 roadmap, make “masked-data feeds for model training” an explicit evaluation scenario now rather than a retrofit later.

FAQs

What is the best data masking tool in 2026? Delphix (Perforce) ranks 1 for masking fused with fast virtualized delivery, Informatica for enterprise breadth, and K2view for entity-grade cross-system consistency with Immuta leading dynamic warehouse masking and DataVeil the low-cost entry.

Static vs dynamic masking which do I need? Static masking rewrites copies for test/analytics environments; dynamic masking transforms results at query time for live systems. They solve different exposures, and regulated estates typically need both.

Does masking satisfy GDPR and similar laws? Properly irreversible masking can take non-production copies out of much regulatory scope, but reversible or poorly keyed masking doesn’t.

Treat masking policy as a legal-plus-engineering decision and verify technique per regulation.

Why do masking projects fail? Broken referential integrity and slow delivery developers bypass anything that blocks a sprint. Buy for integrity and speed, not technique checklists.

Is synthetic data replacing masking? Complementing it. Synthetic data shines for greenfield test cases and AI experimentation; masked production data still wins where realistic distributions and edge cases matter.

Verdict

Delphix makes masked data fast enough to actually use, Informatica and K2view keep it consistent at enterprise scale, Immuta masks the warehouse era at query time enable your bundled floors today, then buy for referential integrity and delivery speed, the two properties demos conveniently skip.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Privacy stopped being a policy problem and became a data-engineering problem: you cannot fulfill a deletion request against data you cannot find, and in 2026 more US states, deeper AI-governance rules, and shrinking DSAR deadlines punish teams still running privacy on spreadsheets.

OneTrust takes 1 as the category’s operating system; Securiti and BigID complete a podium where privacy and data security have visibly merged.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: OneTrust the broadest privacy operations suite, from assessments to consent at web scale.

• Podium: OneTrust (breadth), Securiti (automation on a data-intelligence core), BigID (discovery-first privacy).

• The merge is real: the strongest 2026 platforms fulfill DSARs from discovered data, not from questionnaires.

• Mid-market lane matters: Osano, Ketch, and DataGrail deliver compliance outcomes without enterprise program overhead.

Research-based evaluation: data discovery depth, DSAR automation (find-to-fulfill, not ticket-routing), consent/preference management, assessment workflows (PIA/DPIA/AI), regulatory coverage breadth, and pricing accessibility.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores are excluded from structured data.

The ecosystem advantage compounds: regulators’ expectations, consultancies’ playbooks, and new-hire familiarity all orbit it.

Pros: Unmatched workflow breadth; template and regulatory-update depth; ecosystem gravity.

Cons: Module pricing adds up; depth can feel heavy for small teams.

Bottom line: The default enterprise privacy operating system.

Snapshot: Quote | Data Command Center | DSARs fulfilled from discovered data

Why it earns 2: Securiti builds privacy on a discovery engine: it maps personal data across cloud and SaaS first, then automates DSARs, consent, and breach-scope analysis against that live map.

That ordering data first, workflow second is why its fulfillment automation goes deeper than questionnaire-driven rivals, and its AI-governance extensions ride the same core.

Pros: Best-in-class correlation; privacy and DSPM from one scan.

Cons: Workflow surface lighter than OneTrust’s.

Why it earns 4: TrustArc pairs platform workflows with the research depth of its Nymity lineage and assurance programs few rivals offer when the deliverable is a defensible, verifiable program rather than just tooling, that pedigree counts.

Pros: Regulatory research depth; assurance/verification options.

Cons: Less data-layer automation than the podium.

Bottom line: The program-assurance veteran.

Why it earns 5: Osano gives lean teams working compliance in days cookie consent, subject-rights intake, and vendor privacy monitoring with published pricing and a no-consultant deployment path that mid-market buyers actually finish.

Pros: Transparent pricing; genuinely fast time-to-compliant.

Cons: Enterprise workflow depth limited.

Bottom line: Compliance outcomes without a privacy department.

6. Ketch — Best Programmatic Consent

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Consent & preference infrastructure | Developer-friendly APIs

Why it earns 6: Ketch treats consent as infrastructure: policies defined once propagate to tags, SDKs, and downstream systems programmatically, which is the right architecture when consent decisions must reach warehouses and ad stacks, not just cookie banners.

Pros: Consent that actually propagates; strong APIs.

Cons: Narrower than full-suite rivals.

Bottom line: Consent plumbing built like engineering, not banners.

7. DataGrail — Best DSAR-Focused Value

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | SaaS-integration catalog | DSAR automation core

Why it earns 7: DataGrail’s deep SaaS connector catalog automates the ugliest DSAR step finding and deleting records across hundreds of third-party apps at a price and complexity point below the enterprise anchors.

Pros: Connector breadth for SaaS estates; focused value.

Cons: Less assessment/RoPA depth.

Bottom line: The SaaS-heavy company’s DSAR engine.

8. Transcend — Best Engineering-Grade Fulfillment

Snapshot: Quote | Data-mapping + erasure infrastructure | API-first

Why it earns 8: Transcend sells privacy as infrastructure engineers respect: discovered data flows, programmatic erasure against internal databases and SaaS alike, and consent enforcement in code the pick when engineering owns privacy delivery.

Pros: Deep technical fulfillment; developer alignment.

Cons: Engineering investment assumed.

Bottom line: Privacy requests as reliable pipelines.

9. Microsoft Priva — Best M365-Bundled Floor

Snapshot: Per-user add-on | Risk management + subject-rights inside M365

Why it earns 9: For estates living in Microsoft 365, Priva finds privacy risks and runs subject-rights requests over Exchange, SharePoint, and OneDrive with Purview-native integration a sensible floor, scoped to the Microsoft estate it serves.

Pros: Native M365 depth; incremental licensing.

Cons: Little reach beyond Microsoft.

Bottom line: The floor you can switch on this quarter.

10. Collibra — Best Governance-Adjacent Entry

Snapshot: Quote | Data-governance catalog with privacy workflows

Why it earns 10: Collibra approaches privacy from the governance catalog: organizations already running it for data stewardship can extend lineage and policy workflows to privacy use cases through Zero Trust data access governance rather than buying a separate suite an adjacency play more than a dedicated privacy platform.

Pros: Leverages existing governance investment.

Cons: Not a dedicated privacy suite; DSAR depth limited.

Bottom line: For Collibra shops extending, not privacy-first buyers.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Fulfill One Real DSAR Before You Sign

Run your actual worst-case request through any finalist’s proof of concept: a former customer who used three email addresses across your CRM, warehouse, and support desk.

Platforms that fulfill from discovered, correlated data (Securiti, BigID, Transcend) will find all three identities; questionnaire-driven workflows will find what someone remembered to register.

If your blocker is program management and assessments, weight OneTrust or TrustArc; if it’s SaaS sprawl, DataGrail’s connectors matter more than suite breadth; if the team is three people, Osano’s published tiers beat any enterprise demo.

And count the 2026 regulatory surface honestly new state laws plus AI-governance obligations because template-update velocity is now a real selection criterion.

FAQs

What is the best data privacy management software in 2026? OneTrust ranks 1 for privacy-operations breadth, Securiti for automation built on data discovery, and BigID for discovery-first fulfillment with Osano and DataGrail leading the mid-market lane and Transcend the engineering-led lane.

What’s the difference between privacy management and DSPM? DSPM secures data against attackers; privacy management operationalizes legal obligations DSARs, consent, assessments. The categories are merging: Securiti and BigID sell both from one discovery engine.

Can DSARs really be automated end-to-end? Increasingly, yes if the platform fulfills from a live data map with identity correlation. Intake-and-ticket tools automate the easy 20%; find-to-fulfill platforms automate the painful 80%.

Is Microsoft Priva enough on its own? For data living in M365, it’s a strong floor. Most organizations also hold personal data in SaaS apps and warehouses Priva doesn’t reach, so it typically complements rather than replaces a platform.

How should consent management be chosen? By where consent must land. If decisions only need to reach a cookie banner, most suites suffice; if they must propagate to warehouses, CDPs, and ad platforms, programmatic infrastructure (Ketch-class) is the differentiator.

Verdict

OneTrust runs the program, Securiti and BigID fulfill from data rather than questionnaires, and the mid-market lane finally has honest options pick by your real blocker (program, discovery, SaaS sprawl, or headcount) and test with your messiest DSAR, not the vendor’s demo record.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Databases hold what attackers came for, and service accounts hold the widest keys database security decides whether either gets noticed.We scored ten options from enterprise DAM anchors to warehouse-era access layers.

Imperva takes 1 for watching-plus-stopping; IBM Guardium and Satori complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Imperva the DAM anchor that blocks policy violations, not just logs them.

• Podium: Imperva (enforcement), Guardium (compliance reference), Satori (warehouse-era access layer).

• Cloud shift: Satori and Cyral govern Snowflake-class platforms agentlessly — classic agents never met these estates.

• Watch the service accounts: widest grants, least rotation, most breaches.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: monitoring depth, blocking capability, estate coverage, warehouse-native support, pricing structure, status currency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: enforcement capability 25%, estate fit 25%, warehouse-era readiness 20%, compliance pedigree 20%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Database Security Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Imperva — Best DAM with Enforcement

Snapshot: Quote | Data Security Fabric | Inline blocking | Thales family

Why it earns 1: Monitoring that can say no policy-violating queries blocked in-line, risk analytics across heterogeneous fleets, and cloud-data reach under the veteran brand.

Pros: Blocking teeth; fleet breadth.

Cons: Thales-era packaging.

Bottom line: The watcher that intervenes.

2. IBM Guardium — Best Compliance Reference

Snapshot: Quote | Agents/taps everywhere | Audit reports regulators know

Why it earns 2: Decades of DAM depth at bank scale when the requirement is provable monitoring with reports auditors recognize on sight, Guardium remains the reference.

Pros: Depth; auditor recognition.

Cons: Deployment weight.

Bottom line: The compliance answer with a paper trail.

3. Immuta — Best Cloud Data Access Governance

Snapshot: Quote | Fine-grained access | Cloud data platforms

Why it earns 3: Centralized policies govern access across cloud warehouses and databases with dynamic masking, attribute-based controls, and native enforcement close to the data, operationalizing principles from the Zero Trust Data Access (ZTDA) framework
alongside leading enterprise data security platforms to protect multi-cloud analytics estates.

Pros: Strong warehouse coverage; policy automation.

Cons: More governance-focused than classic DAM.

Bottom line: Fine-grained data access control for modern cloud estates.

4. Oracle (Audit Vault & DB Firewall) — Best Oracle-Native

Snapshot: Quote | First-party SQL firewall + audit consolidation

Why it earns 4: On its home estate, nothing matches native depth audit consolidation and SQL firewalling with the tightest Oracle integration.

Pros: Native fit.

Cons: Oracle-scoped; licensing complexity.

Bottom line: Oracle estates, first-party guarded.

5. DataSunrise — Best Value Multi-Engine

Snapshot: Published/tiered | Dozens of engines | DAM + masking + firewall

Why it earns 5: Mixed fleets on budgets get monitoring, blocking, and masking across cloud and on-prem engines at value tiers the anchors won’t touch.

Pros: Engine breadth per dollar.

Cons: Enterprise ecosystem.

Bottom line: The heterogeneous fleet’s value answer.

6. Aurva — Best Cloud-Native Database Activity Monitoring

Snapshot: Quote | Agentless + hybrid | Real-time database monitoring

Why it earns 6: Cloud-native monitoring delivers granular visibility into database queries and user activity across modern data stores, establishing database activity monitoring (DAM) as a critical defense layer without forcing a traditional agent-heavy DAM architecture.

Pros: Cloud-native design; broad database coverage; low-overhead monitoring.

Cons: Smaller ecosystem than established DAM leaders.

Bottom line: Modern database activity monitoring built for cloud-native estates.

7. Baffle — Best In-Path Field Protection

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Proxy-delivered | Zero app changes

Why it earns 7: A different answer to the same risk fields tokenized/encrypted in the data path, so even successful access yields protected values.

Pros: No-rewrite protection.

Cons: Not a monitoring suite.

Bottom line: Protect the data, not just watch the door.

8. Tenable Nessus — Best Database Security Assessment

Snapshot: Published tiers | Vulnerability scanning | Compliance auditing

Why it earns 8: Mature vulnerability and configuration assessment identifies database weaknesses, missing patches, and compliance gaps across diverse database environments.

Pros: Assessment depth; broad compliance coverage.

Cons: Not a full database activity monitoring platform.

Bottom line: Find database weaknesses before attackers turn them into access.

9. Microsoft — Best Bundled Floor

Snapshot: Bundled/tiers | Defender for SQL + auditing + Purview ties

Why it earns 9: Azure SQL estates get threat detection, auditing, and classification as platform features the activation-first floor.

Pros: Bundle economics.

Cons: Microsoft-estate scope.

Bottom line: The floor you already license.

10. Trellix — Heritage Line (Status Check)

Snapshot: Quote | McAfee-lineage database security

Why it earns 10: Installed bases persist; roadmap depth warrants pre-renewal verification listed for estate reality.

Pros: Continuity.

Cons: Diligence required.

Bottom line: A renewal conversation, not a shortlist default.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Five Impossible Queries, Then Scale

Enable free native auditing everywhere today, then define five “impossible queries” per crown-jewel database mass exports off-hours, admin reads from app accounts and alert only on those at launch.

Baseline service accounts two weeks before policing them; their legitimate weirdness is pager fatigue otherwise.

Warehouses get access layers (Satori/Cyral), not stretched agents; regulated fleets get the anchors (Imperva/Guardium); and test the blocking path against a synthetic mass-export before trusting it live.

Implementation Notes

Deploy monitoring in audit mode against your five most sensitive databases first and spend two weeks building the baseline before any alerting goes live service-account query patterns are strange everywhere, and policing them unbaselined guarantees pager fatigue.

Define the impossible-query policies with the application teams in the room, because they know which access patterns are legitimate weirdness and which are unthinkable.

Blocking deserves a staged rollout of its own: alert-only, then block-with-override for a sprint, then enforce, with a tested bypass procedure for the 2 a.m. incident where the DAM itself is suspected of breaking production.

For warehouse estates, run the access-layer proof of concept against real workloads, measuring query latency overhead honestly.

And connect database alerts to the SOC with context attached an alert that says which policy, which account, which table saves the twenty minutes that decide whether exfiltration finishes.

FAQs

What is the best database security tool in 2026? Imperva ranks 1 for monitoring with enforcement, Guardium for compliance-reference depth, Satori for warehouse-era access layers with Oracle guarding its own, DataSunrise on value, and Baffle protecting fields in-path.

Do cloud warehouses need classic DAM? They need its outcomes audit, masking, least privilege delivered natively (Satori/Cyral-class). Agents built for on-prem engines never fit these estates.

Monitoring or blocking first? Monitor to learn normal, then block the impossible queries. Enforcement you’ve never test-fired is enforcement you don’t have.

What about protecting the data itself? Pair DAM with in-path protection (Baffle-class) successful access then yields tokens, not treasure.

Which accounts deserve attention first? Service accounts: widest grants, least rotation, present in nearly every database breach. Inventory and time-bound them before perfecting human controls.

Verdict

Imperva watches and stops, Guardium satisfies the strictest auditors, and Satori governs the estates agents never reached floor free with native audit, police the impossible, and make service accounts your first hard problem.

The post SafePay Ransomware Has Affected 600+ Organizations by Exploiting VPNs and Backup Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SafePay ransomware has affected at least 600 separate victims across multiple critical infrastructure sectors, according to a joint government advisory released on October 20, 2026.

Active since August 2024, the group has targeted businesses and essential services across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia, becoming one of the most active ransomware threats in 2026.

The attacks combine stolen passwords, exposed remote access services, and known software flaws. After entering a network, attackers take control of accounts, search for valuable files, steal data, and damage recovery systems before encrypting files.

This sequence puts victims under pressure from both business disruption and the threat of stolen information being published online.

Analysts at CISA and partner agencies noted these SafePay activities in the joint SafePay ransomware advisory, which draws on investigations conducted through August 2026.

Contributors include the FBI, United States Secret Service, German investigators, and UK law enforcement. Their findings describe an operation that relies heavily on trusted accounts and common administration tools.

SafePay Ransomware Has Affected 600+ Organizations

SafePay operators gain access through exposed credentials, repeated password guesses, phishing, and vulnerable internet-facing systems. Earlier reporting on SafePay RDP and VPN attacks also documented the group’s use of compromised remote connections.

The latest advisory adds details about automated exploitation and the abuse of phished account profiles to enter victim networks.

The agencies identified exploitation involving CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269 in edge devices, alongside CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711, and CVE-2024-40766 across internet-exposed systems.

Attackers also connected through Mullvad VPN addresses. That finding describes the service being used during intrusions; it does not mean Mullvad itself was compromised or that its ordinary users are linked to SafePay.

Backup infrastructure is another important target. CVE-2024-40711 affects Veeam Backup & Replication and allows unauthenticated remote code execution.

Previous Veeam ransomware exploitation cases showed attackers combining compromised VPN access with this flaw to create administrator accounts.

Those earlier incidents involved other ransomware families, highlighting a shared weakness rather than proving a direct connection between the groups.

Trusted Tools Help Attackers Spread

Once inside, SafePay operators create accounts or raise the permissions of existing ones. They use PsExec, Windows Remote Management, and Remote Desktop Protocol to run commands and reach other machines.

Since these tools also support normal IT work, defenders need to examine who launched them, where they ran, and whether their use fits approved activity.

The attackers search shared folders for useful files, disable security software, and sometimes change user passwords, locking legitimate staff out. Investigators also observed methods that bypass Windows User Account Control and reuse security tokens to gain higher access.

Code packing helps hide malicious programs, while remote support applications provide another route for moving software onto compromised systems.

For data theft, SafePay uses familiar tools including 7-Zip, WinRAR, RClone, WinSCP, and FileZilla. Some incidents involved OneDrive or Backblaze storage.

These applications are not automatically malicious: the warning signs are their unexpected deployment, unusual data transfers, and connections to accounts outside the organization’s control, particularly when combined with other signs of compromise.

The group’s focus on recovery makes its attacks especially disruptive. Operators stop the Volume Shadow Copy Service and have reset network-attached storage holding backups to factory settings.

Related reporting on SonicWall access control flaws shows why securing remote access matters before attackers can reach internal systems and backup resources.

After stealing data, SafePay encrypts files using ChaCha20 together with RSA. The ransomware can encrypt whole files or selected portions depending on file type and size.

Victims receive a ransom note directing them to a Tor chat portal, while phone calls and threats to publish stolen data add pressure. The malware may delete itself afterward.

CISA and its partners urge organizations to patch exposed systems, require multifactor authentication, and limit administrator rights. Backup copies should remain offline or protected against changes and deletion, with restoration tested regularly.

Separating networks can also restrict the path from a compromised remote access account to servers holding sensitive files and recovery data.

Security teams should review unfamiliar accounts, unexpected remote tools, disabled protections, and unusual outbound transfers together rather than treating each event in isolation.

If an intrusion is suspected, the agencies recommend isolating affected machines, preserving logs, and investigating its scope. They discourage ransom payments because payment does not guarantee file recovery and can support further criminal activity.

The post SBI Confirms Data Breach – 3000+ Customer Records Exposed on Dark Web appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
State Bank of India (SBI) has disclosed a data loss incident after a preliminary review identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information on the dark web. The bank reported the findings in an October 21, 2026, stock exchange filing, while saying investigators still needed to establish the data’s authenticity, completeness, and source.

The disclosure confirms an incident involving data loss, but does not establish how the information was obtained or whether attackers breached SBI’s core banking systems. The bank said its services continued to operate normally, with no material impact on core operations, financial performance, or business continuity.

SBI Confirms Data Breach

SBI said it received alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defense Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In. These communications concerned suspected exposure of customer information on the dark web.

Investigators reviewed approximately 375,000 records and identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information, or PII. The larger dataset should not be described as 375,000 confirmed victims. Record counts can include repeated entries and do not necessarily represent separate people.

The information reportedly included registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, and residential addresses. SBI also listed branch and customer information file identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata linked to loan records, lead records, and related files.

These fields go beyond a contact list. Branch details and loan references could help fraudsters make fake banking calls sound credible. However, the filing does not list passwords, PINs or one-time passwords among the exposed information, and it does not report stolen funds.

Cyber Security News previously covered the SBI data breach claim involving an actor using the name Siriusim. That report described claims involving 375,000 CSV rows and 2,722 PDF files. Those allegations remain separate from the findings SBI has now disclosed, which do not attribute the incident to a named attacker.

SBI quickly activated its procedures to respond to and contain the cyber incident. It also hired an independent cybersecurity agency approved by CERT-In to evaluate the situation and investigate the extent of the suspected breach.

The investigation will examine the data’s authenticity and completeness, identify its potential source, determine the scale of exposure and assess risks to customers and the bank. SBI said remedial and preventive measures were being implemented as required.

The filing does not identify an entry point, exploited vulnerability, malware family or compromised server. It therefore provides no basis for attributing the incident to ransomware, phishing or a specific software flaw.

A separate Bank of Baroda data breach report covered unauthorized access to an employee email account. That case offers banking security context, but does not establish any connection or shared attack method with SBI’s incident.

For customers, targeted phishing is a potential concern rather than a confirmed consequence. CERT-In’s online scam advisory warns that criminals use fake bank messages, urgent account warnings, and requests for personal information to deceive users.

Customers should verify unexpected messages through official banking channels, avoid unfamiliar links and never share PINs or one-time passwords. They should check statements for unauthorized transactions. SBI said it would continue monitoring the situation and take appropriate measures under applicable regulatory requirements. Further findings are needed before the incident’s source and full impact can be established.
