articles.title: Meta Muse AI Privacy Flaw Exposes Confidential Business Data Through Shared Chat Links
articles.description:
Meta has paused Muse AI’s conversation sharing feature after a privacy flaw exposed confidential business records and personal details through discoverable chat links. The problem affected pages users chose to share, not every private Muse conversation. Anyone who found an affected link could open its contents without signing in. The exposure came from how Muse […]

The post Meta Muse AI Privacy Flaw Exposes Confidential Business Data Through Shared Chat Links appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Meta has paused Muse AI’s conversation sharing feature after a privacy flaw exposed confidential business records and personal details through discoverable chat links.

The problem affected pages users chose to share, not every private Muse conversation. Anyone who found an affected link could open its contents without signing in.

The exposure came from how Muse built shared page addresses. Conversation titles and random identifiers appeared in hostnames recorded by passive DNS services, which store observed domain lookups. Those records offered a way to find shared pages without receiving a link from the owner.

Researchers from Claroc identified the issue, naming the exposed pages GhostShares. Their report describes a sharing design weakness, not malware or a confirmed attack.

They reported it to Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8, 2026, after checking pages on October 7 and 8.

Meta Muse AI Privacy Flaw Exposes Confidential Business Data

Muse placed shared content under cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Each share’s hostname combined a readable conversation title with a random ID.

Although that ID made guessing difficult, passive DNS could preserve the complete hostname, including the supposedly secret portion, when participating services observed a lookup.

Researchers could then use those records to rebuild working links. No password guessing, stolen account, or security bypass was needed.

Unlike earlier ChatGPT shared conversation exposure involving search engines, this discovery relied on DNS history rather than indexed search results, making crawler restrictions beside the point.

Muse’s robots.txt asked search and AI crawlers to avoid share paths. That did not restrict who could open a page or prevent DNS records from being stored. Claroc also found more than 75 saved scans of Muse share pages on urlscan.io, showing another discovery route.

After removing unrelated wildcard DNS scan noise, Claroc counted more than 6,800 share hostnames. Researchers opened only a few hundred pages, so that figure does not mean 6,800 sensitive conversations were confirmed.

Most inspected pages were ordinary content; a minority contained sensitive records. Examples included a marketing company’s revenue review marked for its CEO, a small business loan application, and a property investor’s financial report.

Other pages held a bank fraud alert with partial account details and a staff vacation calendar. Earlier Grok shared chat exposure similarly showed how public sharing can widen access beyond intended recipients.

One page contained confidential preparation for an executive search call with a frontier AI laboratory, including an internal contact and meeting time. Such details could support impersonation or targeted fraud.

Claroc found no evidence of misuse and withheld affected names, hostnames, titles, figures, and links. Claroc noted that Muse initially returned little beyond the share title, with JavaScript loading the conversation afterward.

A basic page fetch could therefore miss content that appeared in a normal browser. Researchers used ordinary browser sessions without accounts and stopped when one page requested a password.

They did not contact the affected people or businesses, so they could not confirm whether those users intended their documents to be widely accessible online.

Meta Pauses Sharing as Risks Remain

On October 20, Meta said it had paused the feature while reviewing the findings and considering changes to link discovery.

Claroc rechecked 40 previously accessible shares that day; none opened, and their content hostnames returned errors. Historical DNS records still retained hostnames and titles.

This distinction matters: blocking page access does not erase information already stored elsewhere. Reports of indexed Claude shared chats underline the broader risk of treating public links as private collaboration tools.

However, Claroc’s limited sample cannot establish Muse’s total exposure, how long each page remained available, or whether others accessed it.

Organizations should review employee use of Muse, check whether business conversations were shared, and explain that public links are not restricted to named recipients.

Claroc recommends monitoring share creation as an outbound data transfer and, where adequate controls are unavailable, blocking muse.ai and metaaiusercontent.com through managed proxy or DNS filters.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI has expanded its ChatGPT Chrome extension so the assistant can read information across open tabs and carry out browser tasks.

The update moves ChatGPT beyond answering questions about a single page, adding tools for comparing content, filling forms, sending messages, and organizing tabs.

The announcement appeared on October 16 in India. OpenAI says the extension is available across all ChatGPT plans, bringing browser access to users without requiring a separate paid tier for the extension itself.

ChatGPT’s Chrome extension adds Chat and Work modes, letting users analyze open tabs, gather information, control tabs, download files, and group pages.

OpenAI’s examples include comparing three couches by size, material, delivery time, and return policy. Users can also ask for a plain language explanation of an article or compare pricing pages. These tasks reduce the need to copy information between websites and a chat window.

ChatGPT Chrome Extension Analyzes Open Tabs

The extension also brings ChatGPT into a browser tab, with access to conversation history while users browse alongside it. According to the Chrome Web Store listing, it connects browser tasks with ChatGPT on desktop and the web, including connected local files where available.

OpenAI says tasks can run in the background without taking over the active browsing session. Supported uses include research on signed-in websites, document editing, spreadsheet work, data entry, website testing, and bulk file downloads. The listing also names compatibility with Microsoft Edge, Brave, and Opera.

The main security issue is access. An assistant working inside signed-in websites may encounter private messages, business records, or other sensitive material. That makes the scope of each task important, particularly when browser activity involves company accounts or customer information.

The store’s privacy disclosure lists website content, browsing history, user activity, personal communications, authentication information, health information, and financial information among the data categories handled. These disclosures describe data handling categories, not proof that every category is collected during every task.

OpenAI states that ChatGPT will request permission before referencing browsing history or uploading and downloading files. However, the listing does not establish that every browser action receives a separate approval prompt.

Users should avoid treating those specific permission promises as a guarantee covering all activity. Reading web content also creates a route for prompt injection. This happens when a page contains instructions designed to steer an AI assistant away from the user’s request.

Cybersecurity News previously covered OpenAI’s work to strengthen ChatGPT Atlas against prompt injection. That coverage concerns Atlas, not a confirmed flaw in this Chrome extension.

Installation sources deserve equal attention. Earlier reporting on malicious Chrome extensions stealing ChatGPT conversations showed how fake AI tools can turn browser access into data theft. Users should follow OpenAI’s official download link and verify the publisher rather than trust a familiar name or logo alone.

For workplace use, keep requests narrow, limit signed-in access, and review confirmation prompts carefully. These controls help reduce exposure when an assistant can both read pages and act on their contents.

The post WordPress Backup Plugin Developer Hacked to Inject Malicious Code on Installed Sites appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
TeamUpdraft, the developer behind the UpdraftPlus WordPress backup plugin, has disclosed a website breach that exposed remote management keys. Attackers used those keys to install malicious plugins on connected WordPress sites, turning a trusted management feature into a route for running harmful code.

The company identified unauthorized access to teamupdraft.com during October 17–18, 2026. Attackers likely accessed its customer database, including names, email addresses, billing details, order histories, password hashes, two-factor authentication settings, and connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone.

Attackers Installed Malicious WordPress Plugins

UpdraftCentral lets administrators manage WordPress sites from one dashboard. Connected sites trust commands signed with the dashboard’s private key and run them with the permissions of the WordPress user who created the connection.

Nethemba researchers documented attackers sending the plugin.upload_plugin command with valid keys. Where the linked user could install and activate plugins, WordPress accepted the request and loaded malicious PHP code. On one investigated site, the attempt failed because the linked user lacked those permissions.

This was not a bypass of the earlier CVE-2026-10795 security fix. Nethemba’s affected sites already ran UpdraftPlus 2.26.11. The stolen keys allowed requests to pass normal checks without exploiting that earlier flaw.

Researchers found backdoors disguised as maintenance tools. Working variants could log attackers into existing administrator accounts or create new ones. Some hid from the plugin list, while broken versions caused PHP errors and website outages. A normal administrator list therefore does not rule out compromise.

Both free and Premium UpdraftPlus users may be exposed if their sites held affected cloud UpdraftCentral connection keys. Installing UpdraftPlus alone does not create that connection. However, connecting a TeamUpdraft account can present a checked option to add the site to UpdraftCentral, making forgotten connections worth reviewing.

TeamUpdraft says the plugin itself and its download packages were not altered. This differs from the GravityForms supply chain attack, where malicious code reached users through compromised downloads. Earlier UpdraftPlus backup exposure also involved a separate plugin flaw, not stolen cloud management keys.

The vendor says self-hosted UpdraftCentral and backups stored in customers’ own Google Drive, Dropbox, or Amazon S3 were not affected by its website breach. Sites accessed through UpdraftCentral should still renew storage access as a precaution.

TeamUpdraft says it has closed the access route, signed out customer accounts, rotated service credentials, and reported the breach to authorities. It does not store payment card details, with payments handled through Stripe and PayPal.

Administrators should update to UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 Free or 2.26.13 Premium, or later. The official changelog confirms these releases correct the key removal introduced in 1.26.12. Nethemba also reports a cutoff mismatch that can leave some exposed keys present, so manual checks remain important.

Log into each WordPress dashboard directly and open Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral. Delete old connection keys, inspect plugin files and server logs, and review unfamiliar users. Updating or deleting keys cannot remove backdoors already installed.

TeamUpdraft account holders should change their passwords, replace reused passwords elsewhere, and reset two-factor authentication. Administrators should also change site administrator passwords. If suspicious activity appears, TeamUpdraft advises considering a restore from a backup taken before October 17. Reconnect cloud services only after completing the checks and securing the site.

Updates are scheduled for Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC, giving website owners and hosting providers a short window to prepare. In its official […]

The post PHP Warns of Two Critical 9.2 Security Vulnerabilities, Urges Users to Prepare for Patches appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The PHP security team has warned users about two critical vulnerabilities and urged administrators to prepare for an upcoming security release. Both flaws carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Updates are scheduled for Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC, giving website owners and hosting providers a short window to prepare.

In its official security notice, published on October 20, PHP said it would publish full technical details, affected versions, and fixed releases alongside the patches. The team may release updates earlier if either vulnerability becomes public or evidence of active attacks appears.

Public reporting links the upcoming fixes to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Security firm watchTowr describes them as reported remote code execution vulnerabilities, which could allow attackers to run their own code on affected servers. However, PHP’s advance notice does not name the CVEs or explain how the flaws work.

CERT-EU’s advisory also references both identifiers and warns of possible remote code execution without authentication. Its assessment draws partly on leaked information. Administrators should therefore separate these reports from the narrower facts confirmed directly by PHP.

Reports suggest the vulnerabilities could affect PHP versions from PHP 5 onward. The vendor has not confirmed that broad claim. PHP has not yet established whether default installations are vulnerable, which settings are required, or whether particular operating systems face greater risk.

Some early posts described the issues as having a maximum severity score of 10.0. PHP’s published rating is 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 for each vulnerability. The official score should guide reporting until further details explain the underlying risk and attack conditions.

PHP to Issue Emergency Patch

At the time of its published update, watchTowr reported no known exploitation in the wild. PHP’s warning about a possible early release is a precaution, not confirmation that attacks have occurred. Claims involving leaked demonstrations or exploit code should not be treated as proof of attacks against real targets.

Previous incidents show why administrators should prepare quickly. Cybersecurity News documented active exploitation of CVE-2024-4577, a separate PHP flaw, with exploit attempts detected within 24 hours of disclosure. That history provides context for urgent patch planning but does not establish exploitation of these new vulnerabilities.

The publication also covered PHP SOAP extension vulnerabilities earlier in 2026. Those issues involved different components and fixes. Administrators should not assume that installing patches for earlier PHP flaws will address the two vulnerabilities covered by this upcoming release.

CERT-EU recommends identifying PHP applications now and preparing to patch affected systems as soon as fixed versions become available. Where immediate patching is not possible, organizations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix can be applied. Any isolation decision should account for service availability and business needs.

Teams should use the preparation window to confirm who manages each PHP installation and how updates will reach production systems. Once the release arrives, administrators should check the official affected-version list, apply the relevant fixes promptly, and verify the running PHP version afterward. Until then, no deployment should be declared safe solely because its configuration differs from claims circulating online.

articles.title: eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise Triggers Emergency Action Across Browsers
articles.description:
The private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates have been compromised, prompting emergency blocks across major browsers and software platforms. The affected certificates chain to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome, placing clients that still accept them at risk of trusting forged certificates. However, the public disclosures reviewed do not establish […]

The post eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise Triggers Emergency Action Across Browsers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The private keys behind eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority certificates have been compromised, prompting emergency blocks across major browsers and software platforms. The affected certificates chain to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome, placing clients that still accept them at risk of trusting forged certificates.

However, the public disclosures reviewed do not establish that these keys can be cracked in seconds. They confirm that a researcher demonstrated control of the keys, not how they were obtained or how quickly any cryptographic attack could recover them.

A researcher identified as Wayne reported the compromise to root program teams on October 17, 2026. To demonstrate access, Wayne signed the message “We have a problem here – Wayne” using each affected intermediate CA private key.

The disclosure site, published by Dennis Jackson, provides certificates, public keys, and signatures for independent checks. Researchers can use OpenSSL to extract a certificate’s public key and verify the corresponding signature. This proves signing capability without requiring publication of the private keys themselves.

An intermediate certificate authority helps connect a website’s certificate to a trusted root. If its signing key is exposed, an attacker may create certificates that vulnerable clients accept as genuine. Mozilla warned that someone able to intercept a connection could use fraudulent certificates to impersonate websites and potentially read or change traffic.

The risk echoes earlier reporting on unauthorized HTTPS certificates obtained through compromised domain registries and misissued TLS certificates affecting the 1.1.1.1 DNS service. Those cases involved different failures, but show why certificate trust is a security concern beyond the browser padlock.

Browsers Block Certificates as Software Updates

Mozilla received the report at 20:06 UTC on October 17 and completed its OneCRL blocklist rollout by 22:59 UTC. Standard Firefox configurations received protection without requiring a browser update or restart, according to Mozilla’s incident statement.

The disclosure site says Chrome also blocked the affected certificates on October 17. Apple followed on October 19, while Microsoft’s protection arrived on October 20. eMudhra has also revoked the compromised intermediate certificates.

Revocation alone does not protect every application. Some clients do not receive browser blocklists or check whether a certificate has been revoked. These programs need separate updates to stop accepting the affected certificate chains.

Mozilla released Firefox 158.0.1, ESR 115.43.1 and ESR 153.5.1 to cover users whose settings could prevent OneCRL delivery. Its NSS 3.131.1 update also removes the signing root from the trusted certificate list used by other applications.

The incident response page lists fixes including Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10, Python certifi 2026.10.19, and Rust webpki-roots 1.0.10. Node.js and Composer ca-bundle updates were listed as pending when the page was reviewed.

Users should update browsers and operating systems promptly. Developers should also check certificate bundles shipped with applications rather than assume an operating system update covers every runtime.

Administrators can use the disclosure site’s test endpoints and certificate chains to assess remaining exposure. A certificate rejection indicates that the tested client refuses the affected chain. Manual root removal should remain an expert measure because it can disrupt legitimate connections.

The verified finding is a serious signing key compromise. The available evidence does not establish a seconds-long cracking method or confirm attacks against users. How the keys became exposed remains publicly unconfirmed.

A Google Cloud outage disrupted UK banks, business websites and court video links on Tuesday, October 20, after a power event hit its London infrastructure. Google later said most affected services had recovered, although a small number of customers still faced problems. The incident began around 07:08 BST in europe-west2, Google’s London cloud region. Google […]

The post Google Cloud Outage Knocks UK Banks, Websites and Court Systems Offline appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Google Cloud outage disrupted UK banks, business websites and court video links on Tuesday, October 20, after a power event hit its London infrastructure. Google later said most affected services had recovered, although a small number of customers still faced problems.

The incident began around 07:08 BST in europe-west2, Google’s London cloud region. Google identified a power event in the europe-west2-b zone and reported higher error rates and network failures across multiple services. Its public dashboard listed the incident as active during the afternoon.

Google Cloud Outage

Affected products included Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Filestore. These services help businesses run applications, manage containers and store files. A failure across these layers can stop websites and apps even when their own software has not changed.

Google said the power event had been mitigated and engineers were prioritizing existing workloads. During recovery, customers could still face problems creating new workloads. Google did not immediately explain what caused the power event or provide a technical account.

Revolut reported disruption across several services, including card payments and ATM withdrawals. The bank said customers’ money and data remained safe. Halifax and HSBC also acknowledged service problems, while Lloyds said its apps and online logins were working but some online features were affected.

Not every reported problem was independently linked to Google Cloud. Lloyds did not initially confirm a direct connection, and reports on outage tracking websites alone cannot establish the cause of a service failure.

HM Courts and Tribunals Service confirmed problems with its Cloud Video Platform, used for remote hearings. The Criminal Bar Association said the platform had been down across large parts of England and Wales since 10:00 BST, preventing some trials and hearings from proceeding.

Some patients also lost access to appointment booking through the NHS app. According to BBC reporting, the problem involved a third-party appointment service used by some healthcare providers, rather than the entire app. That issue was resolved around midday.

DPD said its website connection issues had been resolved. Google’s afternoon update said the outage had been mitigated for most customers, while engineers continued working on remaining cases. The company promised an incident analysis after its investigation.

The disruption follows earlier incidents covered by CybersecurityNews, including Google’s API management outage and the major AWS outage. Those events had different causes but showed how shared infrastructure can spread disruption across unrelated businesses.

For affected organizations, the question is whether backup arrangements can keep essential services running when a cloud location fails. Google’s findings should clarify what went wrong and the steps needed to reduce the risk of another widespread outage.

articles.title: FBI Suspects Cybersecurity Executive Helped ShinyHunters Run Extortion Website
articles.description:
Federal investigators suspect an executive at a United States consulting firm helped ShinyHunters operate a website used to pressure hacked companies into paying ransom demands. The allegation raises questions about whether trusted ransomware advisers crossed from helping victims into supporting the criminals demanding payment for stolen data. The suspected website operator has not been publicly […]

The post FBI Suspects Cybersecurity Executive Helped ShinyHunters Run Extortion Website appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Federal investigators suspect an executive at a United States consulting firm helped ShinyHunters operate a website used to pressure hacked companies into paying ransom demands.

The allegation raises questions about whether trusted ransomware advisers crossed from helping victims into supporting the criminals demanding payment for stolen data.

The suspected website operator has not been publicly named or charged. Separately, the FBI arrested Edward Dubrovsky, a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive, on October 8 in Pennsylvania. Reporting does not establish that Dubrovsky operated the website, and allegations against him remain unproven as the federal investigation continues into his conduct.

The website, shinywire[.]com, reportedly operated from approximately May 3 through October 16, 2026. It listed nearly 100 organizations targeted by ShinyHunters. Each listing encouraged the victim to contact the group, discuss payment terms, and avoid the release of stolen information, according to sources familiar with the continuing federal investigation.

Shinywire Turned Stolen Files Into Payment Pressure

Victim pages displayed samples of stolen files to support the demands. Organizations that did not engage within seven days reportedly faced publication of their data on a separate ShinyHunters leak site accessible through Tor. This setup used public exposure and deadlines to push companies toward negotiations with the hacking group.

KrebsOnSecurity cited two sources who said investigators believe an executive at a large American consulting firm actively helped run Shinywire. The publication withheld the executive’s identity and the company’s name because no charges had been filed. It described the firm as having more than 1,000 associates across its consulting business.

Dubrovsky’s arrest forms another part of the investigation. As covered in Cybersecurity News’ earlier report, he faces allegations involving a conspiracy to threaten the release of confidential information for money and interference with commerce through threats. The sealed complaint limits public scrutiny of the conduct prosecutors attribute to the Canadian executive.

The public court docket records his arrest and subsequent commitment to the Eastern District of Texas. It also shows that federal defenders were appointed and detention was ordered pending a hearing in the charging district. Those procedural records do not establish guilt or reveal the full evidence behind the allegations against him.

Investigators reportedly gained leads after Dutch police arrested ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap in September. Sources told KrebsOnSecurity that officers accessed recent Signal conversations while he was logged in. Those messages allegedly revealed frequent contact with Dubrovsky and an executive at the unnamed American firm now under scrutiny.

According to the reporting, some exchanges suggested the executives knew details about new ShinyHunters victims before those organizations discovered their breaches. Another allegation is that Dubrovsky knew sensitive FBI information had been stolen before the group publicly threatened its release. These claims come from sources, not publicly tested court evidence.

The investigation gained urgency after ShinyHunters targeted the FBI’s recruitment website in September. Reportedly stolen records included Social Security numbers, home addresses, medical information, and details about employee assignments. The sensitivity of those files increased the stakes beyond a standard corporate breach and placed additional pressure on investigators pursuing suspects.

ShinyHunters commonly steals credentials through phishing and uses compromised accounts to take data from cloud services. It then threatens publication unless victims pay. This is extortion based on stolen information, which does not require encrypting a victim’s computers. According to KrebsOnSecurity, the FBI attributes more than $70 million in 2026 payments to the group.

The case also highlights the risks of trusting promises to delete stolen records. In the PowerSchool breach and extortion case, a payment of approximately $2.85 million did not prevent later demands targeting affected school districts. Subsequent attempts used information from the same breach, showing how stolen records can remain a continuing source of pressure.

KrebsOnSecurity also reported concerns about negotiators whose fees rise with the final ransom payment. CyberAcuView chief executive Mark Camillo said that arrangement creates conflicting interests because the adviser benefits from a larger payment. He called for greater transparency around fees, cryptocurrency costs, and the financial interests involved in settling demands.

The FBI’s May 15 ShinyHunters advisory warned that attackers may combine stolen information with threatening messages, calls, and harassment. It advised people contacted directly not to pay or respond to demands. The bureau also urged victims to preserve communications and report suspected activity through IC3 or an FBI field office.

For now, the website allegation remains a reported investigative finding involving an unnamed executive, while Dubrovsky faces separate criminal proceedings. Neither should be presented as a conviction. Public filings and further evidence will be needed to establish who supported ShinyHunters, what they did, and whether their actions broke the law.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Open Banking Services to Test Stolen Credentials Without Paying a Cent
articles.description:
Criminals have found a way to use open banking as a low-cost checking service for stolen bank and card details. In a campaign described by Group-IB, fraudsters abused a spend-management platform’s account-linking process to check whether credentials worked and whether linked accounts held funds. The platform did not lose money through stolen funds, but it […]

The post Hackers Exploit Open Banking Services to Test Stolen Credentials Without Paying a Cent appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Criminals have found a way to use open banking as a low-cost checking service for stolen bank and card details. In a campaign described by Group-IB, fraudsters abused a spend-management platform’s account-linking process to check whether credentials worked and whether linked accounts held funds.

The platform did not lose money through stolen funds, but it unknowingly paid for the checks through its open-banking provider. The scheme also used the platform’s email and payment notices to send phishing messages.

These claimed that a sale through the online marketplace Poshmark was waiting for verification and urged recipients to follow a link. Poshmark was impersonated and was not involved in the activity; Group-IB also said its systems had not been compromised.

Analysts from Group-IB identified the activity while investigating abuse of a client’s fraud-protection environment.

They assessed it as consistent with Classiscam, a scam-as-a-service operation, and described two linked uses of the platform: sending phishing messages and testing stolen credentials.

This was a fraud campaign—not a report of malware infecting the platform. Group-IB’s findings are detailed in its report on the checker scheme.

Hackers Exploit Open Banking Services

Rather than send every message directly, the criminals used the platform’s own notification system. They added recipients to accounts and triggered messages that appeared to be genuine payment alerts.

The emails borrowed the credibility of a real business service, while the message pretended that a Poshmark sale could not be completed until the recipient verified an account.

The link led to a fake page designed to collect personal and payment details. Group-IB says the form could request names, card details, phone numbers, email addresses, billing addresses, one-time passcodes and card balances.

Some versions also sought payment-wallet or online-banking details. A countdown added pressure by suggesting that the recipient had little time to claim the money.

This use of trusted service messages echoes other cases where criminals abuse real platform notifications to deliver phishing content.

Account linking served as a credential checker

The second part of the scheme took place when an account tried to connect a bank account or card. Some spend-management services let users link a bank through an open-banking aggregator.

With the user’s permission, this login-based process can return account details such as a balance and transaction history. That can help a legitimate user manage spending, but it can also confirm to a criminal that stolen credentials are valid and the account is active.

The key detail is who pays. Group-IB says the platform may be billed by its aggregator for successful links, while the fraudster uses the result without paying that fee.

The criminal gets a useful signal; the platform absorbs the service cost. In its estimate, a successful verification may cost about USD 0.30 to USD 1.00.

For one million billable links a year, if 0.5% to 1% were checker activity, the illustrative annual cost would be about USD 2,500 to USD 5,000, using USD 0.50 per link.

Group-IB observed the phishing and checking activity happening in parallel. That meant one-time codes stolen from victims could be used quickly during an account-link attempt.

The same devices were linked to accounts sending phishing messages and accounts testing cards. On 27 April, device identity [496-] was associated with two accounts of each type; on 28 April, identity [524-] was associated with six of each. These links helped investigators connect activity that might otherwise look like separate incidents.

Many fraud teams look for losses on their own company’s records: unauthorised purchases, false reimbursements or account takeovers. Here, the platform was being used as infrastructure rather than directly robbed. The victims could be marketplace sellers or cardholders who were not even customers of the platform, and the cost could appear on an aggregator invoice rather than as a clear fraud loss.

The observed activity also included disposable email addresses and a mix of hosting services, VPNs, data-centre networks, proxies and residential IP addresses. Group-IB found that accounts created from different device identities could share device and location fingerprints.

This helps explain why blocking a single IP address, or relying only on simple rate limits, may not be enough. Criminals also use automated Classiscam phishing sites to create convincing pages that collect financial information.

Group-IB recommends watching for suspicious activity at three points: account creation, the first outbound messages and the first bank or card link.

Signals may include disposable email use, repeated device or location fingerprints, rapid messages to unfamiliar recipients and account links soon after sign-up.

Reviewing these events together can help teams spot connected behaviour rather than treating each action as an isolated case.

Platforms can also set limits or extra checks for new or low-trust accounts, scan links before messages go out and review unusual spikes in account-linking volume. Finance teams can compare aggregator invoices and link counts against normal customer demand.

Group-IB reports that after its team became involved, a client reduced the time to block fraudulent accounts from several hours to under a minute, and stopped more than 230 accounts in May 2026.

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

articles.title: WP2Shell Attack Lets Hackers Create WordPress Admin Accounts and Install Web Shells Without Login
articles.description:
WP2Shell combines two WordPress Core flaws to move from an unauthenticated request to server-side code execution. It can let an attacker create an administrator account and install a plugin-based web shell. Seqrite’s October 16 analysis lists affected releases, but does not establish widespread live exploitation. The report says the flaws were disclosed in July 2026. […]

The post WP2Shell Attack Lets Hackers Create WordPress Admin Accounts and Install Web Shells Without Login appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
WP2Shell combines two WordPress Core flaws to move from an unauthenticated request to server-side code execution. It can let an attacker create an administrator account and install a plugin-based web shell.

Seqrite’s October 16 analysis lists affected releases, but does not establish widespread live exploitation. The report says the flaws were disclosed in July 2026.

The chain matters because it removes the login step. A public site running an affected release may be exposed before an owner sees a suspicious account or plugin.

Analysts at Seqrite identified and documented WP2Shell, combining CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 into a route from a public REST API request to code execution.

Their technical breakdown of WP2Shell explains the sequence and host artifacts. CVE-2026-63030 affects the REST API batch controller at /wp-json/batch/v1, which processes several API requests in one submission.

Seqrite says nested requests can confuse route handling and reach functionality that should require authentication. This flaw alone does not execute code; it provides a path to the second weakness.

CVE-2026-60137 is an SQL injection flaw in the posts endpoint. The public author_exclude parameter maps to author__not_in in WP_Query.

WP2Shell Attack

According to Seqrite, poorly handled input can affect the database query. Chained with the route flaw, it lets an unauthenticated request reach the vulnerable query. The proof of concept then establishes an administrator-level foothold and remote code execution.

In simple terms, SQL injection lets input affect a database query in an unintended way. Here, the first flaw helps an unauthenticated request reach that vulnerable query; the second supplies the database weakness.

The chain’s impact comes from how the two issues work together, not from either flaw being described as a direct web shell by itself. Once code runs on the server, an attacker may have a way to make further changes beyond the WordPress dashboard.

The demonstrated steps matter to defenders. The chain can create an unexpected administrator account, stage a ZIP archive in uploads, unpack PHP files, and move a plugin directory into wp-content/plugins.

The plugin acts as a web shell, an interface for running server commands. Cybersecurity News has covered a separate WordPress account creation vulnerability and recent Comment2Shell vulnerability coverage, where different flaws also lead to account or shell risks.

Seqrite describes temporary write checks under wp-content, followed by archive staging in wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ and extraction under wp-content/upgrade/.

Sample archive

The sample archive is wp2shell_4e9b3641.zip; extracted files and plugin folders use a wp2shell_<hex> pattern. The report says httpd.exe may perform file writes, as it can during normal plugin operations.

That process name alone is not proof of compromise. More useful signs are the WP2Shell filenames, new PHP files, and unexpected administrators. A WordPress poisoned plugin supply-chain incident also involved a web shell, but used a different delivery method.

The report lists WordPress 6.9.0–6.9.4 and 7.0.0–7.0.1 as vulnerable to the full chain. Versions 6.8.0–6.8.5 are affected by CVE-2026-60137.

It lists 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed. Upgrade to the appropriate fixed release or a later supported version, and verify the update completed.

Restricting unauthenticated access to sensitive REST API features may reduce exposure where practical, but does not replace patching.

After updating, review accounts for unfamiliar administrators, inspect plugin and cache folders for new or changed PHP files, and check logs for suspicious batch-endpoint requests.

Look for temp-write-test-* files, wp2shell_*.zip archives, and wp2shell_<hex> plugin folders. If found, preserve evidence, disable suspicious plugins, reset affected credentials, and investigate persistence. A patched version number alone does not prove an earlier compromise has been removed.

articles.title: Hackers Use Generative AI to Build Custom Malware and Bypass Traditional Security Detection
articles.description:
Hackers are using generative AI to build custom malware, rewrite harmful scripts, and make phishing messages harder to spot. The shift puts pressure on security tools that mainly depend on known file signatures, while helping ransomware operators move faster from their first foothold to data theft and encryption. The danger is not that every AI-generated […]

The post Hackers Use Generative AI to Build Custom Malware and Bypass Traditional Security Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using generative AI to build custom malware, rewrite harmful scripts, and make phishing messages harder to spot.

The shift puts pressure on security tools that mainly depend on known file signatures, while helping ransomware operators move faster from their first foothold to data theft and encryption.

The danger is not that every AI-generated program escapes detection. Instead, attackers can produce unfamiliar code more quickly, reducing the value of rules built around older samples.

At the same time, better language support helps their fake emails and websites blend into normal business activity, making familiar warning signs less dependable.

Researchers from Zscaler noted these changes in an analysis of AI-enabled ransomware published on October 16, 2026. Written by principal information security researcher Phil Hagen, the report describes how attackers use AI across social engineering, data discovery, and malware development.

It examines broader methods rather than identifying a newly named malware family or a single confirmed campaign.

Hackers Use Generative AI

Traditional security products often compare files and network traffic against known patterns. These signatures remain useful for spotting familiar threats, but their limits become clearer when attackers keep changing the code that produces the same harmful result.

Zscaler says generative AI makes those changes faster and easier to produce. Attackers can also build their own tools instead of relying on widely used programs that defenders already track.

Related reporting on AI agents automating cyberattacks describes how code generation and repeated rebuilding can shorten attack workflows. For defenders, unfamiliar tooling means fewer dependable matches against previously collected samples.

This also complicates efforts to identify who carried out an attack. Custom malware once suggested access to skilled developers or substantial funding.

Zscaler warns that readily available language models now give smaller ransomware groups similar development options, making unique tools a weaker clue when assessing an attacker’s resources or identity.

The distinction between AI-assisted development and malware that uses AI while running matters. Zscaler describes rapid script creation and revision, not proof that every payload independently rewrites itself.

Coverage of malware that rewrites itself explores that separate development, where changing code can further weaken checks based on fixed file patterns.

Better Phishing and Faster Data Theft

The attack often begins before any custom malware runs. Generative AI can help criminals write clear emails, create convincing websites, and communicate naturally in a target’s language.

This reduces obvious spelling and grammar mistakes that many employees have been trained to treat as signs of phishing. Zscaler also describes phishing messages that persuade users to run remote monitoring and management software.

These tools have legitimate business uses, but attackers can abuse the access they provide to control a victim’s computer and potentially reach other systems. The initial trick can therefore open a path beyond one device.

Web content creates another challenge. Research covered in GenAI-generated malicious web pages shows how code created after a page loads can change what users encounter.

That browser-based technique is separate from Zscaler’s analysis, but it illustrates why reviewing only a page’s initial content may miss harmful behavior that appears later.

Once inside a network, attackers can use AI to search and classify large amounts of accessible information. Zscaler says this helps them locate valuable material for theft or encryption faster than traditional scripts and playbooks.

Finding sensitive data sooner can increase pressure on victims facing ransom demands or threatened public disclosure.

The central issue is a shorter response window. Faster discovery and custom script development leave defenders less time to connect suspicious activity before files are stolen or encrypted.

Detection therefore needs to consider what a program does, not simply whether its file matches a known malicious sample. Zscaler points to AI-based detection, combined security data, and faster investigation as defensive measures.

Its report describes controls aimed at phishing sites, attacker command infrastructure, suspicious browser content, and ransomware response. These are vendor-described capabilities, not evidence that one product can stop every AI-assisted attack.

articles.title: Thousands of Android Phones Ship With Hidden Malware That Disables Google Play Protections
articles.description:
Thousands of Android phones across more than 150 countries have been found running malware planted in their firmware before purchase. The campaign, called Midnight Mimosa, targets low-cost devices and gives attackers system access without requiring owners to download a harmful app or click a suspicious link. The malware can secretly install and remove apps, load […]

The post Thousands of Android Phones Ship With Hidden Malware That Disables Google Play Protections appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Thousands of Android phones across more than 150 countries have been found running malware planted in their firmware before purchase.

The campaign, called Midnight Mimosa, targets low-cost devices and gives attackers system access without requiring owners to download a harmful app or click a suspicious link.

The malware can secretly install and remove apps, load new code, and generate fake advertising activity. Before installing extra payloads, it temporarily disables the Google Play Store package, then restores it.

Researchers assess this behavior as an attempt to avoid Google Play Protect detection, rather than proof that every protection remains permanently disabled.

Researchers from PolySwarm noted the malware’s firmware-level access in their Midnight Mimosa research report, published October 19.

Their analysis draws on Bitdefender’s investigation, which observed thousands of infected devices over roughly two years.

Mexico, France, and Italy had the highest observed counts, followed by the United States, Germany, Brazil, and Spain. Those figures describe observed infections, not confirmed targeting.

Thousands of Android Phones Ship With Hidden Malware

The infection starts with a malicious system application signed with an Android platform certificate. This trusted position lets it install packages, remove applications, grant permissions, and change protected settings.

Earlier cases of preinstalled Android phone malware show why checking downloaded apps alone cannot address threats already embedded in a device’s software.

The component hides its main functions inside a native library. When loaded, that library uses RC4 encryption to unpack a concealed Java framework.

The framework then contacts command-and-control servers, receives settings, and downloads DEX or JAR plugins. These are Android code modules that let operators change the malware’s behavior without replacing the original system application.

Different plugins handle advertising fraud and silent app installation. Some generate fake ad views, clicks, and conversion events through hidden windows and automated actions.

The activity appears to come from ordinary tools, including weather apps, app lockers, text scanners, and file managers. Bitdefender identified at least 32 disguised applications within the wider payload network.

How the Malware Evades Checks

Temporarily disabling the Play Store creates a window for installing additional software while attempting to avoid detection. Some malicious apps also falsely list Google Play as their installer, despite lacking the signature block applied through Play distribution.

That mismatch can help investigators distinguish a claimed installation source from evidence of how an app actually arrived.

The technique adds detail to earlier Midnight Mimosa firmware findings, which described how the hidden component survives while visible payloads change.

Separately, researchers found 13 related ad-fraud apps distributed through Google Play. These shared malware markers and infrastructure, but did not have the same privileged access as the firmware-installed component.

The enabler also includes functions linked to Accessibility, Notification Access, and SMS permissions, including ways to enable sensitive access automatically.

Researchers did not observe these permissions being used for theft. However, the ability to fetch new code means the campaign’s future behavior cannot be judged only from the advertising modules already examined.

Another payload contains proxy software capable of registering a device and opening two-way TCP tunnels. This could allow outside traffic to pass through an infected phone’s internet connection.

The distinction matters: researchers confirmed the underlying capability, but did not observe actual traffic relaying during their documented test. An initially reported control endpoint was also later identified as a sinkhole.

The wider risk resembles the abuse described in reporting on malicious residential proxy networks, where compromised consumer devices provide network access for other users.

That comparison does not establish a link between operations. For Midnight Mimosa, proxy functionality could expose homes or workplaces to traffic they did not authorize.

Affected devices included inexpensive MediaTek-based phones, counterfeit flagship models, and devices reporting identifiers associated with Doogee and Cubot products.

Some firmware certificates carried identifiers associated with Shenzhen Zediel. Researchers could not determine where the malware entered the supply chain or establish that the certificate owner knowingly participated.

Connections to Joker, Phantom, and Click malware likewise do not prove a shared operator. Removing a visible app may leave the firmware enabler able to install replacements. Cleanup therefore requires attention to the underlying firmware, not just individual payloads.

Google explains that its app safety checks examine applications during installation and scan devices periodically, but this case shows why trusted system components also need scrutiny.

The source lists these 40 sample hashes. Each is reproduced as published; the report does not map individual hashes to specific packages.

The post Hackers Hijack 790 GitHub Repositories to Steal Cloud Credentials and AI API Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A campaign called GhostAction has placed malicious GitHub Actions workflows in 790 repositories, putting cloud credentials, software-publishing tokens, and AI service keys at risk.

The total is OpenSourceMalware’s count of publicly recoverable, validated repositories through October 9, 2026; it is not a claim that every repository leaked credentials or suffered confirmed misuse.

The campaign abuses trusted developer accounts. Once an attacker can write to a maintainer’s repositories, they can add a workflow that runs when code is pushed or when someone starts it manually.

This can expose secrets available to the workflow, turning a stolen account into a route toward cloud systems, package registries, and other projects.

Researchers from OpenSourceMalware identified this latest stage while investigating a malicious PyPI package called claudecord and helping its maintainer respond. They found the malicious workflow and traced related activity across hundreds of repositories.

Hackers Hijack 790 GitHub Repositories

The newer workflow does more than read selected GitHub Actions secrets. It searches files in the repository for strings that resemble credentials, including AWS access keys and tokens for GitHub, GitLab, Google, Slack, SendGrid, OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter.

It also scans reachable Git history, where a key removed from the current version of a file may still appear in an older commit.

To obtain that history, the workflow uses fetch-depth: 0. It then looks for credential-like patterns and, in some cases, gathers nearby lines around AWS key IDs.

Those lines may contain useful context, such as a matching secret key or details about an account or service. The same collection steps can therefore expose more than a standalone key string.

The workflow sends the collected data to attacker-controlled infrastructure over plain HTTP. Because the transfer occurs from a CI runner, it can resemble routine build activity unless defenders inspect workflow changes and outbound network traffic.

For background on a previous GhostAction wave, see Cyber Security News’ GhostAction supply chain campaign report. The number reflects a campaign that has grown over time.

GitGuardian reported 772 affected repositories between August 31 and September 30, 2026. OpenSourceMalware’s later review recovered 790 through October 9, including repositories that may not remain publicly visible.

In a separate October 8 burst, Socket and StepSecurity reported activity across 346 repositories tied to two compromised accounts. These figures cover different periods and evidence sets, so they should not be added together.

That burst included repositories owned by the kitao and henrywoo accounts, as well as Uber’s uber/athenadriver. The activity reached active projects, forks, and repositories that had been dormant for years, suggesting automated discovery of repositories the compromised accounts could change.

The report says some workflows ran successfully, but it had not found malicious PyPI or crates.io releases linked to this latest burst as of October 9.

Why removing the workflow is not enough

A successful workflow run may expose credentials even if the file is later deleted. Removing it does not revoke a stolen GitHub token, invalidate cloud or publishing keys, or remove credentials from old commits.

Teams should preserve relevant workflow files, run logs, commits, and audit records, then revoke the account credentials that enabled the changes and rotate every secret the workflow could access. They should also check package releases, deployments, and cloud activity from the affected period.

For related context, Cyber Security News has covered GitHub Actions PyPI token theft and the financial risk of stolen AI service keys.

GitHub’s secure use guidance for Actions recommends least-privilege access, review of workflow code, and rotation of exposed secrets. Requiring approval for sensitive workflow changes and limiting runner network access can add further checks.

OpenSourceMalware also identified my-github[.]com, which resolves to the campaign’s current collection IP, as a high-priority indicator. The report says the domain is suspicious, but does not prove that the GhostAction operator registered it.

A similarly named GitLab domain is listed only as a watch item, not confirmed campaign infrastructure. Defenders should preserve that distinction when creating alerts.

articles.title: Revolut Outage Disrupts Payments and Banking Services as Google Cloud Reports London Issues
articles.description:
Revolut suffered a major service outage on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, disrupting payments, cash withdrawals, and access to its banking app. The digital bank said customer money and data remained safe while engineers worked to restore affected services. The disruption came as Google Cloud reported problems in its London region. Reuters reported that a person […]

The post Revolut Outage Disrupts Payments and Banking Services as Google Cloud Reports London Issues appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Revolut suffered a major service outage on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, disrupting payments, cash withdrawals, and access to its banking app. The digital bank said customer money and data remained safe while engineers worked to restore affected services. The disruption came as Google Cloud reported problems in its London region.

Reuters reported that a person familiar with the matter linked Revolut’s outage to the Google Cloud disruption. Google said its engineering team was investigating an issue affecting europe-west2, its London cloud region. The reports did not establish the technical cause or provide a confirmed recovery time.

Banking Services Face Widespread Disruption

The outage affected everyday banking tasks rather than a single app feature. Revolut’s status page listed 28 services as partially unavailable, including account sign-ins, card payments, transfers, currency exchange, stock trading and live support chat. Reuters also reported disruption to ATM withdrawals.

For customers, that meant problems could extend beyond opening the app. An affected card payment could interrupt a purchase, while unavailable transfers or cash withdrawals could limit access to funds. Disruption to support chat also affected a channel customers would normally use to ask about payment failures or account access.

“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” Revolut said. The company added that it had been working to fix the issue since identifying it that morning and apologized to affected customers.

The reported connection to Google Cloud places the focus on service availability and cloud dependencies. However, neither the Reuters report nor Revolut’s quoted statement identified malware, ransomware or an intrusion as the cause. The available evidence supports reporting this as an outage, not a confirmed cyberattack or data breach.

A banking service can become unavailable without customer records being stolen. Revolut’s statement addresses the safety of funds and data, while the service reports describe problems accessing banking functions. These are separate questions, and an investigation would need to establish what failed before assigning a more specific cause.

Previous incidents show why the underlying failure matters. Cybersecurity News covered a Google Cloud outage linked to its API management system in June 2025. That incident involved a software failure affecting request processing across services. There is no evidence in the reports reviewed that Tuesday’s disruption shares that cause.

The publication also reported Google Cloud’s accidental deletion of UniSuper’s private cloud account in 2024. Recovery involved rebuilding services and using backups held with another provider. That case offers a separate example of how cloud failures can disrupt financial services, rather than evidence explaining the current Revolut incident.

At the stage described in the cited reports, Google was investigating, and Revolut was working to restore service. Neither report supplied a complete technical explanation or a confirmed time for full recovery. Any later update should distinguish restored functions from services that remain partly unavailable.

For security and operations teams, the immediate issue is understanding the scope of the disruption without confusing downtime with compromise. The unanswered questions include which cloud component failed, how that failure affected Revolut’s services, and whether recovery measures restored all affected functions for affected customers. Those details will determine what lessons can reasonably be drawn from this incident.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

The exposed files showed a wider operation involving cryptocurrency theft tools, Linux attacks, and mobile security testing beyond the banking campaign. Public reporting cited in the investigation said the breaches […]

The post Hackers Target South Korean Banks With AI, Then Accidentally Expose Their Own Attack Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers linked to AI-assisted attacks on South Korean banks left parts of their own infrastructure open, giving researchers a view of their tools and preparations.

The exposed files showed a wider operation involving cryptocurrency theft tools, Linux attacks, and mobile security testing beyond the banking campaign.

Public reporting cited in the investigation said the breaches exposed personal information belonging to at least 68,000 people across at least seven financial institutions.

Different organizations lost different types of data, including customer records and an outsourced developer’s personal details, rather than suffering one identical breach.

Researchers from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified the attack tools while investigating infrastructure linked to the actor, tracked as TAG-217.

Their October 16 research report traced preparations back to August 2026. It described scripts and capabilities, not a newly named malware family, and showed how basic security mistakes exposed the operator’s work.

Hackers Target South Korean Banks With AI

The campaign involved ARTEX, a Chinese-language, open-source framework for penetration testing. Such tools help authorized security teams find weaknesses, but attackers can use them against targets without permission.

Earlier reporting on the AI-assisted bank breach campaign described exposed Claude Code sessions, ARTEX settings, and AI memory files that helped reveal the operator’s workflow.

Public analysis dated October 7 linked the activity to Claude Code, DeepSeek, Grok, and Zhipu AI. Investigators suspected a Chinese-speaking operator, but language clues do not establish nationality or government backing.

Recorded Future assessed that the broader activity likely reflected attempts to make money across several possible targets. The incidents also drew attention to systems outside core banking services.

Reporting on the South Korean security investigation described breaches affecting loan-agent and employee-support systems, showing why security reviews must cover connected business applications as well as customer banking platforms. These supporting services can still hold valuable personal and credit information.

Exposed Files Reveal Earlier Preparations

Open directories and other exposed evidence allowed Insikt Group to reconstruct activity from August 17–22. During that period, TAG-217 tested infrastructure for maintaining remote access and scanned internet-facing systems.

Logs showed repeated connections between the actor’s own servers, but did not establish successful access to victims. By August 22, the operator had assembled tools targeting cryptocurrency mining operations using YiiMP.

Their functions included trying default passwords, stealing wallet configuration and key files, keeping remote access, and sending Telegram alerts when credentials were captured. Other tools targeted known Linux weaknesses to gain higher access or extract protected password data.

By September 5, the workspace included experiments involving iPhone weaknesses and changes to Android system software. Again, the available logs showed testing, not confirmed mobile compromises.

By September 26, records covered target research, traffic routing, payload delivery, and checks involving payment processes, revealing a broader toolkit than the banking attacks alone suggested.

TAG-217 also routed traffic through residential internet connections, likely to hide its source. As reporting on residential proxy network abuse explains, these services make traffic appear to come from ordinary household connections.

The operator also maintained links between servers and copied AI working-memory files across its infrastructure.

The exposed material demonstrates AI use, but it does not measure how much AI accelerated the attacks or prove that an autonomous agent completed every intrusion.

Recorded Future emphasized this limit: the evidence shows the range of environments explored, rather than a confirmed success against every target represented in the toolkit.

For defenders, the lesson is practical. Review internet-facing employee and partner applications, fix exposed weaknesses, and check that users can retrieve only authorized records.

Monitor unusual sign-ins, repeated customer-record requests, unexpected remote access, and abnormal data transfers. Response automation should use clear approval limits, especially when blocking shared proxy addresses could affect legitimate customers.

Announced on October 16, 2026, the service is designed to help security teams find weaknesses in their own networks by running multiple automated tests within a defined, authorized scope. ThreatBook says the agents can work in […]

The post ThreatBook Launches RedAgents AI Platform That Uses Multiple Hacking Agents to Find Security Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
ThreatBook has launched RedAgents, a cloud platform that brings several AI-powered penetration-testing agents together to assess an organization’s systems.

Announced on October 16, 2026, the service is designed to help security teams find weaknesses in their own networks by running multiple automated tests within a defined, authorized scope.

ThreatBook says the agents can work in parallel and show their findings and test logs in one place. The platform takes a different approach from relying on a single testing tool or provider.

Each agent may look for different issues, so combining their results could give defenders a broader view of their exposure.

The launch announcement describes RedAgents as a software-as-a-service platform for security operations teams, rather than a new malware family or a report on a specific intrusion.

ThreatBook’s announcement also notes that the service brings together agents with different origins and capabilities. Those named at launch are Artex Pro, Cyber(YanJi), Yanxun and CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition.

The company says teams can choose one agent or run several against the same approved target, then review results through a shared interface.

ThreatBook Launches RedAgents AI Platform

RedAgents acts as an aggregator: it connects multiple AI penetration-testing agents through one platform and can run them in parallel. A penetration test is an authorized review in which testers look for weaknesses in systems before malicious actors can exploit them.

Running agents side by side may help uncover issues that a single tool misses, though the value of the results depends on how accurately the agents test and report.

ThreatBook says the platform consolidates findings, test data and logs in a unified view. This could reduce the need for teams to move information between separate tools.

The approach is similar to using multiple scanners or testing teams, but RedAgents is designed to coordinate AI agents as part of one assessment.

For readers comparing different designs, Cybersecurity News has covered a multi-agent pentesting toolkit that assigns different testing tasks to specialist agents.

The four named agents have distinct backgrounds. ThreatBook describes Artex Pro as the enterprise version of Artex, an autonomous penetration-testing agent. Cyber(YanJi) is a Python-based agent that searches for a route from a starting point to a defined goal.

Yanxun is described as a system that coordinates specialist agents, while CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition is based on an AI-native testing tool that ThreatBook acquired in September 2026.

These descriptions come from the company’s announcement and should be read as vendor claims, not as independent comparative test results.

ThreatBook reports, for example, that Yanxun can coordinate several dozen agents and that Cyber(YanJi) solved 54 of 54 challenge problems during a validation event.

The release does not provide a controlled, side-by-side benchmark showing how all four agents perform against the same targets.

Scope and data controls

Automated testing tools can cause disruption if they probe systems without permission or exceed an agreed scope. ThreatBook says RedAgents lets customers define an allowlist of approved targets and that agents must operate within those authorized limits.

Organizations should still confirm the scope, timing, rate limits and test conditions before running any penetration test, especially on systems that support business operations.

The company also says customer test data stays within the ThreatBook environment and is not sent to third-party agents. RedAgents supports Zero Data Retention, or ZDR, which ThreatBook says enables complete deletion of test data.

Security teams should confirm how these controls work in practice, including retention periods, access permissions, logging and any contractual terms, before submitting sensitive environment details.

The launch comes as more security products use AI agents to automate parts of testing. Other examples covered by Cybersecurity News include PentestCode’s AI testing agent and Xalgorix’s verification-focused platform.

These products differ in how they are deployed and how they handle findings, so teams should compare scope controls, evidence quality and data handling rather than treating “AI pentesting” as one uniform category.

The main promise of RedAgents is breadth: multiple agents may explore a target in different ways and give teams a combined view of possible weaknesses.

That does not guarantee that every result is valid or that every vulnerability will be found. Security staff still need to review evidence, reproduce important findings safely and prioritize fixes based on business impact and exposure.

ThreatBook says the platform can reduce false positives by combining agent results, but the announcement does not publish independent accuracy figures or a false-positive rate.

It also does not identify a specific customer deployment, measured security outcome or external validation of the service. Those details will matter to organizations assessing whether the platform fits their testing process.

For context, a separate Cybersecurity News report describes Apex’s black-box testing approach, which evaluates applications without source-code access.

RedAgents’ stated distinction is not a single testing method but a central platform for selecting and coordinating several agents. ThreatBook says it plans to add more open-source agents over time, alongside the enterprise tools available at launch.

The company’s announcement and RedAgents product blog provide further product details. RedAgents is available through the company’s website, where ThreatBook says organizations can request a trial.

The post U.S. Government Bans DeepSeek AI and Orders Federal Agencies to Remove All Related Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop buying DeepSeek products and remove related technology from their IT systems. The action covers products from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., its affiliates, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.

The notice was filed for public inspection on October 19, 2026, with publication scheduled for October 20. It creates a government supply chain restriction, not a nationwide ban on private use. Businesses and individuals are not prohibited from using DeepSeek by this order.

U.S. Government Bans DeepSeek AI

The DHS notice sets out two requirements. Federal civilian agencies must exclude DeepSeek and affiliate IT products and services from procurement. They must also remove DeepSeek and affiliate products, including covered third-party implementations, from agency technology systems. That second requirement makes the order broader than a block on new purchases.

The third-party provision is especially important for security teams. An agency may use DeepSeek through another supplier rather than through an application carrying the DeepSeek name. A review limited to branded chat tools could therefore miss products covered by the removal requirement. Agencies need to establish what powers their existing AI services.

The notice does not provide a public list of every affected third-party vendor or product. Suppliers and agency buyers will need to assess whether particular tools use DeepSeek implementations, rather than assuming that a different product name places them outside the order. Contract records and technical documentation can help support that review.

For vendors serving civilian agencies, the order also raises a direct procurement question. They must understand whether their own AI features depend on technology that government customers must now exclude or remove.

DHS cites the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, along with its implementing rules, as the legal basis. The department says the secretary acted after reviewing a recommendation from the Federal Acquisition Security Council and supporting evidence. The notice identifies affiliates through the definition in federal acquisition regulations at 48 CFR 2.101.

The action treats AI as a supply chain issue. For agencies, the question is no longer only whether a chatbot gives accurate answers or whether staff should upload sensitive files. They must also know which companies and underlying technologies support the software they buy, deploy, and connect to government systems.

A key distinction is that this is an exclusion and removal order, not a public report confirming a federal data breach. The published notice does not describe a specific intrusion, identify stolen government records, or establish that every DeepSeek deployment has leaked information. Those claims should not be inferred from the restriction alone.

Separate reporting has shown how attackers can misuse AI models. Cyber Security News previously covered hackers exploiting DeepSeek and Qwen models to develop malware, including efforts to bypass model safeguards. That reporting provides context about AI abuse, but it does not establish the evidence behind this DHS decision.

More recently, Cyber Security News reported on attackers using Codex and DeepSeek AI agents in a campaign against PaperCut servers. The report described AI-assisted exploit work and follow-up activity against vulnerable systems. Such cases show why model misuse attracts attention, while remaining separate from the government’s supplier exclusion process.

A practical response starts with an inventory of AI tools and their dependencies. Security and procurement teams should examine installed applications, hosted services, internal development projects, and supplier agreements for DeepSeek use. These are review priorities based on the order’s scope, not additional requirements quoted from the public notice.

Removing a visible application may not address a service that still routes requests to a DeepSeek model. Teams should check backend model settings and ask vendors to document the models used in their products. Where a covered service supports an important workflow, replacement planning should account for access controls, stored data, and service continuity.

Agencies should also keep a clear record of what they found, which suppliers they contacted, and which products they removed or replaced. That documentation can help distinguish a completed review from an assumption that no DeepSeek technology exists because employees do not use its public chatbot.

The DHS notice directs readers to the signed order in docket DHS-2026-0628 on Regulations.gov and lists CISA’s FASCSA Order Implementation Team as the contact. Agencies should consult that signed text for detailed implementation terms. The central security challenge is identifying covered technology across the full software supply chain, including products sold under another company’s name.
