articles.title: Hackers Exploit Palo Alto VPN Flaw to Bypass MFA and Steal Credentials From VMware Disks
articles.description:
Ransomware operators are exploiting a Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect VPN flaw to bypass multi-factor authentication and enter corporate networks. In one investigated case, attackers reached VMware management systems and stole credentials directly from a domain controller’s virtual disk, avoiding security tools running inside the virtual machine. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 detailed the activity in […]

The post Hackers Exploit Palo Alto VPN Flaw to Bypass MFA and Steal Credentials From VMware Disks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ransomware operators are exploiting a Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect VPN flaw to bypass multi-factor authentication and enter corporate networks. In one investigated case, attackers reached VMware management systems and stole credentials directly from a domain controller’s virtual disk, avoiding security tools running inside the virtual machine.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 detailed the activity in an October 19 threat brief update. Researchers linked exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 to Spikey Scorpius, also known as Qilin, and Tarnished Scorpius, also known as Inc. Separate public reporting connected exploitation to operators using Settra ransomware.

Investigations ongoing since early June have covered healthcare, education, financial services, manufacturing, government, energy, and other sectors. The latest findings show how unauthorized VPN access can develop into credential theft, data theft, and ransomware deployment.

GlobalProtect Flaw Bypasses MFA

The vulnerability affects GlobalProtect portals and gateways in certain PAN-OS and Prisma Access deployments. Exposure requires authentication override cookies to be enabled alongside a vulnerable certificate setup. Palo Alto Networks rates the flaw High, with a CVSS score of 7.8 and its highest suggested response urgency. Panorama and Cloud NGFW are not affected.

Authentication override cookies let previously authenticated users reconnect without repeating the full login process. According to Rapid7’s technical analysis, vulnerable devices decrypt these cookies but do not properly verify that a trusted system created them.

If the cookie certificate is reused for a publicly exposed service, attackers can obtain its public key and forge a cookie. The gateway may accept that cookie as proof of authentication, allowing a VPN connection without the normal login and MFA checks. Cybersecurity News previously covered this GlobalProtect authentication bypass.

After establishing access, attackers use remote monitoring and management tools to explore internal networks. They move between systems through Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block, then prepare tools for credential harvesting, data theft, and ransomware deployment.

The most notable case involved a move from the compromised VPN gateway to VMware’s vCenter management appliance. Attackers then disabled the execInstalledOnly security control on ESXi hosts and used a custom tool to extract credentials offline from a domain controller’s VMDK virtual disk. Unit 42 did not name the tool or provide its implementation details.

Reading credentials directly from the disk bypasses endpoint detection and response controls inside the affected virtual machine. The approach targets the infrastructure beneath the operating system rather than relying on a credential-stealing program running within it. Cybersecurity News has also reported on VMware attacks involving detached domain controller disks.

Unit 42 also observed attackers combining this initial access with tools targeting Veeam backup infrastructure through CVE-2023-27532. That separate flaw can expose encrypted credentials stored in the backup configuration database, potentially opening access to backup hosts.

Defenders should examine GlobalProtect logs for successful gateway-connected events linked to suspicious sources and client details. Reported indicators include 104.207.144[.]154, 146.19.216[.]125, device names GP-CLIENT and DESKTOP-GP01, and host IDs aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and 00:11:22:33:44:55. Earlier monitoring found that many probes did not establish full VPN sessions, making connection events important for investigation.

Organizations should follow the Palo Alto Networks advisory and upgrade every affected portal and gateway. Temporary mitigations include disabling authentication override or generating a new certificate dedicated exclusively to override cookies.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack OVHcloud GitHub Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware
articles.description:
Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases. The October 19, 2026, supply chain attack targeted users downloading the OVHcloud CLI, with malware designed to collect secrets stored on their computers. A customer spotted suspicious release changes and alerted the […]

The post Hackers Hijack OVHcloud GitHub Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases.

The October 19, 2026, supply chain attack targeted users downloading the OVHcloud CLI, with malware designed to collect secrets stored on their computers. A customer spotted suspicious release changes and alerted the cloud provider, which blocked the malicious files within 94 minutes.

OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba said the affected releases were v0.11.0, v0.12.0, v0.13.0, v0.14.0, and v0.15.0. He identified v0.10.0 as clean and announced a safe v0.16.0 release. That replacement is now available on the project’s official GitHub releases page, where it is marked as immutable, meaning its published release files cannot be changed.

OVHcloud Supply Chain Attack

According to Klaba’s account, the compromised files appeared at 14:47 and were detected and blocked at 16:21. OVHcloud’s initial checks found no other affected repository. Those findings limit the confirmed scope to the CLI project, rather than establishing a wider breach across the company’s GitHub organization or cloud platform.

The attacker used an existing developer account to add a malicious binary to the software distributed through GitHub. This placed the threat inside a trusted download location, giving users little reason to suspect that a routine CLI download could expose local credentials. OVHcloud has not explained how the developer account was first compromised.

The customer’s report raised concerns about release files being replaced with a “dirty build” of a later commit. In software builds, that label generally signals changes beyond the recorded source revision. The public issue listing identifies the report as issue #300, covering replaced assets for v0.13.0 through v0.15.0. OVHcloud’s warning named two additional affected versions.

The customer also questioned the account behind the changes and asked whether release files should be locked against replacement. They said they had switched to building through the Go module proxy while seeking clarification. Their report was public because the repository lacked a private vulnerability reporting channel.

Klaba described the added program as a binary whose job was to retrieve secrets from disk. He said its quality was poor but warned that it could still achieve its purpose. The available disclosure does not establish which files it searched, where collected data was sent, or how many users executed the malicious downloads.

The CLI’s normal role makes this threat especially serious. OVHcloud documents the tool as a way to manage cloud services, account resources, and automated workflows. Its supported authentication methods include a local .ovh.conf file containing credentials, alongside environment variables for application keys, application secrets, and consumer keys.

Those documented credential locations explain why a compromised administration tool can create risks beyond the downloaded program itself. However, they are not a confirmed list of this malware’s targets. Until OVHcloud publishes its technical findings, specific claims about stolen SSH keys, browser passwords, persistence, or attacker infrastructure would go beyond the evidence.

The incident fits the broader pattern covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s reporting on trusted software updates used to steal developer and cloud credentials. Attackers can use stolen publishing access to turn familiar software delivery channels into routes for credential theft, without needing users to visit a fake website.

OVHcloud urged users who downloaded the CLI during the incident to update it immediately or delete it. Klaba also advised affected users to change all secrets stored on disk. Rotation is important because replacing the malicious program does not cancel credentials that may already have been copied.

Organizations investigating possible exposure should identify which machines downloaded and ran affected files, preserve available evidence, and review account activity tied to potentially exposed credentials. Their response should extend beyond OVHcloud credentials if other secrets were accessible on those machines. The company’s warning covers local secrets broadly, not only its own service keys.

A related GhostAction GitHub credential theft campaign shows why repository access deserves close attention. That campaign used stolen accounts to introduce malicious workflows under trusted identities. No evidence currently links it to the OVHcloud incident. For OVHcloud users, the immediate priorities remain replacing affected downloads and renewing potentially exposed secrets while the company continues its malware investigation and publishes further technical findings.

The post Hackers Hijack OVHcloud GitHub Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates for Just 5 Minutes to Secretly Install Backdoors
articles.description:
A short-lived change to AOMEI’s software update system gave hackers a way to deliver malware through a trusted route. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant found that attackers repeatedly altered AOMEI’s update settings for only a few minutes at a time between April and July 2026. Any AOMEI Backupper computer checking for updates during […]

The post Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates for Just 5 Minutes to Secretly Install Backdoors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A short-lived change to AOMEI’s software update system gave hackers a way to deliver malware through a trusted route.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant found that attackers repeatedly altered AOMEI’s update settings for only a few minutes at a time between April and July 2026.

Any AOMEI Backupper computer checking for updates during an active window could receive a malicious download instead of a genuine update.

The operation did not rely on a software flaw or require users to open a suspicious file. Instead, the attackers changed two configuration files on AOMEI’s servers, redirecting downloads and using the program’s notification feature to run the malware.

Affected organizations were reported across several sectors and countries, including India, though the full number of impacted systems is not known.

Google Cloud’s GTIG and Mandiant analysts tracked the malware chain as CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD and attributed the activity to a threat group they call UNC7017.

The initial activity was first detected through telemetry shared by ManageEngine’s Threat Analysis Lab, which observed suspicious behavior in late May. AOMEI told Google that it had taken corrective action to secure its distribution servers.

Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates

AOMEI’s update process uses down_html.ini to provide a package version, checksum and download location. A separate file, Notifycfg.ini, guides its notification service, including which local programs to run.

During observed tampering periods, attackers changed both files so the software would accept and launch a harmful ZIP archive.

Researchers recorded three specific windows: ten minutes on May 28, six minutes on July 16 and five minutes on July 20. The attackers restored the original settings after each window.

That made ordinary checks of the live update server less useful: an investigation carried out later could see only the clean files.

The method differs from incidents involving altered software releases or build systems; a Notepad++ update breach is another example of attackers targeting the route that delivers trusted software.

The brief windows did not make the malware itself temporary. A computer that received the altered instructions could continue running malicious files after AOMEI’s servers were repaired.

In July, the attackers also directed one download through a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, after earlier use of Alibaba Cloud storage and domains designed to look connected to AOMEI. This changing delivery setup could make simple domain-blocking rules less reliable.

How the malware chain worked

The first-stage program, CROSSROAD, arrived as upgrade-now.exe. It checked aspects of the computer and could download additional files, create a scheduled task and then delete its own copy.

The task launched a legitimate Radmin program every three hours. However, the Radmin process was placed alongside an attacker-created DLL named BlkScrDl.dll, which it loaded during startup.

That DLL helped start SHINYROAD, a backdoor that could communicate with the attackers’ systems. Later activity also involved ADAPTAGENT, a client for the Adaptix command-and-control framework, disguised as Nitro PDF software.

The use of real administration software and familiar product names can make a malicious process harder to distinguish from normal activity.

Other recent incidents, such as the DAEMON Tools malware supply-chain case, show how attackers can abuse trusted software channels to reach users.

On July 20, attackers added a second risk. They used an invisible, one-pixel notification window to make an AOMEI client request a remote file over WebDAV.

That request could prompt Windows to send NetNTLMv2 authentication data to an attacker-controlled server without a visible prompt. This technique is known as credential coercion: the victim’s computer is induced to attempt authentication to a remote location.

AOMEI’s server-side fix does not remove files already installed on affected computers. Organizations using AOMEI software should review endpoint and network records covering the campaign period, paying particular attention to unusual updater child processes, unexpected Radmin or Nitro-related scheduled tasks, and connections to the indicators below.

Analysts should also examine cached AOMEI configuration files and relevant proxy or firewall logs, since the live server may now return legitimate settings.

The incident also highlights a design issue for software vendors: HTTPS and a checksum supplied in an unsigned configuration file are not enough to prove an update is genuine.

Google recommends signed configuration files, cryptographic verification of downloaded files, and strict limits on which domains an updater may contact. Separating promotional pop-ups from update execution can also reduce the risk of one feature being misused to launch code.

The case echoes other short-lived supply-chain incidents, including a LiteLLM package compromise in which malicious releases were available for a limited period.

In both situations, a brief exposure window can still leave behind a longer incident-response task: find affected systems, assess what ran, and investigate whether credentials or other access were exposed.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

Malicious file hashes

Other file and configuration hashes

Network and host indicators

articles.title: Hackers Compromise Rank Math PRO WordPress Plugin to Install Self-Rebuilding Backdoors
articles.description:
Hackers planted malware in copies of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin, exposing websites to hidden backdoors that can rebuild themselves after removal. Rank Math confirmed that some version 3.0.123 packages distributed during a limited October download window contained malicious code that could compromise websites when activated. The company removed the affected files and released […]

The post Hackers Compromise Rank Math PRO WordPress Plugin to Install Self-Rebuilding Backdoors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers planted malware in copies of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin, exposing websites to hidden backdoors that can rebuild themselves after removal. Rank Math confirmed that some version 3.0.123 packages distributed during a limited October download window contained malicious code that could compromise websites when activated. The company removed the affected files and released clean version 3.0.124.

The affected window ran from October 15, 2026, at 20:02 UTC to October 16 at 07:12 UTC. Rank Math described the impact as limited but did not provide an affected website count in its security advisory. The free Rank Math SEO plugin available through WordPress.org is not affected, and its users need no action for this incident.

Website owners who installed and activated an affected package must treat their sites as compromised. Installing the clean release alone does not complete recovery because malicious files, database entries, accounts, or server changes may remain. Users who installed the package without activating it should delete it, install the clean version, and run a precautionary scan. Downloading it without installation or activation does not establish compromise.

Rank Math PRO Backdoor Survives Removal

Rank Math warns that the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits an infected website. Deleting a suspicious PHP file may therefore provide only temporary relief while the components responsible for restoring it remain active. Deactivating the plugin is also insufficient, according to the vendor’s recovery guidance.

Manual cleanup must begin by deleting the entire rank-math-pro directory. Administrators must then remove malicious records from the WordPress options table before hunting for remaining backdoors.

Rank Math lists three suspicious option_name values, _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb, and _np5pvf754c. Where supported, hosting providers or firewalls should also block outgoing connections to rank1cdn[.]com.

The vendor identifies several places where hidden PHP files may appear, including wp-content/mu-plugins/, other plugin folders, non-default theme directories, and Rank Math’s includes/ folder. Investigators should look for base64_decode combined with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn, proc_open, or PHP-FPM socket code. These are investigation clues that require review within the surrounding file.

Additional warning signs include unfamiliar administrator accounts with usernames beginning wpsupport_ or email addresses ending @wp-mail[.]net. Rank Math also identifies wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php as a fake core file. Its guidance calls for checking .htaccess rules that allow .cache files to execute as PHP and system cron entries tagged #ms6v46. These checks cover several possible routes back into a cleaned website.

The cleanup challenge resembles earlier self-healing WordPress malware covered by Cyber Security News, where surviving components restored deleted files.

Separately, a BdThemes supply chain attack showed how trusted plugin features could become a path to account takeover and persistent access. Neither comparison establishes a link between those attackers and this incident. Recovery Requires More Than a Plugin Update.

Rank Math recommends restoring both website files and the database from a clean backup made before October 15 at 20:02 UTC. Restoring only plugin files could leave malicious database content untouched. After restoration, owners should scan the site, replace exposed credentials, and install Rank Math PRO 3.0.124 from their account.

Without a suitable backup, owners need a wider investigation after disabling the rebuilding mechanism. That includes checking users, scheduled WordPress events, uploads, plugins, and themes.

The vendor also recommends reviewing SSH authorized_keys, running processes, other users’ crontabs, and writable locations outside the website directory. Shared hosting customers should ask their provider to examine areas they cannot access.

All secrets accessible to the compromised website should be treated as potentially exposed, even after a backup restore. Rank Math advises replacing WordPress passwords, database credentials, security keys and salts, payment gateway keys, SMTP credentials, API keys, and hosting access credentials. Administrator two-factor authentication settings also require review. This is precautionary guidance, not confirmation that every affected site suffered data theft.

Finally, owners should scan with tools such as Wordfence or Sucuri and run wp core verify-checksums. Premium plugins may lack public checksums, requiring comparison with official clean copies.

Monitor outgoing connections and returning files over subsequent days. Rank Math urges users to visit its website directly and warns that it will not email login or download links.

articles.title: Hackers Using Fake Google Meet Pages to Steal Google Credentials
articles.description:
Two websites are hosting fake Google Meet pages designed to steal Google account credentials and carry out phishing involving two-factor authentication (2FA), according to threat intelligence shared on October 20, 2026. The pages imitate a familiar meeting service to make a request for account details look more believable. The researcher also reported a serious security […]

The post Hackers Using Fake Google Meet Pages to Steal Google Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Two websites are hosting fake Google Meet pages designed to steal Google account credentials and carry out phishing involving two-factor authentication (2FA), according to threat intelligence shared on October 20, 2026.

The pages imitate a familiar meeting service to make a request for account details look more believable. The researcher also reported a serious security issue on an exposed /install page: it reveals database configuration information and a prefilled database password.

The source does not disclose the password itself. Analysts say this case highlights a risk that goes beyond a lookalike sign-in page. If a user enters a password or verification code on a fake site, criminals may be able to use those details to try to access the account.

The available report does not provide a full account of the page’s design, how victims reach it, or whether any accounts were confirmed stolen.

Anurag (@Malwarehunterr) identified and noted the campaign in a post describing the two domains, the exposed installation page, and the related web paths.

Hackers Using Fake Google Meet Pages

Google Meet is commonly used for work meetings, classes, and personal calls, so a page that looks like a meeting link may not raise immediate concern.

The two domains reported in this case are meet-google[.]cyou and qooglo[.]com. Their names resemble Google-related terms, but neither is the genuine meet.google.com domain.

Users should check the complete website address before entering a password, even when the page uses familiar logos or meeting language.

The researcher’s post describes the pages as designed to steal Google credentials and facilitate 2FA phishing. It does not spell out the exact steps in the sign-in process or explain whether the site relays authentication in real time.

In general, a stolen password can put an account at risk; a captured verification code may add further danger if criminals use it quickly.

Google advises users to choose stronger verification options, such as security keys or Google prompts, and says passkeys are designed to resist phishing.

This matters because an account can hold more than email. Depending on the user’s settings and connected services, access may expose documents, contacts, saved information, or business data.

A successful sign-in can also help a criminal send believable messages from the victim’s account. Google recommends reviewing recent security events and devices if a user suspects unauthorized access. For more background on how attackers can target Google sign-ins and authentication, readers can see this report on a Google account phishing kit.

Exposed installation page raises a separate concern

The reported /install page adds a second issue to the credential theft risk. According to the post, visiting that path exposes database configuration and a prefilled database password.

Such information may help an unauthorized visitor understand how a site’s backend is set up. The report does not say whether the exposed details were used to access the database, and the password value is not included in the source.

A misconfigured setup page should not be publicly available with sensitive information filled in. Site operators should restrict access to installation and setup routes, remove default or prefilled secrets, and review whether any credentials displayed on the page remain valid.

If they do, they should be changed and any systems using them checked. These are practical defensive steps based on the exposure described; the available report does not confirm what response the site owners have taken.

The report also lists web paths associated with the campaign: /meet, /assets/js/demo.js, /api/demo/sessions, /api/demo/sessions/{token}, and /api/demo/sessions/{token}/resend.

These paths may help defenders search relevant web logs, but a path alone does not prove that a system or user has been compromised. The source does not provide a sample file, malware name, IP address, or cryptographic hash.

Lookalike services remain a common theme in phishing. Cybersecurity News has previously reported on a Gmail phishing login flow that sought account details, and on fake Google Forms pages used to collect credentials.

A separate campaign used a fake Meet page to push a malicious command rather than simply request a password, as described in this Google Meet ClickFix report. Those reports describe different campaigns; they should not be treated as evidence that the same operators are behind this one.

Users should open Google Meet by typing its known address or using a trusted calendar invitation, rather than signing in through an unexpected page.

Check the full domain carefully: a padlock or HTTPS connection only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site belongs to Google. Do not enter a password or 2FA code after following an unfamiliar link.

Anyone who may have entered credentials should change the Google password through Google’s official account page, review recent security events, and remove unfamiliar devices or sessions.

If the password was reused elsewhere, change it on those services too. Google’s guidance explains how to secure a compromised account and review account activity. Organizations should also check sign-in logs for suspicious access and alert staff to the reported domains and paths.

articles.title: SBI Data Breach Claim – Hackers Allegedly Claim Access to 3.75 Lakh Users’ Database
articles.description:
An unverified SBI data breach claim alleges that a threat actor named Siriusim posted customer records and banking documents online. The claimed dataset contains 375,000 CSV rows and 2,722 PDF files, but those figures do not establish that 3.75 lakh unique customers were affected. CyberPulse reported the allegation on October 16, 2026. Its post described personal customer […]

The post SBI Data Breach Claim – Hackers Allegedly Claim Access to 3.75 Lakh Users’ Database appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An unverified SBI data breach claim alleges that a threat actor named Siriusim posted customer records and banking documents online. The claimed dataset contains 375,000 CSV rows and 2,722 PDF files, but those figures do not establish that 3.75 lakh unique customers were affected.

CyberPulse reported the allegation on October 16, 2026. Its post described personal customer information, loan applications, supporting documents, account-opening forms and address details. The actor called it the first disclosure of the dataset. The authenticity, source and extent of the alleged exposure remain unverified.

SBI Data Breach Claim

According to India Today, Siriusim posted the claim on BreachForums and shared what it described as four sample customer records. The report said the material may include Know Your Customer (KYC) records, Aadhaar numbers and residential addresses. These details remain allegations rather than confirmed findings from an investigation.

CSV files store information in rows and columns, while PDFs can hold forms and scanned documents. A row count alone cannot show how many people appear in a dataset. Multiple applications or duplicate entries could relate to the same person, and document totals do not prove separate victims.

India Today reported on October 19 that SBI had not addressed the claims when its article was published. The outlet said it had requested comment and could not independently confirm the breach. It also remained unclear whether the material was newly exposed or recycled from earlier leaks.

The available reports do not establish how the alleged records were obtained. Their source could not be traced to SBI itself, a subsidiary or a service provider handling banking applications. There is no verified evidence in these reports identifying an exploited flaw, stolen login or compromised server.

That uncertainty matters because documents bearing a bank’s name do not, by themselves, establish access to its core banking systems. Any investigation would need to validate samples, identify their owner, and check the claimed records against system logs before drawing conclusions about the source or scale.

If genuine, the records could support identity theft, loan fraud and targeted phishing. Criminals could use application details to make fake bank calls or messages sound convincing. Cybersecurity News has previously covered fake SBI reward apps and fraudulent YONO deactivation alerts, both relevant examples of banking impersonation, not evidence connecting those campaigns to this claim.

Customers should verify unexpected bank messages through official channels, avoid shared APK files, and never disclose passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords. SBI should assess the claim, preserve logs, and notify affected customers if an investigation confirms exposure. Until then, this remains an alleged data leak, not a confirmed compromise of accounts.

articles.description:
A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites while spending an estimated $5,000 on AI tokens, according to a Reuters investigation in October. The operation shows how one person can direct software to carry out complex attacks with little ongoing human input. The targets included sites linked to Deere, […]

The post One Hacker Uses AI Agents to Breach Over 100 Company Websites for Just $5,000 appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents to break into more than 100 company websites while spending an estimated $5,000 on AI tokens, according to a Reuters investigation in October. The operation shows how one person can direct software to carry out complex attacks with little ongoing human input.

The targets included sites linked to Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, although the reported impact differed across those companies. After the campaign began on September 25, the agents attempted to compromise more than 1,200 websites, mainly online stores in the United States, Canada, Australia and Japan.

Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at NorForge, uncovered the activity while searching for exposed Cairn installations, an open-source platform that coordinates AI agents. Around October 2, he found roughly two dozen installations apparently being used for malicious activity.

How Cairn Automated the Attacks

Cairn is a general-purpose problem-solving engine rather than a tool built only for hacking. In the attacks described in NorForge’s technical report, operators supplied a target and a goal, then agents searched for weaknesses and worked toward gaining access.

The platform stores findings on a shared project board so its agents can use earlier discoveries to choose their next steps. That allows them to try different paths when an initial approach fails, instead of relying on a single fixed scan.

NorForge tracked the largest Chinese-language activity cluster as AIA0001, linking it to 14 dashboards containing more than 1,100 attack projects. Its target pipeline used Microsoft’s Playwright browser automation tool to check that shopping sites could accept orders before passing them to Cairn.

The task instructions focused on finding ways to run code without signing in, including SQL injection, unsafe file uploads, login bypasses and unsafe handling of stored objects. The apparent aim was lasting access to shopping and payment systems that could later generate money.

NorForge confirmed one claimed breach by checking a reported address on a hardware vendor’s website and finding a live uploader webshell. This server-side script allowed files to be placed on the compromised site, creating a foothold for further attacks.

According to the agent’s own account, that attack combined unauthorized write access to a memcached session store with unsafe PHP object deserialization and older Zend Framework components. The chain turned weaknesses in session storage and object processing into server access, rather than depending on one obvious entry point.

In another case, agents moved beyond a company’s main application after failing to find a weakness. They searched related infrastructure, found an exposed control panel, and spent hours testing its handling of data before reporting that they could run commands on the server.

Low Costs, Long Running Agents

Successful AIA0001 projects took just under 23 hours on average, while one ran for more than five days. Across the observed campaigns, NorForge estimated success at around 10%, although goals and targets varied between operators.

Fagerland estimated the main campaign consumed about $5,000 in tokens, or roughly $50 per successful intrusion. These figures are estimates, not confirmed billing records. NorForge separately put the average task cost near $5 when failed and early-ending attempts were included, warning that uncertainty was substantial.

Worker names suggested a Claude Code setup using a DeepSeek model, but NorForge did not confirm the full model configuration. Chinese-language instructions also do not establish the operator’s nationality, and researchers found no obvious state-backed activity in the exposed panels.

Related reporting on AI agents used to steal retail credit card data described a separate campaign involving Cairn and other tools. Another investigation into DeepSeek-powered credential theft showed attackers using agents to exploit exposed secrets and weak settings, rather than relying on new flaws.

Deere told Reuters it took corrective action and found no indication that attackers accessed sensitive information. SharkNinja said the affected system was a separate product support site and that the threat had been contained. Cummins was investigating a possible attack on a third-party-run website.

Reuters could not determine how much data, if any, was taken across the breaches. NorForge also found hundreds of exposed secrets in the open panels and said it was working with Reuters to notify victims.

The exposure also affected legitimate security testers. NorForge found unsecured testing dashboards revealing customer information, showing that poorly protected AI tools create risk during authorized work.

Defenders should patch public-facing applications, restrict access to admin panels, and watch for unexpected files in web directories. Security teams should also review suspicious web requests and isolate servers where webshells are found, then investigate for stolen data, further access, and other malware before restoring service.

articles.title: Claude AI Detects Hidden Crypto Miner While Building Temperature Monitor App on Mac
articles.description:
An ordinary coding task led to an unexpected security discovery when Claude Code reportedly found a hidden cryptocurrency miner on a developer’s Mac. The AI assistant was building a temperature monitoring app when unusually high sensor readings prompted it to investigate CPU activity. It identified XMRig consuming about 1,175% CPU, described as roughly 12 cores […]

The post Claude AI Detects Hidden Crypto Miner While Building Temperature Monitor App on Mac appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An ordinary coding task led to an unexpected security discovery when Claude Code reportedly found a hidden cryptocurrency miner on a developer’s Mac. The AI assistant was building a temperature monitoring app when unusually high sensor readings prompted it to investigate CPU activity. It identified XMRig consuming about 1,175% CPU, described as roughly 12 cores of processing load.

The developer, posting as u/UntilHEX on Reddit, said Claude checked running processes after reviewing raw sensor data. The discovery offered an explanation for the Mac’s poor performance. However, the account remains a user report supported by a screenshot, rather than a published forensic investigation.

High CPU Usage Exposed the Hidden Miner

According to the shared screenshot, Claude reported that the CPU had peaked at 112°C. “Your Mac is running a cryptominer that I didn’t put there,” the assistant warned. Those figures reflect the reported session and have not been independently verified through hardware logs or a separate examination.

The screenshot identified /tmp/rigupdater as the miner’s running location and pool.hashvault.sh as its mining pool destination. These details provide useful leads for investigators examining this specific device. They do not establish how the software arrived, who installed it, or whether other systems were affected.

XMRig is not inherently malicious. It is mining software with official macOS builds, including support for Apple Silicon. The security concern is its apparent use without the owner’s knowledge or consent. Finding the program alone would not prove an infection without examining its installation, configuration, and activity.

LaunchAgent Reportedly Kept the Miner Running

Claude also flagged a suspicious property list file inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/. The screenshot described a randomly named startup entry dated August 29 that ran a large encoded script through bash, with KeepAlive enabled. Claude said the entry was already present before its development work began.

Apple’s LaunchAgent documentation explains that user agents run within a logged-in user’s session. The KeepAlive setting can tell launchd to keep a job running. That makes the startup entry important because stopping a process without disabling its launcher may allow it to return. LaunchAgents themselves are legitimate macOS features, not automatic proof of malware.

The screenshot also raised concern about credentials available on the Mac, including its GitHub login. That warning describes possible exposure, not confirmed theft. The public evidence does not show that passwords, access tokens, source code, or other files were stolen. The infection route and full scope remain unknown.

Claude initially said it had not killed or removed anything. Instead, it requested permission to stop the startup item and miner, then move files into quarantine. UntilHEX later said the assistant performed cleanup, although one file required manual deletion because of an access issue.

The behavior resembles techniques seen in other Mac threats, without proving a connection. Cyber Security News previously covered fake CAPTCHA attacks that install a backdoor and XMRig. That campaign used a LaunchAgent and could combine mining with password theft, showing why removing a miner alone may leave risks behind.

Separate reporting on CrashStealer’s abuse of Apple crash-reporting branding also documented LaunchAgent persistence. Neither campaign has been linked to UntilHEX’s Mac. Their relevance is the shared use of trusted operating system features to keep unwanted software running.

For affected users, the practical lesson is to investigate unexplained heat and sustained CPU load, review persistence, and check account exposure. Suspected compromise warrants isolation and password changes from a clean device. Claude’s discovery was useful, but the reported cleanup does not establish that every threat was removed.

articles.description:

Tracked as CVE-2026-108097, the flaw affects the Field UI module in Drupal core. The Drupal Security Team published its warning on October 14, 2026. The official security advisory, SA-CORE-2026-014, assigns the issue […]

The post Critical Drupal RCE Vulnerability Could Let Attackers Take Over Websites Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Drupal has released security updates for a critical remote code execution vulnerability that could let attackers take over affected websites without logging in.

Tracked as CVE-2026-108097, the flaw affects the Field UI module in Drupal core. The Drupal Security Team published its warning on October 14, 2026.

The official security advisory, SA-CORE-2026-014, assigns the issue a risk score of 19 out of 25 under Drupal’s rating system. Successful exploitation could expose all private website data and allow attackers to change or delete information. The score is not a CVSS rating.

The most important detail is that Drupal core alone does not provide a direct path to exploit the flaw. However, the security team confirmed that several serious attack paths exist when contributed modules are present. These are additional modules used to extend a website’s features beyond its core functions.

At least one known attack path requires no authentication, meaning an attacker would not need a valid account. Custom website code may also expose the vulnerable functionality. Site owners should consider installed extensions and custom development, rather than judging exposure by Drupal version alone.

Critical Drupal RCE Vulnerability

The public advisory does not name the contributed modules involved or provide a working exploit. Its rating describes exploitation as theoretical, with no public exploit code or development documentation. That wording should not be mistaken for proof of safety, given the confirmed attack paths described by the security team.

The issue follows earlier concerns about Drupal security, including coverage of a Drupal core SQL injection vulnerability. That report concerns a separate flaw.

Its exploitation status should not be applied to this Field UI vulnerability, for which the current advisory does not report attacks in the wild.

The affected ranges cover Drupal versions from 8.9.0 before 10.6.19, 11.0.0 before 11.3.19, and 11.4.0 before 11.4.10. Drupal 12 development releases from 12.0.0-alpha1 before 12.0.0-beta2 are also affected.

The broad version coverage makes it important to check every deployed site, especially where organizations maintain several Drupal installations.

Administrators running Drupal 11.4.x should install Drupal 11.4.10. Those using Drupal 11.3.x should move to 11.3.19, while Drupal 10.6.x users should install 10.6.19. Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, Drupal 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 no longer receive security coverage.

Drupal says uninstalling the core Field UI module (field_ui) protects while sites are updated. Drupal Steward also blocks some known attack paths, but it doesn’t cover every possible exploit. Organizations using that service still need to upgrade rather than treat filtering as a permanent fix.

For teams reviewing possible compromise, guidance on detecting and investigating webshells offers useful background on malicious scripts that enable remote commands. The immediate priority for this vulnerability remains clear.

Apply the supported security release, or uninstall Field UI while preparing the update, without relying solely on partial network protection measures.

Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs.

articles.title: Microsoft Says AI Agents Cannot Be Trusted and Could Become Insider Security Threats
articles.description:
Microsoft warns organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider risks not because they are automatically malicious, but because they can access company data, apps, and tools and act on that access at high speed. The warning, published on October 19, 2026, comes as businesses use agents to handle tasks such as writing code, reviewing […]

The post Microsoft Says AI Agents Cannot Be Trusted and Could Become Insider Security Threats appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft warns organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider risks not because they are automatically malicious, but because they can access company data, apps, and tools and act on that access at high speed.

The warning, published on October 19, 2026, comes as businesses use agents to handle tasks such as writing code, reviewing documents, and processing expenses.

An agent’s actions can change as its instructions, data, or working context change. It may make a mistake, follow harmful directions hidden in a document, or be compromised.

Because agents can act across connected systems, an unsafe action could expose sensitive information or change business records before a person notices. Microsoft’s point is not that every agent is dangerous. It is that organizations should not assume an agent will always behave as intended.

The risk grows when an agent receives more access than its task requires. An agent used to review expense claims, for example, may need to read submissions and check company rules. It should not automatically inherit all the permissions of the employee who set it up. If it encounters hidden instructions in a file or tries to take an unrelated action, security controls should be able to limit what it can do.

AI Models as Insider Threats

Microsoft says those controls should operate outside the AI model. The model can provide answers or plans, but separate security systems should decide what data it can access and which actions it can take.

This matters because a model should not be able to change or bypass the safeguards that govern it. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has described this approach as separating the supply of intelligence from the authority to act.

To support this approach, Microsoft announced plans to expand agent discovery and controls through Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365. The company says it is adding support for 35 more types of local agents, bringing its total to 60, and expanding Microsoft Entra Agent ID so agents can have identities separate from their human sponsors. That separation can help security teams track who owns an agent and distinguish its actions from a person’s.

Microsoft also described Dynamic Permissions, Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The proposed controls would give agents only the access needed for a task and adjust that access as risk changes.

For example, an organization might let an agent continue reading information while blocking it from making changes, restrict the systems it can reach, or require human approval before a sensitive action. At higher risk, the agent could be isolated or stopped.

The company also introduced Guardian Agents, intended to help security teams monitor agent activity and respond to changes at machine speed. Microsoft says people would still set the rules and retain control of important decisions, while Guardian Agents could investigate alerts and apply permitted safeguards. The announcements describe Microsoft’s planned security approach, not a guarantee that every agent-related threat can be prevented.

For security teams, the message is to build agent oversight into deployment from the start. That means tracking which agents exist, assigning clear identities, limiting permissions, monitoring activity, and keeping an independent way to stop unsafe actions.

Related coverage from Cybersecurity News examines Microsoft’s prompt-injection protection for Office 365 and execution containers for securing AI workflows. When agents can act across company systems, visibility and limits are essential to using them safely.

articles.description:

In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, […]

The post Bright Security Introduces STAR Fuzzer, Agentic Fuzzing That Writes Its Own Harnesses and Proves Every Finding appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
San Rafael, United States, October 19th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Built on an evolutionary engine first released in 2018, STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security finds crashes, memory exhaustion and memory-safety bugs in security-critical code without a running application.

In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, and in its first month of availability it produced ten published findings in eight projects, including the Crystal standard library, htop and RIOT OS.

Bright Security, the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, today announced the official launch of STAR Fuzzer, an agentic application fuzzer that automatically identifies security-critical functions, generates a fuzzing harness for each one, searches for faults with an evolutionary algorithm, and delivers every confirmed finding with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it.

STAR Fuzzer is a self-contained mode of the Bright STAR platform and is available now at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

Agentic fuzzing applies AI agents to the parts of fuzzing that have traditionally required a specialist: choosing what to test, writing the harness, and deciding which crashes matter.

STAR Fuzzer uses AI for those steps and an evolutionary search engine for the fuzzing itself, so the parts that need judgment are automated and the search stays fast, repeatable and evidence based.

Why Fuzzing Needed a New Approach

Coverage-guided fuzzers such as AFL++ and libFuzzer are proven and widely used, and programs like Google’s OSS-Fuzz have shown how much they can find.

But they depend on people to write and maintain a harness for every target and to triage the crashes that come back. That cost has kept fuzzing concentrated in specialist teams and a subset of critical projects.

Other testing approaches don’t fill the gap. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tests what an attacker can reach over HTTP, so it rarely exercises the parsing and processing code behind input validation.

LLM-based pentesting is effective at known vulnerability patterns but tends to look where a model expects bugs to be.

The result is a class of outage-level and memory-safety defects, often triggered by tiny malformed inputs, that most AppSec programs never test for.

How STAR Fuzzer compares with traditional coverage-guided fuzzers (such as AFL++ and libFuzzer) and DAST:

  • What it Tests: Traditional fuzzers test functions exposed through a hand-written harness. DAST tests running applications over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions on untrusted-input paths, chosen automatically.
  • Harness: Traditional fuzzers need harnesses written and maintained by engineers. DAST doesn’t use one. STAR Fuzzer generates a harness per function with AI, then verifies it reaches its target.
  • Search: Traditional fuzzers use coverage-guided mutation. DAST sends request-level attack payloads. STAR Fuzzer uses a structure-aware evolutionary search guided by coverage and multiple fitness signals.
  • Running App Needed: Traditional fuzzers, no. DAST, yes. STAR Fuzzer, no.
  • Triage: Manual for traditional fuzzers and built into the scanner for DAST. STAR Fuzzer triages automatically for reachability and impact.
  • Output: Traditional fuzzers return crash inputs and logs. DAST returns a vulnerability report. STAR Fuzzer delivers the file, function and byte-exact payload in a pull request.
  • Fix Validation: Traditional fuzzers need a manual re-run and DAST needs a rescan. With STAR Fuzzer, teams replay the payload.

Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss

Ask an LLM to audit a parser and it will find the bug classes it already knows from training. The zero-days that survive for years in mature, widely deployed code are the ones that match no known pattern.

STAR Fuzzer uses AI to choose targets and build harnesses, but the search that finds the bugs is not an LLM. It doesn’t read the code or guess where a bug might be.

It runs the program millions of times, observes what actually happens, and keeps whatever pushes the target into code it hasn’t reached yet.

In Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss, Bright Security CTO Bar Hofesh gives four reasons LLM code review does not replace fuzzing for zero-day discovery:

  • Scale: A single fuzzing campaign runs 1 million to 10 million concrete inputs against the compiled target. At about 2,000 tokens per reasoned test case, matching one million executions with an LLM would take about two billion tokens for one target, and each of those test cases would still be a prediction.
  • Speed and Ground Truth: A persistent harness runs hundreds to a few thousand inputs per second per worker, across several parallel workers, so one million executions take minutes to tens of minutes. One LLM reasoning pass over one hypothesis takes several seconds, so one million would take months. The fuzzer also observes real behavior, such as a sanitizer reporting a heap read one byte out of bounds. An LLM has to predict how compiled code behaves, including struct layouts, integer widths, allocator behavior and build flags that aren’t visible in the source.
  • Coverage: STAR Fuzzer’s libxml2 harness reaches about 13,600 code regions in a 5-million-execution run. Coverage feedback shows which regions each input reached, and inputs that reach new code become starting points for deeper search. Code review has no equivalent signal for how much of a large parser it has actually covered.
  • The Unexpected: LLMs, code reviewers and static analyzers look for the same known patterns, so in mature code most of those bugs are already fixed. The fuzzer has no expectations about where a bug should be. The target’s own behavior decides what is interesting.

Reproducibility is the other difference. Many plausible-looking LLM findings don’t reproduce, and maintainers need a reproducer before they can act.

A fuzzer finding is a reproducer by construction, and Bright Security replays every one in a fresh container before filing it.

How STAR Fuzzer Works

STAR Fuzzer’s search engine drives any target through a small harness over IPC, so the code under test can be written in C, C++, Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin, Crystal, Node or any language that can read an input and report back.

  • Structure-aware parsing with no per-target grammar: Every seed is parsed into a typed tree of fields by a format-agnostic parsing layer, and the tree serializes back to the original bytes exactly. No grammar or dictionary file is written per target, and each format added to the parsing layer improves every target that uses it.
  • Mutations that get past the first check: Byte-level mutation mostly produces inputs a parser rejects at its first sanity check. Mutating the fields of a valid structured input keeps most executions past framing and validation, so the testing budget is spent on the deeper logic behind them.
  • Evolution with exact replay: Each organism in the population carries a genome, an ordered list of mutations. Each epoch, organisms mutate, run and are scored. Improvements are kept, unproductive changes are reverted, and organisms breed. Replaying a genome reproduces its payload exactly, so every result can be regenerated from a logged random seed.

Results from Open-Source Testing

Before release, Bright Security ran STAR Fuzzer for two days in an automated pipeline against multiple open source projects, from libraries and applications to low-level binary parsers.

45% of the projects tested had High or Critical issues, and 37% of the vulnerable projects are part of Google’s OSS-Fuzz program.

In its first month of availability, STAR Fuzzer produced ten published findings in eight projects written in C, Go, JVM languages and Crystal. Each was replayed in a fresh container before filing:

  • TwelveMonkeys: In the DDS reader, the mipMapCount header field sizes an uncapped array, so a 38-byte file forces a multi-gigabyte allocation (CWE-789). GHSA-fwp7-38wp-mmxw, fixed in 3.15.0.
  • Fider: Upload validation checks an image’s compressed size, then fully decodes it, so a 436 KB PNG expands to about 562 MB. Any authenticated user can trigger it (CWE-409). STAR Fuzzer found it in about 12 minutes, in a release already benchmarked by multiple AI pentesting vendors. GHSA-7cw3-7xh9-529r, fixed in 0.38.0.
  • Crystal standard library (XML): XML::Node#namespace type confusion. ENTITY_DECL is missing from an allowlist, so a field of libxml2’s xmlEntity struct is read as an xmlNs* (CWE-843). GHSA-c267-9cqj-hv9f, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1.
  • Crystal standard library (YAML): YAML::Any#hash overflows the stack on a self-referencing anchor and alias cycle. An 88-byte input causes an uncatchable SIGSEGV (CWE-674). GHSA-fj8w-2r88-5v7w, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1.
  • libsolv: Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-104621 and CVE-2026-104622. Details are under embargo.
  • htop: An out-of-bounds read in the /proc/PID/stat parser, caused by a missing bounds check on field 22 (CWE-125). Fixed (#2101).
  • universal-ctags: A null-pointer member access in foreachEntriesInScope (CWE-476). Fixed in commit 780bd7a (#4497).
  • scrimage: An uncapped width-times-height pixel count lets a 35-byte GIF trigger allocation attempts of about 2 GB, and over 8 GB in a second variant (CWE-789). Fixed in 4.6.8 (#893).
  • RIOT OS: An off-by-one in _dirlist_cb (link_format.c). The bounds check runs after the write, so a NUL byte lands one past the buffer (CWE-193). Fix submitted in PR #22879.

Several of these bugs sit in code that looks correct on review. The Fider upload has a size limit, but it measures compressed size. The TwelveMonkeys field reads as image metadata, not as a length.

The Crystal allowlist looks complete. The YAML hash function is correct for trees, and the bug is a cycle in the input.

The full methodology and results are published in two parts: Part I on brightsec.com, and Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss by Bar Hofesh.

Where STAR Fuzzer Fits Best

STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security is designed for teams whose code handles untrusted input below the HTTP layer, including:

  • Applications that process uploaded files, images, documents or archives
  • Parsers, serialization code and raw binary protocols
  • Non-web software such as embedded and IoT firmware, desktop applications and backend services
  • Codebases with a growing share of AI-generated code that needs testing beyond pattern matching
  • Security teams that want to confirm static analysis (SAST) findings by exercising the flagged functions live

It supports C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal, and runs inside the customer’s environment with no running application, cloud scanner or authentication required.

In persistent mode, harness execution is about 51 times faster than running a new process per input.

Executive Perspectives

“Fuzzing has always found the bugs that matter most, the ones that take a service down or corrupt memory, but it has been too expensive for most teams to run,” said Bar Hofesh, Co-founder and CTO of Bright Security.

“The search was never the bottleneck. The harnesses and the triage were. STAR Fuzzer automates both, so the evolutionary engine we built in 2018 can finally run across a whole codebase.”

“When Nevada opened the Boulder City Bypass in 2018, it took navigation apps months to start sending drivers down it,” Hofesh added. “LLMs auditing code work the same way.

They find the bugs they’ve already seen. The zero-days that have lived for years in mature code are the ones nobody has seen before, and that’s exactly where a fuzzer shines.”

“Security teams are being asked to keep up with code written faster than ever, much of it by AI,” said Gadi Bashvitz, Co-founder and CEO of Bright Security.

“Testing that only looks where bugs are expected won’t keep pace. STAR Fuzzer looks everywhere else, and it hands developers the proof they need to fix what it finds.”

“AppSec teams keep asking us the same thing: if AI is writing more of our code, what’s testing the parts AI can’t, see?” said Eyal Dror, CMO of Bright Security.

“STAR Fuzzer is our answer. In its first month it found ten real bugs in mature open-source projects, and everyone came with the exact input that triggers it. That’s proof a developer can act on the same day, not another alert to argue about.”

Availability

STAR Fuzzer is available now as a mode of Bright STAR. Learn more and book a demo at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

Frequently Asked Questions:

What is Agentic Fuzzing? Agentic fuzzing uses AI agents to automate the judgment-heavy steps of fuzzing: selecting which functions to test, writing and verifying harnesses, and triaging results. The fuzzing itself is performed by a search engine that mutates inputs to trigger faults.

How is STAR Fuzzer Different from AFL++ or libFuzzer? AFL++ and libFuzzer are fuzzing engines that need engineers to write a harness for each target and to triage crashes by hand. STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security selects targets, generates and verifies harnesses, triages faults for reachability and impact, and delivers findings in a pull request with a reproducing payload.

Can LLMs Find Zero-Day Vulnerabilities in Parsers? LLMs are effective at known bug classes, such as an unchecked memcpy length or string-built SQL, but they look where their training says bugs should be. In mature code, the bugs that survive are the ones that match no known pattern, which is where evolutionary, coverage-guided fuzzing is strongest.

Why Use a Fuzzer Instead of LLM Code Review? A fuzzing campaign runs millions of real executions against compiled code and observes what happens, while an LLM predicts behavior from the source. Matching one million executions with LLM reasoning would take about two billion tokens per target. Every fuzzer finding also comes with an input that reproduces it.

How are STAR Fuzzer Findings Verified? Every finding comes with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it, and Bright Security replays each one in a fresh container before filing it. Any result can also be regenerated from a logged random seed.

Does STAR Fuzzer Need Grammars or Dictionary Files? No. A format-agnostic parsing layer turns each seed into a typed tree of fields, so no per-target grammar or dictionary is required.

Does STAR Fuzzer Replace DAST? No. DAST tests a running application from the outside in, over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions from the inside out, without a running application. Bright STAR runs both, with the same agent and the same pull-request output.

What Kinds of Bugs Does STAR Fuzzer Find? Crashes, hangs, out-of-memory conditions and unbounded allocations, memory-safety bugs such as out-of-bounds reads and off-by-one writes, type confusion, stack overflows from recursive input structures, and algorithmic-complexity blow-ups, including decompression bombs triggered by inputs of a few dozen bytes.

Which languages does STAR Fuzzer Support? C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal.

About Bright Security

Bright Security is the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, helping organizations secure software at the speed of AI-driven development.

Its AI-powered Bright STAR platform integrates security directly into the development lifecycle, automating detection, remediation and validation across web applications, APIs and code, and fitting into both developer and AppSec workflows.

Formerly known as NeuraLegion, Bright Security is headquartered in California. Learn more at brightsec.com.

Contact

Eyal Dror

eyal.dror@brightsec.com

NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI agents that act beyond their approved tasks. Published October 16, 2026, the voluntary guidance sets out ten practices for managing incidents during superintelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight. The NIST announcement groups […]

The post NSA, CISA and NIST Release New Security Guidelines to Detect and Shut Down Rogue AI Agents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI agents that act beyond their approved tasks.

Published October 16, 2026, the voluntary guidance sets out ten practices for managing incidents during superintelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight.

The NIST announcement groups the practices into preparation, detection, response, recovery, and reporting. Its main audience is organizations training or testing highly capable agents on lengthy tasks with limited human supervision. The recommendations may also apply to organizations deploying these systems.

The document calls these events SI control incidents. They occur when agents take significant actions without instructions and break policies or security controls that define their task boundaries. Examples include unauthorized contact with outside parties, financial transactions, or access to third-party systems.

NSA, CISA and NIST Issue Rogue AI Agent Guidelines

Importantly, this definition separates independent agent behavior from attacker-directed activity. Prompt injection or a deliberately backdoored model causes instructed actions, not the primary cause of an SI control incident. The guidance also covers near-misses that expose weaknesses before harm occurs.

Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites shows why task boundaries matter when automated systems encounter blocked access. That reporting is separate from the new guidance, which outlines readiness measures rather than announcing a specific breach.

Agencies recommend restricting agents to the data, tools, and systems they need for their tasks. Use strict allowlists for network access where possible, with permitted traffic passing through a monitored gateway. Organizations should also identify routes for hidden communication, persistence, and unauthorized copying of model weights.

Detection should cover the model, its supporting software, host systems, and network activity. Agents should not be able to alter monitoring tools or logs. Where possible, teams should use monitoring models from different families to cross-check findings and reduce shared blind spots.

The guidance also warns that agent outputs may contain exploits aimed at monitoring systems. This adds context to earlier coverage of NIST’s proposed AI security control overlays, which addressed access controls, monitoring and audit records across AI environments.

A central recommendation is shutdown. The joint publication calls for automatically stopping affected agent runs when a control failure or ongoing incident is detected. Depending on severity, organizations should pause related training, evaluation, or deployment until protections are strengthened and verified.

Response teams should preserve model weights, checkpoints, tool calls, rejected actions, and reliable logs. They should revoke exposed credentials, rebuild potentially compromised environments, and remove backdoors or hidden communication paths. Before restarting, teams should test monitoring, access limits, and shutdown controls against the incident’s actions.

Organizations should notify affected parties, meet legal reporting duties, and share relevant incidents and near-misses with government experts. The guidance builds on NIST SP 800-61r3 and established incident response practices, extending them to autonomous systems.

articles.description:
Hackers are exploiting a command injection flaw in SiteGuard Server Edition, a web application firewall installed directly on protected servers. Tracked as CVE-2026-106931, the vulnerability could let attackers run operating system commands with root or SYSTEM privileges, potentially giving them full control of an affected server. The flaw affects the product’s statistics function, which is […]

The post Hackers Exploit SiteGuard WAF Vulnerability That Could Give Them Full Control of Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are exploiting a command injection flaw in SiteGuard Server Edition, a web application firewall installed directly on protected servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-106931, the vulnerability could let attackers run operating system commands with root or SYSTEM privileges, potentially giving them full control of an affected server.

The flaw affects the product’s statistics function, which is enabled by default. EG Secure Solutions confirmed exploitation and notified customers with direct support contracts on September 29, 2026. Japan’s vulnerability coordination service published its JVN advisory on October 14, while JPCERT/CC also issued an alert.

The weakness is classified as OS command injection under CWE-78. It lets attackers run operating system commands through the affected software’s statistics-processing function.

Those commands may execute with root privileges on Unix systems or SYSTEM privileges on Windows, rather than the attacker’s existing permissions. However, the published severity ratings describe a local attack requiring low privileges and no user interaction.

Hackers Exploit SiteGuard WAF Vulnerability

Administrators should therefore understand this as a path from limited access to higher privileges, not a confirmed login-free remote attack. The vulnerability scores 8.5 under CVSS 4.0 and 7.8 under CVSS 3.0.

Neither advisory identifies the attackers, affected organizations, attack volume, or the exact exploitation method. Similar risks involving security appliances have appeared in Cyber Security News coverage of a Hillstone WAF command injection vulnerability. However, that issue is separate from SiteGuard.

Affected releases start at SiteGuard Server Edition version 2.20 when statistics are enabled. For Apache, Nginx, and IIS editions outside FreeBSD, administrators should upgrade to version 8.00 Update 5. FreeBSD installations using Apache or Nginx should move to version 7.00 Update 6.

There is an important exception for Windows deployments. IIS editions from version 3.10 through version 4.00 Update 4 are not affected. Checking both the installed version and statistics setting is therefore necessary when assessing exposure.

Organizations unable to upgrade can obtain a patch that replaces the files used for statistics processing. The vendor also provides this option for releases whose support has ended.

Administrators must save diagnostic information before installing an update or patch because remediation may erase traces of an attack. In the web management interface, open “Diagnostic Information,” then select “Download Diagnostic Information” and retain the downloaded data before making changes.

This evidence-first approach supports later investigation, as explained in Cyber Security News’ guide to digital forensics and incident response. With exploitation confirmed, affected organizations should preserve diagnostics and promptly apply the appropriate fix.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly registered domain copies Microsoft Teams’ login page and interface, raising concerns about a phishing attempt targeting workplace users.

Security researcher Steven Lim reported that teams-cloud[.]live was just five days old when he flagged it on October 18, 2026. He urged organizations to block the address before employees encounter the fake site.

The alert highlights phishing built around a familiar business tool. A copied Teams screen could persuade employees to trust a sign-in request. However, the available report does not establish how many people visited the site, whether passwords were captured, or who operates the domain.

According to Steven Lim, the site mimics both the Teams login screen and its wider user interface. He said it resembles another example he shared on October 8, 2026. That similarity warrants investigation, but it does not confirm that the same attacker controls both sites.

Lim also reported that clicking an option to update Teams downloaded a TXT file. The alert does not provide the file’s contents, a hash, or evidence that it executes code.

Calling it confirmed malware would therefore go beyond the available findings. The unexpected download remains a useful detail for investigators checking browser activity and downloaded files.

Fake Microsoft Teams Domains Used to Steal Credentials

In a pinned comment supplied with the alert, Lim identified amgen[.]teams-cloud[.]live as a healthcare-themed target. The company name appears as a subdomain beneath teams-cloud[.]live. Its presence does not establish that Amgen was breached or that an employee account was accessed.

The concern is the gap between what users see and where they are browsing. A convincing Teams design does not make an unrelated domain a Microsoft service.

Cyber Security News previously covered attackers posing as IT help desk staff through Teams, pushing employees toward downloads or remote access. That separate activity shows how workplace trust can support phishing without a software flaw.

Another report examined fake login pages created through Teams redirects in browsers. No confirmed link exists to this domain, but both cases show why branding alone cannot validate a login prompt.

Defenders should review connections to teams-cloud[.]live and the reported subdomain, then check related downloads and sign-in activity. Lim specifically recommended Tenant blocking and web filtering.

Microsoft documents URL blocking through the Tenant Allow/Block List and custom domain blocking through Defender network protection. Administrators should apply controls suited to their environment and verify coverage rather than assume one setting blocks every route.

Employees should avoid the reported site and verify unexpected Teams update requests through their organization’s established IT support channel before entering passwords or opening downloads.

articles.title: 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Lets Attackers Hack Routers Without Knowing Passwords
articles.description:
A 16-year-old flaw in Broadcom’s Wi-Fi software can let attackers within wireless range take control of affected routers without knowing the network password. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the issue at Hexacon in Paris on October 16, 2026, warning that old code remains in widely deployed devices. According to Kaiser’s research, the flaw has existed […]

The post 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Lets Attackers Hack Routers Without Knowing Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A 16-year-old flaw in Broadcom’s Wi-Fi software can let attackers within wireless range take control of affected routers without knowing the network password.

Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the issue at Hexacon in Paris on October 16, 2026, warning that old code remains in widely deployed devices.

According to Kaiser’s research, the flaw has existed in Broadcom’s software development kit since at least 2010. It affects its proprietary Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) implementation. It allows memory leaks and attacker-controlled code execution before normal WPS enrollment finishes.

The flaw sits in code that joins fragmented Extensible Authentication Protocol messages used by WPS. Weak length checks allow crafted wireless messages to overflow a memory buffer.

16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw

Attackers can then read or change memory and redirect the router’s program flow to run their own code. This is an over-the-air attack, not a password-cracking method. The attacker needs wireless reach to the target but not its network key.

Kaiser demonstrated stealing the saved Wi-Fi password from an Orange Belgium ASKEY TCG3000 router and sending it back through wireless frames. He then joined the network using the stolen password.

A second demonstration against a Proximus BBOX3V+ provided a remote command shell over Wi-Fi frames without a cloud command server. These tests show why a strong password alone cannot stop exploitation of the affected software.

Kaiser confirmed exploitation on devices used by three Belgian internet providers. These include Proximus BBOX3V+, VOO’s Netgear CG3100 and CG3700, Technicolor TC7210 and CGA4233, and Orange’s ASKEY TCG3000. Possible exposure involving Telenet equipment remains unconfirmed.

His estimates place the affected Belgian fleet at roughly 1.56 million gateways across Proximus, legacy VOO, and Orange. These are researcher estimates, not verified provider totals. He warns that the wider issue could affect millions of access points worldwide, although the full count remains unknown.

The finding follows earlier Broadcom-related wireless security concerns, including the separate Kr00k Wi-Fi vulnerability. The new research concerns WPS message handling rather than that earlier flaw.

Kaiser describes a 2018 patch as incomplete. In correspondence reproduced in his slides, Broadcom said it had long known about the issue and had offered replacement software based on hostapd and WPA Supplicant since 2018. That leaves device makers responsible for moving away from the old implementation.

Kaiser reported the eCos issue on July 18 and the Linux issue on July 27. He says Broadcom declined to assign a CVE, and the tested Belgian devices remained unpatched as of October 15.

His detection toolkit includes a wireless fingerprinting script and YARA rules for firmware checks. These are screening tools, not final proof of exploitability. Findings need further review.

The risk also draws renewed attention to Nearest-Neighbor attacks, where compromised nearby systems provide wireless reach. That case used different methods, but shows why nearby Wi-Fi exposure matters.
