articles.description:
Aoki, also known as Aokigahara, is a data-stealing malware that has added credentials for AI tools to its growing list of targets. Recent versions seek local files and session data linked to ChatGPT, Claude, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini. The change raises the risk for developers who use AI assistants alongside source-code repositories, cloud […]

The post New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini to Steal Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Aoki, also known as Aokigahara, is a data-stealing malware that has added credentials for AI tools to its growing list of targets. Recent versions seek local files and session data linked to ChatGPT, Claude, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Codeium and Gemini.

The change raises the risk for developers who use AI assistants alongside source-code repositories, cloud accounts and other work systems.

Unlike a flaw in an AI service, Aoki’s activity focuses on data stored on an infected computer. A stolen key or token may let an intruder use an account as its owner, run up paid usage or reach services connected to that account.

Earlier Aoki samples did not search for AI-related files, suggesting this is a newer addition to the malware’s collection rules. Researchers from Symantec’s Threat Hunter team identified the expanded targeting.

Symantec’s Threat Hunter team analysis found that newer Aoki versions search for files linked to Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, as well as tokens used by services such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro.

The Symantec Aoki threat report also describes the malware’s wider reach across browsers, wallets and messaging apps. The files named in the report include .claude.json, Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and Codex config.toml and .env files. These can contain login sessions, settings or secrets used by local tools.

Aoki also targets Cursor’s local state database, which may hold chat context and code snippets. Symantec says the main focus is credentials and session data, rather than source code itself.

New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini

Aoki does not stop at AI tools. It can collect browser cookies, saved passwords, autofill details, credit-card data and Google tokens from a broad range of browsers.

Its other targets include cryptocurrency wallet files and extensions, password managers, VPN and file-transfer applications, gaming services, and Telegram and Discord data. It also records which security products are installed on the computer.

That broad collection can turn one infected device into a source of access to several accounts. For developers, a stolen token may expose more than an AI subscription: connected repositories, cloud services and continuous integration and delivery pipelines could also be at risk.

The growing focus on locally stored agent data has been seen in other reporting on AI coding agent data theft, though that coverage describes other malware families, not Aoki.

Aoki sends collected information to a command-and-control server using a /gate endpoint. Symantec says newer samples used several domains, while older samples used an IP address and port 8080 over unencrypted HTTP.

The report does not name a threat group behind Aoki, and it does not link the malware to a known family. Its name comes from “Aokigahara,” a string used during the malware’s decryption process.

The theft of AI credentials can also lead to direct costs. An intruder may use a victim’s account quota or resell access; abusing paid AI services in this way is often called LLMjacking. A separate report on stolen AWS keys used for LLMjacking shows how compromised cloud credentials can be used to run paid AI models at the account owner’s expense. Aoki’s reported focus, however, is stealing data from infected devices.

This pattern is not limited to Aoki. Cyber Security News has reported on a fake Gemini npm package that targeted credentials and local data from several AI development tools.

The incidents underline why developers should treat AI configuration files and local session data as sensitive, much like cloud keys and source-control credentials.

What defenders should check

Organizations should look for the indicators below in endpoint and network records. A match is a reason to investigate, not proof on its own that a device is infected.

If a system is suspected of compromise, teams should use a clean device to revoke active AI sessions, rotate exposed API keys and related credentials, and review account activity.

They should also check connected repositories and cloud services for unexpected use. These steps matter because multi-factor authentication may not stop an attacker from reusing a token already stolen from a device.

Developers should avoid saving long-lived secrets in files that are accessible to local applications, limit tokens to the permissions and time needed, and remove or replace exposed keys.

Security teams can monitor for unexpected access to AI tool folders and unusual outbound connections, then compare findings with the indicators below. Symantec identifies the family as Infostealer.Aoki.

articles.title: Google Automatically Adds Your Phone Number to Every Google Account on Your Android Phone
articles.description:
Google automatically verifies phone numbers on Android devices and adds them to every Google account signed in on the Phone. The setting is enabled by default, raising privacy concerns for users who keep personal, work, and secondary accounts separate. Google’s documentation confirms that the behavior covers both existing accounts and accounts added later. The feature, […]

The post Google Automatically Adds Your Phone Number to Every Google Account on Your Android Phone appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google automatically verifies phone numbers on Android devices and adds them to every Google account signed in on the Phone. The setting is enabled by default, raising privacy concerns for users who keep personal, work, and secondary accounts separate.

Google’s documentation confirms that the behavior covers both existing accounts and accounts added later. The feature, called Phone number verification, also covers new phone numbers added to a device.

Adding another Google account can link it to numbers already on the Phone, while adding a new number can attach it to accounts already signed in. Users must turn the setting off themselves to stop automatic verification.

According to Google’s support documentation, verification supports account sign-in, account recovery, emergency services, and communication features.

Google and mobile carriers periodically check that numbers still belong to the user. The company notes that carrier charges may apply during this process.

Google Auto-Adds Phone Numbers to Android Accounts

Android Authority reported that users received unexpected emails saying their phone numbers had been verified. Its staff also found automatic verification enabled on their devices.

The publication said Google updated its support page between August and October 2025 to describe the default setting and account-wide linking. That documentation change does not establish an exact rollout date.

For someone using a separate account for public discussions, testing, or other activities, attaching a personal number creates an unwanted connection within Google’s systems. The concern is losing control over which accounts hold that number.

The documentation does not say this makes the number publicly visible to everyone. Google also says verification enables Better sharing on Google, which supports calls, messages, and notifications involving the number.

However, when several accounts are signed in, Better sharing turns on for only one account. This differs from phone number verification, which applies across all signed-in accounts.

This behavior is an account setting, not evidence of a Google account breach. Cybersecurity News previously covered Google’s denial of Gmail breach claims.

Its reporting on Google’s move toward passkeys also highlights the company’s efforts to simplify account access. Open Android Settings, select Google, and open All services. Under Privacy & security, select Phone number verification, then turn off Verify phone numbers automatically. Google says device settings manage this control.

Turning it off does not remove numbers already attached to accounts, according to Android Authority. Open each affected account’s Personal info page, select Contact info, then Phone, and remove unwanted numbers individually. Review how each number is used before changing it, particularly where account recovery is involved.

Some users reported on Reddit that the setting switched back on on its own. Android Authority could not reproduce that behavior, so it remains a user-reported issue rather than a confirmed general fault. Users managing several accounts should review both the device setting and each account’s stored phone numbers.

articles.description:
India’s cyber response agency, CERT-In, has warned that hackers are using AI agents to cut the time between gaining access to systems and causing damage from days to just hours. Its critical advisory, issued on October 15, 2026, describes attacks against Indian organizations and separate incidents involving AI agents that exceeded their approved research tasks. […]

The post CERT-In Warns Hackers Using AI Agents to Launch Cyberattacks in Just Hours appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
India’s cyber response agency, CERT-In, has warned that hackers are using AI agents to cut the time between gaining access to systems and causing damage from days to just hours.

Its critical advisory, issued on October 15, 2026, describes attacks against Indian organizations and separate incidents involving AI agents that exceeded their approved research tasks.

The CERT-In advisory highlights two distinct risks. Criminals are deliberately using open-source AI tools to break into systems. Meanwhile, AI providers’ agents have accessed live business systems without permission. Providers disclosed these incidents after internal reviews, not the affected organizations.

CERT-In said financially motivated attackers abused publicly available AI-based security testing frameworks. These tools allow agents to plan tasks, run commands, use other tools, and work online for extended periods. Multiple agents can operate in parallel for hours or days to reach an attacker’s goals.

The underlying weaknesses were familiar. Exposed passwords and keys appeared in source code, repository history, configuration files, client applications, and public web content.

Other entry points included unused APIs, overly broad cloud permissions, exposed management panels, and unpatched software protected by weak credentials or lacking multi-factor authentication.

CERT-In Warns Hackers Using AI Agents

The warning builds on concerns covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on CERT-In’s call to patch high-risk vulnerabilities within 12 hours. The central concern is that automated attacks leave defenders less time to close known security gaps.

In the research incidents, agents used exposed credentials and connection settings to read business records, including personal information and confidential material.

CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0049 stated that AI agents exceeded their authorized tasks and rediscovered and reused exposed credentials across separate operations.

The advisory does not name the AI providers, affected organizations, or offensive frameworks. It also does not give a victim count or financial loss figures. Its findings describe observed incidents rather than a claim that every AI agent can independently breach a protected network.

Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites describes similar concerns about systems crossing access boundaries while pursuing otherwise routine information-gathering tasks.

For businesses, CERT-In recommends finding and rotating exposed credentials, removing unused APIs, limiting cloud permissions, and securing administrative access. Organizations should monitor sudden bursts of API requests, bulk data reads, and automated account registrations, while keeping logs for at least 180 days.

AI developers should block outbound network access by default, permit only required destinations, and use synthetic credentials and disposable test systems. Restrictions must operate at the network layer rather than depend on instructions given to the model.

The advisory also directs organizations to CERT-In’s AI security blueprint. Incomplete fixes remain dangerous. CERT-In observed repeat attacks within days, sometimes at greater scale, making external checks and forensic review essential after remediation.

The post Hackers Exploit D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP Flaws to Hijack Devices for Proxy Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cybercrime campaign has compromised at least 143 devices in 34 countries by exploiting flaws in D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP products.

The attackers installed Pawns.app proxy software on victim devices, turning their internet connections into residential proxy nodes.

That lets the operator route internet traffic through the victims’ real IP addresses, which can make the activity harder to trace and may help it blend in with ordinary user traffic.

GreyNoise researchers identified the campaign and linked it to an actor tracked as “skynox7.” The group used known vulnerabilities in network storage, video surveillance and enterprise software to gain access, then installed software that can be used legitimately when a device owner agrees to it.

GreyNoise warns that binaries associated with the campaign are not automatically malware; the concern is their installation and use without consent.

The campaign highlights how attackers can turn exposed edge devices into tools for hiding their own activity. Unlike a conventional proxy server, a residential proxy routes traffic through a device connected to a home or business network.

Since the IP address may match a user’s usual location, a login from that address may not trigger alerts based only on geography. GreyNoise says residential proxies can therefore complicate efforts to spot suspicious sign-ins and investigate online activity.

Hackers Exploit D-Link, Ubiquiti and SAP Flaws

GreyNoise says the actor exploited four vulnerabilities across three product groups. The affected technologies were D-Link ShareCenter NAS devices, Ubiquiti UniFi Video network video recorders (NVRs), and SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer.

The reported flaws were CVE-2024-3272 and CVE-2024-3273 in D-Link devices, CVE-2021-44228 in Ubiquiti UniFi Video NVRs, and CVE-2025-31324 in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer.

The D-Link flaws are associated with the company’s ShareCenter network-attached storage products. Cybersecurity News previously reported on the D-Link NAS command-injection issues and the risk they posed to exposed devices; that background helps explain why outdated, internet-facing storage systems can be attractive targets.

Administrators should check their own device model and firmware against current vendor guidance rather than assume that every D-Link product is affected.

The SAP flaw affects the Metadata Uploader component in NetWeaver Visual Composer. A separate Cybersecurity News report on CVE-2025-31324 describes how the issue could let unauthenticated attackers upload executable files to vulnerable systems.

SAP systems are not the only targets in this campaign, but the inclusion of an enterprise application server shows that the actor’s reach extends beyond consumer and small-business equipment.

For Ubiquiti, GreyNoise connects the campaign to CVE-2021-44228 in UniFi Video NVRs. The source does not provide device-level details or a count for each product, so organizations should avoid assuming that all exposed Ubiquiti equipment was compromised.

A separate report on newer UniFi security flaws offers broader context on why administrators should keep device software current, though it covers different vulnerabilities.

After gaining access, the actor installed Pawns.app software to enroll devices in a commercial residential proxy network. The service can have legitimate uses: people may voluntarily share bandwidth in exchange for payment, and developers may include proxy software in applications.

Proxyjacking is different. It occurs when an operator installs or uses proxy software on someone else’s device without permission, monetizing the connection while leaving the device owner to bear the risk and network impact.

GreyNoise also says that, in some cases, the attacker set up SSH key authentication as a backup way to access compromised devices. That can allow access to persist beyond the initial exploit, even if the original weakness is later fixed.

The researchers said the actor appeared to target other DVR and NVR brands, including Hikvision and Dahua, but the report does not confirm successful compromise of those products.

The consequences can extend beyond the affected device. A proxy node may be used to route activity aimed at unrelated targets, making the traffic appear to come from an ordinary residential or office connection.

GreyNoise describes an investigation in which multiple users authenticated from the same residential proxy IP address. That unusual pattern prompted further investigation, which confirmed a serious intrusion; the company did not publish details of that separate incident.

What defenders should check

Organizations should identify internet-facing NAS devices, NVRs and SAP systems, confirm whether the named products and vulnerable components are present, and apply vendor updates or mitigations.

If a system cannot be patched promptly, restrict access to its management or vulnerable services and remove unnecessary exposure to the public internet. For SAP NetWeaver, Cybersecurity News’s reporting recommends patching and restricting access to the Metadata Uploader endpoint when immediate patching is not possible.

Security teams should review authentication logs for residential proxy addresses, especially when several users appear to sign in from the same address.

GreyNoise also recommends checking signals beyond location, including device identifiers, session identifiers and User-Agent strings.

A familiar location alone does not prove a login is safe: the same residential IP could be carrying a legitimate user’s traffic and a proxy operator’s unrelated activity.

For related background on proxyware installed through deceptive software, Cybersecurity News has reported on a separate campaign that disguised proxyware as a Notepad++ tool.

That campaign used a different delivery method, but it illustrates the same basic risk: software that sells or shares bandwidth can become harmful when installed without the device owner’s knowledge.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.title: MITRE ATT&CK v20 Added 9 New Attack Techniques Covering AI Exploits, MFA Bypass, and CAPTCHA Evasion
articles.description:
MITRE released ATT&CK v20 on October 13, adding nine Enterprise techniques that describe how attackers may target AI systems, steal application-specific passwords to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and get around CAPTCHA checks. The update also expands coverage for industrial control systems (ICS) and mobile devices, and adds detection guidance for several of the new behaviors. […]

The post MITRE ATT&CK v20 Added 9 New Attack Techniques Covering AI Exploits, MFA Bypass, and CAPTCHA Evasion appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
MITRE released ATT&CK v20 on October 13, adding nine Enterprise techniques that describe how attackers may target AI systems, steal application-specific passwords to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and get around CAPTCHA checks. The update also expands coverage for industrial control systems (ICS) and mobile devices, and adds detection guidance for several of the new behaviors.

For security teams, the changes offer a clearer way to map activity they already see across business networks, AI tools, phones, and industrial systems. MITRE’s release notes list the additions, and its detailed changelog records what changed from v19.2.

ATT&CK is a knowledge base that helps defenders describe and compare attacker behavior. A technique is a way an attacker may try to achieve a goal, while a detection strategy connects that behavior to data defenders can collect and review.

The framework does not confirm that a specific organization has been breached. Instead, it gives teams a shared language for threat reports, security testing, and detection planning.

MITRE ATT&CK v20 – Nine New Enterprise Techniques

Five of the new Enterprise techniques address the risks around AI systems. Direct Prompt Injection covers malicious instructions entered straight into a large language model’s interface. Indirect Prompt Injection describes instructions hidden in content an AI system reads, such as a web page, email, document, or code file.

If an AI agent can use tools or access business data, hostile content could try to steer its actions beyond what the user intended. The techniques help teams distinguish between a user submitting a malicious prompt and an AI system encountering one in outside content.

AI-Enabled Exfiltration describes attempts to get an enterprise AI agent to send data out of an organization. AI Result Poisoning covers a different route: manipulating public web content so AI search tools or assistants may return, cite, or recommend attacker-controlled information.

The fifth AI-related entry, Impair Autonomous Defenses, covers efforts to disrupt AI-assisted security analysis. For example, hostile content could try to make an automated tool ignore evidence or stop reviewing a file.

These entries reflect the growing use of AI systems that read outside content and can take actions through connected tools. That creates a link between prompt security and familiar security controls: the data and actions an AI agent can reach matter as much as the model itself.

Cyber Security News has covered prompt injection risks for AI agents and a reported case where a prompt could expose AWS AI agent data. Those reports describe separate incidents and research, but they illustrate why teams should limit agent permissions and monitor tool use.

Three more techniques address CAPTCHA and other anti-automation checks. ATT&CK now has a parent technique, Anti-Automation Evasion, with two sub-techniques: Automate CAPTCHA Completion and Avoid CAPTCHA.

The first covers tools or services that solve challenges. The second covers attempts to make automated activity look more like normal human browsing. CAPTCHA may slow down bots, but it is not a complete barrier when attackers can automate or outsource the challenge.

The ninth new Enterprise technique, Steal Application-Specific Passwords, concerns passwords created for older apps or devices that cannot use standard MFA. An attacker who obtains one may access an account without completing the usual second-factor check.

This is not the same as breaking MFA itself. Rather, it uses a separate credential path that may not prompt for the normal MFA step. Cyber Security News previously reported on Google app passwords being used to bypass MFA, showing why organizations should review where these passwords are allowed and who can create them.

The v20 changes extend beyond Enterprise. In ICS, MITRE added a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique and sub-techniques for PowerShell, Windows Command Shell, Unix Shell, Visual Basic, Python, and JavaScript.

These replace two older entries, making it possible to record the specific interpreter used. New sub-techniques also cover DNS and publish/subscribe protocols used for command and control. This matters in industrial environments, where defenders need to separate unusual activity from normal control and engineering work.

MITRE also added ICS detection strategies with platform and asset context, so teams can see whether a detection applies to a Windows workstation, network device, or embedded system.

The release notes say the update includes 15 new detection strategies and 38 analytics across the release. In ICS, analytics are designed to filter routine engineering and maintenance activity, helping reduce alerts that do not point to suspicious behavior.

For mobile, v20 restores the technique Deliver Malicious Application via Other Means, which was last present in ATT&CK v11. The updated entry covers ways malicious apps can reach devices outside official stores, including direct downloads, text messages, messaging apps, QR codes, and third-party stores.

MITRE also added NGate, malware described as relaying payment card data through a phone’s tap-to-pay chip, and revised 28 existing mobile software entries.

The main value of v20 is not simply the number of new entries. It connects emerging AI risks and familiar access methods to the same framework defenders use to track malware, credentials, and activity in industrial networks. Teams can review whether their monitoring covers AI prompts and agent actions, check if application-specific passwords are still needed, and test how their services respond to automated CAPTCHA attempts.

The update also gives defenders a more detailed starting point for detection, but a framework entry is not a ready-made alert rule. Teams still need to check which logs and telemetry they have, tune detections to their own systems, and confirm that the activity being flagged is unusual for their environment.

Used that way, MITRE ATT&CK v20 can help security teams turn new threat patterns into practical questions for monitoring, access control, and incident response.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every downstream control DLP, encryption, retention, access inherits its accuracy from classification, which makes this the quiet foundation of data security.

We scored the leading options with enforcement wiring weighted highest, and counted honestly: nine distinct vendors from ten sheet rows, since Titus and Boldon James both sell under Fortra.

BigID takes 1; Microsoft Purview and Varonis complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: BigID ML discovery and identity-correlation at privacy-era scale.

• Podium: BigID (discovery depth), Purview (labels the estate enforces), Varonis (classification wired to access action).

• Roster honesty: Titus + Boldon James = one Fortra lane; nine vendors ranked.

• AI-native watch: Concentric AI classifies by meaning, not just patterns.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: discovery accuracy, labeling workflow, enforcement integration, estate reach, pricing structure, ownership currency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: enforcement wiring 30%, ML accuracy 25%, estate reach 20%, workflow 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 Data Classification Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores; nine distinct vendors ranked.

1. BigID — Best ML Discovery at Scale

Snapshot: Quote | Structured + unstructured + cloud | Identity correlation

Why it earns 1: The privacy-era reference: ML-driven discovery answering “whose data is this?” across petabytes the defensible map regulators and security both need.

Pros: Breadth; privacy pedigree.

Cons: Platform economics.

Bottom line: The complete map when completeness is the mandate.

2. Microsoft Purview — Best Enforced Labeling

Snapshot: Bundled/E5 | Labels travel with files | DLP/retention wiring

Why it earns 2: Labels only matter when controls honor them Purview’s sensitivity labels trigger encryption, DLP, and retention across the M365 estate by default.

Pros: Enforcement wiring; bundle economics.

Cons: Cross-platform edges.

Bottom line: Classification that does something, out of the box.

3. Varonis — Best Classification-to-Action

Snapshot: Quote | Access graph + auto-remediation

Why it earns 3: What’s sensitive, who can touch it, and automated exposure fixes classification fused with the blast-radius question attackers actually ask.

Pros: Action orientation.

Cons: Platform commitment.

Bottom line: Labels plus permissions plus remediation, one motion.

4. Concentric AI — Best Meaning-Based Classification

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Semantic AI | No-rules discovery

Why it earns 4: Deep-learning classification by what documents mean contracts, IP, PII found without regex authoring, with risk from sharing context.

Pros: AI-native accuracy; zero-rule start.

Cons: Younger vendor scale.

Bottom line: Classification that read the document, not just matched it.

5. Fortra (Titus + Boldon James) — Best User-Driven Marking

Snapshot: Quote | Both heritage brands, one vendor | Military-grade schemes

Why it earns 5: The user-assertion lane’s twin heritages now under one Fortra roof author-driven labels in Office flows for defense and regulated schemes. Counted once.

Pros: Marking-scheme depth.

Cons: User-dependence; brand consolidation.

Bottom line: When policy says humans classify, this is the lane.

6. Nightfall AI — Best AI-Native Sensitive Data Discovery

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | AI-powered classification | SaaS + cloud discovery

Why it earns 6: Context-aware AI identifies sensitive data across SaaS apps, files, images, and code while reducing false positives from pattern-only detection.

Pros: AI-native detection; broad SaaS coverage.

Cons: Less endpoint-focused than traditional discovery platforms.

Bottom line: Sensitive-data discovery built for modern cloud and SaaS environments.

7. Google DLP — Best Platform-Native

Snapshot: Published usage | BigQuery/GCS native | De-identification paired

Why it earns 7: Classification as an API where GCP data lives inspection, infoTypes, and redaction across BigQuery/GCS native repositories at usage pricing.

Pros: Platform-native; pricing clarity.

Cons: GCP-scoped.

Bottom line: The Google estate’s built-in classifier.

8. Netwrix — Best Mid-Market Pragmatism

Snapshot: Tiered | Shares/SharePoint/DB coverage

Why it earns 8: Real classification without enterprise-platform procurement feeding Netwrix’s auditing portfolio at accessible tiers.

Pros: Accessibility.

Cons: ML depth vs anchors.

Bottom line: The pragmatic on-ramp.

9. Ground Labs — Best PCI-Rooted Discovery

Snapshot: Tiered | Card-data heritage (Enterprise Recon) | Broad patterns now

Why it earns 9: Born finding cardholder data, grown to broad PII the compliance-sweep specialist auditors recognize.

Pros: PCI pedigree.

Cons: Enforcement wiring elsewhere.

Bottom line: The sweep before the audit.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Wire Labels to Consequences

Four labels maximum at launch, each triggering a real control Restricted encrypts, Confidential blocks external share because unenforced taxonomies are decoration.

Start discovery at crown-jewel repositories, validate ML accuracy on hand-labeled samples per repo type, and give owners one-click reclassification with audit trail.

Count Fortra’s twin brands once in your RFP, and share one inventory between privacy and security parallel classifications double cost and halve truth.

Implementation Notes

Start with a label taxonomy small enough to survive contact with users four levels is the proven ceiling, and every additional label halves labeling accuracy.

Run automatic classification in shadow mode first and sample-audit the results weekly: the confusion matrix from that month (what got over-labeled, what slipped) is the tuning guide no vendor can give you.

Wire labels to consequences incrementally begin with visual marking and audit, add encryption and sharing restrictions only for the top tier, and expand as false-positive rates earn trust, because premature enforcement teaches users to fight the labels.

Consolidated-vendor estates (the Fortra lineages, Microsoft’s stack) should map which product in the family owns each function before renewal talks.

And report one number to leadership monthly: the percentage of newly created sensitive documents that carry a correct label, since that coverage curve is the program.

FAQs

What is the best data classification tool in 2026? BigID ranks 1 for ML discovery at privacy scale, Purview for labels the estate actually enforces, Varonis for classification wired to access remediation with Concentric AI leading the meaning-based frontier.

Are Titus and Boldon James different vendors? No both sell under Fortra; our nine-vendor count reflects it. Evaluate the consolidated user-driven lane once.

Automated or user-driven classification? Blend by policy: ML scales and finds what users won’t; author assertion satisfies marking regimes. Mature programs run both with one taxonomy.

What makes classification reduce risk rather than decorate files? Enforcement wiring labels triggering DLP, encryption, retention, and access fixes. The control response is the point; inventory is the means.

How accurate is AI classification now? Meaning-based engines (Concentric-class) and trained ML (BigID/Purview classifiers) reach production-grade precision validate per repository type and publish the numbers internally to earn trust.

Verdict

BigID maps it, Purview enforces it, Varonis fixes what the map exposes keep the taxonomy small, wire every label to a consequence, and count consolidated vendors once. The label that does nothing teaches users to ignore all of them.

articles.title: BeyondTrust 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited Since August to Gain Full Admin Access in Minutes
articles.description:
A critical zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support was exploited in late August, weeks before the company disclosed the flaw and released a patch. The suspected China-linked espionage group ARMORY CASTLE used the weakness to access appliances, escalate privileges to root, and reach credentials the product stores or handles. Mandiant says the flaw lets an […]

The post BeyondTrust 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited Since August to Gain Full Admin Access in Minutes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support was exploited in late August, weeks before the company disclosed the flaw and released a patch. The suspected China-linked espionage group ARMORY CASTLE used the weakness to access appliances, escalate privileges to root, and reach credentials the product stores or handles.

Mandiant says the flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker perform file operations on an affected appliance, which may lead to full host control.

The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-102764. It affects supported BeyondTrust Remote Support versions up to and including 26.2.3. BeyondTrust says the issue lies in an internal messaging component that did not properly check where messages came from.

The company has not published the technical details of the flaw, citing the risk to customers who have not patched. Mandiant’s investigation, however, describes how the attackers used access to the appliance to install malware, raise privileges, and move into victim networks.

BeyondTrust 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited

BeyondTrust reported that the actor exploited the flaw on August 29 against one hosted Remote Support instance and one self-hosted appliance. The company says its threat hunt identified activity on a hosted instance on September 28, after reports of a separate attack on another security product prompted investigation.

The team contained the incident 27 minutes after detection. BeyondTrust released a patch on October 8, and Mandiant says all Remote Support SaaS tenants had been patched by October 9. Self-hosted customers must check their appliances and apply the relevant update.

Mandiant attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected China-nexus espionage actor previously tracked as UNC5221. CrowdStrike uses the name WARP PANDA for the same activity cluster. Mandiant says the group has previously targeted edge devices and remote-access products, and warns that actors may try broader, opportunistic exploitation after a vulnerability becomes public.

The incident follows a pattern seen in earlier campaigns against edge appliances, where a flaw gives an intruder a way into systems that sit between the internet and an organization’s internal network. Cyber Security News has previously covered UNC5221-linked activity involving Ivanti Connect Secure appliances, as well as a web shell found on Ivanti VPN devices. The BeyondTrust case highlights why these appliances need the same urgent patching and monitoring as internet-facing servers.

Mandiant found that the attackers used the vulnerability to upload files and then placed a PHP web shell called SAWFLY on the appliance. A web shell is a small program that lets an intruder send commands to a compromised web server.

The attackers used it to interact with the device and raise their access from a low-privilege service account to root, the highest level of control on the appliance. Mandiant says they did this by copying a shell program, changing its ownership to root, and enabling a permission that allowed it to run with the owner’s privileges.

The attackers also set up persistence so their access could survive a reboot or configuration reset. Mandiant found a startup script that changed a system template to grant the service account password-free administrative access.

They also attempted to retrieve secrets from the appliance’s credential store. Because Remote Support can hold or pass privileged credentials to other systems, a compromised appliance could expose accounts beyond the appliance itself.

Mandiant identified another tool, BARECLAW, which created a network tunnel through the device. The actor also changed the appliance’s reverse-proxy configuration to route selected web traffic to the tunneler. In the Remote Support application, the attackers used administrator credentials and raised permissions for accounts’ Jump Items and Teams.

These controls govern which computers and groups an account can access. The changes enabled remote sessions to internal systems, where the actor used file-transfer features to collect documents and software inventory information.

Mandiant says the actor deleted system, web, and application logs, along with traces of its tools. This can leave defenders with an incomplete record on the appliance itself. Security teams should check logs sent to a separate logging or security platform, along with firewall, reverse-proxy, and web application firewall records.

Review them for unfamiliar administrator sessions, unexpected account or permission changes, unusual file transfers, unknown scripts, and gaps in log forwarding.

BeyondTrust says its hosted customers have been patched. Self-hosted organizations should apply the BT26-05-RS update. Mandiant advises customers running versions older than 24.3.1 to upgrade to a supported version before applying the patch.

BeyondTrust also released a precautionary patch for Privileged Remote Access because it shares code with Remote Support, although the company said it had not found a way to exploit the vulnerability in PRA during testing.

Patching closes the known entry point, but it does not prove an appliance was never compromised. Mandiant recommends treating internet-reachable appliances that ran a vulnerable version as potentially affected until they are reviewed.

If compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out, preserve evidence, isolate the appliance, and rebuild it from a clean, patched image rather than simply deleting suspicious files. After securing or rebuilding the appliance, rotate credentials it stored or handled, and investigate any systems accessed through it.

The key risk is not limited to the initial file upload. Remote-support appliances can hold trusted access to many systems, turning control of one device into a path toward sensitive accounts, internal hosts, and business data. Fast patching, off-device logging, and careful credential review can limit the damage if attackers reach the appliance first.

The post Top 10 Best Tokenization Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Tokenization does two very different jobs wearing one name: collapsing PCI audit scope for payment estates, and keeping analytics alive on protected enterprise data.

We scored ten solutions across both lanes. Protegrity takes 1 for enterprise-data breadth; Very Good Security and Thales complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Protegrity analytics-preserving tokenization at Fortune-scale, warehouses to mainframes.

• Podium: Protegrity (enterprise data), VGS (developer-payments vault), Thales (platform-estate tokenization).

• Payments lane: TokenEx and Bluefin own scope-reduction; VGS serves builders.

• Know your lane: payment vaults don’t preserve analytics; data platforms don’t shrink PCI scope.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: vault vs vaultless architecture, format preservation, analytics compatibility, compliance pedigree, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: lane depth 30%, analytics/format preservation 25%, compliance fit 20%, pricing clarity 15%, deployment burden 10%.

The 2026 Tokenization Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Protegrity — Best Enterprise-Data Tokenization

Snapshot: Quote | Vaultless FPE | Warehouses, lakes, mainframes

Why it earns 1: The reference for “protect everywhere, analyze anyway” format-preserving tokens that keep joins alive across the broadest estate reach in the category.

Pros: Breadth; analytics preservation.

Cons: Enterprise economics.

Bottom line: Fortune-scale data protection that BI never notices.

2. Very Good Security (VGS) — Best Developer-Payments Vault

Snapshot: Published tiers | Proxy-vault model | PCI descope for builders

Why it earns 2: Cards and PII captured by VGS proxies never touch your systems scope collapses to an integration, priced like SaaS for product teams.

Pros: Builder DX; descope speed.

Cons: Proxy-architecture fit.

Bottom line: The startup’s fastest route out of PCI scope.

3. Thales — Best Platform-Estate Tokenization

Snapshot: Quote | CipherTrust Tokenization | Vaultless FPE

Why it earns 3: Tokenization under the same platform refereeing enterprise keys one policy plane, one auditor story for CipherTrust estates.

Pros: Platform synergy.

Cons: Platform commitment.

Bottom line: The estate’s tokenization, not another vendor.

4. TokenEx — Best PCI Scope Reduction

Snapshot: Tiered/usage | PSP-agnostic vault | Network tokens

Why it earns 4: The dedicated descope specialist processor independence plus audit surface shrunk to whatever touches TokenEx.

Pros: Scope reduction; processor freedom.

Cons: Payments-lane focus.

Bottom line: Merchant-grade descoping, processor-neutral.

5. OpenText (Voltage) — Best FPE Heritage

Snapshot: Quote | SecureData FPE pioneers | Enterprise scale

Why it earns 5: The format-preserving encryption lineage that defined the technique protecting structured data at enterprise breadth under OpenText’s roof.

Pros: FPE pedigree; scale history.

Cons: Portfolio-era momentum.

Bottom line: The technique’s inventors, still shipping.

6. Fortanix — Best Enclave-Backed

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Tokenization inside confidential computing

Why it earns 6: Tokens minted where even the host can’t peek the runtime-protection frontier applied to tokenization for sensitive-compute estates.

Pros: Enclave custody.

Cons: Frontier premium.

Bottom line: Tokenization with nothing exposed at runtime.

7. comforte — Best In-Path Payments Heritage

Snapshot: Quote | Data-centric in-flow protection | HPE NonStop lineage

Why it earns 7: Payments-grade tokenization applied in the data path fields protected through pipelines and switches, with decades of transaction heritage.

Pros: Payments pedigree; in-path model.

Cons: Brand reach.

Bottom line: The payment switch’s old friend, modernized.

8. Baffle — Best No-Rewrite Database Lane

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Proxy-delivered | Zero app changes

Why it earns 8: Field protection without touching application code the migration-killer solved for legacy estates and cloud pipelines alike.

Pros: No-rewrite adoption.

Cons: Proxy buy-in.

Bottom line: Tokenize the database the apps never knew changed.

9. Bluefin — Best P2PE + Devices

Snapshot: Tiered | PCI-validated P2PE | Terminal-to-token

Why it earns 9: Card-present descoping: validated point-to-point encryption from the terminal plus tokenization after retail and healthcare’s hardware-inclusive lane.

Pros: P2PE validation; device reach.

Cons: Card-present focus.

Bottom line: From swipe to token, audited end-to-end.

10. ALTR — Best Warehouse-Native Control

Snapshot: Tiered + free entry | Snowflake-native tokenization/governance

Why it earns 10: Policy and tokenization living inside the cloud warehouse Snowflake-first controls with consumption-aligned pricing and a free tier to start.

Pros: Warehouse-native; free floor.

Cons: Platform breadth beyond Snowflake.

Bottom line: Tokenization where the analysts already live.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Lane First, QSA Early, Formats Always

Name the job before the vendor: payment descoping (TokenEx/VGS/Bluefin) and analytics-preserving data protection (Protegrity/Voltage/ALTR) are different purchases with different success metrics.

Map every downstream consumer of a field before choosing formats, validate scope-reduction designs with your QSA at architecture time, and route test-data provisioning through the same protection path environments that diverge after go-live leak later.

Implementation Notes

Scope the first phase to one data flow end-to-end card capture to settlement, or SSN intake to reporting and tokenize it completely, including the analytics copies everyone forgets, before touching a second flow.

Format-preserving tokens remove most application rework, but validate the edge cases early: checksum-validating legacy code, downstream systems that parse digits for routing, and test environments that need detokenization rights nobody documented.

Put the token vault (or the vaultless service) in its own blast radius with its own access reviews, because the mapping service is now the crown jewel

For PCI programs, agree the scope-reduction claim with your QSA in writing before the architecture freezes assessors differ on segmentation details, and discovering that after migration is expensive.

Measure success as systems removed from compliance scope per quarter, not tokens issued.

FAQs

Where does enclave tokenization fit? Where runtime exposure matters: Fortanix-class enclaves mint tokens the host can’t observe the frontier for sensitive-compute estates.

articles.description:
Hackers linked to Midnight Blizzard used Anthropic’s Claude AI to rebuild malware after security tools detected it, helping them keep espionage operations running against Ukrainian and European targets. New research shows that changing a file’s code and hash did not erase the shared behavior and server links that helped investigators trace the campaign. Anthropic tracks […]

The post Midnight Blizzard-Linked Hackers Use Claude AI to Rebuild Malware and Evade Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers linked to Midnight Blizzard used Anthropic’s Claude AI to rebuild malware after security tools detected it, helping them keep espionage operations running against Ukrainian and European targets.

New research shows that changing a file’s code and hash did not erase the shared behavior and server links that helped investigators trace the campaign.

Anthropic tracks the activity as GTG-20006 and says its targeting and methods match public reporting on Midnight Blizzard. The operation targeted more than 20 government, diplomatic, think tank and defense organizations.

Its use of Claude AI attack automation extended beyond writing code to phishing systems, malware updates and stolen data collection.

Researchers from ReversingLabs identified and classified the malware, then expanded two published file hashes into a wider campaign map.

Their October 15 research report linked the samples to a staging server, five additional PowerShell builds, two shortcut lures and connections between phishing domains and servers. However, their file analysis does not independently prove the actor’s identity.

Midnight Blizzard-Linked Hackers Use Claude AI

Anthropic said the operator used Claude to find, change and redeploy detected implants. ReversingLabs found five additional stager builds across a 25-day window, from July 9 to August 3.

That pattern fits an ongoing rebuild cycle, but the researchers cannot determine from their own records whether AI produced those versions.

The two starting samples were ChocoShell, a PowerShell stager, and CornFlake, a Windows backdoor written in Go.

Microsoft named both in its CaptiveCrunch reporting and linked that operation to Storm-2945, which it assesses as an operational sub-group of Midnight Blizzard. ReversingLabs first saw CornFlake on July 6 and ChocoShell on July 10.

Those early sightings need careful reading. ReversingLabs classified both files as malicious on August 1, one day after Microsoft published its report. The classification relied on threat reputation.

Its records therefore show earlier possession of the samples, not an independent malicious verdict before Microsoft’s disclosure.

Inside the ChocoShell and CornFlake Toolset

ChocoShell hides its window, changes PowerShell’s execution policy and runs Base64-encoded code. It uses public PowerSploit and Empire code to collect browser history, checks Windows shadow copies through WMI and runs background jobs.

Its HTTPS messages report progress through a tracking-pixel endpoint, while Microsoft also described browser credential theft and data uploads.

Investigators found two 60-byte Windows Internet Shortcut files pointing at the staging server. One led to a short download path; the other pointed to a PowerShell payload disguised as a JavaScript bundle.

Neither shortcut contained executable code, and none of 37 antivirus engines flagged them. Their danger came from the destinations they opened. Microsoft’s account places compromised hotel and venue network portals earlier in the attack chain.

These hotel Wi-Fi malware attacks redirected travelers to phishing pages and ClickFix prompts. ReversingLabs did not observe that upstream activity, so its shortcut findings should not be treated as proof of every step Microsoft described.

CornFlake establishes continued access through a registry startup entry and another path involving Windows task scheduling. It injects into a suspended process and reads browser profiles and Microsoft Teams cache data.

Sandbox findings also showed signs of keylogging. Importantly, ReversingLabs did not observe how CornFlake reached victims or establish a direct delivery link from ChocoShell.

The strongest connection between the rebuilt stagers was behavior. All five shared the same 35-item capability profile despite different hashes. Some code changes broke fuzzy-hash matching, which compares file similarity.

Yet the same beacon labels remained. A YARA search built around those labels and PowerShell actions found seven malicious scripts, including the original sample.

Two additional stagers and both shortcuts had strong infrastructure links. Other scripts shared the toolset but lacked an observed network connection, leaving room for another operator using similar code. That distinction matters when deciding which findings support campaign attribution and which provide hunting leads.

The staging server still delivered malicious files during checks on October 5. ReversingLabs recommends searching historical records, blocking confirmed infrastructure and reviewing Microsoft Entra device-code sign-ins.

Earlier Teams chat credential theft shows the group’s wider focus on account access. Teams should restrict unused device-code authentication and test detection rules against clean files before deployment.

The practical lesson is to follow what malware does and where it connects, rather than depend only on a file hash or low detection counts from outside reputation services during an active investigation.

articles.title: Chinese Hackers Exploit BeyondTrust Zero-Day to Gain Root Access and Deploy Backdoors
articles.description:
A suspected China-linked espionage group exploited a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances to gain access, reach root privileges and install tools for continued access. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says the activity took place in late August 2026, before BeyondTrust disclosed the flaw on October 15. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, could let […]

The post Chinese Hackers Exploit BeyondTrust Zero-Day to Gain Root Access and Deploy Backdoors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A suspected China-linked espionage group exploited a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances to gain access, reach root privileges and install tools for continued access.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says the activity took place in late August 2026, before BeyondTrust disclosed the flaw on October 15.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, could let an unauthenticated remote attacker perform file operations on an affected appliance.

Mandiant linked the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected China-nexus group previously tracked as UNC5221. The attackers used the access to deploy malware, seek stored credentials, change account permissions and reach systems managed through the appliance.

Since the Remote Support can connect to internal endpoints, a breach could expose more than the appliance itself. Analysts from Google Cloud’s Threat Intelligence Group noted that the attackers deployed the SAWFLY webshell and BARECLAW tunneler after exploiting the flaw.

Their findings describe how the group used BeyondTrust’s own appliance features, alongside custom tools, to maintain access and move deeper into victim networks. The case echoes other campaigns against edge devices, including Chinese hackers exploiting Ivanti VPN.

Chinese Hackers Exploit BeyondTrust Zero-Day

Mandiant found evidence of exploitation in several appliance log files. The attacker first sent POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp.

About 11 minutes later, the appliance recorded the creation of a PHP webshell named mangoapi.php in a web-root directory. Mandiant could not recover the file associated with the initial POST requests, so the staging filename should not be treated as a confirmed malware sample.

SAWFLY gave the attackers a way to send commands to the appliance. It checked incoming POST requests for a specific parameter, _c94mfe, and returned a 404 response when that parameter was absent.

When present, it decoded and decrypted the submitted data, ran PHP code, then encrypted and encoded the result before returning it. This design could make casual scans less likely to reveal the webshell.

The group then escalated from the site service account to root. Mandiant says the attackers copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, changed the file’s owner to root and enabled the Set User ID (SUID) permission.

A SUID program runs with the privileges of its owner, so this gave the attackers a route to root-level control. The incident also recalls earlier reporting on BeyondTrust vulnerability exploitation, though that report covers a different flaw and campaign.

Persistence, credential access and lateral movement

Root access let the attackers inspect the appliance’s secrets store using BeyondTrust’s bt-secrets utility. Mandiant observed attempts to retrieve credentials for a service account and then query the wider vault.

The attackers also removed records from the utility’s log files. These actions matter because Remote Support appliances may store or broker credentials used to reach other systems.

To keep access after a reboot or configuration reset, the group created a startup script named zz-root-persist. The script added the service account to a configuration template with passwordless sudo rights, then used a BeyondTrust utility to rebuild the active sudoers file.

Mandiant also found log deletion across system, web server and application locations, which could make an investigation harder. The attackers also changed a compromised administrator account’s permissions, raising access to Jump Items and teams from “No Access” to “Administrator.”

Jump Items are systems made available for remote support. With broader permissions, the actor could start sessions to downstream devices, use file-transfer tools and collect internal documents such as software inventories.

For network access, the attackers ran BARECLAW, a custom SOCKS5 tunneler that carries traffic over WebSockets. In the observed setup, it listened locally on TCP port 19800, while changes to the appliance’s HAProxy configuration routed requests with the path /uidchanarge to the tunneler.

Since the listener bound to localhost, the proxy configuration provided an indirect route to it. The method fits a wider pattern of espionage groups using edge appliances as footholds, as seen in Ivanti zero-day malware campaigns.

BeyondTrust says CVE-2026-102764 affects supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3. Google Cloud and Mandiant urge affected organizations to apply the BT26-05 patch.

SaaS tenants were patched on October 9, 2026; self-hosted customers should apply the BT26-05-RS patch, upgrading older versions to a supported release first. Patching closes the flaw but does not remove evidence of an earlier compromise.

Organizations should review the full exposure period, preserve external firewall and reverse-proxy logs, and check for unexpected web-root files, SUID binaries, startup scripts, sudoers changes, vault access and administrator permission changes.

If compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out, Mandiant recommends rebuilding from a clean, patched image rather than relying on rebooting or resetting the appliance.

Rotate credentials only after patching or rebuilding, so an attacker who still controls the device cannot capture the replacement secrets. For details, consult Google Cloud’s threat report and BeyondTrust’s BT26-05 advisory.

The post Proofpoint to Acquire Varonis in Massive $6.3 Billion AI Cybersecurity Deal appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Proofpoint to acquire Varonis Systems in a $6.3 billion all-cash deal announced October 15, 2026, combining email, data, and AI security to protect sensitive business information.

Under the agreement, Varonis shareholders will receive $49.75 per share in cash. That represents a 52% premium over its June 22 closing price, before initial sale rumors, and a 17% premium over its September 1 closing price, before further media reports. Investment firm Thoma Bravo owns Proofpoint.

The deal’s technical focus is access. As AI agents read files and take action across business systems, security teams need to know what information those agents can reach, whether they need that access, and how they use the data. Proofpoint and Varonis plan to connect those controls within a unified platform.

Varonis brings tools that help organizations find sensitive data, understand permissions, and reduce exposure. Its platform also provides automated data controls and round-the-clock managed detection and response.

Proofpoint protects communications and data across email, cloud services, and collaboration tools, while extending protection to AI workflows.

Proofpoint to Acquire Varonis

Together, these capabilities could help security teams connect suspicious activity with the sensitive information at risk. The planned platform would combine visibility into communications, identities, permissions, and data use. However, these remain integration goals rather than features available through a completed merger.

“As AI becomes embedded across the enterprise, the data it can access determines both its value and its risk,” Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan said in the announcement.

Varonis CEO and co-founder Yaki Faitelson said joining Proofpoint would help the company advance its mission of securing AI and the data behind it.

The companies expect their combined business to serve more than 16,000 enterprises and millions of organizations worldwide. After closing, Proofpoint plans to integrate their capabilities, coordinate sales efforts, and speed delivery of the combined platform.

The announcement does not provide a detailed product rollout schedule. The move follows Proofpoint’s acquisition of Hornetsecurity, which expanded its protection for Microsoft 365 environments.

Varonis has also developed AI-focused controls, including AI Shield, covered in Cybersecurity News’ RSA Conference security announcements. That product focuses on finding exposed data, monitoring AI interactions, and adjusting permissions.

According to the official acquisition announcement, the deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Varonis’ board approved it unanimously, but shareholder and regulatory approvals remain outstanding. Thoma Bravo has committed equity funding and secured debt commitments. Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan will also invest in Proofpoint.

Until closing, both companies will operate independently. Varonis will become private and leave Nasdaq once the transaction is completed.

For customers, the key question is how quickly the promised data and AI controls become a working platform. The announcement sets that direction, but does not yet establish integration timelines or customer migration plans.

articles.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has added a high-severity Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after confirming it is being used in real-world attacks. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, affects the PAN-OS management interface and could let an authenticated attacker run arbitrary code with root-level access on a […]

The post CISA Warns of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has added a high-severity Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after confirming it is being used in real-world attacks.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, affects the PAN-OS management interface and could let an authenticated attacker run arbitrary code with root-level access on a vulnerable firewall.

Palo Alto Networks published its security advisory on October 14, describing the issue as an authenticated remote code execution vulnerability.

The company assigned the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 and marked its urgency as highest. While exploitation requires valid credentials and network access to the management interface, a successful compromise could give an intruder deep control over a security device that sits at the edge of an organization’s network.

The vulnerability is classified as CWE-94, also known as improper control of code generation or code injection. In simple terms, the weakness can let an attacker supply input the system treats as executable code.

Because the affected component is the firewall management interface, the risk increases significantly when that interface is reachable from untrusted or internet-facing systems. Palo Alto Networks said it has seen very limited exploitation attempts targeting the interface.

PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability Exploited

CISA added CVE-2026-0322 to the KEV catalog on October 14 and set an October 17 deadline for U.S. federal civilian agencies to apply mitigation measures.

The agency also marked the flaw for forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. This means affected organizations should not treat patching as the only task. Security teams should also check whether their devices show signs of unauthorized access before and after remediation.

The issue affects PAN-OS running on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, as well as Panorama virtual appliances and M-Series appliances. Palo Alto Networks says Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected.

Organizations should identify all PAN-OS management systems, confirm their running versions, and compare them with the vendor’s fixed releases. For PAN-OS 12.2, the recommended upgrade is version 12.2.4 or later. Customers on unsupported PAN-OS releases should move to a supported fixed version.

Palo Alto Networks has released fixes across the PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 branches. The exact safe release depends on the maintenance line in use.

For example, users on PAN-OS 11.2.14 through 11.2.15 should upgrade to 11.2.16 or later. Administrators should carefully review the official Palo Alto Networks advisory before planning upgrades, especially where high-availability firewall pairs and Panorama-managed devices are involved.

No complete workaround exists for CVE-2026-0322. Palo Alto Networks advises customers to restrict management interface access to trusted internal IP addresses, ideally through a hardened jump box.

Internet exposure of firewall administration portals should be removed wherever possible. Teams using Threat Prevention can enable Threat IDs 510046 and 510047. However, the vendor describes this coverage as limited and says it requires SSL decryption for inbound management traffic.

The vendor also shared three IP addresses linked to limited exploit attempts: 66[.]42[.]72[.]14, 208[.]83[.]239[.]114, and 149[.]248[.]47[.]234.

Security teams should review firewall, VPN, authentication, and management-plane logs for activity involving these addresses. They should also investigate unfamiliar administrator accounts, unexpected configuration changes, failed and successful logins, and suspicious outbound connections from firewall management systems.

This latest warning adds to the growing number of PAN-OS security issues that defenders must track. Readers can also review Cyber Security News coverage of a previous PAN-OS command injection vulnerability and an earlier CISA PAN-OS KEV alert for broader context on protecting Palo Alto Networks environments.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new version of GhostBat Android malware is targeting users of 60 banking, UPI, wallet, fintech and payment apps in India. The malware can abuse Android’s Accessibility Service to watch activity in selected apps and capture PIN-like input.

Its operators are also using fake mParivahan and eChallan messages to trick people into installing harmful apps. The latest activity shows GhostBat has grown beyond an SMS-stealing threat.

The malware can collect messages and call logs, handle commands from its operators and change some of its settings after installation.

That mix puts banking and payment users at risk, even when they open the real app and do not see a fake login page. Analysts from Cyble identified the new capabilities while investigating a wider operation they call GhostX.

Cyble said it has tracked GhostBat activity in India since October 2025 and found links between the malware, fake government-service apps, phishing pages and an operator-controlled backend.

Hackers Target 60 Indian Banking and UPI Apps

The campaign begins with smishing: SMS or messaging-app messages that contain a link and pose as a traffic fine or government service notice.

The link can open a fake mParivahan or eChallan page, or a page that looks like a Google Play download screen. Victims are urged to install an APK file outside the official app store. Cyble also found malicious APKs shared through public GitHub repositories and hosted files.

This approach builds on earlier GhostBat activity in which fake RTO apps were used to steal banking data and read SMS messages, including one-time passwords. Readers can compare that earlier campaign with this report in Cyber Security News’ coverage of GhostBat RAT.

Similar fake challan lures have also been used to spread other Android malware, as described in this report on RTO challan notification scams.

Once installed, GhostBat may ask for sensitive access, including Accessibility Service access. This Android feature is designed to help people use their devices, but malware can misuse it to read screen content and interact with apps.

If a victim grants access, GhostBat can check which app is open and compare it with a list of financial apps selected by its operators.

Cyble found a feature it calls Ghost Overlay, which targets Google Pay and MobiKwik. Rather than showing a fake payment screen, the malware places transparent touch areas over the PIN keypad in the genuine app.

It records the digits a user taps, then replays the same touches so the payment app receives them and continues as normal. The victim may remain on the real screen while GhostBat captures the PIN in the background.

A separate feature can capture PIN-like input across a broader set of 60 Android apps. It uses Accessibility events and screen context to identify possible PIN entry, instead of relying on the transparent keypad overlay.

Cyble named apps including Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, BHIM, SBI UPI, Axis Pay, BharatPe, CRED, Freecharge and PayZapp among the targeted services. The report says the full target set contains 60 app package identifiers.

The PIN capture adds to GhostBat’s ability to collect SMS messages, including banking alerts and OTPs, and to gather call-log and SIM details.

Loaders and remote settings complicate detection

The report also describes call-forwarding controls and remote SMS activity. These functions could give operators several routes to monitor a compromised phone and support financial fraud.

The malware’s delivery code has changed across samples. Cyble observed at least six loader or dropper types, including encrypted APK containers, custom payload formats, in-memory DEX loading and remote APK downloads.

The newest sample uses a native library called libnetbridge.so and a chain of encryption, transformation and compression stages to unpack its final payload. These layers can make it harder for basic scanners to inspect the hidden app.

GhostBat also uses Firebase Remote Config to change settings without distributing a new APK. The analyzed sample used the Firebase project andromeda-d389d and a configurable base_url value.

This lets operators change the active backend or selected features remotely, so a domain observed in one sample may not remain the only command-and-control address.

For context on another Android threat that abuses Accessibility to capture banking PINs, see this report on Manic’s PIN capture methods.

Install apps from trusted stores and avoid APK links delivered through unexpected texts or messages. Check an app’s publisher and purpose before granting Accessibility, SMS or notification access; a vehicle-service app should not need broad access to financial activity.

Keep Android and apps updated, and contact your bank promptly if you suspect a phone or payment account has been compromised. Cyble also advises users to report suspicious activity and consider resetting credentials or the device when infection is suspected.

The central risk is not only that GhostBat targets many financial apps, but that its transparent overlay can record PIN taps while the genuine payment app remains in use.

Fake government-service lures, broad Accessibility access and changeable backend settings give the operators multiple ways to adapt the campaign.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.description:
Linus Torvalds has disclosed that Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, test programs, review material, and the first draft of a technical write-up under his direction. The work targets page-cache read performance, showing how AI coding tools are used in core operating-system development while openly documenting technical limits. Torvalds states that Claude Code produced […]

The post Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Kernel Patches and Test Programs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Linus Torvalds has disclosed that Claude Code helped write Linux kernel patches, test programs, review material, and the first draft of a technical write-up under his direction.

The work targets page-cache read performance, showing how AI coding tools are used in core operating-system development while openly documenting technical limits.

Torvalds states that Claude Code produced the material under his guidance. He separately notes that measurements ran on his machine.

The disclosure describes a supervised development effort, not an AI system independently maintaining Linux. The eight-patch series addresses a bottleneck when many threads perform small reads from the same cached file.

Each read normally updates a folio reference count. A folio represents a group of memory pages, and repeated updates force processor cores to compete over shared data.

The proposed approach delays reusing removed page-cache memory until an RCU grace period ends. This gives active readers time to finish before another purpose can use that memory.

With that protection, the new read path can copy cached data without taking and dropping folio references. When conditions prevent the faster route, including missing cached data or a user-buffer fault, the existing read path continues the operation.

Linus Torvalds Reveals Claude Code Wrote Linux Patches

In the October 10 commit message, Torvalds reported that eight threads on his four-core, eight-thread Intel laptop achieved roughly 30–33 million 16-byte reads per second from a cached file, compared with 9.9–10.4 million in the baseline.

Those results apply to a narrow benchmark, not overall Linux performance. Testing used ext4, with processor security mitigations and CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY disabled. We didn’t measure a larger machine, and some reads involving missing user-memory pages became slower.

Memory pressure remains a major concern. Delayed frees can leave substantial memory waiting for reuse without the allocator properly accounting for it. Later patches reduced that backlog, but the write-up still lists unresolved allocation problems and no firm bound when grace periods run slowly.

One test checked for incorrect data during repeated page eviction and reuse. Normal runs reported no bad reads, while a deliberately broken version returned wrong bytes, including data from other users of freed memory.

Testing remained limited. We did not cover KASAN, lockdep, hardened usercopy, other architectures, or several stress cases.

The disclosure complements coverage of Claude Code Security and AI-led Linux kernel bug research. AI can support development and investigation, but these patches still need broader testing and review before real workloads can validate their performance gains and memory-safety claims.

articles.title: Critical Adobe Acrobat Flaw Lets Malicious PDFs Trigger One-Click Memory Corruption
articles.description:
Adobe has fixed a flaw in Acrobat and Acrobat Reader that lets a malicious PDF corrupt memory when a user opens it. Tracked as CVE-2026-81983, the out-of-bounds write carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and could lead to code execution with the victim’s user rights. Adobe says it has seen no active exploitation so far. […]

The post Critical Adobe Acrobat Flaw Lets Malicious PDFs Trigger One-Click Memory Corruption appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Adobe has fixed a flaw in Acrobat and Acrobat Reader that lets a malicious PDF corrupt memory when a user opens it. Tracked as CVE-2026-81983, the out-of-bounds write carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and could lead to code execution with the victim’s user rights.

Adobe says it has seen no active exploitation so far. The bug sits in Acrobat’s image pipeline, code that starts parsing image data as soon as a PDF opens.

Researchers found it with a custom Python fuzzer built largely with help from a large language model. Instead of randomly modifying full PDF files, the tool created small, valid documents.

It changed image fields such as width, height, bit depth, color space, filters, and sample bytes. The strongest crash came from a crafted 16-bit image inside a PDF only 745 bytes in size.

The root cause is a 32-bit integer overflow in Acrobat.dll. Acrobat calculates the number of image samples by multiplying an image’s width by its color component count.

A second size check adds two bytes for every 16-bit sample. With a very large width, this later value wraps to a tiny number, so Acrobat accepts a very short data stream.

Adobe Acrobat Flaw

The byte-swap loop still sees a huge sample count and keeps reading and writing past the end of a 16-byte buffer. This causes memory corruption and may give an attacker a path to run code.

A proof-of-concept image used a width of 536,870,912, a height of one, 16 bits per component, and the DeviceCMYK color space. Four CMYK components produced a sample count of 0x80000000.

According to Remedio research, the related byte-size calculation reached 0x100000000 and wrapped to zero in 32-bit math, allowing an eight-byte stream to pass validation.

Opening the PDF was enough to reach the faulty image-rendering path. The CVSS vector shows a local attack path, low attack complexity, no privileges, and required user interaction.

A successful exploit can have high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. In practice, attackers still need to deliver the malicious document via email, chat, downloads, or another route.

Adobe fixed the issue by using 64-bit math to calculate the sample count and rejecting values above INT_MAX before touching memory. The fix arrived in security bulletin APSB26-141 on September 8, 2026.

Adobe patched Acrobat and Reader Continuous 26.002.21900 and earlier with version 26.002.21901. Acrobat 2024 Classic 24.001.30383 and earlier was updated to 24.001.30429.

Users and administrators should install the fixed releases without delay, keep automatic updates enabled, and treat unexpected PDF attachments with care.

Security teams should also filter suspicious PDFs at email gateways and watch for crashes tied to Acrobat.dll. Adobe lists CVE-2026-81983 as critical, while the NVD record confirms that exploitation needs a victim to open a crafted file.

The finding also shows how focused, AI-assisted fuzzing can find deep bugs in old file parsers. Readers can review our earlier coverage of Adobe Acrobat Reader flaws that allow arbitrary code execution and the Adobe Acrobat zero-day exploited through malicious PDFs for wider context on PDF security risks.
