articles.description:
A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-97229 published by researcher Jonah Burgess shows how a flaw in GitLab’s CI/CD regular-expression compiler could be used to run commands on a vulnerable server. GitLab rates the issue Critical with a CVSS score of 10.0. The exploit code is publicly available, raising the risk for organizations that have not […]

The post PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab RCE Vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-97229 published by researcher Jonah Burgess shows how a flaw in GitLab’s CI/CD regular-expression compiler could be used to run commands on a vulnerable server.

GitLab rates the issue Critical with a CVSS score of 10.0. The exploit code is publicly available, raising the risk for organizations that have not yet installed the security updates.

The PoC targets GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. Its author reports testing the included exploit layout against the official Linux amd64 GitLab CE 19.4.1 image. The code uses GitLab’s CI lint endpoint, which checks CI/CD configuration files, as part of the exploit chain.

The exploit has an important access condition. The attacker needs permission to push a branch to a public project on the affected GitLab instance. The PoC then sends a later request to the CI lint endpoint without a token, cookie, or other authorization header.

Jonah Burgess says the command runs as GitLab’s git account, not as an administrator. The public code is an initial release, and its author says further analysis of affected configurations and other possible paths is ongoing.

PoC Exploit Released for Critical GitLab Vulnerability

GitLab’s advisory describes CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler. The PoC details a chain in which CI lint reads a crafted pipeline configuration from an attacker-controlled branch and processes a regular expression against specially named repository paths.

A Unicode path causes Ruby to compile the expression again after GitLab’s size check. The exploit authors say this leads to an integer overflow that redirects the regular-expression engine’s execution and reaches a command-execution function.

The repository reports that the test request usually ends with an HTTP 502 error because the worker process crashes after the command runs. That response alone does not confirm successful exploitation.

Jonah Burgess author’s tests, command output returned through a callback indicated execution. The PoC also requires substantial memory, and the published layout is specific to one GitLab build. The author warns that low memory or multiple concurrent requests could instead disrupt service.

GitLab says the flaw affects CE and EE versions 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. The company released those fixed versions on October 12, 2026, and strongly recommends that self-managed installations upgrade promptly.

GitLab.com is already running a patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action. Administrators should confirm their version and upgrade to the fixed release for their branch or a later supported version.

They should also review recent changes to CI/CD configuration files, especially new or modified regular expressions and project branches. GitLab’s earlier CI/CD regex security coverage and previous security-update reporting provide additional context on why these pipeline components deserve close review.

This PoC does not establish that the vulnerability is being used in real-world intrusions. However, it gives defenders a concrete reason to prioritize patching: the issue has the highest CVSS rating, and public exploit code describes a path from project write access to command execution on a vulnerable server.

articles.title: Critical Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Attackers Escape Virtual Machines and Take Control of Hosts
articles.description:
A critical flaw in the Linux kernel may allow an attacker-controlled virtual machine (VM) to breach its isolation boundary and impact the host system. This vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-99999 and referred to as PwnEscape by researcher Paulos Yibelo, originates from the Linux networking code rather than a specific hypervisor. Paulos Yibelo demonstrated a technique that […]

The post Critical Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Attackers Escape Virtual Machines and Take Control of Hosts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical flaw in the Linux kernel may allow an attacker-controlled virtual machine (VM) to breach its isolation boundary and impact the host system. This vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-99999 and referred to as PwnEscape by researcher Paulos Yibelo, originates from the Linux networking code rather than a specific hypervisor.

Paulos Yibelo demonstrated a technique that exposes host memory and, in their lab, progressed to host-level code execution. The flaw is serious for cloud providers and organizations that run untrusted workloads in virtual machines. VM isolation is meant to stop code inside one guest from reaching the host and other workloads.

PwnEscape shows how a weakness in a host’s packet-processing path can threaten that boundary, even when the underlying issue is not in the hypervisor itself.

PwnEscape Kernel Vulnerability

Linux can delay calculating a network packet’s checksum. This is a normal performance feature: packet metadata tells the kernel where the checksum operation should begin and where the result should be written.

According to Paulos Yibelo’s PwnEscape report, the problem occurred when less-trusted packet metadata could influence a later write into an IPv4 header. Linux had already processed the packet using the header’s earlier contents. But before fragmentation, the deferred checksum operation could change those contents. Later code then relied on the updated IPv4 header length.

In Paulos Yibelo’s test case, the packet initially appeared to have a standard 20-byte IPv4 header. After the deferred write, the header could be interpreted as 60 bytes long. The fragmentation code could then treat bytes beyond the packet’s valid linear data as part of the header and include them in an outgoing packet. He reported that this exposed 32 bytes of host memory.

That disclosure is not the same as code execution. The report describes a separate, controlled lab chain in which researchers used host-memory observations and carefully managed allocation behavior to demonstrate selected kernel-memory writes and run a host-root helper. They say this result was reproduced on researcher-owned systems, not as proof of root execution in a cloud provider’s production environment.

The distinction matters for readers assessing the risk. A host-memory leak can reveal information that should remain outside a guest’s reach. Further steps may be needed to turn that primitive into control of the host, and the report does not establish that every Linux VM or hypervisor is equally vulnerable.

The upstream Linux patch adds a check before certain checksum-completion operations. It verifies that the checksum start is not inside the IPv4 header. If the metadata fails the check, the kernel does not proceed with that checksum write along the affected path. The change covers several consumers, including IPv4 fragmentation.

The commit describes the change as a defense-in-depth measure. It also notes that stronger validation at packet input needs more work. In other words, the patch adds protection at places where the kernel completes checksums, but it is not presented as a full redesign of how all checksum metadata enters the networking stack.

Administrators should review their Linux vendor’s security notices and install an updated kernel that includes the fix. The upstream commit can help identify the change, but Linux distributions may backport security fixes to older kernel versions. A version number alone may not show whether a system is protected, so check the vendor’s advisory and confirm that the system is running the updated kernel.

PwnEscape reminds us that VM security depends on more than the hypervisor. Guest traffic also passes through host operating-system components, including networking code. When metadata can trigger a write later in packet processing, checks made earlier may no longer describe the packet that a later component sees.

The discovery emerged from Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, which invited researchers to test its isolation controls. Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai reported the Linux kernel flaw on the third day while working from a standard sandbox without special access. Vercel called it the program’s most important finding.

The challenge received 1,285 reports over two weeks and paid $242,000 in total bounties, with the kernel flaw accounting for its only critical-rated finding.

Cybersecurity News has also covered Vercel’s confirmation of a KVM escape report and a separate Linux vhost flaw with a public proof of concept. These are distinct issues with different causes. They should not be treated as interchangeable or assumed to be fixed by the same patch.

For defenders, the immediate step is to track vendor updates and patch Linux hosts that run virtual machines. The underlying failure was a mismatch between packet metadata and the IPv4 header that later code trusted. That makes the fix important not only for virtualization providers but also for teams that depend on Linux network processing to keep untrusted workloads contained.

articles.title: Burger King Japan Confirms Data Breach Exposing 11.18M User Records
articles.description:
Burger King Japan has confirmed a data breach that exposed about 11.18 million records linked to members of its official app. BK Japan, which operates the chain in Japan, said an outside party gained unauthorized access to the system used to manage app member information. The company disclosed the incident on October 15, 2026. According […]

The post Burger King Japan Confirms Data Breach Exposing 11.18M User Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Burger King Japan has confirmed a data breach that exposed about 11.18 million records linked to members of its official app. BK Japan, which operates the chain in Japan, said an outside party gained unauthorized access to the system used to manage app member information.

The company disclosed the incident on October 15, 2026. According to its notice, the unauthorized access occurred between October 2 and October 7, and the company confirmed the information leak on October 13. The disclosure concerns member records, not a verified count of unique people.

The exposed information includes member IDs, email addresses, registration type, prefecture, gender, dates of birth, full names in kanji and kana, and phone numbers. The affected fields also include whether members used mobile ordering and whether their email addresses had been verified.

The mobile ordering field describes whether someone used that feature. It should not be presented as evidence that detailed purchase histories or individual order contents were exposed. Likewise, a prefecture identifies a region within Japan, rather than necessarily revealing a complete home address.

BK Japan said it does not hold credit card numbers, so those details were not leaked in this incident. The company also said no leak of login passwords has been confirmed so far. That wording leaves the password finding subject to the ongoing investigation, rather than providing an unconditional guarantee.

How Burger King Responded

The company said it blocked the unauthorized access, formed a response team, and notified Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission. It is also emailing affected members about the incident.

Outside experts are helping investigate the cause and how the attacker first entered the system. BK Japan has not publicly identified an exploited vulnerability or confirmed whether stolen credentials were involved. The disclosed details do not establish ransomware, a payment system compromise, or a connection to another attack.

Reporting by Noticias SIN also cites the company’s plans to strengthen system security and monitoring while working with outside specialists. Those measures address future protection, but the investigation must still determine how the access occurred and which controls failed.

BK Japan said no secondary harm, including fraudulent use of the exposed information, has been confirmed. However, the combination of names, birth dates, phone numbers, and email addresses creates a clear risk of convincing phishing messages.

A scammer could use those details to make a fake Burger King refund, account check, or security alert appear genuine. Messages could direct users to a false login page or ask them to provide payment details. These are potential follow-up threats, not activity confirmed in this case.

The absence of confirmed misuse does not make leaked records harmless, especially when attackers can combine several personal details to make a message sound more believable to recipients.

Restaurant data breaches can expose personal information without exposing card numbers. Cyber Security News previously reported on a McDonald’s breach involving customer contact details in South Korea and Taiwan, while payment information was not included.

The publication also covered separate Burger King drive thru Assistant security flaws in 2025. That report concerned a different platform, and the available evidence does not connect those findings to the Japan app breach.

Affected members should treat unexpected emails, text messages, and calls claiming to represent Burger King with caution. Rather than following a message link, they should open the official app or type the company’s website address directly to check any account notice.

Members should not share passwords, payment details, or verification codes in response to unsolicited contact. Anyone who entered credentials on a suspicious page should change the affected password and replace it anywhere else it was reused.

For now, the key confirmed issue is the exposure of app member information. The initial access method and full technical cause remain under investigation. Future updates should clarify those gaps without confusing confirmed findings with possible risks.

articles.description:
A critical flaw in ChatGPT’s GitHub integration has the potential to turn a routine repository review into a secret-theft attack. A report published on October 15, 2026, describes a scenario in which manipulated repository instructions allegedly lead an AI agent to modify a different private repository and trigger GitHub Actions. According to the researcher Sunil […]

The post Critical ChatGPT GitHub Connector Flaw Could Allow Attackers to Steal Private Repository Secrets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical flaw in ChatGPT’s GitHub integration has the potential to turn a routine repository review into a secret-theft attack. A report published on October 15, 2026, describes a scenario in which manipulated repository instructions allegedly lead an AI agent to modify a different private repository and trigger GitHub Actions.

According to the researcher Sunil Tripathy’s disclosure, the setup involved two separate GitHub accounts. The attacker controlled a public repository containing hidden instructions. The victim account had connected GitHub to ChatGPT with access granted across its repositories.

Tripathy assigns the finding a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. That rating is his assessment, not a confirmed vendor classification. His disclosure says testing used researcher-owned accounts and a dummy secret, with no customer data or third-party systems affected.

A request to review the public repository reportedly caused the agent to follow those instructions as trusted commands. Instead of limiting its work to analysis, it committed a GitHub Actions workflow into a different, private repository using the victim’s existing access.

The workflow allegedly ran automatically and sent the test secret, AUDIT_CANARY, to an external server. Tripathy says the user neither named the second repository nor approved the write operation.

This is an indirect prompt injection scenario, where hostile instructions arrive through material an assistant reads. Earlier AgentFlayer research demonstrated related risks involving malicious documents and connected Google Drive data.

ChatGPT GitHub Connector Flaw

Tripathy reports that direct wording triggered a refusal, while instructions framed as deployment requirements succeeded. He says an innocent-looking workflow reference pointed to a separate custom action containing the data theft logic.

Additional reported outcomes included private repository discovery, attacker-written file commits, and recovery of attack instructions from Git history. These remain researcher-reported findings rather than independently verified results.

A key product distinction remains unresolved. OpenAI’s GitHub documentation describes the standard ChatGPT GitHub app as read-only and directs users to Codex for editing and pushing code. That conflicts with the reported workflow commits, making the exact integration, permissions, and execution path essential to confirming the affected scope.

A separate, previously patched OpenAI Codex command injection flaw also exposed GitHub tokens, but involved unsafe branch-name handling rather than this reported prompt injection chain.

Tripathy says he first reported related behavior on September 4, demonstrated secret theft on September 28, and received an “out of scope” closure on October 14. He says the attack still worked when retested on October 15. These statements do not establish a vendor-confirmed vulnerability or patch status.

For defenders, the clearest precaution is limiting connected repository access to what each task needs. OpenAI confirms that repository access can be changed through GitHub app settings.

Tripathy also recommends reviewing unexpected workflow commits and rotating potentially exposed secrets. His control test reportedly blocked cross-repository writes when access was narrowed to one repository, supporting restricted permissions as a practical safeguard against the demonstrated attack path.

articles.description:
Citrix has disclosed four XenServer vulnerabilities, including three that could let a malicious user with elevated rights inside a virtual machine compromise or crash the underlying host. Citrix published the high-severity bulletin CTX697170 on October 13, 2026, covering XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9. Citrix lists the advisory in its XenServer security bulletin archive. The host-impacting […]

The post Citrix XenServer Vulnerabilities Could Allow Malicious VM Users to Compromise Host Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Citrix has disclosed four XenServer vulnerabilities, including three that could let a malicious user with elevated rights inside a virtual machine compromise or crash the underlying host.

Citrix published the high-severity bulletin CTX697170 on October 13, 2026, covering XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9. Citrix lists the advisory in its XenServer security bulletin archive.

The host-impacting flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-79610, CVE-2026-102700, and CVE-2026-102701. A fourth issue, CVE-2026-79611, has a narrower effect. According to the supplied bulletin, it may allow an unprivileged user inside a guest virtual machine to crash that same guest.

The three host-impacting vulnerabilities require a privileged user within a guest VM. This places the stated threat inside the virtual environment rather than describing an unauthenticated attack against an internet-facing service.

Citrix XenServer Vulnerabilities

The bulletin groups these flaws as issues that may enable host compromise or a host crash, without assigning a specific outcome to each identifier.

That separation matters when assessing exposure. A guest-only crash affects the virtual machine where the attacker operates. A host-level issue reaches the system supporting the virtual environment, broadening the potential impact.

However, the supplied advisory does not establish that every flaw allows code execution or that attackers can automatically access other guests.

CVE-2026-102700 affects XenServer 8.4 only. The remaining three vulnerabilities affect both XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9. Administrators therefore need to check the installed release before deciding which identifiers apply to their systems.

The disclosure follows earlier warnings involving guest access and host stability. Cybersecurity News previously covered a Citrix XenServer and Hypervisor vulnerability that allowed malicious guest administrators to crash or leave a host unresponsive. That earlier issue involved different identifiers and affected releases, so it should not be confused with this update.

Separate reporting on XenServer VM Tools for Windows vulnerabilities described flaws that could raise an attacker’s privileges within a Windows guest. Those issues affected guest drivers, not the host-level impact described in the latest bulletin.

Security teams should use CTX697170 as the reference for this disclosure and consult the latest vendor guidance before planning remediation.

Citrix’s bulletin archive recommends applying published security updates promptly. The supplied XenServer excerpt does not identify fixed builds, patch package names, or restart requirements, so those details should not be assumed.

The provided material also contains no exploit instructions, technical root-cause details, or statement confirming active exploitation. For readers assessing urgency, the confirmed concern is the stated possibility of host compromise or disruption from a privileged guest account, alongside a separate guest-only denial-of-service risk.

articles.description:
Hackers are using ClickFix tricks to install malware loaders and Python tunnels on Windows systems, creating access that could support ransomware attacks. A late September incident shows how a user running a command can start an infection chain built around trusted Microsoft programs, hidden code, and encrypted network traffic. The attack was stopped before ransomware […]

The post Hackers Use ClickFix and Python Tunnels to Prepare Systems for Ransomware Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using ClickFix tricks to install malware loaders and Python tunnels on Windows systems, creating access that could support ransomware attacks.

A late September incident shows how a user running a command can start an infection chain built around trusted Microsoft programs, hidden code, and encrypted network traffic.

The attack was stopped before ransomware reached the affected systems. However, the tools and methods matched activity previously linked to Vice Society, a cybercrime group associated with Rhysida ransomware.

That connection points to a likely ransomware goal, not proof that encryption occurred or that the group carried out this incident.

Researchers from Forescout identified Lorem Ipsum Loader during the investigation and examined five samples alongside 39 AxolotlLoader samples.

Their technical analysis of both loaders, published October 14, describes a new installer-based delivery method, shared command traffic, and important differences between the malware families.

Hackers Use ClickFix and Python Tunnels

ClickFix persuades people to run commands presented as verification steps or fixes. Its TerminalFix variant directs users toward Windows Terminal or PowerShell.

Earlier reporting on fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA prompts showed how this approach can lead to a reverse tunnel into corporate networks without exploiting a software flaw.

In the incident Forescout examined, ZIP archives contained a signed Microsoft executable, a malicious DLL, and a batch script.

Starting the trusted program caused it to load the nearby malicious library, a method called DLL sideloading. The script also created a registry startup entry and a scheduled task that ran hourly.

The malicious DLL carried an added section containing encoded instructions. A dictionary of 260 random five-letter words helped decode the hidden payload.

Another layer used XOR decoding, while an embedded JPEG acted as a decoy. These steps concealed the downloader before its code ran in memory. The loader then restored parts of a Windows library from a clean disk copy, a step intended to interfere with endpoint monitoring.

It launched another copy of its host program, injected code into that process, and ended the original process. A unique marker and mutex helped prevent duplicate instances.

Python Tunnel Gives Attackers a Route Back

To locate its command servers, Lorem Ipsum read encoded information from profiles on a legitimate public forum. This “dead-drop” method separated the server list from the malware itself.

After registration, the loader checked for tasks every five seconds, using traffic that claimed to come from Firefox. The final downloaded tool was a Python tunnel client. It connected over encrypted TLS traffic on port 443 and switched to WebSocket communication.

Related ClickFix Python proxy attacks have used different tools for a similar purpose: keeping a route into a compromised environment after the first infection.

Through the tunnel, the remote server could request TCP connections to specified destinations and relay data in both directions. Several connections could remain active at once.

Keepalive messages maintained access, while a shutdown command let the operator stop the client. Browser-like headers helped the connection appear less suspicious.

Forescout also found a separate delivery chain using a modified Teams MSI installer and two PowerShell stages. One script unpacked a GZIP-compressed payload, which then allocated memory and executed code.

Earlier coverage of fake Microsoft Teams installers documents another ransomware-linked campaign abusing the same trusted software brand, although its payloads differed.

The comparison found three AxolotlLoader variants spread across different host programs. Unlike Lorem Ipsum’s word-based encoding, Axolotl used embedded PNG data to decode shellcode.

Both families shared registration patterns and hosting links, but their code differed. Forescout considered an evolutionary relationship likely, while stressing that it could not confirm one. That distinction matters because a loader or tunnel does not prove ransomware execution.

Coverage of ClickFix ransomware lateral movement shows how other malware chains can support later activity, but investigators must establish each stage separately. Here, containment interrupted the chain before the suspected final payload arrived.

Forescout recommends user training alongside checks for unusual PowerShell process chains, DLL loads outside normal Windows folders, and matching registry entries and scheduled tasks.

Defenders should also review non-browser access to forum profiles and suspicious registration traffic. Shared hosting addresses and the reported TLS fingerprint should support investigation rather than serve as standalone proof of compromise.

articles.description:
A Chinese-run phishing network has been linked to one billion phishing emails targeting 75,000 organizations, according to a report published on October 14, 2026. The operation centers on Iron Man System, a paid phishing platform that lets criminals deploy fake websites and collect sensitive information without building their own tools. The report lists those headline […]

The post Chinese Phishing Network Linked to 1 Billion Messages Targeting 75,000 Organizations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Chinese-run phishing network has been linked to one billion phishing emails targeting 75,000 organizations, according to a report published on October 14, 2026.

The operation centers on Iron Man System, a paid phishing platform that lets criminals deploy fake websites and collect sensitive information without building their own tools.

The report lists those headline figures but does not explain their measurement period or counting method. Its detailed findings document 2,360 phishing templates covering 130 countries and areas.

These numbers describe the network’s reported reach and available tools, not confirmed breaches at every targeted organization.

Researchers from Resecurity identified and mapped the operation after buying a license and running the software in an isolated lab.

Their technical investigation into Iron Man describes a phishing kit rather than malware installed on victims’ devices. The team also entered communities managed by Chinese threat actors to investigate its developers and associates.

Chinese Phishing Network Linked to 1 Billion Messages

Iron Man System uses a Go backend and arrives as a container image, allowing buyers to run the package on their own servers.

Its Chinese-English control panel manages fake pages, brand settings, and license status. Researchers tested version 6.3.1, which displayed a subscription countdown and configured payment-related lures.

This commercial model lowers the skill needed to run phishing campaigns. Earlier reporting on Chinese language phishing services explains how ready-made templates and shared panels help criminals target several countries at once.

That wider trend provides context, but does not establish that separate services share Iron Man’s operators. The template library impersonated couriers, banks, tax agencies, retailers, telecom providers, and public bodies.

DHL had the largest individual template count, with 37, followed by DPD with 24 and Apple with 23. Delivery-related brands formed the largest category, reflecting the appeal of familiar parcel notices as phishing bait.

Comparable tactics appeared in the Panda Shop smishing kit, which used fake delivery and banking pages to collect financial information. Iron Man’s confirmed scope is distinct: its library included 551 lure-type tags, with entries updated as recently as October 1, 2026.

Exposed Builds Reveal Shared Infrastructure

Researchers found a publicly accessible Gitea server holding the kit’s code and container registry. It exposed 911 published image versions and eight registered accounts. Recent releases showed continued development, while matching project names tied the registry directly to the tested package rather than an unrelated mirror.

Build settings revealed S3-compatible storage and a MariaDB database configured on internal addresses. Static credentials appeared across historical builds, although Resecurity withheld their values.

Code analysis also linked product catalogs and uploaded images to captured records containing selected goods and payment-card fields.

The reusable design resembles the business approach described in the Darcula phishing service report, where subscribers receive branded templates and ongoing updates. However, the Iron Man findings do not establish that it uses Darcula’s messaging channels or shares its developers.

The lab panel checked its local license status roughly every 20 seconds, triggering server-side contact with the vendor’s authorization host.

This dependency offers defenders a central disruption point: disabling the licensing service could affect many deployments together instead of requiring separate action against each fake website.

Resecurity said Microsoft led the wider operation and its Digital Crimes Unit helped disrupt developers and infrastructure. Still, recent builds indicated ongoing activity. Attribution remains limited: the report links infrastructure and accounts, but confirms no operator’s real-world identity.

articles.title: Just Viewing an Online Ad Can Infect Your Device With Spyware, Researchers Reveal
articles.description:
Simply viewing an online advertisement can be enough to infect a device with powerful spyware, without the user clicking, downloading a file, or seeing any warning. Citizen Lab researchers documented what they call the first public technical proof of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The method, named “AdFection,” infected devices at international news […]

The post Just Viewing an Online Ad Can Infect Your Device With Spyware, Researchers Reveal appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Simply viewing an online advertisement can be enough to infect a device with powerful spyware, without the user clicking, downloading a file, or seeing any warning.

Citizen Lab researchers documented what they call the first public technical proof of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The method, named “AdFection,” infected devices at international news network Al Jazeera with spyware linked to Israeli vendor Candiru, which now operates as Integrity Labs.

According to the Citizen Lab investigation, published on October 15, 2026, at least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted during 2024 and 2025. Network logs showed that infected systems first contacted Discover-Tech infrastructure after an ad was displayed. They then connected to a Candiru validation server, which checked the device, followed by a command-and-control server used by the spyware.

0-Click Spyware Infects Devices

Discover-Tech is an Israeli company that presents itself as an advertising business. Citizen Lab says it acted as a link between the online ad market and several commercial spyware groups. Its Controlium platform allowed customers to target people through mobile advertising IDs, browser cookies, and IP addresses.

Once an ad loaded, code inside it could contact a Discover-Tech server. That server decided whether the visitor was a chosen target. If the details matched, it could return JavaScript that loaded more code and began the infection process. No click was needed.

This method works because modern ads are not always simple pictures or videos. They can include code for measuring views, tracking users, and loading content from other companies.

Real-time bidding systems also share data within a fraction of a second so advertisers can decide whether to buy an ad slot. That data may include a device ID, IP address, location, and browser details. AdFection used this design to find selected devices and send code only to them, making the activity harder for ad platforms and security researchers to catch.

The scale of the operation was far larger than the confirmed infections. Researchers examined about four billion Discover-Tech bidding records covering four months in 2026.

The company’s ads appeared on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android or iOS apps across dozens of countries. Millions of devices were also quietly directed toward Candiru-linked servers, likely for tracking and checks before possible targeting. However, seeing a Discover-Tech ad does not prove that a device was infected. Most viewers were not selected to receive the spyware code.

Investigators recovered a Windows DLL from one compromised device and linked it to Candiru with high confidence. The sample used COM hijacking to remain active and a distinct 48-byte repeating XOR method to hide strings. It also contained two command-and-control domains and shared key behavior with an earlier Candiru toolchain.

Its SHA-256 hash is 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8. Readers can find more background in Cyber Security News coverage of Candiru’s DevilsTongue spyware and this guide to dangerous malware types.

Citizen Lab also connected Discover-Tech with Intelos and Bindecy. A separate actor named DARK CARTOGRAPHER reportedly used the same infrastructure to link advertising IDs with phone numbers by abusing weaknesses at mobile carriers. That activity could reveal the real identity behind an advertising profile. Citizen Lab plans to publish further technical findings about this operation in a separate report.

The findings also raise serious questions about security checks inside the advertising industry. Discover-Tech had appeared on approved or certified vendor lists and served ads through major networks, including Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. After researchers shared their findings, Google removed Discover-Tech from its advertising platforms.

IAB Europe suspended it from its approved vendor list, while Beeswax removed it from its platform. Vungle paused access, and Eskimi blocked related accounts and domains.

For users and organizations, the case shows that careful clicking alone cannot stop every infection. Security teams should block known Discover-Tech and Candiru infrastructure, inspect unusual ad-related traffic, limit advertising IDs, and use trusted ad blocking.

Browser isolation and strict controls on third-party scripts can add protection on sensitive networks. People should also reset mobile advertising IDs and turn off personalized ads when possible. Citizen Lab urged ad companies to improve vendor checks, scan ad code, share threat data, and stop unknown third parties from running code without strong review.

AdFection changes the risk around online advertising because victims may do nothing beyond opening a normal webpage or app. The confirmed Al Jazeera infections show that targeted advertising can become part of a spyware delivery chain, while the huge reach of these ads shows why the issue goes beyond one newsroom.

Stronger advertising controls, faster platform action, and better network monitoring are now needed to prevent online ads from becoming hidden paths into user devices.

articles.title: AI Agents Create an Unseen Credential Surface That Exposes API Keys and Cloud Secrets
articles.description:
AI agents can expose API keys and cloud secrets during ordinary work, even when no malware is present. When an agent runs a command, reads a configuration file or fetches a secret to complete a task. Even sensitive data can move from protected storage into command histories, logs, agent transcripts and the model’s context. The […]

The post AI Agents Create an Unseen Credential Surface That Exposes API Keys and Cloud Secrets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
AI agents can expose API keys and cloud secrets during ordinary work, even when no malware is present. When an agent runs a command, reads a configuration file or fetches a secret to complete a task.

Even sensitive data can move from protected storage into command histories, logs, agent transcripts and the model’s context. The risk is easy to miss because the agent may use the same trusted tools as a developer.

In research published on October 14, Trellix describes this as an “unseen credential surface”: the path secrets take as they move from protected stores into more exposed places.

Researchers from Trellix noted that the problem does not require malware; it can arise from normal agent behavior and the way credentials are handled.

AI Agents Create an Unseen Credential Surface

The risk begins when an agent needs a credential to perform a task. For example, it may retrieve an OAuth token from an operating system’s secure store and place it directly in a command-line argument.

That can make the token visible to process-monitoring tools, other local processes and shell history. If the agent also records the command in its transcript or sends the result to an external model provider, the secret may leave the device.

Reading a .env file or cloud configuration is another common route. A developer may inspect a file locally, but an agent can pass its contents into the model context as part of the task.

The same concern applies when an agent prints environment variables, uses a command-line tool to retrieve credentials, or reads a secret from a cloud vault. The vault may be working as designed; the exposure happens after the agent retrieves the value.

The issue connects to wider risks in AI coding tools. Cyber Security News has reported on malware targeting local agent data, including tokens, saved connections and prompt histories, which could give criminals access to connected services.

It has also covered prompt injection through GitHub comments, where untrusted text can try to direct an agent with access to secrets. These are separate scenarios, but both show why agent permissions and stored data matter.

Trellix groups the risky behaviors into ten classes, ranging from command-line credentials and credential-file reads to cloud secret retrieval, weakened certificate checks, hidden command execution and changes to startup files.

An agent might also create an unprotected SSH key to avoid an interactive prompt. None of these actions alone proves an attack: developers and automation tools use many of the same commands every day.

Why security tools may miss the chain

A single event often looks routine. A command such as curl, git, cat or a cloud CLI may be used by an engineer, an agent or someone who has gained access to a workstation.

An alert for every read of .env, for example, could trigger repeatedly because editors, build tools and other applications access configuration files during normal work.

The risk becomes clearer when events are linked. A sequence that shows an agent accessing a credential, using it and then sending data outside the device gives defenders more context than any one action alone.

Trellix says investigations should connect those steps to the agent process that began them, rather than relying only on single-event alerts.

The approach also aligns with MITRE’s description of unsecured credentials, which includes secrets kept in files, private keys and other exposed locations.

Prompt injection can make an existing exposure more dangerous. If an agent processes hostile instructions hidden in a web page, code repository or issue, an attacker may try to redirect actions the agent can already perform.

Cyber Security News has covered a separate AWS agent case in which researchers reported that broad permissions and access to secrets could increase the reach of a manipulated agent.

The report recommends keeping secrets out of command-line arguments and preventing credential values from entering an agent’s context in the first place.

Where possible, applications should use provider SDKs or secure ways to pass credentials to tools, such as standard input or restricted file descriptors. Agent frameworks can also block unsafe command patterns, redact credential-like values and limit access to untrusted instructions.

Organizations deploying agents should give each one only the permissions it needs, restrict network access and use short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials.

If a token is exposed, a short expiry can limit how long it remains useful. Security teams should also treat agent-enabled workstations and containers as sensitive systems because they may access cloud accounts, repositories, databases and other services.

The central lesson is that an agent’s normal workflow can create a credential exposure path, even without a malware infection or a software flaw.

Keeping secrets out of prompts and transcripts, and tracing related actions as a sequence, can help reduce the chance that an ordinary task becomes a security incident. Read the original Trellix credential exposure research for the full analysis.

articles.title: UK Legal Aid Agency Data Breach Exposes Personal Records Dating Back to 1978
articles.description:
The UK Legal Aid Agency (LAA) has confirmed that its 2025 cyberattack stole personal records dating back to 1978. An updated investigation found approximately 250,000 records from before 2007, widening the known scope of a breach that affected legal aid applicants, providers and some probation service users. In its October 14, 2026 update, the agency […]

The post UK Legal Aid Agency Data Breach Exposes Personal Records Dating Back to 1978 appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The UK Legal Aid Agency (LAA) has confirmed that its 2025 cyberattack stole personal records dating back to 1978. An updated investigation found approximately 250,000 records from before 2007, widening the known scope of a breach that affected legal aid applicants, providers and some probation service users.

In its October 14, 2026 update, the agency said most affected data concerned applications, claims, payments or cases active between January 2007 and May 16, 2025. Most older records came from the 1990s and 2000s, with very few dating from before 1990.

The LAA first detected the attack on April 23, 2025, and warned legal aid providers that information, including financial details, might have been compromised. On May 16, investigators established that attackers had accessed and stolen a significant amount of personal data, making the incident more serious than initially understood.

Technical teams have since examined data spread across several complex systems. Much of the material was unstructured, split into separate parts or left incomplete, making it hard to determine exactly what attackers took. The latest findings reflect further analysis of the original incident rather than a newly disclosed attack.

Personal, Financial and Court Records Affected

Depending on the person and case, stolen information may include names, addresses, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, financial assessments and legal case details. Some Crown Court records contain charges, pleas, convictions and sentences. Other records may include information about partners, family members and parties involved in civil proceedings.

The oldest category includes benefit checks linked to civil legal aid between 1978 and 2012. Provider information may include bank account names, account numbers, sort codes, payment records and online portal user details. However, the agency stressed that neither every person nor every listed data field was necessarily affected.

The breach also highlights the sensitivity of court information, an issue seen in the separate NSW Online Registry data breach, where approximately 9,000 court documents were downloaded without permission. That incident is not linked to the LAA attack.

Investigators also found probation data belonging to a relatively small number of people supervised between 2010 and 2017. More than 99% related to supervision during 2016 and 2017. Exposed fields included some names, birth dates, nationalities and case references. The agency said this probation data did not concern crime victims.

The LAA says it has no indication that stolen information has been published or shared. Its update does not identify the attackers or explain their entry method. Security work includes stronger authentication, tighter access controls, better monitoring, vulnerability fixes, and isolating or retiring higher-risk technology. Such measures also involve patch management practices

People who believe they may be affected should watch for unexpected messages and independently verify requests for personal or financial information.

The NCSC’s data breach guidance recommends contacting organizations through official channels, avoiding contact details supplied in suspicious messages, replacing reused passwords, and checking accounts for unusual activity following a breach.

articles.title: KGB RAT Malware Bypasses Windows Defender to Steal Credentials and Control PCs
articles.description:
A Windows remote access trojan called KGB RAT gives attackers a way to spy on infected computers, collect credentials and control a victim’s desktop. The malware is sold as a service and advertised with a “fully undetectable” crypter that its sellers claim can bypass Windows Defender and other antivirus products. That claim should be treated […]

The post KGB RAT Malware Bypasses Windows Defender to Steal Credentials and Control PCs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Windows remote access trojan called KGB RAT gives attackers a way to spy on infected computers, collect credentials and control a victim’s desktop.

The malware is sold as a service and advertised with a “fully undetectable” crypter that its sellers claim can bypass Windows Defender and other antivirus products.

That claim should be treated carefully: Group-IB’s report documents the advertised evasion and observed malicious behavior, but does not show that every version can reliably defeat Defender on every system.

Analysts and researchers from Group-IB identified and analyzed KGB RAT, finding a tool that combines credential theft, keylogging, remote control and ransomware features.

The researchers also found that its operators use a separate Telegram channel to receive infection alerts, while the malware contacts command-and-control (C2) servers for instructions.

KGB RAT Malware Bypasses Windows Defender

Group-IB said KGB RAT was promoted on underground forums from late 2025, but traces of an early version of its server infrastructure date to January 2022.

The malware is sold through a malware-as-a-service model, meaning buyers can rent access rather than build their own tool. The seller advertises daily crypter updates and a payload builder that can create files in formats including EXE, BAT, HTA and REG.

The product is presented as a legitimate remote administration tool. Its advertised features include file access, webcam and microphone control, password recovery, hidden desktop access and tools for managing multiple infected computers.

Group-IB’s analysis found samples based on an obfuscated version of NjRAT, a known remote access trojan. This connection matters because KGB RAT is not simply a new name: it builds on existing malware code and adds a commercial package around it.

The report also shows why a RAT can be dangerous even when it does not use a new technique. A related NjRAT campaign abusing Microsoft Dev Tunnels shows how familiar malware can use trusted online services to hide its network traffic. KGB RAT takes a different route, using Telegram for alerts and direct C2 connections for remote control.

In Group-IB’s tested sample, the original program copied itself into a temporary folder and relaunched as svchost.exe, a name that resembles a real Windows process.

It then created a scheduled task called ChromeUpdate to run again when a user signs in. The malware also changed a Windows setting that controls the display of hidden system files and modified a setting related to security-zone warnings.

The malware checks the computer before carrying out its work. Group-IB observed it querying Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for information about the operating system, running processes and installed security products.

It also checked for signs of virtual machines and analysis tools. These steps can help malware avoid running in a research sandbox or reveal which defenses are present.

How KGB RAT takes hold and stays active

For credential theft, researchers observed the sample accessing Windows Credential Manager files. These can hold saved sign-in details for websites, network resources and applications.

KGB RAT also includes a keylogger that can record keyboard activity, as well as features for screenshots, clipboard monitoring and remote desktop control.

Its hidden VNC feature is designed to give an operator a remote view or control session that may not be visible on the victim’s desktop. Readers can learn more about this method in Cybersecurity News’ article on hidden VNC remote desktop control.

Group-IB observed the malware looking up a victim’s public IP address through ip-api.com and sending an infection notification through Telegram’s Bot API.

The report also describes a Crypto Clipper feature in one analyzed sample. This type of tool watches copied cryptocurrency addresses and may replace them with an address controlled by the attacker.

KGB RAT’s sellers claim its crypter can bypass or disable Windows Defender. A crypter changes or wraps malware code to make it harder for antivirus products to recognize a file by its signature.

The seller’s claim is not proof that all builds evade protection. Group-IB says its own Malware Detonation Platform detected samples by observing their behavior, including after obfuscation or unpacking.

That distinction is useful for defenders: a file may change, but its actions can still raise alarms. In the analyzed sample, warning signs included a program running from a temporary folder, an unfamiliar ChromeUpdate task, registry changes, suspicious child processes and connections to Telegram or the listed C2 servers.

A Cybersecurity News report on Silver RAT antivirus bypass methods provides further context on how RAT sellers use crypters and other evasion claims.

Organizations should keep endpoint protection active and updated, restrict unapproved software, and alert on scheduled tasks created by programs running from user-writable folders.

Security teams should review unusual process chains and outbound connections, especially when Telegram or the listed geolocation service is contacted by a non-browser process.

If infection is suspected, isolate the device, preserve logs and investigate from a clean system before resetting exposed credentials and sessions.

articles.title: Critical Next.js Vulnerabilities Allow Hackers to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
articles.description:
Next.js has released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers run malicious code without logging in. A third, high-severity flaw could stop affected applications from serving requests. The issues involve cached functions, SVG image processing, and Server Actions, with fixes available in Next.js 16.4.1 and 15.5.28. Published on October 14, 2026, […]

The post Critical Next.js Vulnerabilities Allow Hackers to Execute Malicious Code Remotely appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Next.js has released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers run malicious code without logging in. A third, high-severity flaw could stop affected applications from serving requests.

The issues involve cached functions, SVG image processing, and Server Actions, with fixes available in Next.js 16.4.1 and 15.5.28. Published on October 14, 2026, the advisories describe separate attack paths with different requirements

Both remote code execution flaws score 9.5, while the denial-of-service issue scores 8.2. Application settings and enabled features determine exposure, so version checks are only one part of risk assessment.

The first vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr, affects App Router applications using Cache Components. An application becomes vulnerable when a use cache function returns multiple typed arrays. Under these conditions, attackers could achieve remote code execution without authentication or user interaction.

Next.js releases 16.0.0–16.4.0 are affected by the flaw, which is fixed in version 16.4.1. Developers should upgrade immediately, as no workaround or CVE identifier is available.

Critical Next.js Vulnerabilities

Earlier React and Next.js RCE reports highlight server-side risks, but the newly disclosed cache flaw has a separate trigger and is unrelated to React2Shell.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-96889, involves a memory-related weakness in an upstream library the Image Optimization API uses to handle SVG files. It can lead to remote code execution on Next.js deployments running on glibc-based Linux. The advisory lists no required privileges or user interaction.

The official image optimization advisory lists affected versions as 10.0.0 through 15.5.27 and versions above 16.0.0 through 16.4.0.

Developers can address this issue by ensuring Next.js uses sharp 0.35.5 or later. Installing the patched Next.js releases ensures package managers provide a fixed dependency.

The third vulnerability, GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r, affects App Router applications with at least one Server Action. Crafted requests can drive excessive CPU usage, preventing the same process from handling further requests. Applications using Pages Router, or those without Server Actions, are not vulnerable.

Affected versions include 13.0.0 through 15.5.27 and 16.0.0 through 16.4.0. There is no workaround besides upgrading. Previous coverage of Next.js security patches highlights related feature-specific risks, but those earlier fixes do not replace this update.

Developers should install Next.js 15.5.28 or 16.4.1 as appropriate. Updating only sharp addresses the image flaw, not the separate cached-function or Server Actions vulnerabilities.

articles.description:

The collection reportedly includes editable animation projects, character designs, storyboards, and production guides from The Amazing World of Gumball, Adventure Time, and Regular Show. However, the archive’s full size, source, and […]

The post Cartoon Network Gigaleak Exposes 200GB of Internal Animation Files and Production Secrets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A reported Cartoon Network gigaleak has exposed more than 200GB of internal animation material, offering a rare look at how popular cartoons were made.

The collection reportedly includes editable animation projects, character designs, storyboards, and production guides from The Amazing World of Gumball, Adventure Time, and Regular Show. However, the archive’s full size, source, and authenticity remain unconfirmed.

Reports began spreading across online communities around October 9 and 10. Fans named the collection the “Classic CN Gigaleak,” with some posts claiming a wider archive approaching 1TB.

IndiaTimes reports the Cartoon Network material at over 200GB, noting that neither the full volume nor its origin has been independently verified. These figures should therefore be treated as reported estimates, not verified measurements.

Unlike finished episodes, these files reportedly contain production assets. The collection includes Flash projects, editable character rigs, layered Photoshop documents, model sheets, storyboards and animatics.

Character rigs let artists move separate parts of a digital character, while model sheets help teams keep designs consistent. Animatics show how planned scenes flow before final animation is completed.

Cartoon Network Gigaleak Exposes

Early Gumball material has drawn particular attention. According to the IndiaTimes report, files from Seasons 1 and 2 allegedly include episode source projects and puppet rigs.

Regular Show folders reportedly contain character portraits, size charts, backgrounds and style guides. Adventure Time material is said to total around 90GB, although its exact contents and completeness remain unclear.

Other reported titles include The Powerpuff Girls, Dexter’s Laboratory, Johnny Bravo, Foster’s Home for Imaginary Friends and Ed, Edd n Eddy.

A Google Drive collection and points to an anonymous X account called “totallynotaburner.” That identifies an apparent sharing point, not a confirmed attacker or the source of the files.

Available reporting does not establish whether the files came from a compromised company system, an exposed archive, a former worker, or another source. No verified attack method, stolen account, or software flaw has been identified. Calling this a confirmed network intrusion would go beyond the evidence currently available.

The difference matters when comparing entertainment industry incidents. Cybersecurity News previously covered a Disney hacker who stole 1.1TB of internal data, where malware and stolen employee credentials provided a documented access path.

That case offers useful context, but it does not explain how the Cartoon Network material surfaced. No shared attacker or technical connection has been established.

For aspiring animators, the reported archive could reveal how professional teams planned scenes and organized projects. However, public availability does not make copyrighted production files open-source.

Yahoo’s coverage reports that links were removed following copyright complaints, showing that preservation interest and permission to distribute are separate issues.

Readers should also avoid treating download links as trustworthy. Cybersecurity News has documented fake download sites spreading malware.

This does not establish that Cartoon Network downloads contain malware, but it supports caution around unfamiliar files and lookalike websites. Until stronger evidence emerges, the reported exposure remains significant, while its cause and complete scope remain unresolved.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Fortinet Vulnerabilities to Deploy Stealthy PEERSTITCH Malware on FortiGate Firewalls
articles.description:
Attackers compromised a telecommunications managed service provider by exploiting vulnerabilities in Fortinet’s centralized management and firewall systems, then deployed PEERSTITCH, a stealthy malware implant that runs inside FortiGate processes. Unit 42 says the activity began with a breach of a FortiManager appliance and exposed configurations and sensitive data linked to more than 500 managed FortiGate […]

The post Hackers Exploit Fortinet Vulnerabilities to Deploy Stealthy PEERSTITCH Malware on FortiGate Firewalls appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers compromised a telecommunications managed service provider by exploiting vulnerabilities in Fortinet’s centralized management and firewall systems, then deployed PEERSTITCH, a stealthy malware implant that runs inside FortiGate processes.

Unit 42 says the activity began with a breach of a FortiManager appliance and exposed configurations and sensitive data linked to more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls.

The researchers say this exposure did not confirm that the clients’ firewalls were also compromised. In the September 2024 intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2024-47575, also known as FortiJump, against FortiManager.

The flaw let an unauthenticated remote attacker send crafted requests through the device’s management channel and run commands. Unit 42 reported that the attackers registered a rogue device, created an archive and stole it.

The archive included firewall configurations, network details, credentials and cryptographic trust material. Analysts from Unit 42 identified PEERSTITCH while investigating the intrusion, which they track as CL-STA-0954, also known as UNC5820.

Their technical report on the FortiGate implant describes a multi-stage operation that moved from FortiManager compromise to credential use, network monitoring and malware deployment.

The stolen archive gave the attackers a map of the managed environment: device serial numbers and public IP addresses, network routes, firewall rules, and management relationships.

It also contained encrypted administrative and VPN credentials and certificates used to establish trust between FortiManager and managed devices. Unit 42 says researchers were able to recover administrative and VPN passwords from the stolen configuration files.

After a period of inactivity, the attackers used the compromised management platform to push unauthorized packet-capture settings to some managed firewalls.

These rules monitored unencrypted HTTP traffic and selected services, including remote administration and network discovery. The researchers also observed captures aimed at TFTP, RADIUS and LDAP traffic, which could reveal files, authentication data and directory activity.

Hackers Exploit Fortinet Vulnerabilities

Using recovered credentials, the attackers then opened unauthorized FortiGate VPN sessions and reached internal network-management areas.

The operation shows how a compromise of a central management system can expose other connected devices: the attackers used stolen trust material and device information to continue their activity beyond the first appliance.

Cybersecurity News has previously covered the FortiManager zero-day vulnerability exploited and the mass compromise of FortiManager devices, which provide background on the earlier exploitation of CVE-2024-47575.

Unit 42 says the attackers exploited a second flaw, CVE-2025-61624, through FortiOS’s system.auto-script feature. The path traversal issue allowed an authenticated administrator to write files outside the intended directory, with the script running at root level.

That access helped the attackers move from a restricted administrative interface to control of the firewall’s underlying operating system.

The attackers used a traversal string in an auto-script object to place a loader on selected devices. The loader fetched several files, including JavaScript and WebAssembly components, plus a native ARM64 executable named lldprx.

After a delay, the deployment script launched the executable, which searched for two FortiOS processes: miglogd, responsible for logging, and iked, which handles IKE and IPsec VPN functions.

The injector attached to both processes and created a 16-kilobyte memory area with read, write and execute permissions. It placed its payload there and altered execution paths in the daemons.

PEERSTITCH then used process memory to pass session tags between miglogd and iked. When VPN traffic matched specific markers, the implant could take an alternate code path that bypassed normal FortiOS security checks.

This design makes the implant difficult to find with routine checks. It does not leave a persistent malware binary on disk, open a listening port or make its own outbound connection. Instead, it hides its activity inside legitimate system processes and their existing traffic.

A second channel and efforts to hide activity

The researchers also found that the attackers misused Apache’s mod_md module, which supports automated certificate management, to set up a reverse shell.

They altered configuration so that certificate-validation activity could run commands through Node.js and repeatedly contact attacker infrastructure. This gave the attackers a separate route for remote control alongside the memory-based implant.

To make investigation harder, the attackers stopped logging services, cleared crash logs, removed rogue accounts and auto-script objects, and replaced a malicious Apache configuration file with harmless-looking text. The lldprx injector also deleted its own file and stopped the staging process before exiting.

Organizations should review FortiManager and FortiGate records for unexpected device registrations, unfamiliar administrator accounts, suspicious VPN sessions, and auto-script entries containing path traversal strings such as ../../.

They should compare firewall configurations with known-good backups and treat credentials, certificates and trust material stored on a compromised management server as exposed.

Cybersecurity News has also covered a FortiGate firewall configuration leak, a reminder that stolen firewall settings can reveal credentials and network design.

For PEERSTITCH-specific hunting, Unit 42 recommends examining the memory maps of miglogd and iked for anonymous 16-kilobyte regions with read, write and execute permissions. Investigators should also check for memory patches at the offsets listed below, cross-process writes to /proc/<pid>/mem, relevant daemon crashes, and suspicious auto-script objects.

articles.title: Firefox Enterprise Adds DLP and AI Controls to Block Sensitive Data Leaks
articles.description:
Mozilla released Firefox Enterprise 158.0 on October 13, 2026, introducing its first dedicated enterprise browser with built-in data loss prevention and AI-use controls. The browser combines Firefox with a self-hosted Admin Console, giving security teams central control over browsing, web access, and how employees share company data. According to Mozilla’s Firefox Enterprise release notes, organizations […]

The post Firefox Enterprise Adds DLP and AI Controls to Block Sensitive Data Leaks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Mozilla released Firefox Enterprise 158.0 on October 13, 2026, introducing its first dedicated enterprise browser with built-in data loss prevention and AI-use controls.

The browser combines Firefox with a self-hosted Admin Console, giving security teams central control over browsing, web access, and how employees share company data. According to Mozilla’s Firefox Enterprise release notes, organizations must deploy the console on their own infrastructure.

Supporting services, including browser updates, Sync, telemetry, and crash collection, also run within the organization’s environment. This setup keeps management data under company control rather than relying on an external management service.

The main addition is DLP, which lets administrators block or warn about pasting, file uploads, downloads, and printing on selected websites.

Teams can display custom messages explaining restrictions. For example, they can block employees from pasting company information into unapproved AI tools while keeping approved services available.

Firefox Enterprise Adds DLP and AI Controls

Built-in checks run locally in the browser, so content doesn’t travel over the network for inspection. Organizations using a third-party DLP agent through Firefox’s Content Analysis interface retain that setup.

Firefox Enterprise turns off its built-in DLP and hands inspection to the existing agent. Warnings and blocks appear in the Admin Console, though administrators can turn off that logging.

The focus on browser data controls comes as AI tools create new exposure risks. Cyber Security News previously covered the BioShocking AI browser attack, where researchers manipulated browsing context to make AI agents expose sensitive information. Firefox’s release notes describe controls over data movement, not a specific fix for that attack.

Employees must sign in through the company’s single sign-on provider before browsing. Firefox Enterprise supports OpenID Connect and follows the provider’s multi-factor authentication requirements.

Administrators can also require device security conditions, including disk encryption and running endpoint protection, before allowing access. Firefox signs employees out if their device no longer meets those conditions.

Profile encryption is enabled by default. Browsing history, form data, saved logins, and TLS session tokens are encrypted using a key supplied by the Admin Console.

A copied profile folder cannot be decrypted without that key. Optional watermarks can show an employee’s email address and the time on sensitive pages, helping trace shared images without physically preventing screenshots.

The console supports more than 130 enterprise policies, including restrictions on extensions and update controls. These controls address risks highlighted in earlier reporting on AI browser extension vulnerabilities that exposed private sessions and data. Lockdown Mode can disable JavaScript JIT compilation, block service workers, prevent HTTP downgrades, and isolate selected sites.

Security event logging is optional for each event type, with records sent to the organization’s console rather than Mozilla. Teams can integrate with SIEM systems and remotely sign out lost devices. Firefox Enterprise also inherits security fixes from Firefox 158, while access requires a deployed console and an early-access request.

articles.title: CISA Warns of Hackers Exploiting Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day to Steal Credentials
articles.description:
CISA urged administrators to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances after attackers exploited CVE-2026-104935, a zero-day flaw that allows remote authentication bypass and command execution, enabling credential theft and data exfiltration. CISA issued its warning and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 13, 2026. The warning covers Ivanti Connect Secure versions […]

The post CISA Warns of Hackers Exploiting Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day to Steal Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA urged administrators to patch Ivanti Connect Secure appliances after attackers exploited CVE-2026-104935, a zero-day flaw that allows remote authentication bypass and command execution, enabling credential theft and data exfiltration.

CISA issued its warning and added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 13, 2026. The warning covers Ivanti Connect Secure versions 25.1.1.1 and earlier, 25.1.2.2 and earlier, and 22.8R2.4 and earlier. Organizations should follow the vendor’s security advisory to select the right update for their deployment.

CISA also directed administrators to Ivanti’s migration guide because upgrade requirements differ between hardware, cloud, and virtual appliances.

According to Volexity’s investigation, an unknown threat actor tracked as UTA0576 began exploiting the weaknesses on October 3. Researchers investigated suspicious activity on October 5 and traced it to a Connect Secure appliance running version 22.8R2.4, which was fully patched at the time. The attack combined an authentication bypass, a file upload weakness that enabled code execution, and a separate privilege escalation flaw.

Together, these weaknesses gave attackers root access, the highest level of control on the appliance. Ivanti tracks the authentication bypass and remote code execution components under CVE-2026-104935.

Attackers used the compromised appliance to collect stored domain credentials, query Active Directory, and search for local administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

Researchers also observed password spraying, network discovery, and attempts to recover credentials from captured traffic. CybersecurityNews previously covered the Ivanti zero-day used to steal Active Directory data.

CISA warned that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may miss evidence of this attack because malicious commands execute in memory. Volexity found that attackers changed library code in memory, restored configuration changes, and removed selected log entries to hide their activity.

The researchers did not identify a web shell or backdoor used to maintain command access. Instead, the attacker repeatedly ran the exploit chain and received command results through HTTPS responses. This makes network and memory analysis important when checking whether an exposed appliance was breached.

CISA Urges Ivanti 0-Day Patch

Volexity reported that Ivanti released fixes for the authentication bypass and code execution flaw on October 13. A fix for the separate privilege escalation weakness remained under development when the research was published. Administrators should not delay the available update while waiting for that additional fix.

The CISA alert recommends backing up the appliance configuration before recovery. For suspected compromise, organizations should perform a factory reset and install the latest version. Cloud and virtual deployments should be rebuilt and upgraded before administrators restore the saved configuration.

Recovery must also address stolen secrets. CISA recommends resetting domain, administrator, and local account passwords, revoking and reissuing stored certificates, and resetting stored API keys and license server credentials. Installing a patch alone does not replace these recovery steps.

Administrators can review CybersecurityNews’ earlier coverage of the affected and fixed Ivanti releases alongside vendor guidance. Organizations using the 22.8 branch should also plan migration before its January 31, 2027 end-of-life date.
