articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Windows 11 Update Issue that Causes Black Screen Errors or Windows Explorer crash
articles.description:
Microsoft fixed a Windows 11 update issue that could leave users staring at a black screen after signing in or cause Windows Explorer to crash. The problem mainly affected Azure Virtual Desktop hosts using FSLogix, and some existing user profiles were more likely to fail to load the desktop. Microsoft marked the issue as resolved […]

The post Microsoft Fixes Windows 11 Update Issue that Causes Black Screen Errors or Windows Explorer crash appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft fixed a Windows 11 update issue that could leave users staring at a black screen after signing in or cause Windows Explorer to crash.

The problem mainly affected Azure Virtual Desktop hosts using FSLogix, and some existing user profiles were more likely to fail to load the desktop. Microsoft marked the issue as resolved on October 13, 2026.

The fix is included in KB5127646 for Windows 11 version 26H1 and later updates. Microsoft recommends installing the latest available update on each device. Systems running the October 13 update or later no longer need the temporary workarounds for this issue.

According to Microsoft’s Windows release health notice, the problem began after the August 2026 non-security preview update, KB5120996. It continued through subsequent updates for Windows 11 version 26H1; that originating update carried OS Build 28000.2804.

Affected users could sign in but found their desktop session did not load automatically. Instead, a black screen appeared, leaving them unable to access the desktop until they started the session manually. Application event logs could also show Windows Explorer crashes, giving administrators a useful sign when checking affected systems.

Microsoft Fixes Windows 11 Update Issue

Microsoft lists Windows 11 versions 26H2, 26H1, 25H2, and 24H2 as affected client platforms. This issue does not affect Windows Server. Although reports mainly involved Azure Virtual Desktop environments using FSLogix, Microsoft did not describe every device running those Windows versions as affected.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the Windows 11 update bug causing black screens, including the temporary recovery steps available before this fix. The new resolution removes the need to rely on those measures once an affected device receives the appropriate update.

Users still running an update released before October 13 can temporarily restore desktop access by pressing Ctrl+Shift+Esc to open Task Manager. They can then select Run new task, enter explorer.exe, and choose OK. Microsoft provides this method as a workaround, not a replacement for installing the fix.

For enterprise-managed devices, administrators can also use Known Issue Rollback, or KIR, through a special Group Policy. The supplied notice identifies KB5124006 260924_20071 for Windows 11 26H1 and KB5124010 260924_20021 for Windows 11 26H2, 25H2, and 24H2.

Administrators must install and configure the policy that matches their Windows version, then restart affected devices. This turns off the change responsible for the issue.

Cybersecurity News also reported on another Windows 11 update fix that replaced a temporary rollback, showing why a workaround and a permanent update aren’t the same.

First, match the symptoms to Microsoft’s health notice and confirm the installed Windows version and update level. Reported signs include a black screen after sign-in, failure to load the desktop, and Windows Explorer crashes. The notice does not identify malware or an attack as the cause.

Microsoft’s Windows 11 release information lists KB5127646 as the October 13 security update for version 26H1, bringing it to Build 28000.3231. Administrators should use the update appropriate for each supported Windows release rather than assume the same package applies across every affected version

articles.title: Ransomware Attacks Intensify: Criminals Shift Focus to Target Employees and Their Families
articles.description:
Ransomware gangs are moving beyond locked files and stolen data. Criminals now threaten employees, executives, and their families to force companies to pay. According to the Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, 37% of successful attacks included threats against workers’ friends or relatives. The findings show that ransomware is no longer only a technical crisis. It […]

The post Ransomware Attacks Intensify: Criminals Shift Focus to Target Employees and Their Families appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ransomware gangs are moving beyond locked files and stolen data. Criminals now threaten employees, executives, and their families to force companies to pay.

According to the Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, 37% of successful attacks included threats against workers’ friends or relatives.

The findings show that ransomware is no longer only a technical crisis. It can become a real safety and mental health emergency.

Ransomware Attacks Target Employees and Their Families

Semperis surveyed 1,200 IT and security professionals from organizations hit by successful ransomware attacks during the previous 12 months. The study covered nine countries and eight sectors during the first half of 2026.

Among respondents, 57% reported threatening texts, letters, or packages. Another 19% faced threats of physical intrusion, 17% reported threats of abduction, and 13% saw threats of bodily harm.

Attackers carried out their threats in 53% of reported cases, according to the survey. The personal impact was severe. One quarter of affected organizations said employees or family members were doxxed, meaning private details were exposed online.

About 23% reported swatting, where criminals make a false emergency call that can send armed police to a victim’s home. A further 25% said people needed medical or mental health care, while 24% hired personal security.

In 14% of cases, staff or relatives changed jobs, offices, or homes. This pressure marks the next stage of extortion. Ransomware groups first relied on file encryption. Many later added data theft and threats to leak it.

Now, criminals can study social media, breached data, public records, and company pages to identify relatives, addresses, schools, and daily routines. Such details let them build messages that feel direct and credible. The goal is simple. Make resisting the ransom seem more costly than paying it.

Artificial intelligence is also changing how ransomware operations work. The report says 84% of surveyed victims experienced attacks that used AI in some way.

This included 40% who faced AI-based attacks and 44% where criminals abused the victim’s own AI agents or systems. AI can help criminals write convincing messages, research targets, change malware, and run work at a larger scale.

However, the survey data reflects what victims reported. It does not prove exactly how AI was used in every incident. Security teams should treat the figures as a strong warning while still checking logs, malware samples, identity events, and attacker communications before linking activity to AI.

Personal pressure is growing, but identity systems remain central to ransomware. Semperis found that 87% of attacks targeted Active Directory, Entra ID, or Okta. Active Directory was targeted in 51% of cases.

Yet only 50% of surveyed organizations had dedicated identity backups, and 42% had automated identity recovery tools. This gap matters because identity control can give criminals broad access, help them move across a network, and allow them to disrupt recovery.

A recent Qilin ransomware investigation showed how attackers abused Active Directory replication to collect domain credentials. Another PAYLOAD ransomware case showed criminals using Group Policy to disrupt a Windows domain without encrypting files.

Organizations should update ransomware plans to cover threats outside the network. The plan should name who contacts law enforcement, who supports targeted staff, who handles public messages, and how the company protects personal data.

Firms also need a trusted communication channel outside normal email and chat systems, since attackers may watch or disable them. Realistic exercises should include doxxing, swatting, threats to children, and contact with relatives.

Employees also need a safe, blame-free way to report suspicious contact. Companies should offer privacy checks, counseling, and clear advice for family members, while avoiding public comments that could expose victims or disrupt a criminal investigation.

Technical steps still matter. Security teams should enforce multifactor authentication, limit privileged access, segment networks, patch exposed systems, keep tested offline backups, and prepare clean recovery for identity services.

The CISA StopRansomware Guide also advises organizations to isolate affected systems, preserve evidence, keep leaders informed, and report incidents to CISA or law enforcement.

Paying does not guarantee safety, data recovery, or an end to pressure. The FBI says it does not support ransom payments because victims may receive nothing and payments support further crime.

Semperis found 59% of victims paid at least once, while 69% suffered multiple successful attacks. That pattern makes fast containment, trusted identity recovery, staff care, and early police contact just as important as restoring servers.

articles.title: Microsoft Windows Server 0-Day Flaw Lets Attackers Crash Servers With a Single Packet
articles.description:
Microsoft patched a Windows Server vulnerability that lets a network-adjacent attacker crash a server with a crafted Distributed File System (DFS) referral response. Tracked as CVE-2026-70111, the flaw affects Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. Corelight researchers reported the issue after finding it while testing Microsoft Remote Procedure Call (MS-RPC) and DFS interfaces. The company […]

The post Microsoft Windows Server 0-Day Flaw Lets Attackers Crash Servers With a Single Packet appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft patched a Windows Server vulnerability that lets a network-adjacent attacker crash a server with a crafted Distributed File System (DFS) referral response. Tracked as CVE-2026-70111, the flaw affects Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025.

Corelight researchers reported the issue after finding it while testing Microsoft Remote Procedure Call (MS-RPC) and DFS interfaces. The company said it had not seen signs of active exploitation when it disclosed the flaw on October 13, 2026.

The vulnerability poses a denial-of-service risk, not server takeover. An attacker needs network access to make the target connect to a malicious SMB server, which returns a malformed DFS referral that crashes the service a process Corelight says can take seconds.

Windows uses DFS to direct users and systems to files stored across a network. When a Windows Server resolves a DFS path, a component called mup.sys requests referral information over SMB. Corelight found that a crafted response can reach a vulnerable code path while the driver processes a DFS referral.

The reported cause is a missing length check. In a particular NameList referral, an offset can point to an empty string. The server code does not reject that value before processing it, and the kernel can hit an invalid memory reference. The result is a blue screen and an unexpected reboot.

Corelight reproduced the crash 11 out of 11 times on Windows Server 2022 and 3 out of 3 times on Server 2019. Those results show the issue was repeatable in the researchers’ lab.

Microsoft Windows Server 0-Day Flaw

However, they don’t show how often organizations use it. Corelight said Windows 10 is not affected because it retains checks absent from the affected Server builds.

Windows Server may restart automatically after a kernel fault, which can limit the length of a single disruption. However, an attacker who can repeatedly trigger the flaw may keep a system offline.

The impact depends on which servers are reachable and targeted. Repeated crashes of important systems, such as domain controllers, could disrupt key services across an organization.

Corelight says reboots may leave little evidence beyond Windows System log Event IDs 41 and 6008, which indicate an unexpected shutdown without explaining the cause, making network monitoring essential to identify activity before and after the crash.

Microsoft’s October 2026 security update, released October 13, addresses CVE-2026-70111 on Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. Organizations should apply the relevant update and prioritize servers that actively use DFS.

Corelight advises monitoring internal, or “east-west,” SMB traffic between servers and domain controllers, not only traffic crossing the perimeter.

Its researchers say Zeek connection logs may show sessions going silent during a crash and reset activity after the server returns. A sudden cluster of connection states such as S1, RSTR, or RSTRH involving the same Server may merit investigation. However, those signs alone do not prove exploitation.

For more background on Windows authentication coercion, see Cyber Security News’ coverage of Windows authentication coercion attacks.

Its earlier report on Windows denial-of-service vulnerabilities offers related context on service availability risks. CVE-2026-70111 shows how an overlooked input check in a kernel driver can turn a network response into a server outage.

Patching affected systems and monitoring internal SMB transactions are key steps to reduce the risk. The technical findings and patch details are described in Corelight’s disclosure.

articles.title: PoC Released for Critical Fortinet FortiClient EMS Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
articles.description:
A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-35616, a critical authentication and authorization bypass in Fortinet FortiClient Endpoint Management Server (EMS), lets defenders test whether affected systems are exposed. The Python tool’s repository says the flaw can allow unauthenticated access to protected API endpoints. Fortinet has confirmed that the vulnerability was exploited in the wild, making prompt […]

The post PoC Released for Critical Fortinet FortiClient EMS Authentication Bypass Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public proof-of-concept (PoC) for CVE-2026-35616, a critical authentication and authorization bypass in Fortinet FortiClient Endpoint Management Server (EMS), lets defenders test whether affected systems are exposed.

The Python tool’s repository says the flaw can allow unauthenticated access to protected API endpoints. Fortinet has confirmed that the vulnerability was exploited in the wild, making prompt patching the priority for organizations running affected versions.

The PoC is published on GitHub and names FortiClient EMS versions 7.4.5 and 7.4.6 as affected. Its README identifies version 7.4.7 as containing the fix.

It provides a command-line interface that accepts a target and optional port. The author warns that testing must be limited to systems covered by explicit written permission.

Fortinet classifies CVE-2026-35616 as improper access control, or CWE-284. In practical terms, a remote user without valid credentials may send crafted requests that bypass protections on the EMS API and execute unauthorized code or commands.

The risk is serious because EMS manages FortiClient deployments so that a compromise could give an attacker access to a central endpoint-administration system.

PoC Released for FortiClient EMS Vulnerability

The issue affects FortiClient EMS 7.4.5 through 7.4.6. Fortinet says the 7.2 branch is not affected, and that FortiClient Cloud and FortiSASE have already been remediated. Organizations should confirm the exact product and version they operate rather than applying the advisory to every Fortinet service.

The GitHub repository shared by Alaatk includes a Python script and instructions for running it against a specified host, with an optional port. That makes the code relevant to security teams validating their own systems.

However, public exploit code can also help unauthorized users test exposed servers. The repository does not indicate how many systems are vulnerable or confirm whether any organization has been compromised.

Fortinet’s advisory is the key remediation reference. It urges customers on versions 7.4.5 and 7.4.6 to install the relevant hotfixes. It says the fix is included in version 7.4.7 or later. Administrators should follow the instructions for their exact release and verify the resulting version after maintenance.

Organizations should also limit access to the EMS management interface to trusted networks, review available logs for unusual API requests or unexpected changes, and investigate signs of unauthorized activity.

If the server was reachable from the internet while unpatched, teams should prioritize reviewing it. A PoC test can confirm exposure, but it should not replace patching or a broader compromise check.

The most important step is to identify all FortiClient EMS deployments and determine whether any run 7.4.5 or 7.4.6. Apply the vendor hotfix or upgrade to 7.4.7 or later, then confirm the change. Do not run the PoC against systems outside the organization or without written authorization.

For additional context, see CybersecurityNews’ coverage of the FortiClient EMS zero-day and emergency hotfix and its report on exposed FortiClient EMS instances. The official Fortinet PSIRT advisory and the CVE-2026-35616 PoC repository provide the primary technical and remediation references.

articles.title: Anthropic Warns AI Agents Can Now Automate the Entire Cyber Kill Chain
articles.description:
Anthropic has warned that attackers use AI agents to automate every stage of a cyberattack, from finding targets and stealing credentials to moving through networks and exfiltrating data. Its September 2026 threat report describes campaigns in which Claude became an active part of attack operations, rather than simply helping hackers write code. The findings cover […]

The post Anthropic Warns AI Agents Can Now Automate the Entire Cyber Kill Chain appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic has warned that attackers use AI agents to automate every stage of a cyberattack, from finding targets and stealing credentials to moving through networks and exfiltrating data.

Its September 2026 threat report describes campaigns in which Claude became an active part of attack operations, rather than simply helping hackers write code.

The findings cover activity disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026. Anthropic said suspected state-backed groups, criminals, and individual hacktivists used Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models. Across these cases, AI reduced the time, staff, and technical knowledge needed to attack multiple victims.

According to Anthropic’s threat intelligence report, publicly available agent frameworks can now automate each step of the cyber kill chain.

These systems connect AI models with tools that scan systems, test weaknesses, run commands, and process stolen information. Human operators still choose targets and review results, but agents increasingly handle the work between those decisions. This builds on the earlier AI-led cyber espionage campaign reported in November 2025.

Anthropic now says similar methods have spread beyond suspected state-backed hackers to smaller criminal groups and lone operators. Frameworks such as PentAGI provide reusable systems for coordinating agents, making these workflows easier to adopt.

Anthropic Warns AI Agents

One case involves GTG-20006, a group whose activity Anthropic says is consistent with public reporting on Midnight Blizzard. The actor targeted Ukrainian and European government, military, diplomatic, and defense organizations, with particular interest in drone technology and its suppliers.

Its AI workflows supported phishing infrastructure, credential theft, command-and-control systems, and data collection. Agents also monitored whether security products detected deployed malware. When detection occurred, the workflow modified and rebuilt the tools, retested them, and prepared updated versions for deployment.

That feedback loop could weaken defenses based only on known malware signatures. Rather than waiting for developers to rewrite a detected tool, attackers can delegate repeated changes to agents. Anthropic cautioned that this may let capable groups bypass detections faster than defenders can create and deploy replacements.

Another cluster, tracked as GTG-50014, involved suspected ShinyHunters affiliates. One operator ran a credential-harvesting pipeline across 10 AWS EC2 workers, downloading 1.8 million Android application packages and scanning them for exposed secrets. The operator sent verified findings to Telegram for further use.

In another intrusion, attackers dumped more than 2,100 Azure AD token sets across over 40 corporate tenants in about 34 hours. Anthropic said AI agents performed nearly all the work. These cases show how stolen access can quickly expand into data theft across customers of a compromised software provider.

Anthropic stressed that automation does not mean attackers have removed people from campaigns. Humans remain involved in target selection, reviewing stolen material, and turning access into profit. Greater autonomy also does not automatically mean greater harm. Some serious breaches involved human direction at every step.

The company banned linked accounts, strengthened safeguards, and shared intelligence where appropriate. Its warning also highlights AI credentials as valuable targets.

Stolen API keys can fund further attacks at victims’ expense, so protecting them is as important as other production credentials. Anthropic said the customer-key thefts described did not compromise its own systems.

articles.title: UAT-6275 Hackers Exploit WinRAR Flaw to Target CIS Government Organizations
articles.description:
UAT-6275 hackers have used a known WinRAR flaw to plant malware on Windows systems while targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The activity shows how an unpatched archive tool can turn a routine attachment into lasting remote access, with the malicious program starting when the victim next signs in. The campaign […]

The post UAT-6275 Hackers Exploit WinRAR Flaw to Target CIS Government Organizations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
UAT-6275 hackers have used a known WinRAR flaw to plant malware on Windows systems while targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

The activity shows how an unpatched archive tool can turn a routine attachment into lasting remote access, with the malicious program starting when the victim next signs in.

The campaign involves CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw that lets crafted archives write files outside the folder chosen for extraction.

Researchers observed the group adding this method in April 2026, alongside older attacks using Word macros, executable downloaders, and malicious shortcuts. The wider activity reviewed ran from June 2025 through August 2026.

Cisco Talos researchers, working with Recorded Future’s Insikt Group, identified the malware and linked the activity to UAT-6275, tracked by Recorded Future as TAG-193.

Their October 14 research report describes custom reverse shells named PickleShell, Chvost, and Laplas. These tools let attackers send commands to infected computers and receive the results through remote connections.

UAT-6275 Hackers Exploit WinRAR Flaw

The WinRAR attack, classified as Chain D, used a RAR archive containing two visible PDF decoys. Hidden inside were payload records that abused NTFS alternate data streams, a Windows file feature.

The WinRAR path traversal flaw allowed those records to place PickleShell in the current user’s Startup folder instead of the expected extraction location.

The archive included ten hidden stream names pointing to the same payload, with different numbers of parent-folder steps. This approach helped account for different extraction locations.

A successful write placed the executable in Startup without requiring administrator rights. The malware then ran at the next sign-in, giving the attacker a foothold without another prompt.

PickleShell is a C#/.NET reverse shell that poses as a Windows service component. The analyzed payload starts a hidden command shell and passes command input and output to its control server. Later builds used encrypted connections.

Researchers also found a stable identifier across nine samples, offering defenders another way to hunt for related files despite name changes.

Earlier activity began with macro-enabled Word documents in June 2025. When a victim enabled macros, the document downloaded and ran another program.

From July, PS2EXE downloaders packaged PowerShell scripts as Windows executables, fetched reverse-shell payloads, and created scheduled tasks to keep running. These stages show that the WinRAR exploit expanded an existing toolkit rather than replacing it.

Four Delivery Paths Support Access

From October 2025, malicious shortcuts launched PowerShell to retrieve scripts from GitHub. Later versions also downloaded PickleShell into Startup.

Earlier Silent Lynx phishing campaigns used similar government-themed attachments and shortcuts. Talos reported overlap with Silent Lynx but continues to track UAT-6275 separately from YoroTrooper because direct indicator or toolset overlap between those two groups was not observed.

Three exposed staging directories and a previously unreported GitHub repository gave investigators access to payloads, tool lists, and infrastructure changes.

The repository’s history helped trace malware updates and control-server changes. Similar GitHub malware delivery methods appear in unrelated campaigns, underlining why defenders should examine script behavior rather than assume that downloads from a trusted platform are safe.

Observed victims and lure themes covered Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus.

The targeted work included diplomacy, economic planning, agriculture, environmental management, and energy. Decoys included an Armenian diplomatic letter and a proposal involving Turkmenistan’s Turkmennebit and Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery, suggesting interest in regional talks and resource supplies.

Talos assessed a Kazakhstan connection with medium confidence, citing language clues, testing submissions, infrastructure access, and working hours consistent with UTC+5.

That assessment does not establish government sponsorship. Investigators also recovered Linux-compatible tools and a public FortiWeb exploit, but the joint paper did not confirm that this actor had exploited FortiWeb systems in the wild.

Organizations should update affected WinRAR installations to a supported release containing the fix introduced in version 7.13. Other WinRAR exploitation campaigns show why archive software deserves regular patch checks.

Security teams should review unexpected Startup-folder files, new scheduled tasks, hidden PowerShell sessions, and scripts downloaded from public repositories, especially when these events follow archive extraction or suspicious email attachments.

The finding also calls for careful incident review: removing the original RAR attachment does not remove a payload already written to Startup. Defenders should connect file creation, process execution, and outbound traffic when checking suspected infections.

Talos published ClamAV signatures and Snort rules for coverage, while the joint technical paper provides hashes and network indicators that can support searches across endpoint records and retained logs during incident response and threat hunting.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DLP’s old reputation blocking legitimate work while real exfiltration walked out died with the pattern-only era.

The 2026 winners judge context, ride enforcement points you already run, and explain every block.

Microsoft Purview takes 1 on bundled reach; Netskope and Zscaler complete a SASE-heavy podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Microsoft Purview DLP woven through the M365 estate most enterprises already license.

• Podium: Purview (bundled), Netskope (SASE-delivered context), Zscaler (inline at cloud scale).

• Classic depth persists: Fortra’s Digital Guardian for IP-critical endpoints; Symantec strictly as renewal continuity.

• SMB lane: CoSoSys Endpoint Protector (now in Netwrix’s family) keeps device DLP accessible.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: detection approach, enforcement-point fit, false-positive management, pricing structure, acquisition currency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: context quality 30%, enforcement-point economics 25%, estate fit 20%, usability 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

The 2026 DLP Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Microsoft Purview — Best Bundled Estate DLP

Snapshot: Bundled/E5 | Exchange/Teams/endpoint/labels

Why it earns 1: Policies riding licensing most enterprises hold, labels that travel with files, and insider-risk pairing activation beats procurement for M365 estates.

Pros: Bundle economics; label integration.

Cons: Cross-platform edges; E5 gating.

Bottom line: The baseline every dedicated purchase must beat.

2. Netskope — Best SASE-Delivered

Snapshot: Platform quote | Inline + API | SaaS-context depth

Why it earns 2: Data policy enforced where traffic already flows cloud-app instance awareness (corporate vs personal) that pattern-era tools never had.

Pros: Context; enforcement-point economics.

Cons: SASE commitment assumed.

Bottom line: DLP as an SSE feature done seriously.

3. Zscaler — Best Inline Cloud-Scale

Snapshot: Platform quote | Zero-trust exchange inline

Why it earns 3: Inspection at exchange scale with EDM/IDM precision for Zscaler-routed estates, data protection is a toggle, not a deployment.

Pros: Scale; inline position.

Cons: Platform path.

Bottom line: The other SASE giant’s serious answer.

4. Proofpoint — Best People-Centric

Snapshot: Quote | Email-rooted + insider threat (ObserveIT heritage)

Why it earns 4: The channel where leaks actually happen email plus endpoint insider-risk telemetry, unified around the humans doing the leaking.

Pros: Email depth; insider lens.

Cons: Suite assembly.

Bottom line: DLP organized around people, not just patterns.

5. Forcepoint — Best Policy-Depth Veteran

Snapshot: Quote | Risk-adaptive enforcement | SSE delivery

Why it earns 5: Decades of policy templates and regulated-industry pedigree, modernized onto the edge with behavior-scaled responses.

Pros: Template depth.

Cons: Packaging evolution.

Bottom line: Mature policy on modern rails.

6. Fortra (Digital Guardian) — Best IP-Endpoint Rigor

Snapshot: Quote | Kernel-level endpoint visibility

Why it earns 6: Trade-secret defense at manufacturing/pharma depth the classic endpoint lane where IP theft is the threat model.

Pros: Endpoint rigor; managed option.

Cons: Classic-gen architecture.

Bottom line: Where the crown jewels are files, this guards them.

7. Palo Alto Networks — Best Platform-Integrated

Snapshot: Quote | Enterprise DLP across NGFW/SASE/CASB

Why it earns 7: One DLP engine spanning the Palo Alto estate firewall, Prisma Access, SaaS for platform-committed shops.

Pros: Estate unity.

Cons: Platform scope.

Bottom line: Data policy wherever Palo Alto already sits.

8. CoSoSys (Endpoint Protector) — Best SMB Device DLP

Snapshot: Published-friendly | USB/device control + content aware | Netwrix family

Why it earns 8: Device and content DLP that SMBs can actually deploy cross-platform endpoints at accessible pricing, now under the Netwrix umbrella.

Pros: Accessibility; Mac/Linux coverage.

Cons: Enterprise-estate breadth.

Bottom line: The pragmatic device-control lane.

9. Trellix — Heritage Endpoint Suite

Snapshot: Quote | McAfee-lineage endpoint DLP

Why it earns 9: Large installed bases persist across enterprise data loss prevention software deployments; evaluate roadmap depth and capabilities to stop endpoint data exfiltration at renewal rather than assuming momentum.

Pros: Estate continuity.

Cons: Diligence required.

Bottom line: A renewal conversation, honestly had.

10. Broadcom (Symantec) — Renewal-Estate Continuity

Snapshot: Quote | The long-reigning enterprise suite

Why it earns 10: Massive estates still run it; the honest framing is continuity management under Broadcom-era pricing posture negotiate hard, or migrate deliberately.

Pros: Install-base maturity.

Cons: Roadmap/pricing posture.

Bottom line: Manage the renewal; don’t greenfield it.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Activate, Contextualize, Explain Every Block

M365 estates activate Purview first its bundled reach resets every case. Route enforcement through edges you already run (Netskope/Zscaler lanes) rather than parallel infrastructure, and reserve classic endpoint rigor (Digital Guardian) for estates where files are the crown jewels.

Run every new policy in audit mode for thirty days, pair blocks with in-context explanations and fast exceptions, and report prevented-exfiltration stories not alert counts upward.

Implementation Notes

Run the first thirty days in monitor-only mode and resist every request to block early: the incident reports you generate in that window who moved what where buy the political capital that blocking policies will spend later.

Start with two or three data classes you can define crisply (payment card numbers, source code repositories, a named M&A folder) rather than a generic PII dragnet, and tune per channel, because the same policy that works on email will drown you on endpoint file events.

Decide the agent question honestly: endpoint coverage matters most where your risk lives (departing employees, USB, unmanaged uploads), so weight the pilot toward the leaver scenario HR notifies, policy tightens for that user, evidence collects automatically.

And assign a named owner for policy exceptions with a weekly review, since unreviewed exceptions are how DLP programs quietly die.

FAQs

What is the best DLP software in 2026? Microsoft Purview ranks 1 on bundled M365 reach, Netskope and Zscaler lead SASE-delivered enforcement, Proofpoint owns the people-centric email lane with Digital Guardian holding IP-endpoint rigor and CoSoSys serving SMB device control.

Is Purview enough without dedicated DLP? Often for M365-centric estates activation plus tuning beats many dedicated deployments. Cross-platform depth and IP-grade endpoint rigor remain the graduation reasons.

Why did SASE eat DLP? Enforcement economics: traffic already transits the edge, so data policy there needs no new infrastructure and cloud-app context (instance awareness) beats patterns.

Should new buyers consider Symantec or Trellix DLP? Existing estates: manage renewals with eyes open. New programs: the bundled, SASE, and people-centric lanes above are where the momentum lives.

How do we stop DLP from blocking real work? Audit-first rollouts, business-unit review of hits, explained blocks with minute-fast exceptions, and intent-clear channels enforced before ambiguous ones.

Verdict

Purview resets the baseline, the SASE pair enforces where traffic lives, and Proofpoint watches the humans activate before buying, explain every block, and let prevented-leak narratives, not alert dashboards, defend the budget.

articles.description:

The post Top 10 Best Malware Analysis Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every SOC question eventually becomes “what does this file actually do?” and the answer’s cost ranges from a free hash lookup to hypervisor-grade detonation.

Evaluating detonation environments alongside the best malware sandbox tools for security teams and dynamic malware analysis tools demonstrates that modern adversaries actively design payloads with anti-evasion, sleep timers, and conditional triggers to bypass traditional automated inspection.

We scored ten analysis tools by the job they serve, from instant context through evasion-resistant depth. Google’s VirusTotal takes 1 as the universal starting point; ANY.RUN and VMRay complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: VirusTotal the lookup that starts nearly every investigation on earth.

• Podium: VirusTotal (context), ANY.RUN (interactive analysis the analyst drives), VMRay (evasion-resistant depth).

• Never upload sensitive samples publicly private tiers exist because public submissions leak.

• Legacy watch: Cuckoo’s original is dormant (adopt the maintained revival); Trellix’s lineage warrants status checks.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: evasion resistance, interactivity, throughput, verdict quality, pricing transparency, project-status currency.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: analysis depth 30%, usability/interactivity 25%, evasion resistance 20%, pricing clarity 15%, ecosystem 10%.

The 2026 Malware Analysis Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. OPSWAT MetaDefender Cloud — Best Multi-Engine Threat Context

Snapshot: Free entry + commercial tiers | Multi-engine scanning + reputation

Why it earns 1: Fast context on files, hashes, URLs, IPs, and domains, combining multi-engine verdicts, sandboxing, and reputation intelligence in one investigation layer.

Pros: Broad lookup coverage; multi-engine analysis.

Cons: Smaller community and corpus footprint than VirusTotal.

Bottom line: The multi-engine starting point for malware triage.

2. ANY.RUN — Best Interactive Sandbox

Snapshot: Free tier + published plans | Analyst-driven detonation

Why it earns 2: The sandbox the analyst actively steers in real time allowing researchers to click phishing lures, enter document passwords, solve CAPTCHAs, and intercept staged payloads as they execute.

Through innovations in the ANY.RUN interactive malware analysis sandbox, analysts can combine manual interactive steering with automated multi-stage chain execution across Windows and Linux virtual environments.

Pros: Interactivity; training value; pricing clarity.

Cons: Public tier visibility; Windows-centric depth.

Bottom line: Analysis as a hands-on session, not a queue.

3. VMRay — Best Evasion Resistance

Snapshot: Quote | Hypervisor-level monitoring

Why it earns 3: Agentless, hypervisor-based observation malware can’t detect the reference answer for samples that sleep through hooked sandboxes.

Pros: Transparency ceiling.

Cons: Premium economics.

Bottom line: For the samples that know they’re watched.

4. Joe Security — Best Cross-Platform Depth

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Windows/macOS/Linux/Android/iOS

Why it earns 4: The deepest reports across every OS that matters hybrid analysis catching what single-platform pipelines ignore.

Pros: Platform breadth; report depth.

Cons: Analyst time to digest.

Bottom line: The whole estate’s sandbox.

5. ReversingLabs — Best File-Intelligence Scale

Snapshot: Quote | Billions-of-files reputation + static decomposition

Why it earns 5: High-speed static analysis and reputation at software-supply-chain scale verdicts on millions of files where detonation can’t keep up.

Pros: Throughput; supply-chain fit.

Cons: Complements dynamic lanes.

Bottom line: Static intelligence at industrial volume.

6. Intezer — Best Genetic Triage

Snapshot: Tiered | Code-reuse mapping | Autonomous verdicts

Why it earns 6: “Whose code is this?” answered automatically family lineage and tier-1 verdicts that clear queues without humans.

Pros: Automation depth.

Cons: Pairs with sandboxes.

Bottom line: Triage that names the family first.

7. CrowdStrike (Hybrid Analysis) — Best Free Community Sandbox

Snapshot: Free community | Falcon Sandbox engine above

Why it earns 7: Real behavioral reports at zero cost the community lane every budget-constrained team should exploit for non-sensitive samples.

Pros: Free; capable.

Cons: Public visibility; queues.

Bottom line: The free deep-dive, used wisely.

8. Palo Alto (WildFire) — Best Inline-Estate Verdicts

Snapshot: Subscription with NGFW estate | Verdicts feed prevention

Why it earns 8: Analysis wired to enforcement: unknown files detonated and verdicts pushed to the firewall estate in minutes analysis as prevention pipeline.

Pros: Estate integration.

Cons: Palo Alto-platform path.

Bottom line: The sandbox your firewalls already talk to.

9. Hatching Triage — Best Modern Self-Hosted Sandbox

Snapshot: Cloud + self-hosted | Multi-platform | Interactive analysis

Why it earns 9: Modern malware detonation with Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android coverage, analyst interaction, automated behavioral analysis, and a self-hosted option for sensitive samples.

Pros: Multi-platform depth; active development; private deployment.

Cons: More operational effort than fully managed sandboxes.

Bottom line: The modern self-hosted sandbox for teams that need control.

10. Trellix — Heritage Suite (Status Check)

Snapshot: Quote | McAfee-lineage sandbox/IVX line

Why it earns 10: Installed bases persist; roadmap and support depth warrant pre-renewal verification listed for estate reality, not momentum.

Pros: Estate continuity.

Cons: Diligence required.

Bottom line: Renewal decision, not greenfield pick.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Lookups First, Depth Where Earned

Start free and disciplined: VirusTotal context plus Hybrid Analysis detonation covers tier-1 for non-sensitive samples with a written submission policy before anything else.

Add interactivity (ANY.RUN) where analysts learn by driving, genetic automation (Intezer) where volume drowns humans, and hypervisor depth (VMRay/Joe) for the evasive minority that earns it.

Wire every verdict into detection engineering the same day; analysis that never becomes a rule is expensive curiosity.

Implementation Notes

Stand up the pipeline before the headline tool: a submission queue (email gateway, EDR quarantine, analyst uploads), an automated first pass through sandbox detonation, and a routing rule that sends only the ambiguous residue to human analysts.

Decide the cloud-versus-on-prem question on data-governance grounds early detonating samples that embed internal documents in a public multi-tenant sandbox can itself be a disclosure event, which is why regulated teams keep a private detonation lane for sensitive submissions.

Feed verdicts back automatically: hashes and IOCs from analysis should flow into blocklists, SIEM watchlists, and threat-intel platforms without a human copying strings between consoles.

And rehearse the surge scenario a phishing wave can multiply daily submissions tenfold, so know your per-sample cost curve and queue depth before the day you need them.

FAQs

What is the best malware analysis tool in 2026? VirusTotal ranks 1 as the universal context layer, ANY.RUN for interactive analyst-driven sandboxing, VMRay for evasion-resistant depth with Joe Security covering every OS and Intezer automating family-level triage.

Can free tools carry a SOC? Tier-1 triage, substantially: VirusTotal plus Hybrid Analysis handles non-sensitive volume. Paid lanes buy privacy, interactivity, evasion resistance, and automation.

Why do samples behave differently in sandboxes? Evasion: malware detects hooks, timing, and artifacts, then sleeps.. Hypervisor-level transparency (VMRay-class) and interactive driving (ANY.RUN-class) are the counters.

Is Cuckoo still safe to adopt? Via the maintained revival lineage only verify project status and budget real ops; the abandoned original is reference material.

What’s the biggest analysis mistake? Public submission of sensitive files a convenience that becomes breach disclosure. Write the submission policy before the first upload.

Verdict

VirusTotal opens every case, ANY.RUN lets analysts drive, and VMRay catches what hides layer free context, interactive skill-building, and earned depth, then turn every verdict into tomorrow’s detection rule.

articles.description:

The post Top 10 Best DevSecOps Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DevSecOps succeeds when security rides the pipeline instead of blocking it and fails when ten scanners produce ten backlogs nobody owns.

Modern engineering teams aligning with enterprise DevSecOps playbooks recognize that vulnerability volume is a vanity metric; the true measure of a program is whether developers actually remediate what their tooling flags.

We scored ten platforms on the metric that matters: whether developers actually fix what the tools find.

GitLab takes 1 for making the whole discipline one product decision; GitHub Advanced Security and Snyk complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: GitLab pipelines, repos, and scanning as one platform with published pricing.

• Podium: GitLab (all-in-one), GitHub Advanced Security (native to the code), Snyk (the workbench developers chose).

• Watch the fix-rate: adoption beats scanner depth the platform engineers use wins.

• Runtime closers: Datadog and Prisma Cloud connect pipeline findings to production truth.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: coverage breadth, developer-adoption evidence, pipeline nativity, pricing transparency, runtime connection. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: adoption/fix-rate potential 30%, coverage 25%, pipeline nativity 20%, pricing clarity 15%, runtime tie 10%.

The 2026 DevSecOps Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. GitLab — Best All-in-One Platform

Snapshot: Published tiers | SAST/secrets/deps/DAST built in | Compliance pipelines

Why it earns 1: One product covers the entire SDLC: security scanning delivered as native merge-request primitives, compliance frameworks managed as code configurations, and vulnerability findings surfaced directly where peer code review occurs.

While organizations must maintain diligence regarding critical GitLab vulnerabilities and emergency security updates, GitLab Ultimate remains the gold standard for all-in-one coherence with published tier pricing.

Pros: Platform coherence; pricing transparency.

Cons: Per-scanner depth trails specialists.

Bottom line: DevSecOps as a single buying decision.

2. GitHub Advanced Security — Best Code-Native

Snapshot: Per-committer pricing | CodeQL + push protection + Copilot Autofix

Why it earns 2: Where the majority of the world’s production source code resides, security checks belong natively: semantic code analysis via CodeQL, secrets blocked pre-commit, and enterprise Actions governance.

With GitHub Copilot Autofix automated vulnerability remediation, developers receive contextual, AI-generated code fixes directly in their pull requests, collapsing time to remediation.

Pros: Native gravity; Autofix era.

Cons: GitHub-scoped.

Bottom line: The platform’s own immune system.

3. Snyk — Best Developer Workbench

Snapshot: Free tier + per-dev | Code/deps/containers/IaC | Fix PRs

Why it earns 3: The developer experience benchmark that engineering teams adopted voluntarily long before corporate mandates arrived.

Standing out among the developer-first static application security testing (SAST) tools, Snyk provides instant feedback in the IDE, automated fix pull requests, and unified coverage across proprietary code, open-source dependencies, container images, and IaC templates.

Pros: Adoption gravity; breadth.

Cons: Per-dev economics at scale.

Bottom line: The security tool engineers don’t route around.

4. Aqua Security — Best Cloud-Native Chain

Snapshot: Trivy OSS + tiers | Build-to-runtime enforcement

Why it earns 4: Built on the widespread adoption of its open-source scanner Trivy, Aqua connects container build scanning with Kubernetes admission control and active runtime protection.

Even while navigating ecosystem risks like the supply chain incident affecting the open-source Trivy scanner, Aqua delivers a cohesive container-era security chain under a single enterprise umbrella.

Pros: OSS reach; runtime tie.

Cons: Platform assembly.

Bottom line: Kubernetes-native DevSecOps with a free floor.

5. JFrog — Best Artifact-Centric

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Artifactory + Xray + signing

Why it earns 5: DevSecOps anchored where binary artifacts actually live. While security teams must track operational updates such as JFrog Artifactory vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild, the combination of Artifactory and JFrog Xray provides deep recursive binary inspection, software bill of materials (SBOM) validation, and cryptographic release signing directly at the enterprise artifact source of truth.

Pros: Registry leverage; custody story.

Cons: JFrog-platform gravity.

Bottom line: Security fused to the artifact backbone.

6. Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud) — Best Code-to-Cloud Context

Snapshot: Quote | Pipeline findings with cloud consequences

Why it earns 6: Connects code-level vulnerabilities, IaC templates, and pipeline configurations directly to live cloud infrastructure posture.

It protects environments against scenarios where threat actors leverage CI/CD environments to compromise cloud resources, correlating static code flaws with cloud permissions to prioritize issues that expose real runtime attack paths.

Pros: Context breadth.

Cons: Packaging shifts.

Bottom line: Findings ranked by where they land.

7. Checkmarx — Best Enterprise AppSec Depth

Snapshot: Quote | Checkmarx One suite | Policy governance

Why it earns 7: Enterprise-grade analytical depth built for dedicated application security programs that require granular tuning and centralized policy orchestration across complex codebases.

Addressing security transparency alongside incidents like the Checkmarx GitHub repository breach and dark web exposure, the Checkmarx One platform delivers deep, highly configurable SAST, SCA, and API inspection under a single governance umbrella.

Pros: Depth + governance.

Cons: Cost; tuning investment.

Bottom line: The enterprise program’s platform.

8. Harness — Best Delivery-Platform Security

Snapshot: Tiered | STO orchestration + OPA policy

Why it earns 8: Security testing embedded as a first-class citizen inside the continuous deployment pipeline.

Through Security Testing Orchestration (STO), Harness normalizes, deduplicates, and correlates findings across dozens of third-party scanners, applying declarative Open Policy Agent (OPA) pipeline guardrails to halt risky builds directly within deployment pipelines.

Pros: Pipeline-native design.

Cons: Harness-scoped.

Bottom line: Security woven into deployment itself.

9. Datadog — Best Observability-Fused

Snapshot: Published usage | Code security + runtime protection on APM agents

Why it earns 9: The platform distribution play: static code analysis and software composition analysis delivered alongside runtime application self-protection (RASP) on the monitoring agents organizations already run.

Leading among modern Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tools, Datadog connects live production trace context to pre-production code flaws without requiring developers to install additional security agents.

Pros: Zero-new-agent; pricing clarity.

Cons: AppSec depth vs dedicated lanes.

Bottom line: DevSecOps through the telemetry you already pay for.

10. Cycode — Best Factory-First

Snapshot: Quote | VCS-to-pipeline risk graph

Why it earns 10: The dedicated platform built specifically to protect the modern software factory against tampering.

Grounded in intelligence such as Cycode research uncovering authentication and SDK vulnerabilities, Cycode maps developer access, source-control configurations, CI/CD pipelines, and secrets into a single risk graph to prevent poisoned pipeline executions.

Pros: Factory depth.

Cons: Quote-based.

Bottom line: The software factory, governed.

Buying Advice: Adoption Is the Spec

Activate what your host includes first GitLab tiers and GHAS reset every business case. Then pick by what engineers will actually use: the deepest scanner ignored loses to the shallower one adopted.

Gate on new findings only, consolidate dashboards into the tracker developers already open, and measure fix-rate monthly the only DevSecOps metric that survives contact with reality.

Keep runtime context (Datadog/Prisma/Aqua lanes) feeding priority, because exploitable-in-production beats severity labels.

Implementation Notes

Sequence the rollout around developer trust: enable scanning in observe-only mode for the first two sprints, publish the false-positive rate you measured, and only then turn on merge-blocking for the two or three rule classes the team agreed were non-negotiable (secrets, critical-severity reachable vulnerabilities).

Budget time for ownership mapping most DevSecOps platform value leaks away when findings route to a queue nobody owns, so wire code-owner files and service catalogs into the triage flow before the first report lands.

Negotiate contributor-based licensing carefully: shared repositories, bots, and contractors all inflate counts, and the difference between list and realistic pricing is often the cost of the enablement you actually need.

Finally, agree on one metric with engineering leadership before launch mean time to remediate reachable criticals is the honest one and report it monthly, because a platform that cannot move that number is shelf-ware with a dashboard.

FAQs

What is the best DevSecOps platform in 2026? GitLab ranks 1 for all-in-one coherence with published pricing, GitHub Advanced Security for code-native depth, Snyk for the developer workbench with Aqua owning the cloud-native chain and Datadog fusing security into observability.

One platform or best-of-breed stack? Adoption decides: a platform developers use beats specialists they ignore. Consolidate where culture is young; compose where teams are strong and someone owns the unified queue.

How are DevSecOps platforms priced? GitLab and GitHub publish (tiers/per-committer), Snyk per-developer with a free floor, Datadog usage-based enterprise suites quote. Budget enablement and triage culture beside licenses.

How does DevSecOps protect against software supply chain attacks? Modern platforms look beyond first-party code, pairing with software supply chain security tools to inspect open-source dependencies, generate software bills of materials (SBOMs), verify cryptographic artifact signatures, and lock down CI/CD runner environments.

Where do most DevSecOps programs fail? Gates before trust: blocking on day-one backlogs teaches bypass. New-findings-only gates, named repo owners, and visible fix-rate metrics succeed where big-bang enforcement fails.

Does DevSecOps include pipeline security itself? It must poisoned-pipeline attacks made the factory first-class attack surface. Platforms with Actions/pipeline policy (GitHub, GitLab, Cycode) reflect that; code-only scopes don’t.

Verdict

GitLab wins the single-decision simplicity, GitHub proves the host can guard itself, and Snyk keeps developers in the fight activate the native floor, pick for adoption, gate gently, and let fix-rate arbitrate every renewal.

Embedding automated security guardrails directly into continuous deployment pipelines provides the verifiable operational integrity required to sustain an authentic Zero Trust architecture.

articles.title: Fake Chrome App on Google Play Evades Detection and Reaches 100,000+ Downloads
articles.description:
A fake Google Chrome app appeared on Google Play with a screenshot showing more than 100,000 downloads, raising fresh concerns about app checks and paid search results. The listing copied Chrome’s name, icon, and description, but its developer was Hizbartech rather than Google LLC. The app reportedly appeared above the real browser as a sponsored […]

The post Fake Chrome App on Google Play Evades Detection and Reaches 100,000+ Downloads appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A fake Google Chrome app appeared on Google Play with a screenshot showing more than 100,000 downloads, raising fresh concerns about app checks and paid search results.

The listing copied Chrome’s name, icon, and description, but its developer was Hizbartech rather than Google LLC. The app reportedly appeared above the real browser as a sponsored result.

However, the download badge does not prove that 100,000 people installed it while it carried Chrome’s branding. Available reports also do not establish password theft, a banking Trojan, or a confirmed malware payload.

Researchers at PiunikaWeb noted the deceptive app after a user on Reddit’s r/browsers community flagged it. Their October 14 report described an adware listing and said a search for the developer’s name still found it, although they could not reproduce the sponsored Chrome search result themselves.

Fake Chrome App on Google Play

PiunikaWeb traced the app to a game called Ball Bounce, which reportedly appeared in August before changing its branding in late September.

Android Authority reported an August 22 listing and a September 30 change, while SammyGuru found an archive suggesting July availability. The exact launch date remains uncertain.

The key concern is the change in identity. A listing that once presented itself as a game later borrowed the appearance of a trusted browser.

Earlier coverage of malicious Google Play apps shows how apps can change after release, although those separate cases do not establish what this copycat contained.

The suspicious package identifier, com.ballbounce.Hizbartech, also linked the listing to its earlier game identity. Unlike an app’s visible name and icon, this identifier gave investigators another way to connect the two versions.

It is a useful search clue for device checks, not proof of specific malicious functions. PiunikaWeb cited Reddit users who installed the 42 MB app and found a contacts-style interface with AI avatars rather than a browser.

Android Authority described a chat app with prepared responses. These accounts explain the mismatch between the listing and its behavior, but they are not a published code review.

No reviewed report supplied evidence of browser password theft, remote control, or hidden banking screens in this app. Past reporting on fake Chrome installation pages describes SpyNote delivered through lookalike websites, but that was a different campaign.

Its capabilities and indicators should not be assigned to this Google Play listing. Likewise, saying the app “evaded detection” describes its apparent passage through store checks, not a verified technical method.

What the App Actually Did

The available evidence does not show encrypted payloads, checks for test devices, delayed code downloads, or an Android security flaw. The documented issue is impersonation and a reported sponsored placement.

Later coverage said the listing appeared to have been removed. SammyGuru reported that its link returned a not-found message on October 14, but cautioned that this did not confirm worldwide removal.

It also found conflicting download figures: 100,000+ in a screenshot and 10,000+ in an indexed listing. These limits matter because install totals, store availability, and confirmed infections are different measures.

Reporting on Google Play stealth loaders explains a separate method involving fake updates and later malware delivery. There is no published evidence connecting that technique or the Anatsa banking Trojan to Hizbartech’s app.

Users should check that the official Chrome listing names Google LLC as its publisher and uses com.android.chrome as its package identifier. Anyone who installed the Hizbartech copy should remove it and run Google Play Protect.

A familiar icon, sponsored placement, or large download badge should not replace checking the developer. For security teams, the package name offers a clearer starting point than searching only for Chrome.

Review affected devices for the listed app and unexpected permissions, while keeping any findings separate from confirmed data theft. The public record still leaves that question unanswered.

articles.description:
Microsoft has disclosed three Active Directory vulnerabilities that could let a remote attacker bypass a key security feature in Windows domain environments. The issues are tracked as CVE-2026-69982, CVE-2026-96252, and CVE-2026-108131, and administrators should review Microsoft’s Security Update Guide entries and deploy the available fixes as soon as possible. Active Directory is the central identity […]

The post Multiple Active Directory Vulnerabilities Let Attackers Bypass Security Feature Remotely appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has disclosed three Active Directory vulnerabilities that could let a remote attacker bypass a key security feature in Windows domain environments.

The issues are tracked as CVE-2026-69982, CVE-2026-96252, and CVE-2026-108131, and administrators should review Microsoft’s Security Update Guide entries and deploy the available fixes as soon as possible.

Active Directory is the central identity service many organizations use to manage users, computers, permissions, and access to business systems.

A weakness that bypasses a security control in this environment can be serious because domain services sit at the center of authentication and trust. If an attacker can reach an exposed or poorly protected domain service, they may be able to weaken protections that are meant to block unauthorized activity.

Microsoft has classified the three issues as security feature bypass vulnerabilities. This means the flaws do not necessarily give an attacker full control of a server. Instead, they may let an attacker bypass protections that would normally limit access, validate requests, or prevent unsafe behavior.

Multiple Active Directory Vulnerabilities

Security teams should treat this as a high-priority patching event, especially in networks where many internal systems can reach Active Directory services. The disclosed CVEs affect Microsoft Active Directory-related components, according to the vendor’s Security Update Guide pages.

Microsoft’s public entries should be the source of truth for affected products, update packages, severity ratings, and mitigation guidance because details can change as the company publishes more information.

Organizations should also confirm that all domain controllers and supporting Windows servers have received the latest cumulative updates.

The remote nature of these flaws increases the concern for large enterprise networks. Attackers who already have a foothold in a network often look for ways to move toward domain controllers, where they can target identity systems and gain broader access.

A security feature bypass could support that process by helping an intruder avoid a control that would otherwise stop or detect suspicious activity.

Administrators should first identify every domain controller, including older systems, backup domain controllers, and systems in remote offices. Test patch deployment in a controlled group where possible, then roll it out quickly across production servers.

Teams should verify successful installation through their endpoint management platform or Windows update reporting, rather than assuming that an update was applied.

Network controls remain important during patching. Domain controller services should not be exposed directly to the public internet. Organizations should limit which hosts can communicate with directory services, separate administrative systems from user networks, and require strong authentication for privileged accounts.

Organizations should also review monitoring tools for unusual authentication failures, unexpected privilege changes, new service accounts, or suspicious activity involving domain controllers. This update is another reminder that identity infrastructure needs the same urgent patching process as public-facing applications.

Organizations have repeatedly faced serious risk from flaws in network and identity products, including recently disclosed issues affecting remote-access infrastructure such as Citrix NetScaler and Gateway vulnerabilities.

Security teams can also review broader coverage of Microsoft security vulnerabilities to track related Windows and enterprise software updates. Microsoft has not provided evidence in the accessible update information that these specific flaws are being actively exploited.

Still, defenders should not wait for confirmed exploitation before applying updates. Security feature bypass bugs can become more valuable when combined with credential theft, phishing, lateral movement, or another vulnerability.

Organizations should review Microsoft’s advisories for CVE-2026-69982, CVE-2026-96252, and CVE-2026-108131 and confirm that all relevant Active Directory systems are updated.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Palo Alto PAN-OS 0-day Flaw to Gain Root Code Execution on Firewalls
articles.description:
Hackers are exploiting a high-severity flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS that allows authenticated attackers to run code with root privileges on affected firewalls. Tracked as CVE-2026-0322, the vulnerability affects the management interface, with the company confirming “very limited exploitation” and urging customers to apply fixes as soon as possible. Palo Alto Networks published its […]

The post Hackers Exploit Palo Alto PAN-OS 0-day Flaw to Gain Root Code Execution on Firewalls appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are exploiting a high-severity flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS that allows authenticated attackers to run code with root privileges on affected firewalls. Tracked as CVE-2026-0322, the vulnerability affects the management interface, with the company confirming “very limited exploitation” and urging customers to apply fixes as soon as possible.

Palo Alto Networks published its security advisory on October 14, 2026, assigning the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.6 and its highest remediation urgency. The company credited internal researcher Suraj Siddharudh with discovering and reporting the issue. It has not named the attackers or disclosed how many organizations were targeted.

PAN-OS 0-Day Vulnerability

The flaw is a code injection weakness, classified as CWE-94. An attacker must have authenticated access with high privileges and network access to the management interface. Successful exploitation allows code execution as root, giving the attacker the highest level of control over the affected firewall. No user interaction is required.

This is not an unauthenticated attack path. The requirement for an existing privileged login limits who can exploit it, but internet-facing management interfaces carry the greatest risk. No special configuration is needed for a vulnerable PAN-OS installation to be affected.

Affected products include PA-Series hardware firewalls, VM-Series virtual firewalls, and Panorama deployments running on virtual systems or M-Series appliances. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected and require no action for this vulnerability

The management interface has featured in earlier PAN-OS attacks. Cyber Security News previously covered active exploitation of CVE-2025-0108 and attackers chaining PAN-OS vulnerabilities to compromise devices. Those reports concern separate flaws and do not establish a connection to the current activity.

Fixed Versions and Protection Measures

Fixed releases include PAN-OS 12.2.4, 12.1.10-h2, 11.1.16-h3, and 10.2.18-h12, with additional hotfix options for earlier maintenance releases. PAN-OS 11.2 fixes include 11.2.4-h22, 11.2.7-h21, 11.2.10-h15, and 11.2.13-h3. Version 11.2.16 was listed with an expected release date of October 15. Administrators should follow the advisory’s upgrade path for their installed version.

Palo Alto Networks says no known workaround exists. Restricting management access to trusted internal IP addresses, ideally through a dedicated jump box, reduces exposure but does not replace patching. Its management access guidance warns against exposing administrative interfaces to the internet or other untrusted networks.

Palo Alto identified 66[.]42[.]72[.]14, 208[.]83[.]239[.]114, and 149[.]248[.]47[.]234 as addresses linked to threat activity and limited exploit attempts.

Security teams can use these indicators when reviewing management traffic, while prioritizing upgrades and tighter access controls. The advisory warns that attack variations may evade current signatures, making a supported fixed release the recommended protection for affected systems.

articles.title: Cisco Secure Email Gateway 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
articles.description:
Cisco has warned that attackers are actively exploiting a critical zero-day vulnerability in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that can give them root access to affected appliances. Tracked as CVE-2026-76519, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows attacks through specially crafted email attachments without requiring a login. Cisco published its advisory on October […]

The post Cisco Secure Email Gateway 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cisco has warned that attackers are actively exploiting a critical zero-day vulnerability in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that can give them root access to affected appliances. Tracked as CVE-2026-76519, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows attacks through specially crafted email attachments without requiring a login.

Cisco published its advisory on October 14, 2026. The company said its security response team became aware of active exploitation in October. Public reporting has not identified the attackers or established how many devices have been compromised, leaving the scale of the campaign unclear.

The vulnerability sits in the Advanced Malware Protection feature, known as AMP. Cisco says the gateway fails to handle certain email attachments safely when its File Reputation service is enabled. An attacker can send a malicious attachment through an affected device to write arbitrary files and potentially execute commands with root privileges.

Root access gives an attacker control over the underlying operating system. The entry point is the gateway processing an attachment, rather than a user opening a file. Cisco has not described a requirement for a recipient to click a link or launch the attachment.

Cisco Secure Email Gateway 0-Day Vulnerability

Both physical and virtual appliances are affected when they run vulnerable AsyncOS software and meet two conditions. File Reputation must be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools package must be older than version 25.3.0.5525. Cisco Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not affected.

This disclosure follows another actively exploited Secure Email Gateway flaw, CVE-2026-76461, reported in September. Earlier coverage of CVE-2025-20393 also documented attacks against Cisco email appliances, although that vulnerability involved the Spam Quarantine feature rather than AMP.

Administrators can check File Reputation under the Advanced Malware Protection settings for incoming or outgoing mail policies. The contentscannerstatus command shows the installed Content Scanner Tools version.

For investigation, Cisco recommends running grep "System Security" system_logs and checking every device in a cluster. A suspected compromise message requires incident response, while an incomplete security scan requires support from Cisco’s Technical Assistance Center.

A clean result does not rule out an attack. Cisco warns that intruders with root access may hide or delete evidence. Security teams should also review independent firewall and network logs for unexpected uploads from the gateway or downloads from suspicious addresses.

Patching closes the entry point but does not establish whether attackers previously gained access. Organizations that find suspicious activity should contact Cisco TAC and preserve available evidence to support a detailed investigation.

Fixed Versions and Immediate Action

Cisco lists AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 as fixed releases. Customers on version 16.0 should migrate to a fixed release. Cisco strongly recommends moving installations earlier than version 16.5 to 16.5.0-780.

The fix is also available through Content Scanner Tools version 25.3.0.5525 or later for licensed, supported AsyncOS releases. This package update does not require a full software upgrade or restart. Administrators who disabled automatic updates can request it using contentscannerupdate, then verify the installed version.

There are no workarounds. Customers with automatic updates enabled should confirm that the fixed package has actually arrived rather than assume protection.

Cisco says it has already deployed the corrected package across Secure Email Cloud Gateway, so those customers do not need to apply the update themselves. For affected organizations, updating the gateway and checking for earlier compromise should proceed together.

articles.title: Multiple NGINX Flaws Let Remote Attackers Crash Servers and Execute Malicious Code
articles.description:
F5 has disclosed three serious security flaws in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source that can let remote, unauthenticated attackers crash worker processes by sending crafted HTTP requests. In certain setups, the memory errors could also allow code execution, although F5 says that outcome requires Address Space Layout Randomization, known as ASLR, to be disabled […]

The post Multiple NGINX Flaws Let Remote Attackers Crash Servers and Execute Malicious Code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
F5 has disclosed three serious security flaws in NGINX Plus and NGINX Open Source that can let remote, unauthenticated attackers crash worker processes by sending crafted HTTP requests.

In certain setups, the memory errors could also allow code execution, although F5 says that outcome requires Address Space Layout Randomization, known as ASLR, to be disabled or bypassed. All three issues affect the NGINX data plane, which handles user traffic, rather than its control plane.

The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-97205, CVE-2026-93479, and CVE-2026-15176. F5 published the three advisories on October 14, 2026, and rated every issue High at 8.1 under CVSS v3.1 and Critical at 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.

The bugs do not make every NGINX server vulnerable by default because each one needs a specific software version and configuration.

Multiple NGINX Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-97205 is a use-after-free flaw in ngx_http_core_module. It can be triggered when asynchronous file I/O, or AIO, is enabled and NGINX processes a Server Side Includes page containing an include virtual command.

The worker may keep using memory after that memory has been released, leading to memory corruption or an unexpected worker shutdown. F5 credits security researcher Cyberlanc3r with reporting the issue.

CVE-2026-93479 is a heap buffer overflow linked to the NGINX map directive and regular expression matching. The unsafe condition can appear when the root directive or an access-log format uses the map’s regex capture variables before the map output variable.

A related path involves a non-cacheable variable used in a string expression. Crafted requests can then make a worker write beyond the allocated memory area and restart. F5 credits Matt Suiche of Tolmo and Mateusz Gierblinski for coordinated disclosure.

CVE-2026-15176 is a separate heap buffer overflow in ngx_http_core_module. It affects a location block that combines alias with rewrite and a set or return directive that refers to $request_filename.

The same risk can exist when $request_filename appears in an access log_format. F5 says a remote attacker can trigger the flaw without authentication, but the required server-side conditions remain outside the attacker’s control. The company found this issue internally.

The affected range is broad. CVE-2026-97205 and CVE-2026-15176 affect NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 through 1.31.6 and 1.0.0 through 1.30.5, while the older 0.x line is also listed for CVE-2026-15176. CVE-2026-93479 has a narrower open-source range of 1.31.2 through 1.31.6 and 1.30.0 through 1.30.5. NGINX Plus 37.0.0 through 37.0.4 is affected by all three bugs.

Related products, including NGINX Instance Manager, F5 WAF for NGINX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and some NGINX Ingress Controller releases, are also affected.

Administrators should upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.31.7 or 1.30.6. NGINX Plus users on the 37.x line should move to 37.0.5.1 or 37.1.0.1.

Fixed releases also include NGINX Instance Manager 2.24.0, F5 WAF for NGINX 5.16.0 or 5.14.2, NGINX Gateway Fabric 2.8.0, and NGINX Ingress Controller 5.7.0. Some older branches have no update, so F5 advises moving to a supported branch that contains a fix.

Where patching cannot happen at once, configuration changes can lower the risk. For CVE-2026-97205, F5 recommends disabling either AIO or SSI. Turning off AIO may reduce performance for large static files or media streaming under heavy load, while disabling SSI stops NGINX from processing SSI tags.

For CVE-2026-93479, administrators should replace unnamed regex captures with named captures and use them only inside the matching block. For CVE-2026-15176, F5 recommends avoiding alias inside a location block and avoiding $request_filename where possible.

Teams should first run nginx -T to review the full active configuration, including included files, then compare the installed build against each advisory. After any change, nginx -t can check the syntax before the configuration is reloaded. These checks matter because the presence of an affected version alone does not prove that the needed configuration is active.

The disclosure follows several other NGINX memory-safety fixes in 2026. Cybersecurity News previously reported three NGINX flaws involving heap overflow, memory disclosure, and use-after-free conditions and an earlier group of NGINX bugs that could cause code execution or denial of service.

F5’s advisories do not report active exploitation of these three newly disclosed flaws. Still, internet-facing NGINX systems should be reviewed quickly because a successful request can restart workers and disrupt service, while a working ASLR bypass could raise the impact to code execution.

Applying the fixed release remains the strongest response because the workarounds cover only the known unsafe configuration paths.
