articles.title: 24 Security Vulnerabilities Patched in curl Used Across 30 Billion Installations
articles.description:
The curl project released curl 8.23.0 on October 14, 2026, announcing 24 security fixes affecting the widely used data transfer tool and its underlying library, libcurl. The vulnerabilities include credential leaks, authentication errors, command injection, and flaws that can disrupt applications. The release also removes SMB and SMBS protocol support, making compatibility checks important before […]

The post 24 Security Vulnerabilities Patched in curl Used Across 30 Billion Installations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The curl project released curl 8.23.0 on October 14, 2026, announcing 24 security fixes affecting the widely used data transfer tool and its underlying library, libcurl.

The vulnerabilities include credential leaks, authentication errors, command injection, and flaws that can disrupt applications. The release also removes SMB and SMBS protocol support, making compatibility checks important before deployment.

According to security firm AISLE, it discovered 18 of the vulnerabilities announced with this release, representing 75 percent of the total.

Its dedicated audit produced 24 CVEs across two releases, with six addressed in curl 8.22.0 and another eighteen associated with 8.23.0. Those figures describe AISLE’s audit findings, not the complete security count for either release.

curl Security Vulnerabilities

One notable flaw, CVE-2026-86414, allows an HTTP proxy to trick libcurl into handing over credentials intended for the destination server.

During a CONNECT tunnel request, the proxy can return a 401 response with a WWW-Authenticate header instead of the expected proxy authentication response.

This can expose a Basic authentication password or a Negotiate/Kerberos ticket. The issue affects versions 7.10.8 through 8.22.0.

Another vulnerability, CVE-2026-94266, can expose passwords through CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL when curl obtains credentials from a .netrc file. The command-line tool can reveal the same information through its url_effective output variable.

Applications that record these returned URLs could therefore place credentials in logs. Versions 7.62.0 through 8.22.0 are affected.

These findings extend a recurring security concern around credential handling. Cybersecurity News previously covered a curl password leak involving redirects and .netrc files, where credentials could reach an unintended host under specific conditions.

The official advisory for CVE-2026-87864 explains an IMAP command injection flaw involving message uploads and CURLOPT_CRLF. Curl advertised the original message size but sent additional bytes after converting line endings.

A mail server could interpret those extra bytes as commands within the authenticated session. This concerns IMAP commands, not operating system shell commands.

Importantly, this flaw was already fixed in curl 8.22.0, although its advisory was published on October 14. It affects versions 7.30.0 through 8.21.0 and carries a low severity rating. Avoiding CURLOPT_CRLF with IMAP is the documented workaround. Recently, cURL patched a 25-Year-Old Vulnerability with version 8.21.0.

Other AISLE findings involve stale AWS signing headers, credentials crossing redirect boundaries, client certificate mix-ups, damaged cookie storage, and incorrect HSTS cache handling. Additional issues can cause an endless loop or exhaust the process stack. These failures often emerge when settings or connection state persist after the destination or identity changes.

Administrators should upgrade affected curl and libcurl installations to 8.23.0 or apply the relevant patches. Check applications that bundle libcurl, since updating the standalone tool may leave embedded copies unchanged.

Review the settings for proxy authentication, credential logging, and IMAP uploads while planning deployment. Before rollout, check the release announcement for any compatibility changes.

articles.description:
As MSSPs take on more clients, alert volumes grow fast. Analyst capacity usually doesn’t. That gap shows up in triage and response first. Teams spend too much time checking IOCs, switching between tools, rebuilding context, and escalating cases that could have been closed earlier. Across thousands of investigations, those extra minutes turn into slower response, more […]

The post How MSSPs Can Cut Tier 1 Bottlenecks Eating into Profit Margins  appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
As MSSPs take on more clients, alert volumes grow fast. Analyst capacity usually doesn’t. That gap shows up in triage and response first.

Teams spend too much time checking IOCs, switching between tools, rebuilding context, and escalating cases that could have been closed earlier.

Across thousands of investigations, those extra minutes turn into slower response, more pressure on Tier 2, and higher delivery costs. 

Let’s look at the triage and response bottlenecks that quietly drive up MSSP workload, and how to remove them before they start eating into margins. 

See Where Triage & Response Put Pressure on MSSP Margins 

For an MSSP, the time spent on each investigation directly affects how much it costs to serve a client.

A few extra minutes on one case may not seem significant, but repeated across hundreds or thousands of alerts, they consume analyst capacity that could be spent handling other incidents or supporting more customers. 

The result is a simple scaling problem: as more analyst time goes into each case, it becomes harder to increase client volume without also increasing headcount, stretching SLAs, or putting more pressure on margins. 

The more of these bottlenecks remain in the workflow, the harder it becomes to grow the client base without growing operational costs alongside it. 

Remove the bottlenecks behind slower investigations.Keep analyst workload from eating into MSSP margins. Cut Triage & Response Friction 

Bottleneck #1: Too Much Time Goes into Basic Alert Validation 

Before analysts can decide what to do with an alert, they first need enough context to understand whether it is actually malicious. 

That often means checking hashes, IPs, domains, and URLs across different sources, looking for related activity, and piecing the findings together manually.

None of these steps may take long on their own. The problem is how often they repeat across clients and investigations. 

For an MSSP, that repetition has a direct cost. The more Tier 1 time goes into basic validation, the fewer cases each analyst can handle.

As alert volumes grow, the MSSP either accepts longer queues and greater SLA pressure or adds more analyst capacity, both of which put pressure on margins. 

Give Tier 1 the Context to Decide Faster 

With ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup, analysts can investigate suspicious indicators and related activity from one place instead of rebuilding context across multiple sources. 

They can search hashes, IPs, domains, URLs, processes, registry activity, and other artifacts, then pivot into connected infrastructure and previous malicious activity.

This gives Tier 1 more evidence earlier in the workflow, helping analysts decide faster whether a case can be closed or needs deeper investigation. 

Cutting routine validation work gives Tier 1 more capacity for cases that actually need investigation.

Bottleneck #2: Too Many Cases Get Pushed to Tier 2 

When Tier 1 doesn’t have enough context to close a case confidently, escalation becomes the safer option. But every unnecessary handoff pulls a more experienced analyst into work that may not actually require Tier 2 expertise. 

The cost goes beyond the escalation itself. Tier 2 may need to review the alert, reconstruct what has already been checked, fill in missing context, and only then continue the investigation.

Repeated across multiple clients, that eats into senior analyst capacity and makes each case more expensive to handle. 

Keeping more routine cases at Tier 1 reduces the amount of senior analyst time each client consumes. 

Help Tier 1 Close More Cases on Their Own

Even when an investigation is complete, analysts still have to package what they found for the next person, another team, or the client. 

That often means pulling together IOCs, screenshots, behavioral evidence, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, verdicts, and recommended actions manually.

If the handoff is incomplete, the next analyst may need to reopen the investigation, recheck evidence, or ask for more context before they can act. 

For MSSPs, that extra work adds time to every case. It also ties up both sides of the handoff: the analyst preparing the report and the analyst waiting to continue the response.

This matters most when escalation is unavoidable. Tier 2 can start with a well-formed investigation record instead of spending the first part of the case rebuilding context that Tier 1 has already collected. 

Faster handoffs cut duplicated work and keep analyst time focused on response instead of report assembly, helping MSSPs handle more cases without adding the same pressure to margins. 

Bottleneck #4: Outdated Threat Data Adds to the Triage Queue 

Threat infrastructure rarely stays still for long. Attackers rotate domains, IPs, and URLs, while new infrastructure can appear faster than traditional threat lists are updated. 

For an MSSP protecting multiple client environments, stale intelligence creates a wider problem than a missed indicator.

Activity linked to emerging infrastructure may continue generating new cases across customers before detection systems recognize it for what it is. 

That leaves analysts reacting to threats later in the cycle, when more investigation work is already required.

At scale, even a small gap in threat-data freshness can translate into a larger queue and more incidents competing for the same team.

Keeping detection closer to what attackers are using now helps stop the triage queue from growing with threats that could have been recognized earlier. 

Bottleneck #5: Disconnected Tools Add Friction to Every Response 

MSSP workflows rarely happen in one platform. Analysts may investigate a file or URL in one tool, manage alerts in a SIEM, enrich cases in a TIP, and coordinate response through a SOAR or ticketing system. 

When those systems are disconnected, investigation results have to be moved manually. IOCs get copied from one platform to another, case context gets rewritten, and analysts spend time making sure the same evidence exists everywhere it needs to.

The post Microsoft’s Recent Windows Updates Break Remote Desktop Services With Error “0xC000000D” appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has confirmed a Windows 11 Remote Desktop issue that can prevent non-admin users from connecting to remote computers with Administrator protection enabled. The problem follows the September 22, 2026, non-security preview update, KB5124010, or later updates. It mainly affects company-managed computers used as Remote Desktop hosts.

Failed connections may return error 0xC000000D and display the message, “The token that was passed to the function is invalid.” Microsoft opened the issue on October 13 and updated its status to “Mitigated” that morning. A temporary workaround is available, but the company is still developing a permanent fix.

Affected Windows 11 Systems

Microsoft lists Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, 26H1, and 26H2 as affected. Windows Server is not affected by this specific issue. The failure occurs when Administrator protection is enabled on the remote host, regardless of how administrators turned on the feature.

This makes the host’s security settings an important part of troubleshooting. Support teams investigating matching failures should check the installed Windows updates, confirm the reported error, and review whether Administrator protection is active before making policy changes. These checks help identify computers that match Microsoft’s description of the problem.

Administrator protection limits how Windows grants powerful system permissions. As explained in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Windows 11 Administrator protection, the feature creates a separate, temporary admin token after the user approves an administrative task. Windows removes that token when the process ends, helping prevent malware from silently gaining admin rights.learn.microsoft+1

Organizations using Microsoft’s Windows security baselines should review their settings carefully. The baselines for Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 enable Administrator protection unless the organization has changed the policy. Microsoft’s updated 26H2 security baseline also recommends testing the configuration against business needs.

Microsoft advises IT administrators to temporarily disable Administrator protection on affected Remote Desktop hosts through their existing management tools. The workaround requires resetting the “User Account Control Type Of Admin Approval Mode” policy through Microsoft Intune or Group Policy.

Because this removes an added security safeguard, organizations should limit the change to affected devices and record the exception for later review.

Cyber Security News previously covered separate Remote Desktop credential prompt failures. Administrators should not assume those earlier fixes address this issue. Microsoft’s current release-health notice says a future Windows update will provide the permanent resolution, with further details to follow.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake WatchGuard VPN Download Site to Steal Login Credentials
articles.description:
Hackers used a fake WatchGuard VPN download website to steal login details before offering visitors the real, digitally signed VPN installer. The attack collected a VPN server address, username, and password through a browser pop-up, leaving victims exposed without installing a malicious client. The campaign shows how a normal software search can lead to credential […]

The post Hackers Use Fake WatchGuard VPN Download Site to Steal Login Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used a fake WatchGuard VPN download website to steal login details before offering visitors the real, digitally signed VPN installer.

The attack collected a VPN server address, username, and password through a browser pop-up, leaving victims exposed without installing a malicious client.

The campaign shows how a normal software search can lead to credential theft. Similar search engine poisoning attacks have pushed fake websites into trusted search results, making a high ranking a poor guide to whether a download page is safe.

Researchers from Huntress identified the campaign while investigating an October 7 incident involving an administrator at a managed service provider.

Their October 13 report described phishing, not a malware-laced installer: the theft happened inside the browser before the genuine software download.

Hackers Use Fake WatchGuard VPN Download Site

The administrator searched Bing for “watchguard vpn sll download,” then opened the fake website eight seconds later. Investigators traced the visit through Bing’s normal search-result redirect.

That evidence supported search engine optimization poisoning, rather than a paid malicious advertisement, as the route into the trap.

The landing page used WatchGuard branding, product information, and a questions section to appear useful. A download button led to a fake support page offering clients for different operating systems.

A footer called it an independent fan site, despite the download flow presenting itself as a support service. Selecting any download option opened a prompt requesting Server, Login, and Password.

Those fields match the details needed for a normal VPN connection, making the request appear familiar. Earlier fake Ivanti download sites used similar vendor impersonation, although that campaign delivered altered installers rather than collecting everything through a browser form.

The capture logic used roughly 150 lines of readable JavaScript. It placed the submitted values into JSON and sent them through an HTTP POST request to a separate collection server. Each submission included a label showing whether it was the first or second attempt.

The script always rejected the first entry, cleared the fields, and displayed an “Incorrect data” message. This could prompt victims to correct a mistyped password or try another one, giving attackers another set of details.

How the Credential Theft Worked

Failed network requests only generated a browser-console warning, avoiding a visible error. After the second submission, the message turned green and a hidden link started downloading WatchGuard Mobile VPN with SSL version 12.11.5 from the vendor’s official content delivery network.

Huntress verified that its digital signature remained valid and that the signed content had not changed. This differs from earlier VPN credential theft linked by Microsoft to Storm-2561, which used fake installers and malicious DLLs before directing victims toward genuine software.

Huntress did not establish that the same operators controlled both registrations of the reused phishing domain. In the investigated incident, browser history showed no download from WatchGuard’s delivery network.

Huntress said this suggested the administrator had not completed both prompts, although a first submission remained possible. Managed Defender flagged the activity 21 seconds after the page loaded, allowing responders to provide remediation guidance before escalation.

The lure domain was offline by October 13. Organizations should reset exposed passwords, treat submitted VPN server addresses as known to attackers, enforce multifactor authentication, and review unusual VPN logins.

Staff should use bookmarked links to the official WatchGuard software portal rather than search results. A valid installer signature does not prove that the website supplying it handled credentials safely.

Announced on October 13, 2026, the operation led to 28 arrests and the rescue of 117 people forced to work inside scam centers. The United Kingdom’s National Crime […]

The post Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI Join Global Crackdown on West African Scam Networks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI joined an international crackdown on West African scam networks that removed more than 3.7 million Facebook and Instagram accounts, pages and groups.

Announced on October 13, 2026, the operation led to 28 arrests and the rescue of 117 people forced to work inside scam centers.

The United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency hosted the effort in London, bringing together technology companies and law enforcement partners from ten countries.

The Joint Disruption Week began on October 6, with investigators sharing intelligence on operations in Nigeria, Ghana and other African countries, according to the Department of Justice announcement.

Investigators from the Department of Justice and analysts at Meta identified scam networks and abusive online activity, not a named malware family.

Neither organization’s published account disclosed malware samples, file hashes or an infection chain. The findings instead describe coordinated social engineering, fake identities and payment fraud spread across online platforms.

Meta, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI Join Global Crackdown

Meta said most removed accounts appeared to target people in the United States and United Kingdom using profiles that posed as American and British users.

These removals extend the platform’s broader work on Meta’s latest anti-scam tools while taking away accounts that criminals used to reach potential victims.

Microsoft suspended accounts suspected of links to the scams. Google and OpenAI also participated, although the announcements did not provide separate takedown totals for either company.

OpenAI said it shared insights with partners and used AI to help identify scam networks across platforms. Authorities received leads on more than 30 suspected scam centers. In Sasaabi, near Accra, Ghanaian officers arrested 19 people and seized 303 electronic devices.

They also identified 117 trafficking victims awaiting return to Nigeria and 89 fraud victims whose losses totaled about $8.3 million.

Nigerian authorities arrested another nine people and seized 53 devices. The trafficking victims must be distinguished from suspects: Meta said people rescued in Ghana had been held against their will, lacked adequate food and suffered physical and psychological abuse.

The latest figures add detail to earlier reporting on the Ghana scam center raid and underline why arrest totals cannot be treated as counts of everyone found inside a compound. People forced to send scam messages can themselves be victims of the criminal operation.

How the Scam Networks Worked

The networks used several fraud models rather than one technical attack. Investment scams began with fake romantic or professional relationships before victims were directed toward false investment offers, including cryptocurrency schemes.

Other operations involved fake military identities, goods that never arrived and claims that criminals could recover previously stolen money.

Law enforcement impersonation and digital arrest schemes used threats to pressure victims into paying. Job and task scams offered simple work but demanded fees or transfers from applicants. These methods rely on trust, fear and false authority rather than a disclosed software vulnerability.

The technical response connected online accounts, web infrastructure, communication channels and financial activity.

Silent Push said it mapped more than 35,000 malicious domains and nearly 700 communication channels tied to African scam centers, helping investigators link online operations to physical locations and operators.

For readers assessing suspicious offers, earlier FBI warnings about fake work-from-home job scams explain why requests to pay cryptocurrency before receiving work deserve close scrutiny. The same payment pressure appeared among the fraud types identified during this operation.

Industry partners identified more than $11 million in potentially freezable funds. That figure does not mean the full amount was frozen, seized or returned. Separately, Coinbase identified more than 65 active scam victims and stopped over $415,000 in potential losses before payments occurred.

The operation shows why account removals alone are insufficient. Platforms can interrupt contact with victims, while financial tracing can expose payment routes and police can seize devices and arrest suspected organizers.

Investigators now have additional leads, but the announcements do not establish that every linked scam center has been closed.

Anyone targeted should preserve chats, payment records and transaction details to help investigators. Stop sending money, contact the payment provider and report the suspected online fraud. Avoid anyone promising to recover lost cryptocurrency in exchange for another upfront payment.

articles.title: PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw Enabling Root Privilege Escalation and VM Escape
articles.description:
A public proof of concept for Vghost, a high-severity Linux vhost flaw tracked as CVE-2026-74580, shows how the bug can let a local user gain root access or, in certain virtual machine setups, break out of a guest and affect the host. The issue has a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8 and is fixed in […]

The post PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw Enabling Root Privilege Escalation and VM Escape appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public proof of concept for Vghost, a high-severity Linux vhost flaw tracked as CVE-2026-74580, shows how the bug can let a local user gain root access or, in certain virtual machine setups, break out of a guest and affect the host. The issue has a CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8 and is fixed in updated Linux kernel releases.

Vhost is a Linux kernel system that helps virtual machines handle network and other device traffic more quickly. It uses shared virtual queues, called virtqueues, to carry device data between a guest and the host. The flaw lies in how vhost caches IOTLB mappings used to find those queues in memory.

The problem occurs when a virtual ring is reconfigured. Linux updates the ring’s address or size but doesn’t clear the cached mapping for the ring’s descriptor, available, or used data.

A later cache hit can therefore skip the expected address check and translate the new address using an old mapping. The resulting pointer may reach kernel copy routines with an invalid target.

Researchers on the Seclists mailing list traced the bug to two earlier kernel changes: one introduced the metadata cache, while the other deferred guest I/O address validation.

PoC Released for Linux Vhost Flaw

For local privilege escalation, an attacker first needs permission to open a vhost device such as /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. The PoC primes the cache, changes a ring address without clearing the cached entry, then triggers the queue. The researchers say this can read and write kernel memory.

The demonstrated chain uses a kernel memory read to work out the address randomization offset, then writes to the kernel’s modprobe_path setting. Triggering a kernel module request can then run an attacker-controlled helper with root privileges.

The researchers report reproducing the chain on Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. Device permissions differed: the tested Ubuntu system limited access to the kvm group, while the other listed test systems exposed the device to ordinary users.

That difference makes device permissions an important exposure check, but it does not replace patching. Membership in kvm or another group with access to vhost devices should be treated as privileged while a system remains unpatched.

The second path starts inside a virtual machine. It requires a vhost device using a virtual IOMMU, iommu_platform, and the virtio queue-reset feature VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. A guest can reset and re-enable a queue, leading the host to reconfigure its ring while the stale metadata remains cached.

When the guest then triggers the queue, the stale mapping can send a used-ring write beyond guest memory and into the QEMU process heap. The researchers say the corruption can crash QEMU or affect its control flow. This is a configuration-dependent VM escape risk, not a claim that every virtual machine can be escaped through the flaw.

The upstream fix clears the vring metadata cache when the ring address or size is changed, so the new configuration must pass IOTLB validation.

The first fixed upstream stable releases listed for the affected series are 5.10.265, 5.15.216, 6.1.183, 6.6.152, 6.12.104, 6.18.45, 7.1.9, and 7.2. Administrators should install a fixed kernel or a vendor backport and reboot into it.

Until then, restrict access to all vhost device nodes, including /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*. Do not pass these devices to untrusted containers.

For unpatched virtualization hosts, avoid exposing vhost devices with iommu_platform behind a virtual IOMMU to untrusted guests. Permission changes do not revoke file descriptors that are already open, and they do not address the guest-triggered path.

For related coverage, see Cyber Security News’ reports on Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws and KVM guest-to-host escape risks. The technical analysis and PoC are available from Tencent Zhuque Lab and GitHub.

CrowdStrike disclosed the joint operation on October 13, describing it as the start of a wider effort against the group’s domestic support network. The farms […]

The post FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used to Infiltrate U.S. Companies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The FBI disrupted several U.S. laptop farms used by North Korean threat group FAMOUS CHOLLIMA in late September 2026, cutting off infrastructure that helped fake remote workers enter American companies.

CrowdStrike disclosed the joint operation on October 13, describing it as the start of a wider effort against the group’s domestic support network.

The farms housed company laptops that overseas operatives controlled remotely while posing as U.S. employees. This setup helped them hide their locations, collect salaries for North Korea’s regime, and keep access to employer systems.

CrowdStrike said dozens of affected organizations operated across aerospace, energy, finance, healthcare, cybersecurity, defense engineering, government technology, and consumer technology.

CrowdStrike researchers identified false identities, technical indicators, and U.S. computers supporting the scheme between April 2025 and June 2026.

Their report on the disruption describes remote access tools and hardware abuse, not a newly identified malware family. The team combined device activity with targeted investigations to uncover local facilitators and share findings with the FBI.

FBI Disrupts North Korean Famous Chollima Laptop Farms Used

The operation depended on a simple gap: a worker hired under a stolen identity could not easily receive a company laptop abroad without raising questions.

As earlier reporting on North Korean identity fraud explains, local helpers provide the addresses and equipment needed to make overseas workers appear domestic.

CrowdStrike observed operatives filing false police reports claiming laptops had been stolen, then requesting replacements at farm addresses.

Others claimed sudden moves to redirect deliveries or rotated through residential addresses to hide the final destination. Some obtained jobs through IT staffing firms, allowing client devices to reach farms without those firms knowing.

Once a laptop arrived, a facilitator added hardware and software for remote control. The physical device stayed in the United States while its operator worked elsewhere.

This local presence helped the group pass location checks, handle employer equipment, and support identity and financial checks needed to receive wages.

The farms also supplied a trusted local presence for financial checks. CrowdStrike described facilitators as providing a physical address, a legal identity, and a route through bank due diligence requirements.

That makes the support network more than a place to store laptops: it connects hiring, access, and payment. Taking a farm offline forces operators to rebuild that chain, even when the wider group can move elsewhere.

Device Spoofing Complicates Detection

Since May 2026, CrowdStrike has observed FAMOUS CHOLLIMA spoofing device hashes, including making a video capture card appear to be a webcam.

Researchers also saw the same disguised device across separate victim organizations, suggesting operators reused device identifiers while trying to avoid detection.

Farm networks shared identifiers across several fake worker identities at the same time, offering another clue to coordinated activity.

The findings complement earlier coverage of remote interview fraud tactics, where stand-ins and remote desktop tools helped hide who was actually completing interviews and technical work.

The distinction matters for defenders: a legitimate tool can support an illegal operation without being malware. CrowdStrike names Astrill VPN, AnyDesk, OBS Studio, and PiKVM as technologies to review in context.

Their presence alone does not prove compromise, but unexplained use alongside identity or shipping inconsistencies deserves investigation.

CrowdStrike recommends standard background checks and reviews for reused phone numbers, email addresses, bank accounts, resume wording, and website content across profiles.

Other warning signs include differences between identity documents and video appearances, suspicious job references, new public profiles, and login activity inconsistent with a worker’s claimed location.

The latest disruption follows earlier nationwide laptop farm searches reported in June 2025, but the operations should not be treated as the same case. CrowdStrike did not disclose an exact farm count, arrest total, or seized device count for the September 2026 action.

CrowdStrike warned that the disruption will likely have a limited local effect rather than stop the wider operation.

FAMOUS CHOLLIMA remains active and is expected to adapt, making continued checks on worker identity, device delivery, and remote access important beyond the initial hiring process.

The post VirusTotal Integrates Threat Intelligence With ChatGPT for Malware Analysis appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
VirusTotal can now bring threat intelligence into ChatGPT through VirusTotal AI (VTAI), allowing users to investigate suspicious files, URLs, domains, and IP addresses within a conversation.

The connection helps analysts retrieve existing reports and explain detection results while keeping the source, analysis date, and coverage visible.

The integration uses Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard that connects AI tools with external services. VirusTotal’s ChatGPT connection guide describes setup through Developer mode and an OAuth connection. Users sign in with Google through VTAI without supplying a VirusTotal API key. Availability depends on account and workspace settings.

VirusTotal ChatGPT Integration

For an explicitly authorized ChatGPT attachment, the connector can fetch and hash the original file content. It checks whether VirusTotal already knows that hash before uploading anything.

Known files return existing reports, while only confirmed unknown files are submitted. Creating the connection alone does not prove attachment support works.

This approach separates report retrieval from file contribution. Retrieving an existing report consumes query quota, including repeated lookups and analysis status checks.

At Cybersecuritynews, we have successfully integrated VirusTotal with ChatGPT to enhance our analysis capabilities. Recently, we conducted an in-depth check on a PDF file, and here are the results.

Uploading a confirmed unknown file does not spend that quota, although separate contribution limits apply. Receipt recovery is free, helping users resume interrupted work without resubmitting the same sample.

For network investigations, users can request URL submissions or domain and IP reanalysis when authorized. Keeping each request identifier helps track the registered analysis after an interruption.

These checks extend workflows covered in Cyber Security News’ VirusTotal threat research guide, bringing report review into a conversational interface.

The connection also builds on VirusTotal’s earlier use of AI, including Code Insight for malware analysis. However, threat report access should not be mistaken for a final security verdict.

Missing reports mean the result is unknown. Pending analysis and zero detections do not establish that a file or website is safe.

Privacy remains a concern. Standard submissions share content with VirusTotal and may expose it to security community members and partners. Analysts should obtain permission before submitting personal documents, internal code, credentials, or sensitive data.

Complete submitted URLs can disclose information carried in query strings and fragments, making review before submission essential. According to the VTAI overview, access is free within quotas. Permissions and allowances apply across account connections, not per chat.

For security teams, the benefit is easier access to evidence, not a replacement for investigation. Analysts still need to assess report age, coverage, and context before deciding whether to block, isolate, or escalate.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researchers earned a $250,000 reward from Google after building a full-chain Chrome exploit with AI agents. The XBOW team says the work took six days and about $40,000 in computing costs, using OpenAI’s publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model. Google has fixed the flaws.

XBOW disclosed the work on October 13, 2026. Its chain linked three bugs to move from JavaScript in a Chrome tab to code execution outside the browser’s renderer sandbox. The company estimated that the issue could affect about one billion users worldwide, while the demonstration targeted Windows.

Google Awards $250K for Chrome Exploit

A sandbox limits what a compromised web page can do. A full chain joins bugs to cross Chrome’s defenses in sequence. XBOW demonstrated a crafted page launching a program on a test system. It did not report the exploit being used against people.

The first flaw was in V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine. XBOW says a bug in the Maglev compiler let separate JavaScript objects share a changeable number during deoptimization, when V8 moves from optimized code to a less optimized path. Changing the value could mislead optimized code and give the exploit memory access inside V8’s protected region.

The second flaw affected animated WebP images. The decoder could use frame details saved from one image while reading changed image data. That mismatch caused an out-of-bounds write and allowed the chain to leave the V8 sandbox.

The third flaw was in Crashpad, Chrome’s crash-reporting system. On Windows, Crashpad could retry a failed memory read using a length based on the rest of a page. The code assumed the renderer would not change.

XBOW’s exploit changed page access during the retry, causing an oversized read and memory corruption in the handler outside the renderer sandbox.

XBOW says its researchers guided the work. They chose targets, split tasks, checked AI results, and prepared backups. The team replaced an early chain after Google said one part was already known. A modular design let it swap in another bug. The company said it developed the final chain from August 2 to August 7.

Google’s Chrome Vulnerability Reward Program offers $250,000 for an eligible full-chain exploit that works from web content on an active Chrome release. The rules require a working demonstration and responsible testing. The award recognizes a reported flaw, not a confirmed compromise of users’ devices.

Users should keep Chrome up to date and relaunch it when an update is ready. XBOW says Google fixed all three flaws. Cybersecurity News has covered an XBOW AI agent finding a Linux kernel flaw and a Chrome update fixing multiple vulnerabilities. Here you can find more details on Google’s reward rules.

AI may shorten the time needed to find complex flaws. Software teams should use these tools to test their own products, with human review and coordinated fixes central to security work.

articles.title: Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability Enables Privilege Escalation Attacks
articles.description:
Microsoft has released fixes for a Windows SmartScreen vulnerability that allows an attacker with local access to gain higher privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-85851, the flaw was disclosed on October 13, 2026, and carries a CVSS base score of 7.8. Microsoft rates it Important. The issue involves a use-after-free memory error and affects several Windows 11 […]

The post Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability Enables Privilege Escalation Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has released fixes for a Windows SmartScreen vulnerability that allows an attacker with local access to gain higher privileges.

Tracked as CVE-2026-85851, the flaw was disclosed on October 13, 2026, and carries a CVSS base score of 7.8. Microsoft rates it Important. The issue involves a use-after-free memory error and affects several Windows 11 releases and Windows Server 2025.

According to the supplied Microsoft advisory, successful exploitation lets an attacker move from a low integrity level to a medium integrity level. This is a specific increase in access, not a confirmed path to administrator or SYSTEM privileges. The attacker must already have low privileges on the affected device, but the attack requires no user interaction.

The flaw falls under CWE-416, use-after-free. This error occurs when software continues to access memory after that memory has been released. Another operation may reuse the same memory, leaving the original code working with data that no longer belongs to it. Such errors can cause memory corruption, crashes, or other security problems.

Microsoft identifies local privilege escalation as the impact for this vulnerability. Its CVSS vector lists low attack complexity, low privileges required, and no user interaction. Those conditions describe an attacker who already has a foothold on the device, not someone exploiting SmartScreen directly over the internet.

Windows SmartScreen Vulnerability

Microsoft credits researcher yhw with reporting the issue. At publication, the advisory marked it as neither publicly disclosed nor exploited and assessed exploitation as “Exploitation Less Likely.” Those findings do not remove the need to patch, but they do not support describing this flaw as an actively exploited zero-day.

Earlier SmartScreen attacks involved different weaknesses. Cyber Security News previously covered SmartScreen bypass attacks delivering malware through CVE-2024-21412 and Water Hydra’s SmartScreen zero-day campaign. Those reports concern bypassing security warnings and should not be confused with the newly disclosed local privilege escalation flaw.

Microsoft also disclosed CVE-2026-83504, a Windows SmartScreen information disclosure flaw rated CVSS 4.7 and classified as a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition.

An attacker who successfully exploits this second flaw could view heap memory from a privileged process. Exploitation requires winning a race condition, which explains its high attack complexity.

It also requires local access and low privileges and needs no user interaction. Microsoft credits its Offensive Research & Security Engineering team and reports no exploitation at publication. The supplied material does not establish an exploit chain between the two flaws.

For CVE-2026-85851, the supplied update list covers Windows 11 versions 23H2, 24H2, 25H2, 26H1, and 26H2 across x64 and ARM64 systems. Windows Server 2025, including Server Core, is also listed.

The listed fixes are KB5126653 for Windows 11 23H2, KB5127648 for 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2, KB5127646 for 26H1, and KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025.

Administrators should match each device to its release and architecture, then verify installation against Microsoft’s update records. The two advisories list different update packages, so check their patch details separately before deploying across affected systems.

articles.title: Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits Can Fully Compromise iPhones From a Single Web Visit
articles.description:
Two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, show how a visit to a malicious or compromised website can put an outdated device at risk. The kits can link several software flaws together to break out of the browser and reach deeper parts of iOS. Depending on the device’s software version and the kit used, […]

The post Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits Can Fully Compromise iPhones From a Single Web Visit appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, show how a visit to a malicious or compromised website can put an outdated device at risk.

The kits can link several software flaws together to break out of the browser and reach deeper parts of iOS. Depending on the device’s software version and the kit used, an attacker may then steal sensitive information without needing the user to install an app or tap through extra prompts.

These are not ordinary malicious webpages. An exploit kit is a set of tools that checks a visitor’s device and selects code designed for its software.

Coruna contains five complete exploit chains and 23 exploits targeting iOS 13.0 through 17.2.1. DarkSword uses a six-flaw chain against iOS 18.4 through 18.7. The two kits target different iOS ranges, so the risk depends on the version installed.

Researchers from iVerify identified and studied DarkSword with Google and Lookout, and iVerify has also reported on newer variants in the wild.

In an investigation published in October 2026, its researchers described a modified strain called P7 DarkSword, which can steal keychain and cryptocurrency wallet data.

Coruna and DarkSword Exploit Kits

The attack starts when Safari loads a malicious page or content hidden inside a compromised website. The page checks the iPhone’s model and iOS version, then serves code suited to that device.

A WebKit or JavaScriptCore flaw can let the code run in the browser. Further flaws help it escape the browser’s safety limits and gain higher system access.

That chain matters because the browser normally runs in a restricted area called a sandbox. A sandbox is designed to limit what a webpage can reach.

Coruna and DarkSword use additional flaws to break past those limits; the later stages can reach kernel-level access, which gives the attacker much broader control over the device. Earlier Coruna exploit research describes the range of exploits and iOS versions involved.

The tools can then collect valuable data. Reporting on DarkSword describes theft of passwords, messages, browsing records, location information and cryptocurrency wallet contents.

iVerify’s P7 analysis adds on-device keychain collection and two-way communication with the attacker’s server. That information can put both personal accounts and work access at risk, especially when the phone holds saved credentials or is used to approve sign-ins.

From targeted tools to wider criminal use

Coruna’s history shows how a powerful exploit can move between different users. Google tracked its use from a surveillance customer to espionage activity against Ukrainian users and later to financially motivated campaigns using fake finance and cryptocurrency websites.

The kit’s final payload, called PlasmaLoader, is designed to target cryptocurrency wallets and search Apple Notes for recovery phrases.

DarkSword also moved beyond limited use after its source code was leaked publicly in 2026. That made the kit easier for other attackers to obtain and adapt.

Separate reporting has described attackers combining DarkSword’s route into a device with Coruna’s wallet-theft tools, a development covered in this DarkSword and Coruna platform report.

A public leak does not mean every copy works on every iPhone, but it can make reuse and changes easier. The threat can be difficult to spot. Some implants run inside normal system processes and may remove parts of their activity when finished.

Browser or network monitoring can also miss what happens after the exploit code reaches the device. iVerify reported that some DarkSword variants leave useful traces, including Safari history and crash logs, while Coruna artifacts may remain after a reboot or iOS update.

Installing the latest iOS update available for the device is the most important step. Updates close known flaws used in these chains; Apple has also issued security fixes for older supported devices. Users should check Settings for Software Update and install the version offered for their model.

Lockdown Mode can provide extra protection for people at higher risk, but it is not a replacement for updates. It works best when enabled before opening a malicious page and can limit some features.

Users should also avoid signing in through unexpected finance or cryptocurrency pages, even when a site looks familiar. Organizations should track iOS versions across work devices, review which accounts each phone can access and have a plan to isolate a suspected device for investigation.

If compromise is suspected, treat credentials stored on that phone as exposed: change them from a trusted device, revoke active sessions where possible and involve the organization’s security team. A loaner phone can help staff keep working while investigators preserve the original device.

articles.title: Hackers Breach Meta GitHub Repositories, Steal Source Code and Data of 1,500 People
articles.description:
Hackers used an employee’s stolen credentials to access some of Meta’s GitHub repositories, taking product source code and personal information linked to roughly 1,500 people. Most affected individuals are Meta employees in the United States, according to the company’s disclosure to SecurityWeek. Meta confirmed the breach on October 13, 2026, when it began notifying affected […]

The post Hackers Breach Meta GitHub Repositories, Steal Source Code and Data of 1,500 People appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers used an employee’s stolen credentials to access some of Meta’s GitHub repositories, taking product source code and personal information linked to roughly 1,500 people. Most affected individuals are Meta employees in the United States, according to the company’s disclosure to SecurityWeek.

Meta confirmed the breach on October 13, 2026, when it began notifying affected people. The company said it detected the intrusion several weeks earlier, blocked the attackers’ access, and brought in GitHub and law enforcement to support its response.

Stolen Credentials Opened Repository Access

Meta said attackers entered through stolen employee credentials, not a flaw in a Meta product. The company also said its internal systems were not breached. The disclosed incident involved business data held in GitHub repositories.

The report does not explain how the credentials were stolen or identify the attackers. Meta said its investigation with GitHub had not indicated that the group specifically targeted Meta’s data. That assessment remains based on the investigation so far.

According to Meta, 99% of the stolen material was business data, consisting of software code related to some products. Personal information accounted for the remaining 1%. Those percentages describe the stolen material, not the share of employees affected.

Meta has not named the affected products or detailed the repository contents. The disclosure does not say that attackers changed code, published it, or used it to compromise other systems.

Meta told SecurityWeek it mistakenly placed personal information in the repositories, despite company rules that prohibit storing it on GitHub. The company has not disclosed which types of personal information were taken, leaving the full privacy impact unclear.

A significant portion of material that appeared to contain personal information was synthetic or anonymized test data, Meta said. The company believes this could make it harder for attackers to separate genuine records from test records. However, that does not remove the need to protect people whose real information was exposed.

Meta is notifying regulators and offering affected individuals credit monitoring and dark web monitoring services. These measures form part of its response while it addresses the repository exposure and its handling of personal data.[securityweek]

Meta Rotates Secrets and Adds Data Checks

Meta said it rotated secrets found in the affected repositories and strengthened product security to address risks from the stolen business data. It is also introducing proactive scans to detect user information uploaded by mistake and working with GitHub on additional repository protections.

GitHub’s guidance on leaked secrets explains why replacing exposed credentials matters. Removing a secret from source code alone is not enough. Teams must revoke it through its provider and generate a replacement where needed to prevent further use.

The incident follows other repository thefts covered by CybersecurityNews, including CrowdSec’s loss of about 170 private GitHub repositories through a compromised former employee account. Separate reporting on hundreds of thousands of active credentials exposed on GitHub highlights the need to revoke leaked keys promptly.

Neither report establishes a connection to Meta’s breach. Together, they show why repository security must cover both account access and the data stored inside code projects.

articles.title: Attackers Breach European Bank Through Third-Party Gateway and Target WSUS Server
articles.description:
A European bank was breached through a poorly secured, third-party gateway before an attacker tried to exploit its Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) infrastructure. The case shows how stolen login details and weak access controls can put a bank’s central software systems at risk without a complex attack chain. The bank’s security team uncovered unauthorized […]

The post Attackers Breach European Bank Through Third-Party Gateway and Target WSUS Server appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A European bank was breached through a poorly secured, third-party gateway before an attacker tried to exploit its Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) infrastructure.

The case shows how stolen login details and weak access controls can put a bank’s central software systems at risk without a complex attack chain.

The bank’s security team uncovered unauthorized VPN access attempts stretching across several months after spotting unusual activity on its central IT system.

Investigators traced the intrusion to an external gateway managed by a third party, where strict authentication had not been properly enforced.

Researchers from Unit 42 identified the intrusion and its attempted code execution, but their report does not name any malware family.

Published on October 13, 2026, the investigation describes an opportunistic attacker whose noisy actions exposed basic security gaps rather than a confirmed, advanced spying operation.

Attackers Breach European Bank

The attacker used compromised credentials to sign in to internal systems through the gateway. Unit 42 did not name the appliance vendor or explain how those credentials were first obtained.

The confirmed entry point was weak authentication on the externally managed device, not a disclosed gateway software exploit. That distinction matters because valid accounts can give an intruder access without requiring a new vulnerability.

Earlier reporting on brute-force attacks against VPNs describes separate incidents involving weak passwords and appliances lacking multifactor authentication, showing why remote access settings deserve close review. Those incidents are not linked to this bank.

Once inside, the intruder repeatedly scanned hosts and networks across several protocols, interacting with thousands of systems.

Instead of quietly following one narrow path, the attacker searched broadly for more opportunities to gain access. Unit 42 said the volume of scanning and use of common system identifiers showed little effort to stay hidden.

Over several months, the attacker also ran repeated password-guessing campaigns against internal systems, with administrator accounts a key focus.

These attempts sought additional access while the intruder explored the environment. Separate coverage of automated VPN login attacks illustrates how repeated credential testing can threaten remote access services, although the bank’s reported password guessing occurred internally.

The activity extended beyond logins. Automated web requests scraped internal pages and attachments, while the attacker searched operational and network shares.

This exposed documentation during the intrusion. However, the report does not give a stolen data volume, identify affected customers, or confirm that customer banking records were taken.

WSUS Exploit Attempt Stopped

The attacker later targeted a remote code execution vulnerability in WSUS on the bank’s central configuration management server.

That server handled software distribution across the organization, making it an attractive place to seek higher privileges and lasting access. Control of such a central service could have widened the incident’s impact.

Unit 42 did not disclose the vulnerability’s CVE identifier. Although separate reporting on active WSUS vulnerability exploitation covers CVE-2025-59287, that identifier cannot be assigned to this bank incident from the published evidence.

Keeping those cases separate avoids turning a related technical risk into an unsupported finding. Cortex XDR detected the attempt to run unauthorized code and contained the threat before it escalated.

Unit 42 reported that the attacker was stopped from establishing persistent access or spreading further through the network. This containment followed earlier scanning, authentication attempts, and access to internal documentation; it did not prevent the initial breach.

Responders reviewed endpoint records across thousands of systems and logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. They found no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors.

Bank leaders reviewed the exposed documentation and rotated all compromised credentials. The bank also expanded its Cortex XDR and Cortex XSIAM coverage and incident response support.

The investigation highlights authentication, timely patching, and endpoint detection as core safeguards. Third-party management did not remove the bank’s exposure to a weak gateway configuration, while containment and follow-up hunting helped limit the damage.

For security teams, the lesson is to review vendor-managed access with the same care as internal systems. The report calls for strict identity controls, timely updates, and endpoint monitoring. Checking these controls together is important because a valid login can otherwise turn an outside gateway into internal access.

articles.description:
Gear of War: E-Day players faced login failures, sudden disconnects, and other online service problems after distributed denial-of-service attacks targeted the game’s online services. The official Gears Community account confirmed the cause on X, linking the disruption to DDoS activity and ending speculation about the source of the failures. The Gears Community reported attacks on […]

The post Gears of War: E-Day Hit by DDoS Attack, Causing Login Failures and Disconnects appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Gear of War: E-Day players faced login failures, sudden disconnects, and other online service problems after distributed denial-of-service attacks targeted the game’s online services.

The official Gears Community account confirmed the cause on X, linking the disruption to DDoS activity and ending speculation about the source of the failures.

The Gears Community reported attacks on its online services that caused intermittent disconnects, login issues, and other disruptions, but did not identify the attackers, disclose traffic figures, or specify affected services, limiting details about the attack’s scale and method.

A separate update from the same account said the login issue had been resolved and that the team would continue closely monitoring services.

Earlier messaging had flagged extended login times and said the issue was improving. The updates show progress toward recovery, but the login fix should not be read as proof that every reported service problem had ended.

Gears of War: E-Day Hit by DDoS Attack

Players may experience delayed or failed logins, intermittent disconnections, and difficulty reconnecting, symptoms confirmed by the Gears Community during the online service disruption.

The available statement does not establish that the attacker accessed player accounts or stole personal information. It describes an attack against service availability. Reporting the incident as a confirmed data breach would go beyond the evidence released by the Gears Community team.

A DDoS attack uses multiple machines to overwhelm a target with traffic or requests. The aim is to make a system or network unavailable to legitimate users. Compromised devices can form a botnet, allowing attackers to send traffic from many sources at once, according to CISA’s DDoS response guidance.

This can exhaust network capacity or system resources, preventing the system from handling normal requests. However, the Gears update does not identify a botnet, a traffic flood type, or an attack rate. There is no published basis in that statement for assigning the incident to a known group or connecting it to another campaign.

Gaming infrastructure has faced similar availability threats before. Cybersecurity News previously covered DDoS malware targeting Valve Source Engine game servers, with several supported attack methods. That report provides useful background on game-server threats. However, it does not link to the E-Day disruption.

Another report examined a 3.15-billion-packets-per-second attack against a Minecraft server. The case shows why packet volume matters alongside bandwidth when assessing attacks. No comparable measurements have been shared in the available Gears statement.

CISA recommends confirming DDoS activity through network monitoring and traffic analysis, then applying measures such as traffic filtering and rate limits. These are general defensive steps, not confirmed details of the Gears team’s response.

Official updates confirm the reported cause, player impact, and login recovery, but leave the attack’s scale and technical handling undisclosed. The team’s stated recovery approach still includes monitoring after the service disruption.

articles.title: Multiple Google Chrome Flaws Could Enable Memory Corruption and Code Execution Attacks
articles.description:
Google released a Chrome security update that addresses 37 vulnerabilities, including seven critical flaws that raise concerns about memory corruption and possible code execution. Published on October 13, 2026, the update covers Windows, Mac, and Linux, with fixes spanning graphics, PDF handling, media processing, networking, and other browser components. According to Google’s Stable Channel Update […]

The post Multiple Google Chrome Flaws Could Enable Memory Corruption and Code Execution Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google released a Chrome security update that addresses 37 vulnerabilities, including seven critical flaws that raise concerns about memory corruption and possible code execution.

Published on October 13, 2026, the update covers Windows, Mac, and Linux, with fixes spanning graphics, PDF handling, media processing, networking, and other browser components.

According to Google’s Stable Channel Update for Desktop, the patched versions are 155.0.8059.79/.80 for Windows and Mac, and 155.0.8059.79 for Linux. The release includes seven critical, 29 high, and one medium-severity security fixes.

Google says it will continue distributing updates over the coming days and weeks. The critical vulnerabilities include CVE-2026-110152, a buffer overflow in ANGLE, Chrome’s graphics translation layer. Zhenpeng “Leo” Lin at depthfirst reported the issue on September 30.

Buffer overflows can corrupt memory when software writes beyond the space reserved for data, potentially creating opportunities for attackers to change program behavior.

The remaining six critical entries are use-after-free flaws. CVE-2026-110149 affects Browser, CVE-2026-110136 affects PDF, CVE-2026-110161 affects Network, and CVE-2026-110165 affects Core.

Multiple Google Chrome Vulnerabilities

Google also patched CVE-2026-110148 in SVG and CVE-2026-110151 in Media. These findings involve Google researchers and Xinyang Ge.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when software continues accessing memory after releasing it. Depending on the bug, attackers may influence that memory’s contents, causing crashes, corrupting data, or potentially running malicious code. However, the flaw category alone does not enable an attack against every affected component.

Cybersecurity News previously covered Chrome’s update fixing 247 vulnerabilities, including four critical use-after-free issues. The latest release continues that focus on memory safety across multiple browser features rather than a single isolated component.

Among the high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-110169 affects V8, Chrome’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine. Rapid7’s vulnerability record states that a crafted HTML page could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside Chrome’s sandbox in versions before 155.0.8059.79.

That limitation matters. Code execution inside the sandbox does not, by itself, prove an attacker can take control of the entire operating system.

Google’s release announcement does not describe a complete attack chain or confirm that these newly patched vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild.

Google credits Xinyang Ge at Anthropic, assisted by Claude, with reporting CVE-2026-110169. Other high-severity fixes address V8 type confusion, buffer overflows in Animation and PDFium, a Passwords information leak, Installer privilege elevation, and authorization problems in ReadingMode, Updater, and Mojo.

For background, Cybersecurity News’ coverage of earlier ANGLE and V8 security fixes explains how memory-handling issues repeatedly affect graphics and script processing.

Users should open Chrome’s menu, select Help, then About Google Chrome to check for updates. After installation, select Relaunch to apply the fixes. Linux users should update through their package manager. Google’s Chrome update guide explains these steps.

Google may restrict detailed bug reports until most users receive patches. Restrictions may also remain if affected third-party libraries haven’t been fixed elsewhere, limiting the technical information currently available to readers and defenders.

articles.title: Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Days Exploited to Steal Active Directory Credentials
articles.description:
Attackers chained three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances to gain root-level access without logging in, then searched for credentials and sensitive Active Directory data. The activity, which began on October 3, 2026, targeted a fully patched appliance running version 22.8R2.4, showing that keeping a device current did not protect it from these […]

The post Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Days Exploited to Steal Active Directory Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers chained three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances to gain root-level access without logging in, then searched for credentials and sensitive Active Directory data.

The activity, which began on October 3, 2026, targeted a fully patched appliance running version 22.8R2.4, showing that keeping a device current did not protect it from these previously unknown flaws.

Volexity found the intrusion while investigating suspicious activity at a customer and worked with Ivanti to examine the affected device. The security firm tracks the previously unknown actor as UTA0576.

Its analysis found attempts to steal domain credentials, Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and other directory information.

Researcers at Volexity found that the chain combined an authentication bypass and a file-write weakness that Ivanti tracks together as CVE-2026-104935, followed by a separate privilege-escalation flaw.

The first two issues let the attacker reach a protected script and run code as the appliance’s cgi-server user. The third flaw then let UTA0576 run commands as root.

Ivanti released a fix for CVE-2026-104935 on October 13, while the privilege-escalation issue remained under development for a future update.

Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Days Exploited

Volexity said the initial bypass misused the appliance’s handling of web requests. A request to a public login script could include an X-DSCGI-PATH header that directed the appliance to a different, protected script.

The attacker then abused the file-upload handler to briefly place a script on the device. By sending repeated requests quickly, UTA0576 could run the file before the appliance deleted it.

After gaining initial code execution, the actor used the privileged dsinvoked service to raise access to root. The exploit changed configuration data in memory, asked the service to run a task with an attacker-supplied script, and then restored the original settings.

It also removed selected entries from Ivanti debug and Linux audit logs. Because the changes happened in memory and were reversed, Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool might not show signs of compromise.

The actor did not install a web shell or backdoor, according to Volexity. Instead, it sent commands through the same HTTPS exploit channel and received results in the responses.

This made the activity harder to spot through a search for persistent malware alone. Organizations following the full Ivanti zero-day report should note that a clean file scan or the absence of a web shell cannot by itself rule out an intrusion.

Once inside, UTA0576 used the VPN appliance’s Active Directory service account to query a domain controller over LDAP. The searches included LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery data, password-bearing account fields, logon script paths, and other user details.

The actor also extracted credentials stored on the appliance, reviewed authentication logs for valid usernames, and tried password spraying against Active Directory accounts.

The operation also included network discovery and data collection. A packet-capture tool searched traffic for LDAP credentials, HTTP Basic Authentication credentials, and NTLM challenge-response hashes.

Lateral movement

The actor attempted to export captured traffic and directory results through the exploit channel. Volexity assessed with high confidence that the activity pointed to preparation for lateral movement, though the investigation did not establish the actor’s ultimate goal.

This focus on VPN appliances and directory credentials echoes other activity Volexity has investigated, including the SonicWall VPN credential theft campaign.

The incidents involved different products and threat actors, but both show why edge devices can expose sensitive internal traffic. They should not be treated as the same campaign.

Administrators should install the latest Ivanti update that applies to their appliance and investigate devices that may have been exposed.

Volexity recommends watching for repeated requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, especially when the X-DSCGI-PATH value points to a different location.

Teams should also check for unusual files and activity under /tmp/ and review network evidence. Suspected cases need memory and network forensics because log tampering and memory-only changes can hide traces from routine checks.

Volexity published indicators related to the case, but its report does not provide file SHA values. The listed address and artifacts below come from the report; they are clues to investigate, not proof on their own that a device was compromised.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft fixed three Windows BitLocker vulnerabilities CVE-2026-85920, CVE-2026-88070, and CVE-2026-83500 that could enable privilege escalation or bypass security protections in its October 2026 updates.

BitLocker is a core Windows disk-encryption feature designed to protect data if a laptop, desktop, or storage drive is lost or stolen. It helps prevent someone from reading protected files by removing a drive and connecting it to another system.

The newly disclosed issues do not mean BitLocker encryption has been broken. Instead, they affect parts of the Windows BitLocker implementation that an attacker can abuse after gaining local or physical access to a target device.

CVE-2026-85920 is an elevation-of-privilege vulnerability caused by a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition. This flaw occurs when Windows checks a condition and then uses the result later.

Meanwhile, an attacker changes the relevant data in the short gap between those actions. An authenticated local user may exploit this weakness to gain higher permissions on an affected Windows device.

The second issue, CVE-2026-88070, is an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in Windows BitLocker. Microsoft classifies it as an elevation-of-privilege issue, while third-party vulnerability tracking data lists a CVSS severity score of 7.8.

Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities

A local authenticated attacker could use the flaw to access memory outside expected bounds and elevate privileges, which may lead to system-level access under certain conditions.

CVE-2026-83500 is different because it bypasses a security feature. The issue stems from an open redirect condition in Windows BitLocker and requires physical access to the affected machine.

An attacker could use the flaw to bypass a security control, making device access protections especially important for laptops, workstations, and systems in shared spaces.

Organizations should treat these BitLocker bugs as a reminder that full-disk encryption is only one part of endpoint protection. Privilege elevation flaws normally require the attacker to already have local access, often through a compromised account, malware execution, or physical access.

Security teams should therefore reduce unnecessary local administrator rights, require strong sign-in protections, and closely monitor unusual privilege changes on Windows endpoints.

Administrators should install the latest Microsoft security updates as soon as their testing process allows. Microsoft’s Security Update Guide provides the affected-product and update details for CVE-2026-85920, CVE-2026-88070, and CVE-2026-83500. Microsoft’s October release included all three BitLocker issues among a much wider set of Windows vulnerabilities.

For systems that leave the office, IT teams should confirm that BitLocker uses TPM protection with a startup PIN where appropriate, and that recovery keys are securely stored.

Physical controls also matter because the bypass issue depends on direct access to the device. Endpoint detection tools can help identify suspicious local activity that attackers may use before attempting privilege elevation.

Readers can also review Cyber Security News coverage of Windows security updates and BitLocker vulnerabilities for related reports. The key action is simple: patch affected Windows systems quickly and make local access harder for untrusted users.
