articles.title: Hackers Abuse Google Search to Attacks ITadmins with Weaponized PuTTY Installer
articles.description:
IT administrators searching Google for PuTTY may see a convincing fake download result mixed with legitimate links. Researchers documented a campaign that uses a lookalike website to deliver a malicious Windows installer disguised as the popular SSH client. The installer opens a working PuTTY window as a decoy while secretly starting a separate malware chain […]

The post Hackers Abuse Google Search to Attacks ITadmins with Weaponized PuTTY Installer appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
IT administrators searching Google for PuTTY may see a convincing fake download result mixed with legitimate links. Researchers documented a campaign that uses a lookalike website to deliver a malicious Windows installer disguised as the popular SSH client.

The installer opens a working PuTTY window as a decoy while secretly starting a separate malware chain in the background.

The campaign targets people who use remote access and system tools as part of their work. A poisoned search result leads to a fake PuTTY page, and its download link supplies a trojanized MSI installer.

The page copies the title of the genuine PuTTY download site, helping the fake result seem credible. This method echoes earlier campaigns involving fake PuTTY downloads targeting IT admins, but the newly reported chain uses Node.js and a different command system.

Analysts from Unit 42 identified the campaign and reported that the MSI installs an obfuscated Node.js loader alongside an unmodified, signed PuTTY 0.85 program.

Their findings describe a multi-stage infection that can give an operator the ability to send new JavaScript instructions to an infected computer. The report also notes the use of Ethereum smart contracts to find the active command-and-control, or C2, server.

Hackers Abuse Google Search

The reported delivery site, puty[.]ink, imitates PuTTY’s download page. Clicking its download link retrieves Putty-x86_64.msi from a Backblaze B2 storage bucket.

When a victim opens the installer, Windows Installer drops four files into a folder under the user’s Local AppData directory. The MSI also opens putty.exe, a legitimate, Sectigo-signed copy of PuTTY 0.85. Because the program looks and works normally, a user may believe the installation is safe.

Meanwhile, the installer starts a batch file named 44JYYsqg.cmd. The script hides its console, checks whether Node.js is already installed, and downloads the official Node.js 18.20.5 runtime if it is not.

It then uses a small JScript file to launch Node.js with an obfuscated JavaScript payload. The runtime itself is legitimate; the danger comes from the attacker’s script and the way it is used. This approach resembles other cases where attackers use Node.js as a malware launcher.

Rather than relying only on a fixed server address embedded in the malware, the JavaScript loader queries an Ethereum smart contract through seven public RPC services.

It compares the replies and uses the most common valid URL as its C2 address. The malware checks for an updated address every five minutes, making it harder for defenders to rely on blocking just one server.

The technique, known as EtherHiding, has also appeared in other campaigns that hide malware infrastructure on Ethereum. After finding a server, the malware checks in about every 500 milliseconds.

Its requests resemble downloads of ordinary image or style files, using extensions such as .png, .jpg, .css and .ico.

If the server returns more than 10 bytes, the loader passes the response to JavaScript execution with access to Node.js features. That means the operator can send new capabilities without replacing the original installer.

Why IT teams should take notice

Unit 42’s findings describe commands for collecting system details, including the operating system, antivirus products, domain membership, graphics hardware and active SMB sessions.

The researchers also observed browser-profile and cookie collection, installation of a WebSocket package, and a PowerShell routine that captured roughly five desktop screenshots per second.

Those images were saved as encoded files in the temporary folder, enabling near-live monitoring of the user’s screen. The campaign does not rely on a software flaw in PuTTY.

It depends on a user trusting a search result and running an installer from a fake page. That is especially concerning for administrators, whose computers may hold browser sessions, saved access details or active connections to internal systems.

Similar search-result lures have been used to deliver trojanized utilities, as seen in earlier fake PuTTY and WinSCP campaigns targeting IT teams.

Teams should direct staff to verified software sources and consider maintaining an approved software portal for commonly used tools.

Security teams can investigate unexpected node.exe activity from user AppData folders, especially when it runs with an .ini file argument.

They should also review MSI launches that create the named campaign files, and check for outbound traffic to Ethereum RPC services from computers that have no business using them.

PuTTY’s legitimate download page and Node.js’s official release source can help users verify where trusted software should come from: PuTTY’s official site and Node.js 18.20.5 for Windows.

Unit 42’s campaign announcement is available on X. A familiar program window or a valid signature on one bundled file does not prove that the installer itself is safe.

The post Microsoft Windows Shell 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has patched an actively exploited Windows Shell zero-day vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web protections. Tracked as CVE-2026-96951, the flaw was addressed in the October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates. It carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and is rated Important by Microsoft.

The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before the update, but Microsoft confirmed that exploitation had already occurred. Its “Exploitation Detected” assessment signals a confirmed attack rather than a possible future threat. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index advises customers to give applicable updates in this category the highest priority.

Windows Shell 0-Day Exploited

The flaw involves command injection, where Windows Shell fails to properly handle special elements used in a command. Microsoft describes the outcome as a security feature bypass available to an unauthorized attacker over a network. Successful exploitation allows the attacker to evade Mark of the Web defenses.

Mark of the Web identifies files that come from the internet and helps Windows apply warnings or other protective checks. Bypassing this protection can remove an important barrier between a downloaded file and a user opening dangerous content. However, the reported impact is a security bypass, not a standalone remote code execution flaw.

Attackers can deliver a specially crafted file through email or instant messaging and use social engineering to persuade the target to open it. Exploitation requires user action. This means the flaw should not be treated as a zero-click attack, despite its network-based delivery path.

Earlier reporting on Windows LNK Stomping attacks described another way attackers bypassed Mark of the Web through Windows shortcuts. Separately, a WinZip Mark of the Web vulnerability showed how archive extraction could lose internet-origin tags. These are separate vulnerabilities, not confirmed techniques used in the current attacks.

The supplied Microsoft advisory credits Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo of Fujitsu Limited, Benoit Sevens using Claude with Anthropic, and researcher yhw. It does not identify the attackers, their targets, the malicious file format, or the scale of exploitation. Those missing details limit conclusions about the campaign and its reach.

Security teams should prioritize applicable Windows updates and check Microsoft’s Security Update Guide for affected products. Testing and deploying the fix quickly is especially important because exploitation is confirmed. Users should remain cautious with unexpected attachments, since this attack depends on persuading someone to interact with attacker-controlled content.

The post OpenAI Engineer Arrested for Planting Spyware Device in an Executive Conference Room appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An OpenAI engineer has been arrested for allegedly hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco offices. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, and appeared in federal court on October 13, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

Prosecutors charged him with using or attempting to use a device to intercept spoken communications. Although described as a spyware device in the headline, the hardware was a hidden audio recorder. The public announcement does not describe malware installed on OpenAI computers.

OpenAI Engineer Arrested for Planting Spyware

According to the complaint, OpenAI staff discovered the first device around September 30. It was plugged into a USB port behind a television, wrapped in toilet paper, and contained encrypted data. OpenAI determined that it had been installed around September 28.

The room hosted highly confidential discussions about research, product plans, business opportunities, government engagements, and technical progress. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan, who joined OpenAI in July 2025, had no authority to enter the room or attend those meetings.

Office CCTV allegedly showed him near the room on several dates before the discovery. Footage from October 5 reportedly showed him entering the room and looking behind the television.

Investigators also examined searches made through a productivity tool. Before September 28, Alfozan allegedly asked about building addresses, room calendars, meeting capacities, leadership locations, and meetings with outside partners.

The complaint describes related prompts from a chatbot account associated with his spouse. Authorities said that account shared several identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s account. Between September 24 and September 30, it requested help with continuous audio recording, Wi-Fi connectivity, live listening, remote access, concealment, and SD card encryption.

Prompts submitted on September 27 and September 28 allegedly referenced the first recorder’s custom header and unique MAC address. These details form part of the evidence linking the account activity to the recovered hardware. However, requests about remote access do not establish that recordings were transmitted outside OpenAI.

On October 5, security staff also found a similar recorder inside a bag Alfozan allegedly left unattended elsewhere in the office. The bag contained his wallet and identification.

The case concerns alleged physical eavesdropping, not a confirmed network breach. The Justice Department announcement does not identify a foreign recipient or establish that confidential recordings reached another party.

Separately, Cybersecurity News has covered OpenAI’s response to AI reasoning extraction and researchers reaching internal repositories through a forum security flaw. Those reports concern different security paths and are not evidence of a connection to this case.

The FBI is investigating. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker is prosecuting, with support from National Security Division attorney Kate Tagert. According to the Northern District of California announcement, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release if convicted. The charge remains an allegation, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes 1,118 Vulnerabilities in October Patch Tuesday and Introduces New Risk Cohorts
articles.description:
Microsoft’s October 2026 Patch Tuesday briefing outlines 1,118 vulnerabilities across 15 risk groups, alongside a new approach designed to help security teams review large update releases. Called risk cohorts, these groups bring together flaws that require similar questions about an organization’s systems, users, and exposure. Microsoft’s accompanying document maps individual CVEs to these shared areas […]

The post Microsoft Fixes 1,118 Vulnerabilities in October Patch Tuesday and Introduces New Risk Cohorts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft’s October 2026 Patch Tuesday briefing outlines 1,118 vulnerabilities across 15 risk groups, alongside a new approach designed to help security teams review large update releases.

Called risk cohorts, these groups bring together flaws that require similar questions about an organization’s systems, users, and exposure. Microsoft’s accompanying document maps individual CVEs to these shared areas of assessment.

The goal is to reduce repeated work without removing the need to review each vulnerability. Instead of asking the same deployment questions hundreds of times, analysts can assess a common area once and use that information across several CVEs. Microsoft describes the approach as exploratory, not a replacement for its existing update guidance or individual vulnerability assessments.

The release follows other large update cycles covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s September 2026 Patch Tuesday report and August 2026 Patch Tuesday coverage. Those reports show the broad range of Microsoft products that enterprise teams must consider when planning security updates.

Why Microsoft Is Exploring Risk Cohorts

Traditional vulnerability review starts with each CVE. Analysts check its severity, affected products, attack requirements, and exploitation status. They then decide how quickly their organization needs to respond. That process remains necessary, but a large release can force teams to repeat many of the same checks.

For example, several flaws may require analysts to establish whether untrusted files reach a Windows component. Others may depend on whether users with limited permissions can run code locally. Server vulnerabilities may require checking whether a particular role is installed and reachable.

A risk cohort groups vulnerabilities around those shared questions. The flaws do not need to have the same root cause or CVSS score. Their connection is the assessment needed to understand exposure in the customer’s environment.

Microsoft highlights that these provisional groups are not official vulnerability categories. They do not change patching instructions, determine urgency on their own, or replace checks for active exploitation, user interaction, attack paths, and product guidance.

Windows and Office Dominate the Groups

The largest listed cohort covers Windows filesystems, storage, and backup, with 136 CVEs. Its shared assessment focuses on features and backup paths that handle untrusted input, disk images, media, or workloads. Office document and mail clients follow with 135 CVEs, while Windows graphics, media, and content processing accounts for 131.

For Office, the useful questions concern installed applications and versions, incoming documents and messages, and how updates reach users. Graphics and media reviews focus on systems that process untrusted content and the permissions under which those components operate.

Windows core and kernel privilege boundaries contain 109 CVEs. Installation, deployment, and update services contain another 103. These groups focus attention on whether code running with limited permissions can interact with more privileged parts of Windows.

Device, peripheral, and print surfaces account for 76 CVEs, matching the 76 assigned to DNS, DHCP, and network address infrastructure. Remote access and RDP deployments contain 65, authentication and cryptography contain 61, and the Windows networking stack contains 53.

The remaining listed groups cover virtualization and isolation with 45 CVEs, network file sharing with 39, endpoint management and security controls with 38, web and messaging services with 27, and directory, federation, and certificate infrastructure with 24. Microsoft provides the individual mappings in its October cohort PDF.

The practical value lies in connecting vulnerability details to actual deployment. For remote access, teams need to identify clients, gateways, and servers, then examine permitted access paths and identities. For virtualization, the shared question is where untrusted guest or workload code is allowed to run.

Those answers can support several reviews, but they cannot settle every patching decision. Two flaws in the same cohort may have different attack requirements, affected versions, or exploitation status.

Microsoft’s Security Update Guide remains the reference for individual advisories. Teams should use cohort assessments alongside those records, not instead of them. The approach offers a way to organize a heavy workload while keeping each vulnerability’s specific risks visible throughout the patching process.

Published on October 13, 2026, the disclosure is tracked under […]

The post Critical FortiSandbox GUI Vulnerability Allows Remote Attackers to Bypass Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Fortinet disclosed a critical authentication-bypass vulnerability in the FortiSandbox graphical user interface that could let remote attackers access protected functions without valid credentials. Tracked as CVE-2026-107656, the flaw carries a reported CVSSv3 score of 9.6 and affects both FortiSandbox appliances and selected FortiSandbox PaaS releases.

Published on October 13, 2026, the disclosure is tracked under Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-185. Fortinet lists the potential impact as execution of unauthorized code or commands. Its advisory marks known exploitation as “No,” meaning the disclosure does not establish that attackers have already used this vulnerability in real attacks.

The weakness is classified as CWE-288, Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel. A remote attacker could send crafted HTTP requests to bypass GUI authentication. The supplied CVSS vector describes a network attack with low complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction.

The advisory does not provide specific request paths, an exploit payload, or a detailed attack chain. Those limits matter when assessing exposure. Security teams should not assume that this flaw shares the same exploit method as earlier FortiSandbox authentication bypass vulnerabilities, which involved different components and vulnerability classes.

Affected Versions and Required Updates

FortiSandbox versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.6 are affected and require an upgrade to 5.0.7 or later. Versions 4.4.0 through 4.4.9 require an upgrade to 4.4.10 or later. FortiSandbox 5.2 is not affected.

For FortiSandbox PaaS, versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.6 require an upgrade to 5.0.7 or later. All PaaS 4.4 versions are affected, and Fortinet directs customers to migrate to a fixed release. PaaS 5.2 is not affected. No virtual patch is listed.

Fortinet credits Adham El Karn of its Product Security team with discovering and reporting the issue internally. The company also acknowledges Jason McFadyen of TrendAI Research for responsible disclosure.

A separate FortiSandbox sensitive data exposure vulnerability previously affected the web interface, but its fixes should not be treated as protection against this new flaw. Administrators should check their exact product and release against the new advisory before selecting an upgrade. This avoids confusing separate security fixes.

The post TFG London Cyberattack Disrupts IT Systems Used by Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles Brands appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
TFG London has confirmed a cyberattack that disrupted IT systems supporting Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles. South Africa’s The Foschini Group detected the incident on October 11, 2026, and disclosed it to shareholders on October 13. Several systems remained unavailable, although stores continued trading.

According to the company’s shareholder announcement, Inside Story and White Stuff were not affected. TFG Africa and TFG Australia also remained unaffected because they operate on separate systems. The confirmed disruption is therefore limited to part of the group’s UK business, rather than its global operations.

TFG London Cyberattack

TFG activated its incident response and business continuity plans after discovering the attack. External cybersecurity specialists are helping contain the incident, and the company has informed relevant UK authorities.

Its investigation is still examining whether personal or other sensitive information was compromised. Customers face disruption, even as stores remain open. Some website functions may be unavailable, and orders placed on or after October 11 could be delayed. Customers have been told not to resubmit those orders.

Purchases placed before Sunday are expected to be processed and delivered normally. In customer communications, TFG London said a third-party provider handles payment processing. Based on its investigation so far, it has “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk.”

However, the company has not ruled out exposure of other customer information and will directly notify people whose data was affected.

TFG has not disclosed the attackers’ identity, their entry point, or whether ransomware was involved. It has also not provided a deadline for full system recovery. These gaps matter because system unavailability alone does not show whether attackers encrypted files, stole data, or caused another form of disruption.

The separate systems used in Africa and Australia provide an important boundary to the reported impact. However, TFG has not published enough technical detail to establish which UK applications were affected or how access across the three brands was disrupted.

TFG’s June financial results described an earlier cyber incident affecting a key online concession partner. That disruption was one of several pressures on its UK portfolio.

Adjusted operating profit fell 65.4%, excluding brand impairment and acquisition costs. This figure should not be presented as the cost of October’s attack.

The wider retail context includes the Marks & Spencer cyberattack, which disrupted payment and collection services, and the Harrods supplier data breach, which exposed customer records.

Neither report links to TFG. For now, the central questions remain how they gained access, whether they stole information, and when affected services can safely return.

articles.title: Critical Docker Hub Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Users and Push Container Images
articles.description:
Docker has disclosed a critical Docker Hub vulnerability that could let attackers impersonate other users and publish container images under trusted names. Tracked as CVE-2026-105445, the flaw affected personal access tokens transferred during account conversions. Docker resolved the issue on September 30, 2026, stating its investigation found no evidence of exploitation. This issue posed a […]

The post Critical Docker Hub Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Users and Push Container Images appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Docker has disclosed a critical Docker Hub vulnerability that could let attackers impersonate other users and publish container images under trusted names. Tracked as CVE-2026-105445, the flaw affected personal access tokens transferred during account conversions.

Docker resolved the issue on September 30, 2026, stating its investigation found no evidence of exploitation. This issue posed a software supply chain risk, as attackers could potentially alter images that developers relied on.

Depending on the token’s permissions and the target user’s access, they could pull, push, or delete images in personal repositories and connected organizations. However, the flaw did not allow full account takeover.

Docker Hub Vulnerability

Docker Hub allows users to convert a personal account into an organization while keeping existing repository names. This helps teams preserve image references used by applications and build systems.

During conversion, the user selects an existing Docker Hub account to become the organization’s owner. Starting August 26, 2024, this process also transferred the original account’s personal access tokens, known as PATs, to the selected owner. Docker changed the ownership record without changing or revoking the token secret. The new owner was neither asked to approve the transfer nor notified that it happened.

An attacker could therefore create an account, generate a PAT, and convert that account into an organization while naming a victim as its owner. The attacker still knew the token secret, but Docker Hub now linked that token to the victim. Registry requests using it could authenticate as the target user.

This was a failure in credential-ownership handling rather than a stolen-password attack. The token remained usable after its identity changed. Docker says the exposure window lasted from August 26, 2024, at 20:33 UTC until September 30, 2026, at approximately 19:10 UTC, when the production fix went live.

Publishing an image under a legitimate repository name could expose downstream users to unexpected code.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the Trivy supply chain attack involving compromised Docker images, illustrating why trusted publishing paths matter. That incident is separate from this vulnerability, which Docker found no evidence attackers exploited.

The affected tokens did not provide access to the Docker Hub website. Attackers could not use this flaw to change a victim’s password, email address, or two-factor authentication settings.

The impact stayed at the registry level and depended on the token’s scope and the user’s repository permissions. Researchers Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com reported the issue through Docker’s vulnerability disclosure program.

According to Docker’s security advisory, the company reproduced it with internal test accounts and deployed a fix less than four hours after receiving the report.

Docker reviewed every account conversion since the flaw appeared and checked registry authentication logs, usage data, and token records. Investigators examined approximately 304,000 image pushes made with transferred tokens.

All went to repositories belonging to the converted organization or the new owner, with none reaching unrelated accounts. Docker also inspected higher-risk public images without running them. It found no malware, cryptominers, credential theft, persistence, or tampering.

However, registry logs record token use rather than token existence. Docker therefore treated every transferred PAT as potentially affected, including tokens that never appeared in usage logs.

Docker notified exposed users and organization owners on October 2. On October 8, it deactivated transferred tokens, except those owners requested to retain. Account conversion no longer transfers PATs.

Docker is also adding owner consent, notifications, and records of token ownership changes. Docker says users who received no notification were not exposed and need no incident-specific action.

It recommends revoking unfamiliar or unused PATs and using organization access tokens for organizational automation. Related container image scanning tools provide context for teams reviewing image security alongside credential controls.

The post CrowdStrike Joins Anthropic Defense Program to Advance AI-powered Defense for Critical Infrastructure appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CrowdStrike has joined Anthropic’s Critical Infrastructure Defense Program to help strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity across energy, water, manufacturing, and transportation systems.

Announced on October 8, 2026, the partnership combines CrowdStrike’s experience protecting business and industrial networks with Anthropic’s advanced Claude models, technical support, and cybersecurity research.

The initiative targets a difficult security challenge. Critical infrastructure often connects modern information technology, or IT, with older operational technology, or OT, that controls physical equipment.

These industrial systems can remain in service for decades. Taking them offline for updates may interrupt essential services, leaving known security weaknesses unresolved for years.

Anthropic Defense Program

According to Anthropic’s announcement, the program brings Claude models, on-site engineers, and threat research to trusted security providers and equipment manufacturers.

CrowdStrike is among 11 founding partners, alongside organizations including Dragos, Nozomi Networks, Rockwell Automation, Palo Alto Networks, Accenture, and Deloitte. The approach puts AI support in the hands of teams that already understand industrial environments.

The program forms part of the broader Anthropic Cyber Mission, which also supports open-source software security. Anthropic says several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers address weaknesses.

Its initial focus is learning which defensive methods work safely and effectively, rather than treating AI as a complete solution for industrial security.

CrowdStrike will contribute security data, threat intelligence, and experience from its Falcon platform. In its partnership announcement, the company describes an opportunity to connect its knowledge of attacker behavior with Anthropic’s AI research.

That context matters because defenders must understand a weakness within the wider network before they can choose a practical response.

A key part of CrowdStrike’s contribution is Falcon for XIoT, which covers industrial and connected devices alongside IT assets. CrowdStrike says it helps discover unmanaged and older equipment, assess exposure without disruptive scanning, and detect threats moving between business and operational networks.

Supported Windows and Linux hosts can help discover and monitor nearby unmanaged devices. The Falcon platform also combines endpoint, identity, cloud, threat intelligence, and OT security data. This shared view gives defenders more context when investigating suspicious activity across connected environments.

The partnership builds on an existing relationship, with Anthropic’s Claude already available within CrowdStrike’s Charlotte AI security assistant. Participation in the program adds technical guidance and access to a community focused on critical infrastructure defense.

The announcement also follows Anthropic’s expanded Cyber Verification Program, which gives eligible security professionals broader model access for approved work. However, finding weaknesses is only part of the challenge.

Anthropic acknowledges that verifying findings and safely applying fixes remain difficult, especially when industrial equipment cannot stop. The collaboration’s value will depend on turning AI findings into safe, practical improvements.

articles.title: Zoom Clients for Certificate Validation Flaw Exposes Sensitive Information via Network Access
articles.description:
Two high-severity certificate validation flaws in Zoom clients could allow attackers without login credentials to access sensitive information over a network, according to advisory text dated October 13, 2026. The issues affect Windows clients and the My Notes feature across desktop and mobile platforms, making updates important for both personal users and business deployments. The […]

The post Zoom Clients for Certificate Validation Flaw Exposes Sensitive Information via Network Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Two high-severity certificate validation flaws in Zoom clients could allow attackers without login credentials to access sensitive information over a network, according to advisory text dated October 13, 2026.

The issues affect Windows clients and the My Notes feature across desktop and mobile platforms, making updates important for both personal users and business deployments.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-108184 and CVE-2026-108185, each carry a CVSS v3.1 score of 7.4. Zoom Offensive Security reported both.

The supplied bulletins describe information disclosure risks but do not identify the exact data that could be exposed, provide an attack example, or state whether either flaw has been exploited.

Zoom Certificate Validation Flaw

Certificate validation helps software check that it is communicating with a trusted service. When those checks fail, an application may accept a connection it should reject.

MITRE describes this weakness as improper certificate validation and explains that it can let attackers impersonate trusted systems or interfere with protected communications.

That general risk does not establish the precise attack method for these Zoom flaws. The supplied disclosures do not say whether the problem involves certificate trust, expiry checks, server identity, or another validation step.

Claims that attackers can steal passwords, meeting recordings, or all user notes would therefore go beyond the available details. Zoom’s descriptions specifically identify information disclosure, not remote code execution or account takeover.

According to security bulletins published by Zoom, CVE-2026-108184 appears in bulletin ZSB-26021 and concerns certain Zoom clients for Windows.

Affected Zoom Workplace releases start at version 7.0.0 and remain vulnerable before versions 7.2.0 and 7.1.9 in their respective branches. This branch wording matters because the correct update target depends on the release line installed.

The same flaw affects Zoom Workplace VDI Client for Windows from version 7.0.11 to before 7.0.13. Zoom Rooms for Windows is affected from version 7.0.0 to before 7.1.7.

Businesses should check these products separately rather than assume that updating the standard Workplace app also fixes virtual desktop clients or meeting room systems.

CVE-2026-108185, described in ZSB-26022, affects certificate validation in My Notes. On Windows, the affected Workplace range begins at 7.1.5. On macOS and Linux, it begins at 7.0.5.

Each desktop platform requires version 7.2.0 or 7.1.9 in its respective branch to move beyond the listed affected range. Zoom Workplace for Android and iOS is also affected by the My Notes issue, starting at version 7.0.5 and continuing before 7.2.0. The bulletin does not explain whether specific feature settings are required for exploitation.

Disabling My Notes should not be presented as a confirmed workaround without further guidance from Zoom. Users should install the latest supported release through Zoom’s official Download Center. Zoom’s security bulletin page also recommends keeping its software current to receive security fixes and improvements.

For managed environments, the affected version ranges provide a practical starting point for checking which installations still need attention.

Administrators should confirm installed versions after deployment, including devices outside the main office and systems maintained by separate teams.

A completed rollout should cover Windows Workplace, VDI, Rooms, and affected mobile and desktop My Notes clients, rather than only the most visible employee laptops.

These disclosures follow earlier Zoom client vulnerabilities and a separate Windows account takeover flaw. Those reports offer useful background, but their attack methods and consequences should not be applied to these new certificate issues.

Tracked as CVE-2026-104935, the flaw carries a high-severity CVSS score of 8.6. Ivanti confirmed that exploitation affected a limited number of customers in its October 13, 2026 advisory. The vulnerability involves […]

The post Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in the Wild appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ivanti has disclosed an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) that allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands without logging in.

Tracked as CVE-2026-104935, the flaw carries a high-severity CVSS score of 8.6. Ivanti confirmed that exploitation affected a limited number of customers in its October 13, 2026 advisory.

The vulnerability involves authentication bypass through spoofing, classified as CWE-290. An attacker can exploit the flaw over a network without credentials or user interaction.

Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day

The CVSS assessment indicates low attack complexity, with a high impact on data confidentiality and lower impacts on data integrity and service availability.

According to Ivanti, its product security team initially discovered part of the vulnerability and patched it in version 25.1.3.0, released in July 2026. Exploitation occurred while the company was working to bring the fix to other supported versions. Ivanti credited Volexity for helping protect affected customers.

The disclosure follows earlier Ivanti VPN exploitation and the MITRE network breach involving Ivanti zero-days. Those incidents involved different vulnerabilities and should not be treated as evidence of the methods used in this campaign.

Affected releases include 25.1.1.1 and earlier, 25.1.2.2 and earlier, and 22.8R2.4 and earlier. Ivanti lists 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1, and 22.8R2.5 as resolved versions. Versions in the 22.7 branch and lower do not contain this vulnerability.

Customers using 25.1.1.1 on ISA6000 or ISA8000 appliances should install 25.1.1.2. Organizations running 22.8 should move to 25.1.1.2 or later, or install 22.8R2.5 if migration cannot happen immediately. Both 22.7 and 22.8 reach end of life on January 31, 2027.

Migration to 25.1.3.0 requires the ISA4500, ISA6500, or ISA8500 platform. Physical deployments need the new servers, while virtual and cloud deployments require newly built devices using the appropriate template.

Administrators should consult Ivanti’s upgrade and migration guide before changing platforms. Ivanti said it currently has no reliable indicators of compromise. Customers who suspect exploitation should follow its recovery instructions.

The advisory does not identify the attackers or provide exploit details, leaving the campaign’s scope beyond the confirmed customers unclear at disclosure.

articles.title: Danfoss Refrigeration Hack Update – 4,980 Hosts Found Exposed to Internet
articles.description:
France accounts for more than half of the internet-facing hosts found in a Shodan search for Danfoss web pages, following a cyberattack that disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems. An update from International Cyber Digest on October 13 reports a total of 4,980 hosts identified, with 2,911 located in France and 517 in South Africa. These findings […]

The post Danfoss Refrigeration Hack Update – 4,980 Hosts Found Exposed to Internet appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
France accounts for more than half of the internet-facing hosts found in a Shodan search for Danfoss web pages, following a cyberattack that disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems.

An update from International Cyber Digest on October 13 reports a total of 4,980 hosts identified, with 2,911 located in France and 517 in South Africa. These findings raise new concerns about exposed cooling controls; however, they do not confirm that every listed host has been hacked.

According to Shodan, Germany ranks third with 171 results, followed by Portugal with 158 and the United States with 141. Poland, Belgium, Sweden, Spain, and the Netherlands also appear among the leading countries.

France represents roughly 58% of the reported total. International Cyber Digest estimates that around eight in ten matching hosts are in Europe.

Danfoss Refrigeration Hack Update

The search looks for Danfoss references in web content, not proof that every result is a vulnerable refrigeration controller. A separate screenshot shows 4,551 results from a more filtered search. Neither image provides firmware versions, confirms successful attacks against individual hosts, or establishes how many supermarkets each controller serves.

The exposure update follows attacks overnight between October 11 and October 12. Reports describe attackers remotely triggering defrost functions at French supermarkets, leaving chilled and frozen goods spoiled.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the supermarket fridge attacks, including reports of temperatures reaching 50°C. Those temperature reports should not be treated as measurements from every affected store.

France’s CERT-FR confirmed numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC devices in an October 12 alert. The agency instructed operators to disconnect the systems or filter access.

Danfoss told news outlets that affected refrigeration management systems were running outdated firmware and repeated its advice to update supported equipment and replace legacy systems.

International Cyber Digest also shared a claim that affected systems used the username admin and a password that changed daily to the current date. Published technical research supports a narrower explanation.

Claroty’s Team82 found a hidden, date-based authentication path in the AK-SM 800A platform that could bypass the configured administrator password.

According to Team82, the controller generates a daily authentication code using its current date. Someone who reproduces the algorithm could generate an accepted code and obtain an administrative session.

This is not the same as proving that the ordinary administrator password simply becomes the date. Investigators have not publicly established that this specific flaw enabled the supermarket attacks.

The issue is tracked as CVE-2025-41450. CISA identifies affected AK-SM 8xxA versions as those earlier than R4.2, which addressed the authentication weakness.

Its advisory also covers CVE-2025-41451, a command injection flaw in email alert settings, and CVE-2025-41452, a web server configuration weakness. Both affect versions before R4.3.1.

Team82 explains that the command injection flaw could allow code execution after authentication. The configuration weakness could let an authenticated attacker alter web traffic handling or disrupt the management interface.

These findings show possible attack paths, not a confirmed account of how the French incident unfolded. The AK-SM 800A manages multiple refrigeration devices through one web interface. Operators can adjust temperature limits, schedules, alarms, and user accounts.

That central role makes exposed management access especially risky because changes can affect physical cooling operations, rather than only digital records. Similar concerns appear in Cybersecurity News coverage of internet-exposed cooling and power controllers.

CERT-FR recommends restricting network access to service providers when compromise is suspected, then performing a factory reset, applying available security updates, changing passwords and other secrets, checking accounts, and fully reconfiguring the system. Recovery should follow a controlled process that protects store operations.

Operators should also remove direct internet exposure, separate control networks from business networks, and use protected remote access. Patching remains essential, but access restrictions are equally important while teams assess, repair, or replace affected equipment. For retailers, the immediate priority is restoring safe cooling without leaving the same access open.

articles.title: CISA Warns of Hackers Exploiting Two Citrix NetScaler 0-Days to Execute Code Remotely
articles.description:
Threat actors are actively exploiting two critical zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, allowing them to execute code remotely on exposed systems. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, received a CVSS v4 severity score of 9.5 out of 10 and have been added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security […]

The post CISA Warns of Hackers Exploiting Two Citrix NetScaler 0-Days to Execute Code Remotely appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Threat actors are actively exploiting two critical zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, allowing them to execute code remotely on exposed systems.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, received a CVSS v4 severity score of 9.5 out of 10 and have been added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

CISA confirmed that it received reports and partner intelligence showing global exploitation activity. Citrix released emergency updates after confirming that exploitation had occurred against unpatched, customer-managed NetScaler deployments. The affected products are often placed at the network edge to provide application delivery, load balancing, VPN access, and secure remote access.

That position makes a compromised appliance highly valuable to threat actors because it can sit between internet users and internal company systems.

CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation issue that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on a vulnerable NetScaler ADC or Gateway.

It affects all vulnerable deployments, including devices using the default configuration. No optional feature needs to be enabled for the flaw to be reachable, making it the broader of the two issues. Citrix said the vulnerability has a low attack complexity rating, meaning a threat actor does not need an account or user interaction to begin exploitation.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-88772, is a memory overflow vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution or denial-of-service conditions. Unlike CVE-2026-88771, this issue requires Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS, to be enabled.

DTLS is enabled by default on NetScaler VPN virtual servers unless administrators have explicitly turned it off. This makes remote-access deployments a key area for security teams to review.

Citrix has provided configuration checks that can help administrators determine whether DTLS is active on a NetScaler virtual server. Both zero-days were disclosed on September 27, 2026, alongside six other NetScaler flaws. Citrix confirmed that attackers were already exploiting the two remote code execution issues before it made fixes public.

CISA Warns of Two Citrix NetScaler 0-Days

Security teams should treat the release as an active incident response matter rather than a routine patching task. Cyber Security News previously reported on Citrix’s confirmation of the two NetScaler zero-days, including the risks facing internet-exposed ADC and Gateway appliances.

The vendor’s security bulletin lists NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1 releases before 14.1-73.37 and 13.1 releases before 13.1-64.23 as vulnerable. NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS builds before 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 13.1-FIPS or NDcPP builds before 13.1-37.279 are also affected.

Secure Private Access Hybrid customers using vulnerable NetScaler instances must upgrade those instances as well. Citrix-managed cloud services are not covered by this bulletin because Cloud Software Group applies updates to those services directly.

Administrators should identify every customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway system, especially appliances reachable from the public internet, and upgrade to the fixed releases as soon as operationally possible.

Citrix recommends 14.1-73.37 or later for the 14.1 branch and 13.1-64.23 or later for the 13.1 branch. FIPS and NDcPP deployments need their matching patched releases. Organizations should also check whether CVE-2026-88772 applies by reviewing DTLS-enabled VPN and other virtual server settings.

According to CISA, patching alone may not remove the risk where a device was already compromised. CISA has advised organizations to look for signs of compromise before applying updates and to send NetScaler logs to a central SIEM or log-retention platform, since local appliance logs can rotate quickly and overwrite evidence. CISA also published a Sigma detection rule resource to support threat hunting for suspicious NetScaler activity.

Where compromise is suspected, organizations should first preserve evidence, including system snapshots, support bundles, memory data where appropriate, and remote syslog records.

Citrix advises isolating the affected appliance, changing credentials and stored secrets, revoking certificates and private keys, investigating connected systems, and rebuilding from a known-good backup that predates the suspected compromise.

Restored passwords, key-encryption keys, and SSL certificates should then be rotated. The situation has expanded beyond the initial two flaws. CISA updated its alert on October 9 to include CVE-2026-107406 and to stress prompt updates for CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88779.

CVE-2026-88779, a separate actively exploited SAML-related NetScaler issue, can cause denial of service and may be used to force a reboot that helps execute code previously injected through exploitation of CVE-2026-88771.

Cyber Security News also covered the actively exploited NetScaler SAML zero-day, which requires affected organizations to apply a newer set of NetScaler updates.

For defenders, the immediate priority is clear: patch exposed NetScaler systems, preserve logs before making major changes, review authentication and administrative activity, and assume that a vulnerable internet-facing device may have been probed or compromised.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

articles.title: Threat Intelligence Guide for US SOC Teams and CISOs: How to Choose the Right Solution
articles.description:
Choosing an enterprise threat intelligence solution is about more than just data volume or integrations. The right provider should deliver relevant intelligence, fit existing workflows, and help security teams investigate threats faster.  While SOCs may prioritize rapid investigation and enrichment at scale, MSSPs may focus more on multi-tenancy and customer separation.  This enterprise threat intelligence […]

The post Threat Intelligence Guide for US SOC Teams and CISOs: How to Choose the Right Solution  appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Choosing an enterprise threat intelligence solution is about more than just data volume or integrations.

The right provider should deliver relevant intelligence, fit existing workflows, and help security teams investigate threats faster. 

While SOCs may prioritize rapid investigation and enrichment at scale, MSSPs may focus more on multi-tenancy and customer separation. 

This enterprise threat intelligence buying guide covers the key criteria to consider, including intelligence quality, integrations, data privacy, scalability, and proof-of-concept testing. 

Start With Your Security Team’s Requirements 

The first step in threat intelligence vendor selection is understanding what your security team needs intelligence to accomplish, rather than comparing feature lists. 

Some organizations may prioritize faster alert investigation and enrichment, while others need intelligence for threat hunting, malware analysis, or proactive monitoring. MSSPs may also require strong customer separation and efficient multi-tenant workflows. 

Start by identifying the teams, workflows, and data involved, then define your threat intelligence requirements around factors such as intelligence freshness, investigation context, API capacity, integrations, privacy, automation, and access management. 

Clear requirements make it easier to focus on capabilities that directly support your security operation. 

For teams that need both intelligence and hands-on analysis, it can also be useful to consider how threat intelligence connects with malware and phishing investigation.

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox provides an environment for analyzing threats in real time, with capabilities including interactive analysis, SOC-ready reporting, and integrations through API, SDK, and security standards.

Its virtual machines start in under 10 seconds, with reports available in about 40 seconds. 

Look at Threat Intelligence Quality and Context 

The size of an intelligence database doesn’t necessarily determine its value. During evaluation, consider the quality and sources of the data, how quickly it becomes available, how indicators are validated, and how much context accompanies each result. 

This is especially important for threat intelligence aggregation. Combining multiple sources can improve coverage, but may also introduce outdated, duplicate, or conflicting data.

Without effective filtering and context, more data can simply create more noise. Analysts often need more than a malicious or benign verdict.

Details such as related domains, URLs, files, malware families, infrastructure, and historical activity can help determine an indicator’s relevance. 

Threat intelligence enrichment provides analysts with the context needed to assess threats and determine what to investigate next. 

For example, ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup (TI Lookup) lets analysts search indicators and event fields and investigate relationships between domains, IPs, URLs, hashes, files, TTPs, and other data.

It delivers each result in about 2 seconds and connects threat intelligence with data from sandbox research sessions, giving analysts additional context for investigations. 

TI Lookup draws on threat intelligence contributed through investigations from 16,000 organizations and more than 700,000 analysts, providing additional context for investigations.

It delivers fresh, up-to-date intelligence on the latest malware and phishing attacks, helping security teams stay informed about emerging threats and attack trends. 

Tap into threat intelligence from 16K+ organizations to stay ahead of emerging threats. Boost DR by 36% and cut MTTR by 21 mins per case. Integrate ANY.RUN  
 

In addition, Threat Intelligence Reports (TI Reports) can provide another layer of context by summarizing emerging threats, attack techniques, malware activity, and relevant indicators.

When evaluating a provider, consider whether reports are timely, well-sourced, actionable, and easy for analysts to connect with ongoing investigations. 

Prioritize Fresh Intelligence 

Threat intelligence can lose relevance over time, especially when used to identify active infrastructure or support automated detection. 

When evaluating a provider, consider how quickly new intelligence becomes available and how outdated indicators are identified, updated, or retired.

Fresh data helps teams respond to current activity, while historical visibility allows analysts to investigate whether an indicator or related infrastructure has appeared before. 

The right balance depends on your use case. Real-time alert enrichment may require frequent updates, while threat hunting may place greater value on extensive historical context. 

Look for clear information on how intelligence is timestamped, validated, updated, and maintained, as these factors directly affect its value in investigations and detection workflows.  

ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds) can support these requirements by providing live malicious IPs, domains, and URLs enriched with sandbox analysis.

TI Feeds continuously update their data, with 99% of unique, high-confidence IOCs undergoing validation before being added. 

Evaluate Correlation, Not Just Individual Indicators 

An indicator is often just the starting point of an investigation. Its real value increases when analysts can connect it to related infrastructure, files, malware, and other activity. 

Threat intelligence correlation helps uncover these relationships. For example, a suspicious domain may be linked to an IP address, URL, malicious file, or malware family, giving analysts a broader view of the threat rather than a single isolated data point. 

This goes beyond IOC management, which focuses on tracking, validating, and distributing indicators.

For more complex investigations, analysts also need to understand how indicators are connected and what those relationships reveal about the activity behind them. 

When evaluating a solution, test common investigation scenarios and see how easily analysts can pivot between related intelligence.

The goal is to determine whether the available context can reduce investigation time and manual research. 

Strengthen your SOC with ANY.RUN. Investigate threats faster, turn analysis into actionable intelligence, and streamline your response. Contact us

Assess Integration Options 

Threat intelligence should fit into the security workflows your organization already uses. 

Enterprise teams may need intelligence to move between SIEM, SOAR, EDR/XDR, firewalls, case-management systems, and other security tools. Integration should therefore be part of the procurement process, not an afterthought. 

ANY.RUN integrates with existing security environments through APIs, SDKs, and ready-made integrations, helping teams bring threat analysis and shared context into their established workflows. 

Beyond API availability, consider request limits, quotas, bulk operations, response times, authentication, SDK support, and automation capabilities, especially when handling thousands of enrichment requests daily. 

Consider STIX/TAXII Support 

STIX/TAXII support can simplify the exchange of structured threat intelligence between security systems and reduce custom integration work. 

TI Feeds support STIX/TAXII alongside API and SDK integrations, making it easier to incorporate intelligence into existing workflows. 

During a proof of concept, test whether the data arrives in the expected format, includes the required context, updates at the right frequency, and works reliably with your existing systems. 

Plan for Scale From the Beginning 

A service that works for a small security team may face different demands as usage expands. More analysts and automated enrichment can increase investigation volume and API requests, while MSSPs may need to support multiple customer environments at once. 

Consider user management, permissions, workspace separation, auditability, API capacity, and data volumes when assessing scalability. MSSPs should also look closely at multi-tenancy to ensure customer data remains properly separated. 

ANY.RUN’s MSSP offering supports high-volume workflows with automation, standardized reporting, API/SDK access, and capabilities designed for multiple customer environments. Interactive Sandbox, TI Lookup, and TI Feeds deliver 3x better SOC performance. 

Scalability also means keeping the service manageable as more teams, analysts, and customers rely on it.
 

Cut Tier 1 workload by up to 20%. Increase analyst capacity, streamline operations, and improve service performance. Boost MSSP efficiency

Test the Analyst Experience 

Threat intelligence should help analysts investigate threats efficiently. Even extensive intelligence can be difficult to use if analysts have to navigate multiple disconnected workflows. 

During evaluation, pay attention to search, filtering, historical visibility, pivoting, and how easily analysts can move between related indicators. 

A practical test is to give analysts a familiar investigation scenario involving a suspicious domain, IP, URL, or file hash.

See how quickly they can determine its relevance, identify related activity, and gather enough context to decide what to investigate next. 

Interactive Sandbox can also support hands-on malware and phishing analysis, allowing analysts to interact with threats in live virtual environments and access findings such as IOCs and TTPs.

For enterprise SOCs, 95% of SOC teams speed up threat investigations, while 94% of users achieve faster triage. 

Determine the Need for Dark Web Monitoring  

Dark web monitoring can help organizations identify leaked credentials, exposed corporate information, or brand-related threats. 

Rather than treating it as a must-have feature, assess whether it addresses a specific security requirement. Consider source coverage, validation, detection speed, and how easily analysts can act on the findings. 

Use Real Data in the Proof of Concept 

A proof of concept should reflect real security workflows, not just provider demonstrations. 

Use representative historical alerts, including malicious, benign, and ambiguous cases. Measure outcomes such as investigation time, enrichment quality, false-positive reduction, manual effort, search performance, and API reliability. 

If automated enrichment is planned, test realistic request volumes to identify potential limitations before deployment. 

Review the Total Cost of Ownership 

The cost of a threat intelligence service extends beyond the subscription. Integration, maintenance, training, analyst time, infrastructure, and API usage can all add to the total. 

Review API limits and additional usage costs, and consider whether the service adds meaningful coverage or context to your existing intelligence sources. 

For example, TI Feeds help identify up to 58% more threats overall and offer a 21-minute reduction in MTTR per case.

When assessing ROI, teams can compare metrics such as these with their own baseline investigation time, detection coverage, and analyst workload. 

Turn Requirements into a Practical Decision 

Once requirements and testing are complete, assess how well each offering fits your security workflows. 

Consider intelligence quality, freshness, enrichment, correlation, integration, automation, privacy, scalability, usability, and cost. The priorities will vary by organization and use case. 

An MSSP may focus more on multi-tenancy and API capacity, while an enterprise SOC may prioritize investigation speed and contextual enrichment. 

A threat intelligence procurement guide should help teams base their decision on requirements, testing, and measurable operational outcomes. 

Conclusion 

Choosing an enterprise threat intelligence offering starts with understanding your security requirements and use cases. 

Assess intelligence quality, freshness, context, enrichment, integrations, privacy, scalability, and automation, then validate those criteria with real-world testing. 

The goal is to turn threat intelligence into useful context that helps security teams investigate threats faster and reduce unnecessary work.

The post G2A.COM Reports 35% Growth in Security Software Orders, Outpacing VPN Growth appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Amsterdam, Netherlands, October 13th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Antivirus and security software orders grow more than twice as fast as VPN orders, accounting for 43% of cybersecurity purchases on the marketplace 

G2A.COM, a digital marketplace that serves more than 35 million users across 180 countries, reports a 35% year-on-year surge in antivirus and security software orders, outpacing VPN orders.   

Released during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the marketplace figures reveal that security software accounted for 43% of cybersecurity-related orders during the period, up from 39% in the equivalent period in 2025.

Overall, orders across cybersecurity products increased by almost a quarter (24%).  

VPNs remain the larger category, but antivirus and security software are taking a greater share of purchases on G2A.COM.

The findings highlight that consumers are increasingly looking beyond privacy and secure connectivity towards broader protection of their devices, accounts and digital activity 

The trend comes as the global cyber threat landscape continues to evolve. According to the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Threat Landscape 2026, ransomware remains the most impactful type of cyber incident in the short term, while social engineering continues to be widely used to exploit trust.  

“What we’re seeing is a shift from privacy-first protection towards a more layered approach to cybersecurity” said Adrian Podkaminer, Chief Information Security Officer at G2A.COM.

“As people move between more devices, accounts and digital services, effective cybersecurity increasingly depends on different safeguards working together rather than relying on a single solution.” 

G2A.COM marketplace data suggests that consumers are taking a more active approach to protecting their digital lives. At the same time, they do not see security as their responsibility alone.

According to the Trust in Digital Commerce report, a survey by G2A.COM and Juniper Research involving 9,000 consumers from nine countries found that half of them think e-commerce sites are mainly responsible for security.

Meanwhile, a third blame banks and payment providers, and 20% say it’s up to the consumers themselves. 

For G2A.COM, that responsibility translates into concrete safeguards. The marketplace works exclusively with verified business sellers and applies KYC, KYB and AML processes, supported by AI-based fraud prevention and continuous monitoring. 

Cybersecurity Awareness Month offers an opportunity for consumers to review both the tools they use and the habits that help protect their accounts. G2A.COM encourages users to: 

  • Secure important accounts: use strong, unique passwords and enable multi-factor authentication wherever available, particularly for email, shopping and payment accounts. 
  • Keep devices updated: install operating system, browser and application updates promptly. 
  • Check before clicking: treat unexpected login requests, downloads and urgent payment messages cautiously, and visit the official website or app directly. 
  • Understand the protection purchased: check what a security product covers, its compatibility with existing devices and any subscription or renewal terms. 

About G2A.COM 

G2A.COM is the world’s largest marketplace for digital entertainment, serving over 35 million users from 180 countries with more than 200 million visits in 2025.

As a true gateway to digital entertainment and a rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, G2A.COM gives access to over 125,000 digital offerings, including vouchers, games, DLCs, in-game items, and non-gaming items such as gift cards, subscriptions, software, or e-learning, sold by sellers from all over the world.

A compliance-driven organization audited by Deloitte for over a decade, G2A.COM is a leader in online security, recognized by the prestigious American CNP Award alongside industry giants like Microsoft and PayPal.

Today, the company is a key gateway for recognized global brands, leveraging its scalable infrastructure to drive the next phase of e-commerce through agentic AI and global M&A – continuously expanding its role as the Gate 2 Adventure in the digital world.

articles.title: ICMacOS Malware Evolves to Steal Credentials and Provide Persistent Remote Mac Access
articles.description:
ICMacOS malware has grown from a tool that steals passwords and cryptocurrency wallet data into a remote access trojan that can keep attackers connected to infected Macs. Its newer version adds a live command channel and a startup mechanism, giving criminals access beyond the first round of data theft. The change raises the stakes for […]

The post ICMacOS Malware Evolves to Steal Credentials and Provide Persistent Remote Mac Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
ICMacOS malware has grown from a tool that steals passwords and cryptocurrency wallet data into a remote access trojan that can keep attackers connected to infected Macs.

Its newer version adds a live command channel and a startup mechanism, giving criminals access beyond the first round of data theft.

The change raises the stakes for Mac users and businesses. Rather than leaving after collecting saved logins, the malware can remain active, run commands, and collect more information.

Developers face particular risk because stolen cloud keys, SSH credentials, and project secrets can expose systems outside the infected device.

Researchers from SOCRadar’s Threat Research Unit identified ICMacOS, also called Icarus macOS, in September 2026.

Their October 12 report describes two versions: an initial information stealer and a newer build with persistent remote access. The malware is promoted by a Russian-speaking actor using the name GlowComa.

ICMacOS Malware Evolves

GlowComa advertises ICMacOS on Russian-speaking cybercrime forums, including XSS, Exploit.in, and Rehub, with updates shared through Telegram. Prices start at $699 weekly and reach $1,699 monthly.

Buyers receive a management panel for tracking infected devices, stolen passwords, cookies, files, and wallets, alongside Telegram alerts when stolen data arrives. The panel is written in Go and uses MySQL to store records, giving buyers a central view of stolen assets.

The infection starts with ClickFix pages that persuade victims to paste malicious commands into Terminal. This approach also appears in macOS ClickFix credential theft campaigns, where fake verification prompts turn the user into the trigger for malware execution.

ICMacOS uses an initial Bash script to retrieve a campaign-specific dropper. That dropper changes Terminal preferences to hide window details, then uses AppleScript to display a fake “System Preferences” password dialog.

It checks the supplied password by trying to unlock the user’s login Keychain, allowing up to five attempts. A successful check gives the malware a verified password for later theft.

Next, the script checks whether the Mac uses Intel or Apple Silicon and downloads the matching payload. It launches the malware in the background with the stolen password and campaign details as arguments.

Finally, it closes Terminal and displays a fake error message based on settings retrieved from its server. The developer claims support from macOS Sierra onward, but the report does not establish compatibility with every release.

The main payload is a 64-bit Mach-O executable written in Go. Version 1 checks Russian language settings and the device’s public IP country before stealing data.

The researchers describe this as a guardrail intended to avoid Russia and Commonwealth of Independent States countries, consistent with the operator’s advertised restrictions.

Its collection modules target browser passwords, cookies, history, cryptocurrency wallets, and password manager data. Developer files include AWS credentials, Kubernetes settings, SSH keys, Git credentials, and environment files.

Similar developer credential theft risks have appeared in other Mac campaigns, showing how one compromised workstation can expose a company’s wider infrastructure.

ICMacOS also copies messaging data from Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, and Apple Messages, plus Apple Notes and Termius information.

It attempts to decrypt Keychain contents using the captured password and an embedded Go library. If that fails, it uses Apple’s security utility, with additional fake prompts seeking administrator approval where needed.

Collected files are packed into a hidden ZIP archive and uploaded through an HTTPS request. A separate Python payload broadens collection to VPN profiles, Slack, Signal, Zoom, and documents in common user folders. It also converts browser cookies into a format that attackers can reuse for session hijacking.

Persistent Remote Access Changes the Risk

Version 2 adds checks for existing malware processes and available privileges before setting up persistence. It installs a LaunchAgent with an Apple-like name and loads it into the active user session.

Its configuration keeps the process running and includes a 60-minute fallback interval, helping restore access if execution stops. The new build also opens a persistent WebSocket connection using the Gorilla WebSocket library.

Commands received from the server run through the Unix shell, with output returned in real time. This move resembles Atomic Stealer backdoor capabilities that extended another Mac credential stealer into a longer-lived remote access threat.

Version 2 further collects clipboard text, Outlook data, Steam files, browser autofill records, and shell history. Defenders should investigate unexpected password dialogs, suspicious Terminal activity, hidden temporary archives, and newly created LaunchAgents. Suspected devices should be isolated, with exposed credentials reset from a clean system and active sessions reviewed.

articles.title: XWorm Malware Can Spy Through Your Microphone and Hijack Logged-In Browser Sessions
articles.description:
XWorm malware is moving beyond password theft, giving attackers tools to listen through infected computers, track their location, and control browsers where users are already logged in. Its growing plugin collection turns a compromised Windows device into both a spying tool and a route into online accounts, without requiring attackers to steal passwords first. The […]

The post XWorm Malware Can Spy Through Your Microphone and Hijack Logged-In Browser Sessions appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
XWorm malware is moving beyond password theft, giving attackers tools to listen through infected computers, track their location, and control browsers where users are already logged in.

Its growing plugin collection turns a compromised Windows device into both a spying tool and a route into online accounts, without requiring attackers to steal passwords first.

The browser feature is especially concerning because it uses sessions that have already passed login checks. Instead of signing in from another computer, an attacker operates the victim’s browser directly.

This can allow access to authenticated accounts without another multifactor authentication challenge, although it does not mean XWorm can defeat every possible security check.

Researchers from Netskope Threat Labs identified four XWorm versions operating in the wild since their July 2025 report.

In their latest XWorm research report, they recorded 1,236 detection events across more than 100 customer organizations during Q3 2026, four times the volume recorded in Q3 2025.

These figures describe detections, not a confirmed count of unique infected devices. Financial services represented approximately 35% of affected customers, with activity concentrated in India, Brazil, Italy, Panama, and the United States.

The findings extend earlier reporting on XWorm Windows script delivery, which showed how scripts and PowerShell helped install the malware while hiding its execution inside legitimate Windows processes.

XWorm Malware Can Spy

The HBrowser plugin, available since version 6, gives operators an interactive view of a victim’s running browser. An attacker selects a supported browser from the control panel, which sends an OpenBrowser command through XWorm’s command-and-control channel.

The infected computer then accepts remote input and sends screenshots back to the operator. Mouse clicks, cursor movements, scrolling, keyboard input, and pasted text travel through the same AES-encrypted channel.

This creates a working remote browser session rather than a simple collection of stolen browser files. Authenticated tabs become accessible, allowing attackers to use accounts while the victim’s existing login remains active.

The distinction matters: this is not evidence that XWorm breaks MFA itself. It avoids a fresh login by working inside an already authenticated session.

Related reporting on GhostProfile browser session hijacking describes another approach to live account access, but GhostProfile copies browser profiles on macOS, whereas Netskope describes XWorm controlling a running browser on Windows.

XWorm’s Microphone plugin uses the NAudio library’s WaveInEvent function to capture sound from a recording device selected by the attacker.

It first lists available devices through the MICCM command, then records 8 kHz, 16-bit mono audio in 500-millisecond buffers. Each buffer is compressed, encoded, encrypted, and streamed back through the control channel.

Netskope reports roughly half a second of audio latency, with recording continuing while the operator keeps the session open. Commands named CLOSEMIC and ENDMIC stop capture or end the session.

Webcam capture is also available on demand, widening the risk beyond stolen files to conversations and activity around the infected device.

The Maps plugin changes a Windows location-consent registry value to Allow before requesting coordinates. Netskope observed this running without privilege escalation or a visible permission prompt.

It calls GeoCoordinateWatcher.TryStart with a 15-second timeout and falls back to IP-based location lookup when GPS is unavailable. IP-derived location should not be confused with precise GPS coordinates.

Leaked Builders Drive Continued Development

The confirmed plugin count increased from 35 to 46 after Netskope’s July 2025 report. Researchers tracked V6.4, V6.5 “XWorm Reborn,” V7.2, and V7.4, with additions including Rootkit, SteamTokenRecovery, HRDP, Cmstp-Bypass, and ResetSurvival.

This growth builds on XWorm defense evasion techniques, previously reported alongside changing loaders, script formats, and attempts to weaken Windows monitoring.

A cracked builder appeared publicly in June 2025, followed by modified V6.4 source code in August. Netskope linked these releases to higher detection volumes, which remained above earlier levels through 2026.

V7.2 added native-code hiding and six anti-virtual-machine checks, while V7.4 used an XBinder dropper, NTdll unhooking, and LocaltoNet-based control infrastructure.

For defenders, the report highlights the need to investigate device compromise alongside account misuse. Earlier XWorm fake receipt campaigns show how ordinary business documents can lead to infection.

Browser access, microphone capture, registry changes, and remote-control traffic should be examined together rather than treated as unrelated events. A valid account session does not prove that the person using it is legitimate.
