articles.title: Critical Ghostscript Flaw Lets Attackers Use Malicious PDFs to Execute Code
articles.description:
A critical vulnerability in Ghostscript could allow attackers to use specially made PDF files to run code on vulnerable servers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-39919, affects Ghostscript versions before 10.08.0 and has a CVSS severity score of 9.8 out of 10. Ghostscript is widely used to render PDFs, create document thumbnails, and convert PostScript files […]

The post Critical Ghostscript Flaw Lets Attackers Use Malicious PDFs to Execute Code appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical vulnerability in Ghostscript could allow attackers to use specially made PDF files to run code on vulnerable servers.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-39919, affects Ghostscript versions before 10.08.0 and has a CVSS severity score of 9.8 out of 10. Ghostscript is widely used to render PDFs, create document thumbnails, and convert PostScript files into images.

The issue is especially important for websites and services that accept uploaded PDFs. WordPress sites, document portals, print services, email gateways, invoice platforms, and file-conversion APIs may all call Ghostscript behind the scenes when they process user-supplied files.

A malicious PDF can therefore reach the vulnerable component even when the main application has no direct Ghostscript code.

Researchers from Wordfence identified the vulnerability during a WordPress 7.1 security assessment using its Argus testing system.

This is not a malware campaign, and researchers have not reported active exploitation in the wild. Instead, the finding shows how a crafted PDF can trigger memory corruption and, in certain server builds, lead to unauthenticated remote code execution.

Wordfence reported the flaw to Artifex on August 23, and the vendor confirmed it the following day before releasing the fix on September 8.

Critical Ghostscript Flaw

CVE-2026-39919 is a heap-based buffer overflow in Ghostscript’s JPEG 2000 image decoding path. The issue occurs when Ghostscript processes a PDF containing a JPEG 2000 image with unusual component resolution settings and sub-byte sample values.

In simple terms, the program reserves too little memory for image data and then writes more data than the allocated buffer can hold.

That extra data can overwrite nearby memory used by Ghostscript. In a controlled WordPress test environment, Wordfence researchers showed that this memory corruption could be developed into remote code execution.

The code would run with the permissions assigned to the account that processes the PDF, such as a web server or PHP-FPM user, rather than automatically gaining root access.

The public NVD vulnerability record lists the issue as a heap-based buffer overflow and notes that crafted JPEG 2000 content inside a PDF can corrupt memory.

The risk starts when an application accepts a PDF and attempts to create a preview or thumbnail. On many WordPress setups, the chain is WordPress, Imagick, ImageMagick, and then Ghostscript. The site may appear to be processing a normal document upload, but Ghostscript is the lower-level tool that reads the file.

This is why the issue differs from the earlier WordPress Imagick code-execution flaw, where WordPress upload validation could be bypassed with content disguised as an image. In this case, the memory bug itself sits inside Ghostscript.

Affected Versions and Real-World Risk

The vulnerable code was introduced in Ghostscript 9.21 and affects upstream versions through 10.07.1. Artifex fixed the issue in Ghostscript 10.08.0, and its official Ghostscript CVE page confirms that CVE-2026-39919 was addressed in that release.

However, Linux vendors may backport the fix to an older-looking package version, meaning gs --version alone may not prove whether a server is safe.

Wordfence tested ten package environments, including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, AlmaLinux, Alpine Linux, and an official WordPress Docker image. The researchers found vulnerable builds across those environments during their September 15 tests.

Their proof-of-concept files did not work unchanged across all systems, which means there is no evidence of a single universal PDF that compromises every server. Still, a build-specific exploit continued to work on systems sharing the same Ghostscript executable.

That result matters for hosting providers and companies that deploy many servers from one container image. A threat actor may not need a PDF that works everywhere if several targets use the same vulnerable build.

The concern is similar to the recent malicious HEIC image research, which showed how native media-processing libraries can expose WordPress servers when uploaded files reach vulnerable decoders.

Organizations should install the fixed Ghostscript package provided by their operating system vendor or hosting provider. Teams using containers should rebuild images from an updated base image and redeploy them, rather than simply restarting an existing container.

Managed WordPress customers should ask their hosting provider whether its Ghostscript package includes the CVE-2026-39919 fix and whether uploaded PDFs are converted into previews.

Where updates cannot be installed immediately, administrators should stop untrusted users from uploading PDFs or disable PDF processing through ImageMagick policy settings.

Rate limits and upload limits can reduce repeated processing attempts, but they do not remove the underlying flaw. Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode should also not be treated as a fix because Wordfence reached the vulnerable path while that sandbox setting was enabled.

The incident also adds to growing evidence that document and image conversion services need close review. A Discourse image pipeline chain recently showed how Ghostscript and ImageMagick can become part of a wider file-processing risk path.

While Claude-assisted decoder exploit research demonstrated how flaws in media libraries can be adapted for real service environments.

articles.title: SAP Security Update Patches Critical Code Injection and Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities
articles.description:
SAP has released its October 2026 security updates, fixing critical code injection, access control, and cloud security flaws alongside a high-severity memory corruption issue. The October 13 release includes 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to earlier notes. Four entries carry critical ratings, making this patch cycle important for teams […]

The post SAP Security Update Patches Critical Code Injection and Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SAP has released its October 2026 security updates, fixing critical code injection, access control, and cloud security flaws alongside a high-severity memory corruption issue.

The October 13 release includes 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to earlier notes. Four entries carry critical ratings, making this patch cycle important for teams running SAP business systems.

According to SAP’s October Patch Day bulletin, the fixes cover S/4HANA, NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Commerce Cloud and several development libraries.

Although the headline highlights critical vulnerabilities, the memory corruption flaw is rated High, not Critical. Its published impact concerns service disruption rather than confirmed code execution or data theft.

Across all 22 entries, SAP lists four critical, three high, 14 medium, and one low severity issues, including the two updated notes and four library advisories.

SAP Security Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-89107 carries a CVSS score of 9.9 and affects the Manage Substitution/Validation Rules feature in SAP S/4HANA. SAP lists S4CORE versions 105, 106, 107, 108 and 109 as affected, with the correction delivered through Security Note 3805589.

The weakness lies in how the rule definition feature checks input written in a scripting language used for business rules. An authenticated attacker with specific business privileges can submit crafted input that the system treats as executable ABAP code, SAP’s programming language.

Successful exploitation could give an attacker broad control over the affected system, with serious effects on data privacy, data accuracy, and service availability. The attack requires an account with suitable business permissions, but the published CVSS vector indicates low attack complexity and no need for another user to interact.

CVE-2026-58249 affects the Internet Communication Manager component in SAP NetWeaver and SAP Web Dispatcher. Rated 7.5, the flaw is addressed by Security Note 3765424. A remote attacker does not need to authenticate before sending a malicious request.

The affected software fails to properly check certain fields in crafted requests handled by an internal protocol component. This can trigger a memory handling error and crash the affected process. The published description reports a high impact on availability, with no impact on confidentiality or integrity.

SAP’s affected version list spans HDB 2.00, multiple kernel and Web Dispatcher releases, Content Server, XS Advanced Runtime and SAP Extended Application Services.

Administrators should compare installed components against the full vendor list rather than assume every deployment needs the same update package.

The highest-rated issue is CVE-2026-89111, an OAuth2 server-side request forgery flaw in SAP Cloud SDK for Python, scored 10.0. It affects versions before 0.45.2.

In applications serving multiple tenants on SAP Business Technology Platform, an attacker controlling the tenant_subdomain parameter can redirect token requests to an attacker-controlled server and expose client credentials.

SAP also fixed CVE-2026-89110, a broken access control flaw in NetWeaver Visual Composer VC70RUNTIME 7.50, rated 9.9. Another critical issue, CVE-2026-89108, concerns a missing authorization check in the Configuration Service of Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence versions 15.4 and 15.5, with a score of 9.1.

Earlier reporting on the SAP NetWeaver zero-day exploited in the wild showed how Visual Composer weaknesses became a route into business networks.

Cyber Security News also covered CISA’s warning about the exploited SAP flaw. Those reports concern CVE-2025-31324, not evidence that these newly disclosed vulnerabilities are being exploited.

SAP urges customers to apply the patches as a priority. Teams should identify affected products, read the relevant security notes, and plan updates around business needs.

Cloud SDK users should move to version 0.45.2 or later and check which applications use the affected library. The release also addresses SQL injection in Commerce Cloud, authorization gaps in ABAP Platform, and several cross-site scripting flaws.

The two revised notes cover earlier SSRF and scripting issues. These updates should remain part of the patch review, even when critical fixes take priority.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

articles.title: Kimsuky Hackers Use Malicious Resume Documents to Deploy Funhouse Ransomware
articles.description:
Kimsuky hackers have used a malicious résumé document to deploy Funhouse ransomware through a chain of scripts and remote access tools. The attack begins with a Hangul Word Processor document disguised as a job application, turning a routine work file into an entry point for malware that ultimately encrypts files. The campaign connects document-based deception […]

The post Kimsuky Hackers Use Malicious Resume Documents to Deploy Funhouse Ransomware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Kimsuky hackers have used a malicious résumé document to deploy Funhouse ransomware through a chain of scripts and remote access tools.

The attack begins with a Hangul Word Processor document disguised as a job application, turning a routine work file into an entry point for malware that ultimately encrypts files.

The campaign connects document-based deception with tools used in earlier Endpoint ransomware cases. Opening the résumé drops supporting files, but clicking a link inside it triggers the next stage.

That distinction matters: the visible document acts as bait, while the link starts the process that leads to remote access and ransomware execution.

Researchers from AhnLab Security intelligence Center (ASEC) identified the Funhouse malware delivery case in a report published October 1, 2026. They linked it to earlier Kimsuky activity through shared scripts, Quasar RAT settings, and ransomware traits.

The findings show a change in the initial delivery method rather than a completely new toolset. The public report does not establish how many victims.

Kimsuky Hackers Use Malicious Resume Documents

The malicious file, resume.Hwp, contains embedded Object Linking and Embedding, or OLE, data. When opened, the Hangul process extracts pdf.Exe and pdf.Exe.Manifest into the Windows temporary folder without further user input.

The executable is a VbsEdit script executor, while the manifest contains the malicious script used in the following stage. A hyperlink inside the résumé invites the recipient to open a PDF bearing a person’s name.

Clicking it launches the extracted executable, which runs the manifest script and creates a randomly named batch file. The trigger resembles earlier Kimsuky document tricks: a weaponized HWP research campaign also used embedded files and a clickable link to begin malicious execution.

This is not simply a document that encrypts files when opened. ASEC describes several stages between the résumé and the final payload.

Batch, VBS, and PowerShell scripts run in sequence, followed by a Python-based backdoor, Quasar RAT installation, and Funhouse execution. Quasar RAT serves as the tool used to deploy the ransomware.

The Python stage fits the group’s previous operations. An earlier malicious LNK backdoor campaign used document-themed Windows shortcuts to install a Python backdoor through multiple scripts.

In the Funhouse case, ASEC also found batch code resembling earlier Kimsuky samples. The operators periodically updated this batch component, which provided an additional way to maintain access.

Quasar RAT Connects the Cases

The Quasar RAT sample uses a configuration file with a .dwg extension, storing its command-and-control address, target identifier, and mutex name.

A mutex is a named object programs can use to coordinate activity or avoid running duplicate copies. The latest configuration reports version 4.4.3, compared with version 1.1.8 in the earlier cases.

Although configuration filenames, server addresses, and target details changed, the Quasar mutex stayed the same across the February, June, and September cases.

These matches support ASEC’s assessment of continuity. They also show why investigators should compare settings and code behavior rather than treat each new server or filename as evidence of an unrelated campaign.

ASEC identified Funhouse as a variant of Endpoint ransomware. The June Endpoint and September Funhouse samples share the encryption extension, ransom-note filename, mutex, encryption method, key-generation approach, footer size, and footer marker.

The attacker’s contact address changed, but the underlying file-encryption traits remained consistent. Both samples use HC-128 encryption and a 72-byte footer. Their key-generation process combines CryptGenRandom, Curve25519, and SHA-512.

By contrast, the February Endpoint sample used ChaCha20 encryption and a different key-generation method. These differences trace changes within the ransomware family; SHA-512 here describes a cryptographic operation, not a published sample hash.

ASEC said the shift from recently favored LNK files to HWP documents likely aims to lower suspicion. A résumé is a familiar work item, particularly for staff handling job applications.

Earlier Kimsuky recruiter phishing campaigns similarly used fake résumés and business cards, showing how the group shapes lures around a recipient’s normal tasks.

Defenders should watch the full sequence, not just the attachment type: Hangul writing executable and manifest files, followed by unusual script activity and remote access tooling.

ASEC advises checking document links and sender credibility, avoiding suspicious links, updating Hangul and operating systems, and keeping endpoint protection current.

articles.title: Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses Malicious npm Packages to Target Crypto Founders
articles.description:
A fake Web3 accelerator called Apex has been using malicious npm packages to target cryptocurrency start-ups and founders with what appeared to be free AI credits, coding tools, smart-contract audits, investment access, and invitations to in-person events. Behind the polished Web3 pitch, the operation delivered malware for macOS and Windows, exposed AI-agent data to attacker-run […]

The post Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses Malicious npm Packages to Target Crypto Founders appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A fake Web3 accelerator called Apex has been using malicious npm packages to target cryptocurrency start-ups and founders with what appeared to be free AI credits, coding tools, smart-contract audits, investment access, and invitations to in-person events.

Behind the polished Web3 pitch, the operation delivered malware for macOS and Windows, exposed AI-agent data to attacker-run systems, and provided false security results that could mislead teams into trusting unsafe code.

The campaign used two npm packages, @apexacc/cli and @apexacc/audit, presented as an AI coding agent and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) security-audit tool. Users who ran the packages through npm or npx could trigger a multistage infection chain.

The operation is especially concerning because crypto founders often handle wallet keys, source code, cloud credentials, investor data, and smart-contract material on the same developer systems.

Analysts at Elastic Security Labs identified the malicious @apexacc/cli package after a supply-chain monitor flagged suspicious behavior.

Their investigation linked it to a broader operation posing as the Apex accelerator and later found @apexacc/audit, another malicious package from the same publisher. The packages were malicious when published rather than being legitimate projects that were later compromised.

Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses Malicious npm Packages

Apex presented its main service as “Apex Arena,” a private workspace for Web3 founders. The site claimed more than 200 portfolio projects and more than $124 million raised.

It promoted smart-contract reviews, founder messaging, a directory of vetted talent, investment scoring, free Claude and Gemini credits, and the Apex Copilot coding tool.

The group also used fake reviews and advertised a physical event connected to TOKEN2049 in Singapore, a tactic designed to make the operation look like a real startup programme.

This mix of AI services, crypto branding, public repositories, and live-event activity shows how modern social-engineering campaigns can move beyond a simple phishing page.

Similar risks were seen in a malicious npm campaign targeting Web3 developers, where poisoned packages sought wallet phrases, API tokens, SSH keys, and cloud credentials.

Apex Copilot largely copied the legitimate open-source Oh My Pi coding agent. Elastic found that 1,351 of 1,363 compared source files matched the original project.

The altered code added a bootstrap component that could receive commands from Apex-controlled infrastructure, change AI service routing, and add an attacker-controlled MCP server to the victim’s configuration.

Malware Delivery on Windows and macOS

The npm package launchers used apex.cjs and audit.cjs to download platform-specific files from GitHub releases. On Windows, the code contacted vrf.apexaccs[.]org and received server-selected commands. It then created PowerShell and VBScript staging files before launching wscript.exe, PowerShell, and later malware stages.

The Windows chain led to a custom information stealer through bludness.exe, install.exe or exegis.exe, and updater_loader.exe. The final payload collected system details, clipboard data, screenshots, browser information, Wi-Fi profile names, files, and data from wallet, VPN, remote-access, messaging, and AI-client applications.

It also targeted Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Yandex browser data, including saved credentials and cookies, before archiving collected material and sending it through Telegram.

On macOS, a Rust helper requested a command from the same verification service. The command fetched a script that delivered CloudSyncD, a backdoor which requested the user’s administrator password through a fake prompt and then collected host information before contacting its command-and-control server.

The CloudSyncD delivery method overlaps with the earlier fake Zoom installer CloudSyncD campaign, which also used a counterfeit installer and password prompt to run a privileged backdoor on macOS devices.

Apex Copilot changed OpenRouter-related environment settings so that model requests were sent to arena.apexaccs[.]org, rather than directly to the expected AI provider endpoint.

Elastic confirmed that prompts, conversation history, code snippets, local tool output, and available tool definitions could be sent to the Apex-controlled service.

The package also wrote an apex-copilot MCP entry into ~/.apex/agent/mcp.json, giving the remote server a lasting connection path across later sessions.

This is important because MCP tools may be allowed to read local files, call APIs, or run actions through AI clients. The danger follows a pattern documented in the first malicious MCP server discovery, in which a trojanized npm tool silently copied emails handled by an AI agent.

The second package, @apexacc/audit, claimed to offer 18 smart-contract security tools. Elastic found that every tool returned fabricated results rather than performing the stated checks. Some results were hard-coded, some inserted user-provided labels, and others used random or date-based values.

In one test, Apex’s remote scoring tool returned a score of 51/100 for a fictional project despite receiving no code repository, contract address, team data, or other evidence.

Teams should remove the two Apex packages from developer systems, review shell history and endpoint telemetry, and rotate secrets that may have been exposed.

This includes crypto wallet credentials, seed phrases, API keys, cloud tokens, GitHub credentials, browser sessions, SSH keys, and AI-service tokens.

Organisations should also examine AI-agent configuration files for unexpected MCP entries and review outbound connections to the listed domains.

Developers should verify npm publisher identity, repository ownership, release history, and package behavior before installing unfamiliar Web3 or AI tools.

npm lifecycle scripts can run during installation, while npm’s ignore-scripts setting prevents scripts declared in package.json from running; this can provide a safer review step, although explicitly invoked package commands can still execute.

Security teams should also alert on npm-launched PowerShell, VBScript, curl, or shell activity, especially when it creates files in temporary folders or downloads executable content.

articles.description:
Anthropic warns that small AI models may be months away from self-replicating across poorly secured smart TVs and other internet-connected devices. Its research suggests future AI worms could run on consumer hardware rather than depend on a data center, making them harder to shut down through a single central service. According to research published on October […]

The post Anthropic Warns AI Models Could Soon Self-Replicate on Smart TVs and IoT Devices Without a Data Center appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic warns that small AI models may be months away from self-replicating across poorly secured smart TVs and other internet-connected devices.

Its research suggests future AI worms could run on consumer hardware rather than depend on a data center, making them harder to shut down through a single central service.

According to research published on October 12 by William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, AI agents may be able to install and run models on unfamiliar machines.

Researchers stressed that they have not demonstrated a complete rogue replicator. Their findings show progress toward that threat, not an active AI malware outbreak.

Anthropic Warns AI Could Self-Replicate Across IoT Devices

Researchers ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes costing about $55 each. Every box had 4GB of RAM and stored part of the model. Together, the devices achieved 0.39 tokens per second, showing that cheap hardware can support a large model, although very slowly.

This approach uses distributed inference, where several machines share the work of running an AI model. Instead of fitting everything into one device, researchers split its layers across the boxes.

A future worm could carry model weights, the files containing its learned values, onto compromised devices and use their combined resources. The proposed replication chain involves finding targets, gaining access, setting up inference, and spreading from newly reached hosts.

Anthropic focused mainly on inference setup, which requires choosing suitable software, fixing package issues, and handling different operating systems. A nine-billion-parameter model successfully established inference on eight of nine hardware types tested.

In a separate experiment, researchers used eight Google Cloud machines running Android emulators inside an isolated network. Their Android Debug Bridge ports required no authentication.

GLM-5.2 reached all eight machines in four of five trials and seven machines in the remaining trial while establishing Llama3.1-8B inference. However, the agent’s own model ran on a separate inference server. Researchers spawned new agent copies after checking each successful setup.

This was therefore a simplified test of replication skills, not proof that GLM-5.2 could independently live and reproduce on TV boxes. The easy access path also limits real-world conclusions.

Anthropic estimates smaller models could reach the required skill level by late 2026 if past improvement rates continue. That forecast uses a general AI capability measure rather than a direct replication measure.

Hardware limits would still slow spread, with estimated Qwen3.5-9B inference setup taking roughly 28 to 51 hours.

Existing infections show why this matters. The Kimwolf botnet compromised more than two million devices, including many Android TV boxes.

Unlike fixed malware, future AI worms might adjust their setup methods for unfamiliar systems and pass useful troubleshooting notes to later copies. Defenders should watch for large model downloads, unusual traffic between devices, network scanning, and unexpected outbound connections.

The Kimwolf v7 report also recommends disabling exposed ADB access and separating TV boxes from business networks. Stronger device security and coordinated isolation of infected hosts could reduce opportunities for AI worms to spread.

articles.title: npm Trusted Publishing Flaw With 10 Million Downloads Exposes 1,500+ Packages to Malicious Takeover
articles.description:
A security flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing feature exposed more than 1,500 packages to possible takeover through reclaimed GitHub repository names. The affected packages accounted for more than 10 million total downloads and over one million downloads per month, creating a serious software supply-chain risk for developers, CI/CD systems, and organizations that rely on npm […]

The post npm Trusted Publishing Flaw With 10 Million Downloads Exposes 1,500+ Packages to Malicious Takeover appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A security flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing feature exposed more than 1,500 packages to possible takeover through reclaimed GitHub repository names.

The affected packages accounted for more than 10 million total downloads and over one million downloads per month, creating a serious software supply-chain risk for developers, CI/CD systems, and organizations that rely on npm dependencies.

The issue, named SlugFest, did not require an attacker to steal an npm token, break into a maintainer’s npm account, or access the original GitHub repository.

Instead, a threat actor could claim an abandoned GitHub owner/repository name and use it to receive a valid short-lived npm publishing credential for a package that still trusted that old location.

Analysts at Bloom Security identified the flaw and noted that it was a package takeover path, not an active malware campaign.

However, a successful takeover could allow malicious code, including a harmful postinstall script, to be published under a legitimate package name and delivered to users during normal dependency installation.

This risk is especially important after the recent ChainDrop npm worm showed how compromised releases can spread through developer tools, repositories, and automated build environments.

npm Trusted Publishing Flaw With 10 Million Downloads

Trusted Publishing is intended to make npm releases safer. Rather than storing a long-lived npm token in GitHub Actions or another CI/CD service, a maintainer can connect a package to a repository and workflow through OpenID Connect, or OIDC.

During a release, the workflow obtains a short-lived identity token and exchanges it for an npm publishing credential. This removes the need to place reusable publishing secrets in build pipelines. The problem was in the way npm initially linked a package to its publishing repository.

For an unvalidated configuration, npm stored the human-readable GitHub repository path, known as a slug, such as organization/project, instead of immediately storing GitHub’s permanent numeric repository ID and owner ID.

Repository names can change ownership after a project is renamed, transferred, deleted, or when its owner account changes names.

That means an attacker could create a new GitHub repository using the newly available slug, add a workflow with the expected filename, request an OIDC token, and present that token to npm.

If the configured package had never completed its first trusted publish, npm could accept the repository name as a match and issue a valid publishing credential. The attacker could then release a new version under the legitimate npm package name.

This differs from the token theft used in many earlier npm compromises. As explained in Cyber Security News coverage of GitHub’s npm security improvements, Trusted Publishing was designed to reduce exposure from long-lived automation tokens.

SlugFest showed that a secure short-lived credential can still be abused when the identity binding behind it relies on a reusable name rather than an immutable identifier.

Why AI Coding Agents Increase Exposure

Bloom’s research also focused on the growing role of AI coding agents in package installation. The company found that a typical endpoint installs around 70 packages a month through AI agents, while developer systems may install close to 350 packages per month.

These figures cover direct installations and do not include the additional dependencies pulled in by each package. Tools such as coding assistants and IDE-integrated agents can choose, install, and execute packages with little human review.

If a legitimate dependency is silently replaced with a malicious release, the agent may select the newest version and run its lifecycle scripts as part of a normal setup task. This makes package provenance, version pinning, and review of install-time scripts more important than ever.

The concern also connects with the AI coding agent security risks reported earlier this year, where manipulated content could influence an agent to run attacker-controlled commands.

In the SlugFest case, the dangerous step is not a prompt alone: it is the possibility that an agent installs a package that has been published through an apparently trusted release path.

Bloom reported the issue through GitHub’s HackerOne program on June 6, 2026. The issue was validated on June 9, and the researchers said a fix was implemented on October 2 after more than 120 days.

GitHub now makes newly created but unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations expire after 48 hours. A configuration becomes validated only after its first successful publish, which then binds it to the repository’s immutable identity.

GitHub also blocks Trusted Publishing tokens triggered by issue_comment events, in addition to its existing restriction on pull_request_target events.

Maintainers using affected workflows should move publishing to safer events, such as push, release, or workflow_dispatch. The current npm Trusted Publishing documentation confirms that a new configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days or it will expire.

Package maintainers should review every Trusted Publisher configuration, verify that each linked GitHub repository is still under their control, and remove and recreate bindings after a repository rename, deletion, or transfer.

Teams should also monitor unexpected release activity, pin dependency versions where practical, and review provenance attestations carefully.

As the ChainDrop trusted publishing incident demonstrated, valid provenance can show where a package was built, but it does not prove that the source repository, account, or build environment was safe.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Citrix NetScaler 0-Days to Deploy Platypus Remote Access Tool
articles.description:
Threat actors are exploiting two critical Citrix NetScaler zero-day vulnerabilities to deploy a modified Platypus remote access tool on exposed ADC and Gateway appliances. The activity shows how quickly attackers are moving from initial access to persistent control of edge devices that often sit between corporate networks and the public internet. The campaign targets CVE-2026-88771 […]

The post Hackers Exploit Citrix NetScaler 0-Days to Deploy Platypus Remote Access Tool appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Threat actors are exploiting two critical Citrix NetScaler zero-day vulnerabilities to deploy a modified Platypus remote access tool on exposed ADC and Gateway appliances.

The activity shows how quickly attackers are moving from initial access to persistent control of edge devices that often sit between corporate networks and the public internet.

The campaign targets CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, two actively exploited flaws in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway. Both bugs carry a CVSS score of 9.5 and can allow remote code execution without requiring a valid user account.

Citrix released emergency fixes for affected products, while CISA also added the two issues to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Researchers at Binary Defense investigated incidents involving two NetScaler devices that showed signs of exploitation during a customer’s upgrade process.

One device showed attempted exploitation, while the other contained evidence that attackers had delivered and likely executed a custom-built remote management implant called Platypus.

Platypus is an open-source remote administration framework written in Go. The attackers reportedly modified and compiled the tool for FreeBSD, the operating system used by NetScaler appliances. They then disguised the malware as a Perl-related file to blend in with normal appliance files.

The observed installer used a curl command piped into the shell to retrieve and launch the tool. The payload was stored under paths that could look familiar to NetScaler administrators, including /var/tmp/, /netscaler.local/, and /var/core/. One sample used the filename .ns_09343.pl, although it was an ELF binary rather than a legitimate Perl script.

Hackers Exploit Citrix NetScaler 0-Days

The deployment method matters because it provides attackers with a foothold that may remain even after an organization patches the original vulnerable appliance.

A patch stops further use of the flaw. However, it does not automatically remove web shells, backdoors, stolen credentials, altered configuration files, or remote access implants already placed on the device.

Recent reporting has also documented attackers using the command-injection flaw to install web shells and collect NetScaler configuration data.

CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation flaw that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run commands on vulnerable NetScaler appliances.

Binary Defense researchers found that attackers could place shell commands inside crafted authentication-related input, including usernames. The malicious input is written into NetScaler logs, where a vulnerable error-handling process can later execute the injected command.

The second bug, CVE-2026-88772, is a DTLS memory overflow issue. It affects NetScaler VPN virtual servers where DTLS is enabled, which is the default configuration in many deployments.

A successful exploit can allow code execution or cause a denial-of-service condition by crashing the affected service. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said attackers were actively exploiting the two flaws in NetScaler ADC and Gateway systems.

The command-injection weakness is particularly concerning because execution may not happen immediately. A delayed maintenance process can run the injected command later, making it harder for defenders to match a suspicious login request with follow-on activity.

The recovered Platypus samples were not standard builds of the public project. The custom version reportedly included added modules for privilege escalation, persistence, cleanup, and timestamp manipulation.

It could execute commands through a remote terminal, read and write files, update itself, use plugins, and communicate with a command-and-control server through mutual TLS.

The malware also contained a local peer-discovery feature using the _platypus-mesh_tcp mDNS service. That feature could help an operator identify or link compromised systems on the same network.

Researchers linked the campaign to the domain entretiensol[.]com, which acted as a staging and control server. Other domains reportedly shared infrastructure or certificate traits with the operation, including white-guard[.]pro, gurerasfalt[.]com, garyvard[.]com, and hickoryusedauto[.]com.

Organizations should urgently upgrade vulnerable NetScaler ADC and Gateway systems to fixed releases. Citrix identified version 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 as patched builds for the two original zero-days, including corresponding FIPS and NDcPP releases.

Security teams should also treat patching as only the first step. They should review ns.log, sh.log, bash.log, httpaccess.log, and httperror.log for suspicious authentication strings, unexpected shell commands, curl | sh activity, files with .pl extensions that are actually binaries, and outbound traffic from NetScaler appliances to unknown internet hosts.

Any appliance exposed before patching should be considered potentially compromised until administrators complete forensic checks, rotate reachable credentials, revoke active sessions, and inspect both nodes in high-availability deployments.

articles.description:
Mobile security is two budgets wearing one name: testing finds the flaws before release, shielding hardens the binary against the hostile devices it ships to. cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Mobile security is two budgets wearing one name: testing finds the flaws before release, shielding hardens the binary against the hostile devices it ships to.

When evaluating Mobile Application Security Testing (MAST) tools alongside commercial mobile application penetration testing, engineering teams quickly discover that inspecting source code covers only half the threat landscape.

We scored ten tools across both lanes plus the free floor every team should know. NowSecure takes 1 on MASVS-mapped pipeline testing; Guardsquare and Zimperium complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: NowSecure automated MAST mapped to the OWASP MASVS standard.

• Podium: NowSecure (testing), Guardsquare (shielding + free AppSweep floor), Zimperium (runtime + threat context).

• Free floor: OWASP MobSF the open-source analyzer in every researcher’s toolkit.

• Two budgets: consumer/financial apps need testing and shielding — MASVS-R exists for a reason.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: MASVS coverage, pipeline integration, shielding depth, runtime defense, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: lane depth 30%, standards alignment 25%, pipeline/DX 20%, pricing clarity 15%, ecosystem 10%.

The 2026 Mobile AppSec Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. NowSecure — Best Automated MAST

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | MASVS/MASA-mapped | CI-native

Why it earns 1: Automated testing on real physical devices rather than emulators, mapped directly to OWASP MASVS standards and continuous testing specifications that security teams can audit against.

It plugs into developer CI/CD pipelines to deliver deep static, dynamic, interactive, and API assessments at merge speed.

Standout features: Automated MAST; MASVS mapping; CI integration; store-compliance checks.

Pros: Dedicated depth; standards fluency.

Cons: Testing lane only.

Bottom line: MASVS verdicts at merge speed.

2. Guardsquare — Best Shielding + Free Floor

Snapshot: Tiered/quote + free AppSweep | DexGuard/iXGuard | ProGuard heritage

Why it earns 2: The industry benchmark for code obfuscation and binary shielding (DexGuard for Android, iXGuard for iOS), building on its foundational ProGuard lineage.

Guardsquare provides anti-tamper and dynamic instrumentation defenses against tools like Frida and Ghidra, while offering AppSweep as an accessible, zero-cost mobile vulnerability scanner.

Standout features: Obfuscation; anti-tamper; environment checks; AppSweep free scanning.

Pros: Shielding depth; free entry.

Cons: Protection lane, not full testing.

Bottom line: The binary attackers can’t read, from the vendor with a free floor.

3. Zimperium — Best Runtime + MTD Pairing

Snapshot: Quote | zShield + zDefend | Threat-intel context

Why it earns 3: In-app runtime application self-protection (zDefend) combined with binary hardening (zShield), powered by global threat telemetry from its mobile threat defense (MTD) platform.

As Zimperium security researchers identified privilege escalation via OEM permissions, its on-device engine alerts applications when they execute in compromised or hostile environments.

Standout features: App shielding; in-app RASP (zDefend); MTD signals; key protection.

Pros: Runtime + intel pairing.

Cons: Quote-based.

Bottom line: Defense with a threat feed behind it.

4. Data Theorem — Best Mobile + API Continuous

Snapshot: Quote | App + backend attack path

Why it earns 4: Mobile risk exists equally in the backend services supporting the client. Data Theorem continuously scans the mobile frontend while mapping every API endpoint it queries, providing full-stack visibility alongside API security and backend inventory monitoring to catch data leakage and shadow endpoints.

Standout features: Mobile Secure; API Secure unity; SDK analysis; monitoring.

Pros: Full-path breadth.

Cons: Platform quote.

Bottom line: Tests the app and everything it talks to.

5. Appdome — Best No-Code Defense Fusion

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Build-time protection catalog

Why it earns 5: Automates mobile app shielding, anti-fraud controls, and MTD capabilities into binaries at build time without manual SDK integration.

It provides automated defenses against on-device virtualization and banking trojan techniques, converting security policies into an automated CI/CD build step.

Standout features: No-code fusion; protection catalog; build integration.

Pros: Speed; breadth.

Cons: Config-model fit.

Bottom line: Defense as a build step.

6. Promon — Best Banking-Grade Shielding

Snapshot: Quote | SHIELD runtime protection

Why it earns 6: The financial sector’s dedicated in-app bodyguard: Promon SHIELD protects banking and payment apps on rooted or compromised hardware.

It neutralizes sophisticated threats like banking malware that reconstructs screen-lock PINs and injects overlays, preventing memory dumping and unauthorized screen capture.

Standout features: Runtime shielding; anti-hooking; secure keyboard; SDK delivery.

Pros: Banking pedigree.

Cons: Shielding lane; quotes.

Bottom line: The app that fights back.

7. Veracode — Best Policy-Governed Platform

Snapshot: Quote | Mobile under the attestation plane

Why it earns 7: Mobile application security testing delivered as a governed component within a broader enterprise compliance framework.

Operating alongside enterprise policy attestation and static code analysis, Veracode evaluates iOS and Android binaries to help regulated organizations maintain audit compliance across their mobile portfolio.

Standout features: Platform MAST; policy; unified reporting.

Pros: Governance unity.

Cons: Mobile-depth contests.

Bottom line: Mobile in the compliance story.

8. Checkmarx — Best One-Queue Mobile SAST

Snapshot: Quote | Mobile code in the platform queue

Why it earns 8: Static analysis for mobile source code (Kotlin, Swift, Objective-C, Java) managed alongside the rest of your enterprise application risk in Checkmarx One.

It connects mobile repos with developer-first static code analysis to correlate proprietary code flaws with dependency risks in a unified triage queue.

Standout features: Mobile SAST; platform unity.

Pros: Queue coherence.

Cons: Binary/runtime lanes elsewhere.

Bottom line: Mobile code, same court.

9. Black Duck — Best Platform Mobile Lane

Snapshot: Quote | Coverity-family + SCA on mobile

Why it earns 9: Deep static code analysis and open-source dependency auditing for mobile applications delivered through the Coverity and Black Duck platform.

It pairs mobile engine checks with Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and open-source license compliance, identifying vulnerable third-party SDKs and open-source libraries embedded in mobile packages.

Standout features: SAST/SCA on mobile; platform reporting.

Pros: Estate continuity.

Cons: Dedicated-mobile depth.

Bottom line: The suite’s mobile chapter.

10. OWASP (MobSF) — Best Free Analyzer

Snapshot: Free (OSS project) | Static + dynamic analysis | Researcher standard

Why it earns 10 (as the floor): Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) is an open-source project that delivers static and dynamic analysis for APK, IPA, and APEX packages.

While organizations must maintain diligence regarding security advisories, such as the Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) static and dynamic analyzer vulnerabilities, MobSF remains the default zero-budget baseline across the security research community.

Standout features: APK/IPA static analysis; dynamic instrumentation; API; CI usage.

Pros: Free; capable; ubiquitous.

Cons: You operate and interpret; no vendor support.

Bottom line: The zero-budget floor that finds real bugs.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Two Budgets, One Standard

Run a MASVS-L2 gap assessment on your flagship app the missing lanes will name themselves.

Testing (NowSecure/Data Theorem/MobSF floor) removes flaws; shielding (Guardsquare/Promon/Appdome/Zimperium) raises attacker cost on devices you don’t control consumer and financial apps need both budgets. Start free (MobSF + AppSweep), test every build, shield what faces hostility, and never mistake store review for security review.

FAQs

What is the best mobile app security testing tool in 2026? NowSecure ranks 1 for automated MASVS-mapped testing, Guardsquare for shielding with a free scanning floor, Zimperium for runtime defense with threat context and OWASP’s MobSF anchors the free lane every program should exploit.

Testing or shielding which comes first? Testing catches flaws cheaply pre-release; shielding defends the shipped binary on hostile devices. Sequence testing-first, but consumer/financial apps ultimately fund both MASVS-R codifies the resilience lane.

Is OWASP MobSF adequate for commercial enterprise security? MobSF provides an effective open-source floor for static analysis and basic dynamic inspection.

However, enterprise commercial suites add real physical hardware device farms, automated OWASP MASVS compliance tracking, remediation workflows, and vendor SLAs.

Organizations self-hosting MobSF must also monitor vulnerabilities affecting centralized MobSF servers to protect internal pipelines.

Is MobSF good enough on its own? As a floor, genuinely useful real findings, free, CI-capable. What paid lanes add: real-device depth, MASVS program mapping, support, and the shielding MobSF never claimed to do.

What is MASVS? OWASP’s Mobile Application Security Verification Standard the requirement levels (L1/L2/R) programs audit against. Tools that map findings to it (NowSecure-class) make compliance conversations short.

Do the big AppSec platforms cover mobile adequately? Code and dependencies credibly; binary behavior, resilience, and store-runtime realities still favor dedicated mobile lanes which is why the category persists.

Verdict

NowSecure wins testing, Guardsquare wins the binary, Zimperium arms it with intelligence and MobSF proves the floor is free. Assess against MASVS, fund both budgets where users are strangers, and ship apps that assume the device is the adversary.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Federal buyers, the FDA, and the EU’s CRA era all want your software’s ingredients list and next year’s CVE will interrogate the SBOMs you generate today.

Evaluating these platforms alongside the Top 10 Best Software Supply Chain Security Tools shows that simply creating a static inventory is insufficient; organizations must manage, correlate, and monitor those inventories across the entire development lifecycle.

We scored ten options across generation, management, and monitoring, with a status flag where the roster demanded honesty.

Anchore’s Syft takes 1 as the free generation standard; FOSSA and Cybeats complete the podium.

• Regulated depth: Finite State extracts SBOMs from firmware binaries the device-mandate lane.

• Status honesty: Rezilion’s wind-down makes it a cautionary flag, not a pick.

Research-based: format fidelity (CycloneDX/SPDX), transitive depth, VEX support, monitoring capability, regulatory fit, pricing transparency, status currency.

5. Manifest — Best Supplier-SBOM Ingestion

Snapshot: Tiered | Ingest/normalize/monitor | Federal traction

Why it earns 5: The third-party consumption problem solved: collecting, normalizing, and continuously monitoring the disparate SBOMs your enterprise suppliers deliver.

It acts as an operational bridge for supply chain intelligence and third-party risk analysis, turning supplier PDFs and disconnected JSON files into searchable inventories.

Standout features: Ingestion at scale; normalization; monitoring; sharing.

Pros: Consumption depth.

Cons: Young vendor.

Bottom line: Makes supplier SBOMs mean something.

6. Snyk — Best Dev-Flow Generation

Snapshot: Free + per-dev | Export from existing scans

Why it earns 6: SBOM generation delivered as a natural byproduct of security scanning already active across developer repositories.

Leveraging Snyk’s dependency graph, engineering teams can export CycloneDX and SPDX documents while benefiting from AI-assisted automated remediation and fix pull requests to resolve discovered vulnerabilities before shipping.

Standout features: SBOM export; platform unity; API.

Pros: Zero-new-tool path.

Cons: Management elsewhere.

Bottom line: The export hiding in your current subscription.

7. Sonatype — Best Policy-Tied Platform

Snapshot: Tiered | Lifecycle + Firewall enforcement

Why it earns 7: Ingredients lists directly tied to ingestion policy: generating the SBOM that actively blocks risky components at the door.

Backed by Sonatype Nexus Repository security advisories and Nexus Lifecycle, it prevents malicious or non-compliant dependencies from entering builds.

Standout features: SBOM generation; policy tie; research data.

Pros: Enforcement link.

Cons: Nexus gravity.

Bottom line: The inventory with a bouncer attached.

8. JFrog — Best Registry-Native

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Build-info lineage | Xray-correlated

Why it earns 8: SBOMs generated where binary artifacts live: using Artifactory build-info as the immutable single source of truth.

As organizations track active JFrog Artifactory enterprise security updates, JFrog Xray correlates vulnerabilities and cryptographically signed release bundles directly from the registry.

Standout features: Build-info SBOMs; Xray tie; distribution.

Pros: Source-of-truth fit.

Cons: Platform gravity.

Bottom line: The registry writing its own receipts.

9. Mend — Best Automation-Linked

Snapshot: Tiered | Renovate-connected bills

Why it earns 9: The software inventory that automatically schedules its own updates: connecting SBOM component tracking directly to automated remediation workflows.

Mend couples inventory export with automating dependency updates across CI/CD pipelines, turning outdated components into tracked pull requests.

Standout features: SBOM export; automation tie; compliance.

Pros: Fix-path link.

Cons: Lifecycle depth elsewhere.

Bottom line: From ingredients list to update queue.

10. sbomify — Best SBOM Lifecycle & Sharing Platform

Snapshot: Free + paid tiers | SBOM lifecycle management | VEX + sharing workflows

Why it earns 10: sbomify turns SBOMs into living security artifacts by combining generation, management, vulnerability tracking, VEX, and controlled sharing in one workflow.

Standout features: CycloneDX/SPDX support; VEX; vulnerability monitoring; SBOM sharing; CI/CD integrations.

Pros: Strong lifecycle coverage; free entry; good compliance and sharing workflows.

Cons: Smaller ecosystem and market footprint than larger enterprise platforms.

Bottom line: From SBOM generation to continuous sharing and compliance in one platform.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Generate Free, Then Buy Your Obligation

Syft in CI this week costs nothing and future-proofs every build. Then buy the lane your obligations name: legal workflows (FOSSA), portfolio monitoring (Cybeats), supplier ingestion (Manifest), firmware mandates (Finite State) or export from platforms you already run (Snyk/Sonatype/JFrog).

Attach VEX so ingested bills don’t scream on every CVE, and retire wound-down vendors from shortlists before procurement does.

FAQs

What is the best SBOM tool in 2026? Anchore’s Syft ranks 1 for free generation, FOSSA for license-integrated management, Cybeats for lifecycle monitoring with Finite State owning firmware mandates and Manifest the supplier-ingestion lane.

What regulations demand SBOMs? US federal procurement (EO 14028 lineage), FDA premarket device cybersecurity, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act era plus enterprise contracts citing all three. Generation is table stakes; monitoring makes it real.

CycloneDX or SPDX? Support both serious tools do. CycloneDX (OWASP) leads security use cases and VEX; SPDX (Linux Foundation) leads license heritage. The format war matters less than emitting consistently.

What is VEX and why does it matter? Exploitability statements accompanying SBOMs declaring which component CVEs actually affect the product. Without VEX, every ingested bill looks on fire; with it, triage breathes.

What happened to Rezilion? The runtime-SBOM pioneer wound down a reminder that this young market’s vendors need stability checks alongside feature comparisons.

How do SBOM tools integrate with artifact storage? Modern solutions integrate directly with container registry security tools and artifact managers, storing SBOMs alongside container digests and binary packages as tamper-evident metadata.

Verdict

Syft floors generation free, FOSSA and Cybeats make bills live, and the mandate lanes (Finite State, Manifest) serve the regulators arriving fastest emit today, monitor tomorrow, attach VEX always, and check every vendor’s pulse in a market young enough to bury pioneers.

Maintaining cryptographically verifiable software bills of materials provides the foundational transparency required to uphold an authentic Zero Trust security architecture. Emit inventories from every build, monitor them over time, accompany them with VEX statements, and choose vendors with proven operational stability.

articles.title: Top 10 Best CI/CD Pipeline Security Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
Supply-chain attackers stopped bothering with your code they poison the pipelines that build it. Modern build pipelines execute untrusted third-party code with elevated infrastructure privileges, making CI/CD pipeline security best practices the frontline of defense against software factory tampering. We scored ten options with native-first honesty: what your CI platform already includes resets every business […]

The post Top 10 Best CI/CD Pipeline Security Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Supply-chain attackers stopped bothering with your code they poison the pipelines that build it.

Modern build pipelines execute untrusted third-party code with elevated infrastructure privileges, making CI/CD pipeline security best practices the frontline of defense against software factory tampering.

We scored ten options with native-first honesty: what your CI platform already includes resets every business case, and the dedicated lanes earn their bills on what natives miss.

GitHub Advanced Security takes 1; Cycode and Legit Security complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: GitHub Advanced Security push protection, CodeQL, and Actions policy where most pipelines live.

• Podium: GitHub (native floor), Cycode (VCS-to-pipeline graph), Legit (factory integrity).

• Niche that matters: StepSecurity hardens the runner layer attackers actually exfiltrate through.

• Absorbed lanes: Argon sells inside Aqua, Cider inside Palo Alto evaluate under current flags.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: pipeline discovery, integrity/tamper detection, runner hardening, native coverage, pricing transparency, acquisition clarity. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: attack-surface relevance 30%, discovery/integrity 25%, native-value honesty 20%, pricing clarity 15%, ecosystem 10%.

The 2026 CI/CD Security Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. GitHub Advanced Security — Best Native Floor

Snapshot: Published per-committer | Push protection + CodeQL + Actions policy

Why it earns 1: The factory securing itself: secrets blocked before they land, semantic code scanning, dependency review, OIDC-to-cloud federation, and Actions policies where most of the world’s pipelines already run.

While organizations must manage risks highlighted by GitHub Actions supply chain vulnerabilities and runner token exposures, GHAS establishes the baseline every dedicated tool must justify displacing.

Standout features: Push protection; CodeQL; Actions policies; artifact attestation; dependency review.

Pros: Native; per-committer pricing.

Cons: GitHub-scoped; runner hardening thin (see 4).

Bottom line: Activate before any dedicated RFP.

2. Cycode — Best VCS-to-Pipeline Graph

Snapshot: Quote | Native engines + risk graph | Source-control roots

Why it earns 2: Code, secrets, and pipeline posture connected in one graph the dedicated platform whose roots (VCS and pipeline security) match where attacks moved.

Backed by threat intelligence like Cycode research uncovering authentication and SDK vulnerabilities, it correlates developer identities with workflow permissions.

Standout features: Pipeline posture; secrets; hardening; risk graph.

Pros: Breadth + graph.

Cons: Quote-based.

Bottom line: The factory and its code, one lens.

3. Legit Security — Best Factory Integrity

Snapshot: Quote | Discovery + tamper detection

Why it earns 3: You can’t defend pipelines you can’t name Legit inventories the build estate, watches for tampering, and scores SDLC posture. The SolarWinds lesson, productized.

It defends against incidents like supply-chain attacks targeting build environments and forged pipeline provenance by monitoring the systems that compile application code.

Standout features: Pipeline discovery; integrity monitoring; misconfig governance.

Pros: Integrity depth.

Cons: Pair for code-side scope.

Bottom line: Knows every workflow that can reach production.

4. StepSecurity — Best Runner Hardening

Snapshot: Free + published tiers | Harden-Runner egress control

Why it earns 4: The attack that actually happens malicious dependencies exfiltrating from CI dies at egress control. Action pinning and runner policies close the layer natives leave open, free tier included.

StepSecurity provides actionable defense against campaigns like the GhostAction supply chain campaign that abuses GitHub Actions to steal CI/CD credentials, blocking outbound exfiltration at the operating system layer.

Standout features: Harden-Runner; egress filtering; action pinning; policies.

Pros: Attack-relevant niche; free floor.

Cons: Actions-scoped.

Bottom line: The runner that can’t phone home to attackers.

5. GitLab — Best Single-Platform DevSecOps

Snapshot: Published tiers | Ultimate security suite

Why it earns 5: Scanning, compliance pipelines, and protected environments as platform features one product decision covering the SDLC for GitLab estates.

Despite requiring operational diligence around critical GitLab CI/CD vulnerabilities and API security updates, GitLab Ultimate delivers exceptional end-to-end coherence.

Standout features: Built-in scanners; compliance frameworks; protected envs.

Pros: Coherence; published pricing.

Cons: Depth vs specialists.

Bottom line: The all-in-one answer for its own estate.

6. Arnica — Best Behavioral Defense

Snapshot: Published tiers | Anomalous-dev detection | ChatOps fixes

Why it earns 6: Pipelines fail through people and permissions Arnica watches for anomalous pushes and excess rights, fixing via chat at published rates.

It pairs behavioral tracking with developer-first static code analysis and posture checks to automate real-time remediation directly within Slack and Microsoft Teams.

Standout features: Behavioral detection; permission rightsizing; secrets; ChatOps.

Pros: Behavior lens; pricing clarity.

Cons: Younger ecosystem.

Bottom line: Notices the commit that isn’t like the others.

7. OX Security — Best PBOM Traceability

Snapshot: Tiered | Commit-to-workload lineage | Enforcement options

Why it earns 7: Provides every build artifact with an immutable biography: tracking which commit produced it, which pipeline compiled it, and which production cluster runs it.

Backed by security research including OX Security vulnerability research uncovering command execution flaws, its Pipeline Bill of Materials (PBOM) gives security teams automated enforcement policies that block unverified builds.

Standout features: PBOM; code-to-cloud mapping; native scans; enforcement.

Pros: Lineage clarity.

Cons: Scale checks.

Bottom line: Provenance with teeth.

8. Apiiro — Best Risk-Graph Context

Snapshot: Quote | Material-change detection

Why it earns 8: Highlights which specific pipeline or code change actually altered your organization’s risk profile.

Utilizing AI-driven application risk-graph visualization and deep architecture mapping, Apiiro monitors code changes from initial pull request through build and deployment, identifying risky material changes to authorization boundaries.

Standout features: Risk graph; change detection; SDLC posture.

Pros: Context depth.

Cons: Maturity assumed.

Bottom line: Knows which change mattered.

9. Aqua (Argon) — Best CNAPP-Absorbed Lane

Snapshot: Tiered | Argon inside since 2021

Why it earns 9: Pipeline security delivered within a broader cloud-native application protection platform.

Integrating Argon Security’s technology, it protects software supply chain pipelines even as threat actors launch supply chain attacks targeting open-source scanners and tools, connecting build integrity checks directly to container admission controllers.

Standout features: Pipeline scanning; posture; CNAPP unity.

Pros: Platform path.

Cons: Standalone momentum.

Bottom line: Factory security in the container estate.

10. Palo Alto (Cider) — Best Prisma-Absorbed Lane

Snapshot: Quote | Cider inside since 2023

Why it earns 10: Pipeline security and posture management integrated directly into Prisma Cloud’s code-to-cloud security architecture.

Incorporating Cider Security’s pipeline research, it protects environments where threat actors leverage CI/CD environments to compromise cloud resources, tying misconfigured GitHub Actions directly to production IAM roles.

Standout features: Pipeline inventory; posture; CNAPP context.

Pros: Cloud-context tie.

Cons: Packaging shifts.

Bottom line: Pipeline risk in the platform ledger.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Activate, Harden, Discover

Native controls first GHAS or GitLab Ultimate reset every case. Harden the execution layer next (StepSecurity-class pinning and egress this week, it’s cheap).

Then buy discovery and integrity (Cycode/Legit) when workflows outnumber memory, behavior watching (Arnica) where dev-account risk matters, and evaluate absorbed lanes (Argon/Cider) through their parent platforms. Attestation is a build output now treat it that way.

FAQs

What is the best CI/CD security tool in 2026? GitHub Advanced Security ranks 1 as the native floor most estates should activate, Cycode and Legit lead dedicated posture and integrity, StepSecurity owns runner hardening with GitLab’s platform lane and the absorbed options (Argon/Aqua, Cider/Palo Alto) serving their estates.

What attacks does pipeline security stop? Poisoned pipelines, malicious dependencies executing in CI, runner exfiltration, tampered builds, and stolen deploy credentials the tradecraft behind the decade’s worst supply-chain incidents.

Where do we start this week? Push protection on, actions pinned, runner egress filtered free-to-cheap moves that close the paths attackers actually use. Discovery follows when you can’t name every workflow with production reach.

How does CI/CD pipeline security connect to Application Security Posture Management (ASPM)? Pipeline security governs the integrity of the build factory, while Application Security Posture Management (ASPM) platforms aggregate, deduplicate, and prioritize the vulnerabilities discovered across all scanners running within those pipelines.

What happened to Argon and Cider? Acquired into Aqua (2021) and Palo Alto (2023) respectively both sell inside platforms now; evaluate current packaging.

Native controls or dedicated platforms? Natives first, always then dedicated lanes for what they miss: cross-platform discovery, integrity monitoring, behavioral detection, and runner-layer hardening.

Verdict

GitHub proves the factory can guard itself, Cycode and Legit map what sprawls beyond it, and StepSecurity locks the door attackers actually use activate, harden, discover, in that order, and let attestations flow from every build. The pipeline is the crown jewel now; fund it like one.

articles.title: Top 10 Best RASP Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
RASP’s idea block attacks from inside the running app won so convincingly that observability and edge platforms absorbed it, leaving a thinner standalone market that stale lists misrepresent. Rather than relying solely on pre-deployment scans from static application security testing (SAST) tools, modern engineering organizations deploy real-time runtime protection directly inside running workloads to intercept […]

The post Top 10 Best RASP Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
RASP’s idea block attacks from inside the running app won so convincingly that observability and edge platforms absorbed it, leaving a thinner standalone market that stale lists misrepresent.

Rather than relying solely on pre-deployment scans from static application security testing (SAST) tools, modern engineering organizations deploy real-time runtime protection directly inside running workloads to intercept memory corruption, command injections, and zero-day execution paths.

Our roster resolves to nine real entries (Hdiv sells inside Datadog since 2022; K2 Cyber carries a defunct-status flag). Contrast Security takes 1; Datadog and Waratek complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Contrast Protect the dedicated standard-bearer, testing-to-production on one agent.

• Podium: Contrast (dedicated), Datadog (Hdiv’s engine at APM reach), Waratek (JVM virtual patching).

• Check your toggles: Dynatrace and Datadog estates may already own runtime blocking unactivated.

• Different job alert: Jscrambler protects the browser side client-side shielding, budgeted separately.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: protection depth, overhead reputation, deployment model, consolidation accuracy, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: in-process depth 30%, deployment burden 25%, platform economics 20%, status honesty 15%, ecosystem 10%.

The 2026 RASP Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores. n/r = not rated pending status.

1. Contrast Security — Best Dedicated RASP

Snapshot: Per-app/quote | Protect + Assess continuity | Broad language agents

Why it earns 1: The company that bet on instrumentation executes production protection deepest exploit blocking with code-level context, from the same agents that verified in testing.

It provides native Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) continuity while reinforcing secure coding practices and remediation workflows across development teams.

Standout features: In-app blocking; attack visibility; IAST continuity; language breadth.

Pros: Depth; one-agent story.

Cons: Agent lifecycle; per-app economics.

Bottom line: The pure dedicated play, still standing tallest.

2. Datadog (incl. Hdiv) — Best APM-Delivered

Snapshot: Published usage | Hdiv engine inside | Zero new agents

Why it earns 2: Runtime protection delivered as a toggle on tracing agents already running across your fleet.

Powered by Hdiv’s acquired technology, Datadog leverages its presence among top Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tools to deliver in-app protection with transparent usage-based billing.

Standout features: Exploit blocking; trace-context evidence; APM unity.

Pros: Deployment-free; pricing clarity.

Cons: Dedicated-depth contests.

Bottom line: RASP at the reach of the agent you already run.

3. Waratek — Best JVM Virtual Patching

Snapshot: Quote | Patch without redeploying | Legacy Java’s shield

Why it earns 3: JVM-level rules neutralize vulnerable application behavior without requiring source code modifications serving as the definitive virtual patching solution for Log4j-class emergency vulnerabilities inside legacy enterprise Java stacks that cannot ship rapid updates.

Standout features: Virtual patching; JVM instrumentation; legacy support.

Pros: Patch-without-deploy.

Cons: JVM scope.

Bottom line: The emergency fix that skips the release train.

4. Dynatrace — Best OneAgent Defense

Snapshot: Published usage | Detect-and-block on OneAgent

Why it earns 4: Application Security rides instrumentation Dynatrace estates already deploy exposure-ranked, Davis-prioritized, and activated with a switch.

It injects runtime application self-protection (RASP) rules directly into execution flows to halt injection attempts without external appliances.

Standout features: OneAgent delivery; runtime blocking; exposure ranking.

Pros: Zero-new-agent; usage pricing.

Cons: Platform gravity.

Bottom line: Check this toggle before any RASP RFP.

5. Fastly (Signal Sciences) — Best Edge-Adjacent

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | NGWAF at runtime’s job

Why it earns 5: The Next-Gen WAF that absorbed much of the market demand originally aimed at RASP.

Recognized across enterprise Web Application Firewall (WAF) solutions, Signal Sciences delivers app-aware blocking as a web server module, container sidecar, or edge proxy without invasive in-process code instrumentation.

Standout features: NGWAF; flexible deployment; app-aware rules.

Pros: Pragmatism; developer goodwill.

Cons: Not in-process context.

Bottom line: Why many teams never bought classic RASP.

6. Imperva — Best WAAP-Estate Pairing

Snapshot: Quote | Thales family | Defense-in-depth

Why it earns 6: In-app execution depth positioned behind the perimeter gateway you have tuned for years.

Imperva delivers RASP protection as an integrated defense layer within its modern WAAP portfolio, shielding backend services from attacks that slip past edge heuristics.

Standout features: RASP module; WAAP unity; virtual patching support.

Pros: Estate synergy.

Cons: Standalone momentum.

Bottom line: The layered pick for Imperva estates.

7. Jscrambler — Best Client-Side Lane

Snapshot: Tiered | Browser-side shielding | PCI 6.4.3 tailwind

Why it earns 7 (as its own job): A fundamentally different battlefield: JavaScript code obfuscation, anti-tampering, and skimming defense against Magecart attacks executing within untrusted end-user browsers.

It brings RASP’s defensive principles directly to modern e-commerce checkout environments.

Standout features: JS protection; anti-tamper; skimming detection; PCI-aligned monitoring.

Pros: Owns its lane; regulatory push.

Cons: Not server-side RASP budget separately.

Bottom line: The checkout page’s bodyguard.

8. OpenText (Fortify) — Best Suite-Governed

Snapshot: Quote | SSC integration | On-prem capable

Why it earns 8: Runtime protection managed under sovereign-friendly governance for Fortify-standardized estates.

Fortify delivers in-process shielding alongside runtime vulnerability testing across live web applications and dynamic application security testing (DAST) platforms to satisfy air-gapped compliance mandates.

Standout features: Runtime agents; SSC unity; policy.

Pros: Governance continuity.

Cons: Category momentum.

Bottom line: In-app defense inside the compliance plane.

9. Oligo Security — Best ADR / Runtime Exploit Defense

Snapshot: Commercial | Runtime visibility | Exploit detection and blocking

Why it earns 9: Oligo brings modern application detection and response (ADR) and runtime threat detection to production environments, using runtime behavior and deep application context to identify exploitable risks and active attacks backed by threat intelligence from Oligo Security researchers uncovering critical runtime RCE vulnerabilities.

Standout features: Runtime exploit detection; behavioral context; exploitability prioritization; runtime blocking; application visibility.

Pros: Modern runtime-security approach; strong production context.

Cons: More ADR-focused than traditional in-process RASP.

Bottom line: Modern runtime defense built around what applications actually execute.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Toggles First, Depth Where It Counts

Audit your APM’s security switches before any RFP Datadog/Dynatrace estates often own the capability unactivated.

Buy dedicated (Contrast) where in-process context is the requirement, Waratek where Java can’t redeploy, Jscrambler where the browser is the battlefield and prune dead names (K2) plus absorbed ones (Hdiv) from shortlists before procurement embarrasses itself.

Deployment realism decides outcomes here more than feature matrices. Start runtime protection in monitor-only mode on one tier-one app, measure overhead and false-block rates against real traffic for a sprint, then graduate to blocking on the routes where evidence supports it teams that flip global blocking on day one usually flip it off by day ten.

Pair every in-process layer with your WAAP rather than replacing it: the edge absorbs volumetric noise cheaply, leaving the agent to judge the requests that deserve code-level scrutiny.

And budget the client side separately PCI DSS 6.4.3-era requirements make payment-page script defense (Jscrambler-class) a compliance line item now, not an optional extra.

Common Pitfalls

Global blocking enabled before monitor-mode evidence; RASP purchased while the APM’s included protection sits dark; client-side and server-side lanes confused in one budget; dead vendors surviving on shortlists; and agents deployed without platform-engineering ownership of overhead.

FAQs

What is the best RASP tool in 2026? Contrast Protect ranks 1 for dedicated in-process protection, Datadog (Hdiv’s engine inside) for APM-delivered blocking, Waratek for JVM virtual patching with Dynatrace toggles, Fastly’s edge lane, and Jscrambler’s client-side job rounding the field.

Is RASP dead as a category? The capability thrives; the standalone market thinned. Platforms absorbed the demand our nine-entry honest count (with one defunct flag) tells the story stale lists don’t.

What happened to Hdiv and K2? Hdiv was acquired by Datadog (2022) and powers its runtime protection; K2’s signals point to wind-down verify before any consideration.

How does RASP interact with a Web Application Firewall (WAF)? They operate at different layers: WAAP gateways inspect perimeter traffic at the CDN edge, while RASP evaluates execution context inside the runtime environment.

Even when vulnerabilities affect edge WAF and CDN architectures, in-process RASP agents intercept the underlying malicious payload before execution.

RASP vs WAF both? Different vantage: WAAP filters broadly at the edge; RASP blocks with code context in-process. Common pattern: WAAP everywhere, in-process depth on crown jewels.

What about client-side protection? A distinct job script integrity and skimming defense (Jscrambler-class), now PCI-driven for payment pages. Budget it separately from server RASP.

Verdict

Contrast keeps the dedicated crown, Datadog proves distribution wins, and Waratek owns the emergency-patch niche activate what your agents already can, buy depth where context demands, and let the dead names rest. Nine entries, honestly counted; one idea, thoroughly absorbed.
