articles.title: Attackers Reportedly Hack Supermarket Fridges and Raise Temperatures to 50°C
articles.description:
French supermarket chains are dealing with a major cybersecurity incident after attackers reportedly changed refrigeration settings remotely, causing some chilled cabinets and freezers to heat up instead of cool down. The incident began overnight between October 11 and October 12 and affected stores linked to Intermarché, E.Leclerc, and Système U, according to early reports. The […]

The post Attackers Reportedly Hack Supermarket Fridges and Raise Temperatures to 50°C appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
French supermarket chains are dealing with a major cybersecurity incident after attackers reportedly changed refrigeration settings remotely, causing some chilled cabinets and freezers to heat up instead of cool down.

The incident began overnight between October 11 and October 12 and affected stores linked to Intermarché, E.Leclerc, and Système U, according to early reports.

The cyberattack is believed to have targeted refrigeration-control systems made by Danish industrial technology company Danfoss. These systems manage cooling equipment inside supermarkets, including freezers, chilled food displays, compressors, and temperature alerts. In the affected stores, attackers reportedly changed the settings to trigger continuous defrosting and set temperatures as high as 50°C.

This meant refrigeration units designed to keep food cold reportedly operated like heaters for several hours. Fresh food, dairy items, meat, frozen products, and other temperature-sensitive goods may have become unsafe for sale.

Stores were forced to inspect their stock and discard food that could no longer meet food-safety requirements. BFMTV reported that some locations could face losses reaching hundreds of thousands of euros, while around 150 Intermarché stores were reportedly affected.

Supermarket Fridges Hacked

The incident shows how a cyber incident can quickly become a physical and financial problem. Supermarkets depend on refrigeration around the clock. Even a short disruption can damage stock, interrupt deliveries, create food-safety concerns, and reduce customer trust.

Reports indicate that the attackers may have abused a defrost feature built into the refrigeration-management software. Defrosting is a normal process that removes ice from cooling equipment. However, if it is enabled continuously or configured with unsafe values, the equipment cannot maintain the low temperatures needed to preserve food.

Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Coopérative U, confirmed that cybercriminal activity had affected refrigeration production systems in several stores in the group’s network. He said teams were working with refrigeration specialists to restore operations and that an investigation would be needed to establish how the incident occurred.

Early reporting suggests older software versions may be involved. However, the exact intrusion method, the responsible group, and whether a known vulnerability was exploited have not been publicly confirmed. That distinction is important. A report that legacy software is present does not prove that a specific security flaw enabled the compromise.

The event also places fresh attention on security issues affecting connected refrigeration equipment. Commercial cooling controllers are part of operational technology, or OT. Unlike ordinary office computers, OT systems directly control real-world equipment, including cooling units, pumps, manufacturing machines, and building controls.

Cybersecurity News previously reported on 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland XWEB Pro refrigeration controllers used by supermarkets, warehouses, and hospitals. Researchers showed that compromised controllers could change temperature readings or silently stop cooling equipment. That research involved Copeland products, not the Danfoss systems named in the French incident, but it demonstrates the real-world impact of insecure refrigeration controls.

Danfoss refrigeration products have also been subject to security advisories. CISA advisories discussed flaws affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, including authentication weaknesses, command-injection risks, and settings-control issues in older versions. Danfoss released updates for affected software releases, and organizations should confirm that their equipment is running supported versions.

Retailers using remotely managed refrigeration should urgently review every internet-connected controller, remote-access path, vendor account, and third-party maintenance connection. Systems should not be directly exposed to the public internet, and remote access should use a VPN, multi-factor authentication, and strict account controls.

Security teams should also separate refrigeration networks from point-of-sale, corporate, and guest Wi-Fi networks. Temperature changes, repeated defrost commands, configuration edits, and unusual remote logins should create immediate alerts for both IT and facilities teams.

The supermarket incident is still developing, but its lesson is already clear. When attackers gain control of systems that manage physical equipment, the impact can go far beyond stolen data. In this case, a change in software settings reportedly turned supermarket fridges into a costly food-waste event across France.

articles.title: IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs
articles.description:
IBM patched 22 vulnerabilities in Verify Identity Access and Security Verify Access, including two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated remote code execution across appliance and container deployments. The most severe bugs, CVE-2026-78401 and CVE-2026-78406, each carry a CVSS score of 9.8. Both involve deserializing untrusted data, a process where software rebuilds stored or transmitted data into […]

The post IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
IBM patched 22 vulnerabilities in Verify Identity Access and Security Verify Access, including two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated remote code execution across appliance and container deployments.

The most severe bugs, CVE-2026-78401 and CVE-2026-78406, each carry a CVSS score of 9.8. Both involve deserializing untrusted data, a process where software rebuilds stored or transmitted data into objects without properly checking whether it is safe.

The publicly listed advisory for CVE-2026-78401 confirms the risk of unauthenticated remote code execution. IBM rates both deserialization bugs as network-accessible attacks with low complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction.IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws, Including Critical Remote Code Execution Bugs.

Successful exploitation could seriously affect data confidentiality, integrity, and service availability. However, the supplied bulletin does not identify vulnerable endpoints, describe an exploit chain, or report confirmed attacks.

These critical flaws deserve close attention because attackers do not need a valid account to reach the vulnerable code. Their severity reflects potential impact and ease of attack, not evidence that exploitation has already occurred.

IBM Patches 22 Verify Access Flaws

Three additional vulnerabilities carry scores of 9.1. CVE-2026-16916 allows an authenticated, high-privilege remote attacker to execute arbitrary code because a protection mechanism fails.

CVE-2026-16823 enables attackers to bypass security restrictions, while CVE-2026-19491 allows authentication bypass. Unlike the deserialization bugs, these issues require different access and have different outcomes.

The update follows earlier IBM Identity and Verify Access vulnerabilities reported by Cyber Security News, which covered request smuggling, privilege escalation, and other security weaknesses in the same product family. Do not confuse those earlier fixes with this October patch release.

The bulletin also addresses CVE-2026-18740 and CVE-2026-19482, both rated 8.8. These argument injection flaws let authenticated remote attackers perform unauthorized actions or execute arbitrary commands. CVE-2026-19493, rated 7.5, allows a remote attacker to write files through path traversal.

Other vulnerabilities include cross-site scripting that could expose credentials within trusted sessions, SQL injection that could modify data or disrupt services, and cross-site request forgery that could trigger unauthorized actions.

Additional fixes address audit log forgery, incorrect authorization checks, authentication workflow bypass, and information disclosure in the Snapshot Manager Container. Several denial-of-service flaws affect resource allocation, recursive processing, and memory reads.

IBM also patched a stack buffer write issue that requires administrative privileges and access to the local management interface. Earlier IBM Security Verify command execution coverage provides related background on previously patched appliance flaws.

Affected releases include IBM Security Verify Access and its Container edition from 10.0 through 10.0.9.2. IBM Verify Identity Access and its Container edition are affected from 11.0 through 11.0.3.

IBM directs appliance customers to install Verify Identity Access 11.0.3.1 or Security Verify Access 10.0.9.3 through its Fix Central download links.

Container customers should follow IBM’s container download guidance, which identifies product images and registry locations. IBM renamed Security Verify Access to Verify Identity Access starting with version 11.0.0.

The bulletin lists no workarounds or mitigations. IBM encourages customers to update promptly, and the bulletin lists the supplied fixes as the stated remediation for these vulnerabilities across affected supported deployments.

articles.description:
Hackers are exploiting two flaws in AhsayCBS backup servers to run commands, plant webshells, and install XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised as Microsoft Edge. Huntress first observed exploitation on October 7, 2026, at 23:20:15 UTC. By October 8, its researchers had seen five organizations targeted, with attackers checking systems and setting up tools to maintain access. […]

The post Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Webshells and XMRig Miners appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are exploiting two flaws in AhsayCBS backup servers to run commands, plant webshells, and install XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised as Microsoft Edge.

Huntress first observed exploitation on October 7, 2026, at 23:20:15 UTC. By October 8, its researchers had seen five organizations targeted, with attackers checking systems and setting up tools to maintain access.

The campaign targets Ahsay Cloud Backup Server, a management platform used by managed service providers and system integrators. Administrators use it to manage backup users, policies, and operations. According to Huntress’s investigation, versions up to 10.3.4 are affected, including a release previously described as safe.

The attack chains CVE-2026-105133, a medium-severity authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function, with CVE-2026-105134, a critical flaw in the Replication Receiver endpoint at /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do.

Together, they let attackers bypass login checks and execute commands as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, giving them broad control over the Windows host.

Hackers Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws

The NVD entry for CVE-2026-105134, published October 4, lists a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and describes remote command injection. It still identifies version 10.3.4 as a fix.

However, Huntress’s October 8 update says that the version remains vulnerable, making the conflicting guidance important for administrators assessing exposure.

After gaining access, attackers configured a malicious replication receiver and placed Java Server Page webshells inside the application’s web directory. Huntress also detected suspicious commands launched by cbssvcX64.exe, the AhsayCBS service executable.

This pattern resembles earlier z0Miner attacks against WebLogic servers, where attackers used JSP webshells to maintain access before deploying mining tools. That similarity describes a shared method, not evidence that the campaigns involve the same operators.

Attackers downloaded Taskgmr.ps1, edge.exe, msedge.exe, and config.json into temporary folders from an Alibaba Cloud Object Storage endpoint. The file edge.exe was XMRig, while msedge.exe was a modified copy of NSSM, a legitimate utility that keeps other programs running.

A newly created Windows service, MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc, ran the disguised NSSM binary with SYSTEM privileges. It kept the miner active and restarted it after crashes or reboots. The miner connected to xmr. kryptex[.]network and 51.195.127[.]124 on port 8029.

The use of webshells followed by Monero mining also appears in earlier Apache web server coinminer attacks, highlighting how exposed servers can become income sources for attackers.

The PowerShell script monitored Task Manager and stopped the mining service whenever users opened it. Mining resumed after Task Manager was closed.

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

The script also closed Task Manager at 18:00 local time or after it stayed open overnight for over an hour. Huntress described its comments as suggesting AI assistance, not proving AI authorship.

In one incident, attackers downloaded WinRing0x64.sys, a legitimate but vulnerable driver, using certutil.exe. Huntress linked its use to improved mining performance through low-level hardware access, not to turning off security tools.

Organizations should restrict management access to trusted IP addresses or a VPN while awaiting a confirmed fix. Investigate suspected compromised hosts and rebuild them from trusted backups.

articles.description:
The FBI arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky in Pennsylvania on October 8, 2026, as part of its investigation into the hacking group ShinyHunters. The arrest links a professional involved in ransomware response to an alleged cyber extortion conspiracy. However, the evidence behind the charges remains largely sealed, and the allegations have not been proven […]

The post FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Executive in ShinyHunters-Linked Extortion Investigation appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The FBI arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky in Pennsylvania on October 8, 2026, as part of its investigation into the hacking group ShinyHunters.

The arrest links a professional involved in ransomware response to an alleged cyber extortion conspiracy. However, the evidence behind the charges remains largely sealed, and the allegations have not been proven in court.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, Dubrovsky was associated with Canadian security firm CyberSteward and had planned to attend a cyber insurance conference in Philadelphia.

Sources told the publication that the arrested Canadian was visiting Pennsylvania for the event. The Cyber Risk Summit ran from October 5 through October 7 at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel. The public court docket lists the defendant as Edward Dobrovsky, a slightly different spelling.

FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Executive in ShinyHunters

KrebsOnSecurity reported charges involving conspiracy to threaten the confidentiality of information to extort money and interference with commerce through threats. With the main complaint sealed, the public record does not explain what actions prosecutors allege Dobrovsky took.

An October 9 court order committed the defendant to the Eastern District of Texas. Records also show that a judge appointed federal defenders and ordered detention pending a hearing in the charging district. This updates an important detail in the initial reporting, which said Dubrovsky had not yet received appointed counsel.

Cypfer, another Canadian cybersecurity company, disputed Dubrovsky’s claim that he was a former founder. In an October 10 update, a company spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity that he had served as managing director, not founder or co-founder, and resigned in November 2025. The distinction prevents his arrest from being wrongly presented as the arrest of Cypfer’s founder.

ShinyHunters typically steals login details through phishing and uses compromised accounts to take data from cloud software services. The group then threatens to publish stolen records unless victims pay. KrebsOnSecurity, citing the FBI, reported that the group had extorted more than $70 million from victims during 2026.

The investigation also covers the theft of sensitive information from the FBI’s recruitment portal. The New York Times reported that stolen records included home addresses, Social Security numbers, and sensitive job assignments.

KrebsOnSecurity said the exposed material included medical and psychiatric information. Such records create concerns beyond financial loss because they reveal deeply personal details about bureau personnel.

The case follows the arrest of an alleged ShinyHunters leader in the Netherlands. Dutch police detained a 24-year-old Amsterdam suspect on September 15 with FBI support. A security company executive identified him as Pepijn van der Stap, although Dutch authorities did not publicly name him. His alleged role remains unproven.

Another development involved Saif al-Din Khader, reportedly known online as Rey. Cybersecurity News previously reported that the suspected ShinyHunters member helped FBI investigators after detention in Jordan. That reported cooperation does not establish his role in the FBI breach or validate every claim made by the hacking group.

For readers following the case, the key gap remains Dubrovsky’s alleged conduct. Public reporting establishes an arrest and allegations of extortion, but the sealed complaint limits scrutiny of the evidence. Further court filings may clarify how prosecutors connect his work to ShinyHunters.

articles.title: New Unicode Characters Let Attackers Create Convincing Lookalike Domains for Phishing
articles.description:
Security researchers have found new ways to build fake domains that resemble trusted brands while still appearing as readable Unicode in Chromium-based browsers. The issue can make phishing pages look real because users may see a familiar name and no clear browser warning during normal web browsing. Research by Ian Muscat and Leanne Briffa of […]

The post New Unicode Characters Let Attackers Create Convincing Lookalike Domains for Phishing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researchers have found new ways to build fake domains that resemble trusted brands while still appearing as readable Unicode in Chromium-based browsers. The issue can make phishing pages look real because users may see a familiar name and no clear browser warning during normal web browsing.

Research by Ian Muscat and Leanne Briffa of Have I Been Squatted tested internationalized domain names, or IDNs, against Chromium’s display rules. Their proof of concept included аррӏө[.]com, a Cyrillic copy of apple[.]com.

Chrome 154 displayed it in Unicode instead of its Punycode form, xn--80a6aa68c8d[.]com. The domains were registered for controlled testing, not a real phishing campaign.

New Unicode Characters Make Domain Look Real

The Domain Name System first used English letters, numbers, and hyphens. IDNs later allowed letters from many languages. Punycode converts Unicode names into ASCII that DNS can handle, with encoded labels starting with “xn--.” This supports a global internet, but creates risk because letters from different scripts can look alike.

This method is called a homograph or homoglyph trick. Cyber Security News previously covered new homoglyph attack methods and a phishing trick using a Japanese character that looked like a slash.

Chromium tries to stop these tricks by showing suspicious IDNs as Punycode. Its rules check mixed scripts, unsafe symbols, whole-script copies, and a comparison form called a skeleton. It also compares skeletons with popular domains. The checks use ideas from Unicode Technical Standard 39.

Chrome added a whole-script confusable check after the famous 2017 аррӏе[.]com test. That older domain used only Cyrillic letters that looked like the Latin letters in apple. Chromium now detects it and displays xn--80ak6aa92e[.]com instead.

The research found that this rule works only when every character in a Cyrillic label appears on Chromium’s lookalike list. The Cyrillic letter ө, used in languages including Kazakh and Mongolian, is allowed but is not on that list. Replacing the final Cyrillic е with ө makes the whole check stand down, even though the result can still look like apple[.]com to a person.

A second gap appears in skeleton matching. Chromium removes many accents before comparing names, but marks from letters with hooks or strokes can remain. As a result, oƙta[.]com does not reduce to the same skeleton as okta[.]com, while the bar from ө also stops аррӏө[.]com from matching apple[.]com.

The researchers registered 20 proof-of-concept names. They included Unicode lookalikes for Apple, OpenAI, Skype, SharePoint, Pinterest, SpaceX, Shell, Okta, Nike, and Kickstarter. Their tests also found that Chromium’s later navigation warning did not catch аррӏө[.]com because its skeleton was two edits away from Apple, while that check looks for a closer match in this case.

The risk also reaches email. In tests with 20 internationalized senders, Gmail Web displayed every sender domain in Unicode, while Outlook Web showed every one as an encoded A-label. Gmail showed Punycode only in the separate “mailed-by” field, which many users may never open. The test did not measure spam filters, sender reputation, or link scanning.

A valid certificate does not prove that a domain belongs to the brand it resembles. It only confirms that the browser has an encrypted link to the domain named in the certificate. Attackers who own a lookalike domain may also configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC correctly, so email authentication alone cannot prove that the sender is the real company.

An October 2026 review of .com found 167,226,216 delegated names, including 733,509 IDNs in xn-- form. Researchers identified 161,894 visual lookalike pairs covering 133,953 ASCII domains. These matches are not proof of crime because they may include defensive registrations, real multilingual sites, or unrelated companies.

Organizations should monitor new xn-- domains that resemble their brands, review certificate records, and enable impersonation protection in mail gateways. Teams can tag unexpected IDN senders, keep external sender labels enabled, and inspect DNS and proxy logs for encoded names. Defensive registration can also help with the closest brand copies.

Users should avoid signing in through links in unexpected messages. Opening a saved bookmark or typing the known address is safer. Password managers and passkeys add strong protection because they match the real domain and should not fill or respond on a different lookalike site. Browser updates remain important, but this research shows that reading the address bar alone is no longer enough.

articles.description:
Microsoft is investigating an Exchange admin center access issue that may prevent some administrators from opening the web portal used to manage Exchange Online. Affected admins may encounter an “Internal Server Error” message, according to the Microsoft 365 Status update provided for this report. The company is tracking the incident under EX1500900 and has directed […]

The post Microsoft Exchange Admin Center Issue Blocks Web Portal Access to Admins With “Internal Server Error” appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft is investigating an Exchange admin center access issue that may prevent some administrators from opening the web portal used to manage Exchange Online. Affected admins may encounter an “Internal Server Error” message, according to the Microsoft 365 Status update provided for this report.

The company is tracking the incident under EX1500900 and has directed customers to the Microsoft 365 admin center for further information. The notice describes an access problem affecting some admins. It does not establish a global outage or confirm that users are unable to send and receive email.

“We’re investigating an issue in which some admins may be unable to access the Exchange admin center (EAC) and may encounter an ‘Internal Server Error’ message,” the supplied notice states.

Exchange Admin Center Issue

The Exchange admin center is Microsoft’s web-based console for managing Exchange Online. IT teams use it to manage mailboxes and groups, review mail flow reports, and handle migrations. Microsoft’s Exchange admin center documentation explains that available features depend on the administrator’s assigned roles and permissions.

Losing access can delay these tasks, particularly when teams need to review delivery problems or make urgent mailbox changes. However, an unavailable management portal does not, by itself, show that the underlying email service has stopped working. The supplied incident notice identifies admin access as the reported problem.

The brief announcement does not identify a root cause, affected regions, the number of impacted organizations, or a recovery timeline. It also does not announce a confirmed workaround. Those gaps mean the incident should not be described as a cyberattack or linked to a specific service change.

Administrators should check Health > Service health in the Microsoft 365 admin center and look for EX1500900. Microsoft’s service health guidance explains that this dashboard lists active incidents and advisories, with individual pages providing further details about each issue.

The Microsoft 365 Admin mobile app also supports service health updates and push notifications. This gives teams another way to follow Microsoft’s investigation without relying on the Exchange management interface itself. Updates should be checked against the incident record rather than inferred from reports about unrelated outages.

For essential work, Exchange Online PowerShell provides a separate command-line management interface. It supports Exchange Online administration, including security features. However, Microsoft’s supplied notice does not confirm that PowerShell is unaffected, so it should be treated as a possible alternative rather than a verified workaround.

Cybersecurity News previously covered a Microsoft Exchange admin center outage tracked as EX1051697. That incident involved HTTP 500 errors and reports of an alternative portal address helping some administrators. Those earlier findings do not establish a working fix for EX1500900.

The publication also reported a separate Exchange Online disruption tracked as EX1464935, which concerned broader service functionality. Its different incident number and reported impact underline why administrators should keep individual service events separate when assessing business disruption.

For now, the supported scope remains limited to the access failure described in the supplied announcement. Organizations should follow EX1500900 for confirmed impact, recovery progress, and any approved mitigation. Email delivery failures, if observed, need separate verification rather than being automatically attributed to this admin portal issue.

Update: Microsoft rolled back the change, and the issue is now resolved for admins.

articles.description:
Nippon Columbia Group disclosed a malware infection on October 8, 2026, that may have exposed millions of Daiichi Kosho customer and employee records after a contractor’s employee computer was infected. Daiichi Kosho says data theft and misuse remain unconfirmed, and it has found no impact on its own systems. The estimated total is 8.724 million […]

The post Nippon Columbia Malware Infection May Have Exposed 8.7 Million Customer Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Nippon Columbia Group disclosed a malware infection on October 8, 2026, that may have exposed millions of Daiichi Kosho customer and employee records after a contractor’s employee computer was infected.

Daiichi Kosho says data theft and misuse remain unconfirmed, and it has found no impact on its own systems. The estimated total is 8.724 million records, comprising approximately 8.631 million customer records and 93,000 employee records.

Although the headline rounds the figure to 8.7 million customer records, the full count includes both groups. These figures describe records potentially at risk, not a confirmed number of people whose information was stolen.

Nippon Columbia Group handles personal information on behalf of Daiichi Kosho. According to the company’s initial incident notice, the infected computer temporarily stored personal data linked to this work was temporarily stored on the infected computer. Investigators could not rule out the possibility that information had leaked outside the organization.

BleepingComputer reported that Nippon Columbia notified Daiichi Kosho on October 5 and isolated the affected computer the following day. The contractor also reset passwords and other login credentials while investigating the cause, scope, and possible online release of data.

Nippon Columbia Malware Infection Exposed

The available reporting does not identify a malware family, name an attacker, or explain how the computer became infected. It also provides no technical evidence showing that files were copied outside the network. Those gaps mean the incident should not be described as confirmed ransomware activity or a proven data theft operation.

The affected information may include registered names, gender, dates of birth, email addresses, and telephone numbers. Customers of BIG ECHO, MEGA BIG, Karaoke CLUB DAM, Banana Club, B-GARAGE, and DK Dining may be affected. The records relate to people who registered as members or made reservations through the company’s services.

Daiichi Kosho says passwords are not included in the potentially exposed information. It has also reported no evidence of unauthorized use of loyalty points.

Customers should nevertheless remain cautious about unexpected emails, text messages, or calls asking for payment or personal and financial details.

The case highlights a risk linked to outsourced data handling. Daiichi Kosho’s own systems need not be compromised for a contractor’s information to be exposed.

Related CybersecurityNews coverage of the Veradigm third-party data breach and Fidelity Investments vendor incident offers further context on how incidents at service providers can affect their clients. These are separate cases, not evidence of a shared attacker.

In its October 9 update, Daiichi Kosho announced a dedicated toll-free inquiry hotline at 0120-732-079. The service operates from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays. Customers unable to reach the company by phone can email incident-desk@dkkaraoke.co.jp.

The company apologized again for the concern and inconvenience caused. It said it had not confirmed any unauthorized use of personal information arising from the incident, but the investigation remained ongoing. Daiichi Kosho will continue working with relevant authorities to establish the cause and prevent a recurrence.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Casbaneiro malware is hiding its main command and control traffic until an infected user visits a targeted banking website.

The Windows banking trojan combines phishing messages, location checks, staged downloads, and separate data collection servers to make an active infection appear quiet during routine analysis.

The campaign targets users across Latin America, with activity linked to Argentina, Peru, Colombia, and Mexico. Its key trick is timing: stolen information can leave the computer before the main control channel opens.

A lack of immediate C2 traffic therefore does not mean the malware is inactive. Researchers from Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs identified the campaign in August 2026.

In a technical report published on September 10, researcher Rachael Liao described how Casbaneiro separates email theft, victim registration, and remote control across different servers. The design makes individual connections harder to connect into one clear attack chain.

Casbaneiro Malware Hides C2 Activity

The infection starts with emails and PDF files posing as invoices or legal notices, including claims about court proceedings. These messages create pressure to act quickly.

Some include the recipient’s email address, giving the lure a personal touch that can make a malicious link seem more trustworthy.

That link leads to a webpage that checks the visitor’s IP address. Users outside the selected country are sent to legitimate websites such as Google or YouTube.

This resembles Grandoreiro’s regional filtering tactics, where location checks help banking malware limit delivery and avoid exposing its payload to outside researchers.

Visitors inside the target region receive a page containing a ZIP archive encoded with Base64 inside JavaScript. The script starts the download through the browser’s normal download interface, then redirects to a blank page. This sequence gives the victim fewer visible reasons to question what has just happened.

The archive contains an HTA file, a Windows application format that can run scripts. It loads external JavaScript, which retrieves an XML script package containing JScript.

That code uses Windows Management Instrumentation to check for sandbox environments and confirm that the operating system language matches an approved list.

After those checks, the downloader retrieves three separate components: a legitimate AutoIt interpreter, a compiled AutoIt script, and a compressed payload.

AutoIt Loader Builds the Infection

Random filenames make tracking harder. Splitting the components also weakens file analysis because their combined behavior may not be clear when each file is examined on its own.

A Startup folder shortcut runs the AutoIt script again when the user signs in. The loader shows a fake Windows service window before unpacking the payload and injecting it into RegSvcs.exe, or mobsync.exe if RegSvcs.exe is missing. Related Horabot banking trojan activity also used AutoIt components and Startup shortcuts.

Casbaneiro decrypts stored settings using the same algorithm as Ousaban. It joins fragments of encrypted strings and keys only when needed.

It also rejects systems using German, French, or English as their default language. The shared algorithm does not, by itself, establish that both campaigns have the same operator.

The trojan collects address book contacts and sender and recipient details from Microsoft Outlook messages. It sends that information without encryption.

It also builds a victim identifier by hashing the computer name, username, and executable name with MD5, then uses local markers to avoid repeating some collection tasks. Another server receives Base64 encoded victim information and returns HTTP 403 Forbidden.

Casbaneiro treats this response as the expected outcome, retrying when it receives any other status. Analysts who read the error as evidence of dead infrastructure could miss a working part of the attack rather than a failed connection.

Only a visit to a targeted bank website triggers the main C2 exchange. The available commands include keyboard control, clipboard pasting, file execution, command execution, and fake banking windows.

Similar Ousaban banking session attacks show why tests that never open a targeted bank page may miss important malware behavior.

Fortinet also found HTTP requests without a Host header, unusually large Content-Length values, and bodies sent through many small packets.

These irregularities may complicate traffic inspection. Defenders should connect email, endpoint, and network events, monitor unexpected AutoIt execution and Startup shortcuts, and avoid treating HTTP 403 responses as proof that a suspicious server is harmless.

Organizations should also strengthen email filtering, keep antivirus protection current, and train staff to question unexpected invoice or legal messages. Fortinet says its antivirus service detects the campaign’s phishing PDFs, malicious JavaScript, and Casbaneiro payload.
